docs.title: Java Problem-Solving Playbook
docs.text:
From "I don't know where to start" to expert-level answers. Every problem is solved the way a 15-year interviewer expects: think aloud, start with brute force, find the waste, reach the optimal pattern. You get recursive and iterative/normal versions and a Java 8 Streams take where one fits.

Start with Foundations See the Roadmap

docs.text:
1. Problem + examples + clarifying questions: what to ask before you write a single line.
  2. Thinking process: restate the problem, try brute force, spot the waste, name the pattern.
  3. Approaches, from brute force to optimal: each one with numbered steps and its complexity.
  4. Recursive and Java 8 versions wherever they are natural.
  5. Dry run table: trace the optimal solution by hand.
  6. Code: embedded from the real, compiled and JUnit-tested source in src/main/java.
  7. Edge cases, follow-ups, related problems: what the interviewer asks next.

docs.title: String costs (immutability!)
docs.text:
• s + c inside a loop is O(n²) overall, because every concatenation copies the string. Use StringBuilder.
  • substring copies (since JDK 7u6), so it is O(k), not O(1).
  • s.toCharArray() is O(n) and returns a copy; s.charAt(i) is O(1).

docs.title: Recursion space
docs.text: The stack depth is the space. Recursive reverse of a string of length n uses O(n) stack even if no other data is allocated. Java's default stack overflows at roughly 10⁴–10⁵ frames.

Classic traps

  • == on Integer objects outside −128..127 compares references. Use equals.
  • Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.
  • -7 % 3 == -1 in Java (the sign follows the dividend).
  • list.remove(1) removes index 1; list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the value 1.

docs.title: Problem-solving framework (UMPIRE+)
docs.text:
Use this script on every problem. Say each step out loud in an interview.

  1. Understand. Restate the problem in one sentence. Work through 2–3 examples by hand, including an edge case.
  2. Clarify. Ask about the input range, null/empty, duplicates, negatives, case sensitivity, Unicode, whether you may modify the input, and the output format.
  3. Match. Which pattern does it look like? See the table below.
  4. Brute force first. State it, give its complexity, and don't code it unless asked. It proves you understand the problem.
  5. Find the waste. What does brute force recompute or rescan? That waste is your optimisation.
  6. Implement. Use clean names, handle edge cases at the top, and add a comment for every non-obvious invariant.
  7. Review. Dry-run on your example, check the edge cases, state time and space, and suggest follow-ups.

docs.title: Pattern recognition table
docs.text: If the problem says… Think… "sorted array", "pair with sum" Two pointers, binary search "longest/shortest substring/subarray with…" Sliding window "count / frequency / seen before" HashMap / int[26] "subarray sum equals k" Prefix sum + HashMap "maximum subarray" Kadane "next greater / smaller", "histogram" Monotonic stack "all combinations / permutations / subsets" Backtracking (recursion) "overlapping subproblems", "number of ways", "min cost" Dynamic programming "top K", "Kth largest", "median of stream" Heap "intervals" Sort by start, then merge/sweep "shortest path in unweighted grid" BFS "dependencies / ordering" Topological sort "find pattern in text" KMP / Rabin–Karp / Z "XOR", "single number", "power of two" Bit manipulation

docs.title: What a senior answer sounds like
docs.text: "Brute force is O(n²): for each element I scan the rest. The waste is that I keep re-scanning for something I've already seen, so I'll store what I've seen in a HashMap. That gives O(n) time and O(n) space. If memory is tight and I'm allowed to sort, two pointers gives O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space."

docs.title: The three questions
docs.text:
1. What is the smallest input I can answer directly? That is the base case.
  2. If someone hands me the answer for a smaller input, how do I build mine? That is the recursive case.
  3. Does every call move toward the base case? If not, you get infinite recursion and a StackOverflowError.

Leap of faith

Don't trace every call in your head. Assume f(n-1) is correct and only check that f(n) uses it correctly. This is proof by induction.

docs.title: Recursion tree, and why memoization matters
docs.text:
fib(5) recomputes fib(3) twice and fib(2) three times. That makes it exponential:

                fib(5)
             /         \
         fib(4)        fib(3)
        /     \        /    \
    fib(3)  fib(2)  fib(2) fib(1)
    /   \
 fib(2) fib(1)

Cache each result once and the tree collapses to a line, so the cost drops to O(n). See Fibonacci.

docs.title: Types of recursion
docs.text: Type Shape Example Linear one self-call factorial, sum of digits Tail self-call is the last action tail(n-1, acc*n) Binary / tree two self-calls fibonacci, merge sort Divide & conquer split, solve halves, combine max/min, merge sort, LCP Backtracking choose → explore → un-choose subsets, permutations, N-Queens

docs.title: Converting recursion to iteration ("normal solution")
docs.text:
• Tail recursion becomes a while loop: the accumulator turns into a local variable.
  • Linear recursion becomes a loop that runs from the base case upwards (bottom-up).
  • Tree recursion with overlapping subproblems becomes a DP table filled bottom-up.
  • General recursion becomes an explicit Deque used as a stack.

Java does not optimise tail calls, so for large n prefer the iterative form.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• String is immutable. Each "modification" creates a new object, so build results with StringBuilder.
  • char is a 16-bit UTF-16 unit. c - 'a' maps a..z to 0..25, which is the basis of the int[26] frequency trick.
  • Most string problems reduce to five patterns: two pointers, frequency counting, sliding window, stack, and pattern matching (KMP / Rabin–Karp).

docs.title: Anagram check
docs.text: Easy Frequency counting Sorting

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same counts. "listen" and "silent" → true.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Case-sensitive? Ignore spaces ("dormitory" vs "dirty room")? Unicode?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Quick reject: different lengths can never be anagrams.
  2. Sorting idea: sorted anagrams are identical. That's O(n log n).
  3. Counting idea: one array, +1 for each char of a and −1 for each char of b. Every slot must end at 0. That's O(n).

docs.title: Approach 1 — Sort and compare
docs.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (char arrays).

docs.title: Approach 2 — Single count array (optimal)
docs.text:
1. If the lengths differ, return false.
  2. For each i: count[a[i]]++ and count[b[i]]--.
  3. Return true if every count is 0.

docs.title: Approach 3 — HashMap
docs.text: Works for any alphabet without a 65536-slot array. Return false as soon as any count would drop below zero.

docs.title: Approach 4 — Streams
docs.text: Compare the two groupingBy(counting()) maps.

docs.title: Dry run ("aab" vs "aba", counting a and b)
docs.text: i a[i] b[i] count a count b 0 a a 0 0 1 a b 1 −1 2 b a 0 0 → all zero ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same counts (case-sensitive). */
public final class Anagram {
    private Anagram() {}

    /** Sort both and compare. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean sorting(String a, String b) {
        if (a == null || b == null || a.length() != b.length()) return false;
        char[] x = a.toCharArray(), y = b.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(x);
        Arrays.sort(y);
        return Arrays.equals(x, y);
    }

    /** Optimal: one count array; +1 for a, -1 for b; all zeros at the end. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static boolean optimal(String a, String b) {
        if (a == null || b == null || a.length() != b.length()) return false;
        int[] counts = new int[Character.MAX_VALUE + 1];     // covers every char; use int[26] for a–z only
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length(); i++) {
            counts[a.charAt(i)]++;
            counts[b.charAt(i)]--;
        }
        for (int c : counts) if (c != 0) return false;
        return true;
    }

    /** HashMap version — works for any alphabet, sparse memory. */
    public static boolean hashMap(String a, String b) {
        if (a == null || b == null || a.length() != b.length()) return false;
        Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (char c : a.toCharArray()) freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum);
        for (char c : b.toCharArray()) {
            int left = freq.getOrDefault(c, 0) - 1;
            if (left < 0) return false;                      // b has a char more often than a
            freq.put(c, left);
        }
        return true;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: compare frequency maps. */
    public static boolean streams(String a, String b) {
        if (a == null || b == null || a.length() != b.length()) return false;
        Function<String, Map<Integer, Long>> freq =
                s -> s.chars().boxed().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));
        return freq.apply(a).equals(freq.apply(b));
    }
}

docs.title: Character frequency & duplicate characters
docs.text: Easy Hashing Frequency array

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the occurrences of each character, keeping first-occurrence order. Also list the characters that occur more than once.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: "programming" → {p=1, r=2, o=1, g=2, a=1, m=2, i=1, n=1}, duplicates [r, g, m].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each char, count it with an inner loop. That's O(n²).
  2. Waste: we rescan the string for every char.
  3. Insight: one pass, incrementing a counter per char, gives O(n).
  4. Container choice: LinkedHashMap keeps order. int[26] is fastest when the input is only a–z.

docs.title: Approaches
docs.text:
Approach How Time Space Brute force nested loop O(n²) O(k) HashMap freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum) O(n) O(k) int[26] counts[c - 'a']++ O(n) O(1) Streams groupingBy(identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, counting()) O(n) O(k)

k = number of distinct characters.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/**
 * Count how many times each character occurs (preserving first-occurrence order) and list duplicates.
 */
public final class CharacterFrequency {
    private CharacterFrequency() {}

    /** Brute force: for each char count it with an inner loop. O(n^2). */
    public static Map<Character, Integer> bruteForce(String s) {
        Map<Character, Integer> result = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (s == null) return result;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char c = s.charAt(i);
            if (result.containsKey(c)) continue;             // already counted
            int count = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < s.length(); j++) if (s.charAt(j) == c) count++;
            result.put(c, count);
        }
        return result;
    }

    /** Optimal: one pass with a hash map. O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct chars. */
    public static Map<Character, Integer> optimal(String s) {
        Map<Character, Integer> freq = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (s == null) return freq;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum);
        return freq;
    }

    /** Fixed alphabet trick: int[26] for lowercase a–z only. Fastest; O(1) space. */
    public static int[] lowercaseCounts(String s) {
        int[] counts = new int[26];
        if (s == null) return counts;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') counts[c - 'a']++;
        return counts;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: groupingBy with LinkedHashMap to keep order. */
    public static Map<Character, Long> streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return new LinkedHashMap<>();
        return s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Duplicates: characters occurring more than once, in first-occurrence order. */
    public static List<Character> duplicates(String s) {
        return optimal(s).entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
                .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
                .toList();
    }
}

docs.text:
• Sort characters by frequency (LeetCode 451). Use bucket sort on the counts.
  • Find the max-occurring character. Track the max while counting.
  • Count words instead of chars. See the Java 8 string bank.

docs.title: First non-repeating character
docs.text: Easy Frequency counting Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the first character that appears exactly once, or '\0' if none does. The index variant returns its position, or −1.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output "leetcode" l "loveleetcode" v (index 2) "aabb" none

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each i, scan all j to see whether s[i] repeats. That's O(n²).
  2. Insight: we need the count of each char and the original order.
  3. Two passes: pass 1 counts, pass 2 walks s in order and returns the first char with count 1. That's O(n).

docs.title: Approaches
docs.text: Approach Time Space Nested loop O(n²) O(1) indexOf(c) == lastIndexOf(c) O(n²) O(1) Two-pass count (optimal) O(n) O(1), fixed alphabet Streams: LinkedHashMap + counting() + filter(v == 1) O(n) O(k)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** Return the first character that occurs exactly once, or {@code '\0'} if there is none. */
public final class FirstNonRepeatingChar {
    public static final char NONE = '\0';
    private FirstNonRepeatingChar() {}

    /** Brute force: for each index, scan the whole string. O(n^2). */
    public static char bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null) return NONE;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            boolean repeated = false;
            for (int j = 0; j < s.length() && !repeated; j++) {
                repeated = i != j && s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j);
            }
            if (!repeated) return s.charAt(i);
        }
        return NONE;
    }

    /** Optimal: two passes — count, then find the first with count 1. O(n) time, O(1) (fixed alphabet). */
    public static char optimal(String s) {
        if (s == null) return NONE;
        int[] counts = new int[Character.MAX_VALUE + 1];
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) counts[c]++;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) if (counts[c] == 1) return c;   // second pass keeps original order
        return NONE;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: ordered frequency map, first entry with value 1. */
    public static char streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return NONE;
        return s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()))
                .entrySet().stream()
                .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
                .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
                .findFirst()
                .orElse(NONE);
    }

    /** Index-based variant (LeetCode 387): returns index or -1. Uses indexOf == lastIndexOf. */
    public static int firstUniqueIndex(String s) {
        if (s == null) return -1;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char c = s.charAt(i);
            if (s.indexOf(c) == s.lastIndexOf(c)) return i;  // simple but O(n^2) worst case
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
• Stream of characters (first unique so far after each char): keep counts plus a queue, and pop from the head while the head's count > 1.
  • First repeating character: track a Set and return the first char where add returns false.

docs.text: Medium Hashing Canonical key

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Group words that are anagrams of each other. ["eat","tea","tan","ate","nat","bat"] → [[eat,tea,ate],[tan,nat],[bat]]

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Comparing every pair with an anagram check is O(n² · k). That's too slow.
  2. Insight: give every word a canonical key that is identical for all its anagrams, then group with a HashMap.
  3. Key options: the sorted chars ("aet"), at O(k log k), or the 26-count signature, at O(k).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** Group words that are anagrams of each other. Groups appear in first-occurrence order. */
public final class GroupAnagrams {
    private GroupAnagrams() {}

    /** Key = sorted chars. O(n · k log k) for n words of length k. */
    public static List<List<String>> sortedKey(String[] words) {
        Map<String, List<String>> groups = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (words == null) return new ArrayList<>();
        for (String w : words) {
            char[] c = w.toCharArray();
            Arrays.sort(c);
            groups.computeIfAbsent(new String(c), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
    }

    /** Optimal: key = 26-letter count signature ("#1#0#2..."). O(n · k). Lowercase a–z input. */
    public static List<List<String>> countKey(String[] words) {
        Map<String, List<String>> groups = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (words == null) return new ArrayList<>();
        for (String w : words) {
            int[] counts = new int[26];
            for (char c : w.toCharArray()) counts[c - 'a']++;
            groups.computeIfAbsent(Arrays.toString(counts), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: groupingBy on the sorted-chars key. */
    public static List<List<String>> streams(String[] words) {
        if (words == null) return new ArrayList<>();
        Map<String, List<String>> m = Arrays.stream(words).collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                w -> w.chars().sorted().collect(StringBuilder::new, StringBuilder::appendCodePoint, StringBuilder::append).toString(),
                LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.toList()));
        return new ArrayList<>(m.values());
    }

}

docs.title: Pattern search: KMP & Rabin–Karp
docs.text: Expert Pattern matching LPS table Rolling hash

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return every start index where pattern occurs in text, overlaps included. text = "AABAACAADAABAABA", pattern = "AABA" → [0, 9, 12].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Naive: try every alignment and compare. Worst case O(n·m) ("aaaa…a" vs "aaab").
  2. Waste: after a partial match of j chars fails, naive search moves the text pointer back and re-reads chars it has already matched.
  3. KMP insight: the matched part is a prefix of the pattern, which we know in advance. Precompute, for each prefix, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix (LPS). On a mismatch, set j = lps[j-1]. The text pointer never moves back.
  4. Rabin–Karp insight: compare hashes, and roll the window hash in O(1). Verify the actual chars on a hash hit.

Reading it: lps[4] = 2 because "AABAA" both starts and ends with "AA".

docs.title: KMP search loop
docs.text:
1. j = number of pattern chars currently matched.
  2. While j > 0 and text[i] != pattern[j]: j = lps[j-1] (fall back, don't restart).
  3. If they match, j++. If j == m, record i-m+1, then set j = lps[j-1] to allow overlaps.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Find all start indexes of {@code pattern} in {@code text} (overlaps allowed). Empty pattern → none. */
public final class KmpPatternSearch {
    private KmpPatternSearch() {}

    /** Naive: try every alignment. O(n · m) worst case ("aaaa…a" vs "aa…ab"). */
    public static List<Integer> naive(String text, String pattern) {
        List<Integer> hits = new ArrayList<>();
        if (text == null || pattern == null || pattern.isEmpty()) return hits;
        for (int i = 0; i + pattern.length() <= text.length(); i++) {
            int j = 0;
            while (j < pattern.length() && text.charAt(i + j) == pattern.charAt(j)) j++;
            if (j == pattern.length()) hits.add(i);
        }
        return hits;
    }

    /**
     * KMP: precompute lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix.
     * On mismatch we fall back to lps instead of restarting, so the text pointer never moves back. O(n + m).
     */
    public static List<Integer> kmp(String text, String pattern) {
        List<Integer> hits = new ArrayList<>();
        if (text == null || pattern == null || pattern.isEmpty()) return hits;
        int[] lps = lps(pattern);
        int j = 0;                                           // chars of pattern currently matched
        for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) {
            while (j > 0 && text.charAt(i) != pattern.charAt(j)) j = lps[j - 1];
            if (text.charAt(i) == pattern.charAt(j)) j++;
            if (j == pattern.length()) {
                hits.add(i - j + 1);
                j = lps[j - 1];                              // continue to find overlapping matches
            }
        }
        return hits;
    }

    /** Longest-proper-prefix-which-is-also-suffix table. "AABAACAABAA" → [0,1,0,1,2,0,1,2,3,4,5]. */
    public static int[] lps(String p) {
        int[] lps = new int[p.length()];
        int len = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < p.length(); i++) {
            while (len > 0 && p.charAt(i) != p.charAt(len)) len = lps[len - 1];
            if (p.charAt(i) == p.charAt(len)) len++;
            lps[i] = len;
        }
        return lps;
    }

    /** Rabin–Karp rolling hash (alternative). Average O(n + m); verify on hash hit to avoid false positives. */
    public static List<Integer> rabinKarp(String text, String pattern) {
        List<Integer> hits = new ArrayList<>();
        if (text == null || pattern == null || pattern.isEmpty() || pattern.length() > text.length()) return hits;
        final long base = 256, mod = 1_000_000_007L;
        int m = pattern.length();
        long pHash = 0, tHash = 0, high = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < m - 1; i++) high = high * base % mod;   // base^(m-1)
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            pHash = (pHash * base + pattern.charAt(i)) % mod;
            tHash = (tHash * base + text.charAt(i)) % mod;
        }
        for (int i = 0; ; i++) {
            if (pHash == tHash && text.regionMatches(i, pattern, 0, m)) hits.add(i);
            if (i + m >= text.length()) break;
            tHash = (tHash - text.charAt(i) * high % mod + mod) % mod;   // drop left char
            tHash = (tHash * base + text.charAt(i + m)) % mod;           // add right char
        }
        return hits;
    }
}

docs.title: Longest common prefix
docs.text: Medium Scanning Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the longest prefix shared by all strings. ["flower","flow","flight"] → "fl"; ["dog","racecar","car"] → "".

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The answer can't be longer than the shortest string.
  2. Vertical scan: compare column 0 across all strings, then column 1, and so on. Stop at the first mismatch or when any string ends.
  3. Horizontal scan: start with prefix = strs[0] and shrink it until each string startsWith it.
  4. Sort trick: after sorting lexicographically, the first and last strings are the most different, so their common prefix is everyone's.
  5. Divide & conquer: LCP(all) = LCP(LCP(left half), LCP(right half)).

docs.title: Dry run (vertical scan)
docs.text: col flower flow flight Result 0 f f f ✅ 1 l l l ✅ 2 o o i stop → "fl"

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Longest common prefix of an array of strings ("flower","flow","flight" → "fl"). Empty/null array → "". */
public final class LongestCommonPrefix {
    private LongestCommonPrefix() {}

    /** Vertical scan: compare column by column. O(S) where S = total chars. O(1) extra space. */
    public static String verticalScan(String[] strs) {
        if (strs == null || strs.length == 0) return "";
        for (int col = 0; col < strs[0].length(); col++) {
            char c = strs[0].charAt(col);
            for (int row = 1; row < strs.length; row++) {
                if (col == strs[row].length() || strs[row].charAt(col) != c) return strs[0].substring(0, col);
            }
        }
        return strs[0];
    }

    /** Horizontal scan: shrink the prefix until each string starts with it. */
    public static String horizontalScan(String[] strs) {
        if (strs == null || strs.length == 0) return "";
        String prefix = strs[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < strs.length; i++) {
            while (!strs[i].startsWith(prefix)) prefix = prefix.substring(0, prefix.length() - 1);
        }
        return prefix;
    }

    /** Sort trick: after sorting, only first and last strings need comparing. O(S log n). */
    public static String sorting(String[] strs) {
        if (strs == null || strs.length == 0) return "";
        String[] copy = strs.clone();
        Arrays.sort(copy);
        String first = copy[0], last = copy[copy.length - 1];
        int i = 0;
        while (i < first.length() && i < last.length() && first.charAt(i) == last.charAt(i)) i++;
        return first.substring(0, i);
    }

    /** Divide and conquer (recursive): LCP(left half) ∩ LCP(right half). */
    public static String divideAndConquer(String[] strs) {
        if (strs == null || strs.length == 0) return "";
        return lcp(strs, 0, strs.length - 1);
    }

    private static String lcp(String[] s, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return s[lo];                          // base case: one string
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        String a = lcp(s, lo, mid), b = lcp(s, mid + 1, hi);
        int i = 0;
        while (i < a.length() && i < b.length() && a.charAt(i) == b.charAt(i)) i++;
        return a.substring(0, i);
    }
}

docs.title: Longest palindromic substring
docs.text: Hard Expand around centre DP Manacher

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the longest contiguous palindrome in s. "babad" → "bab" (or "aba"), "cbbd" → "bb", "forgeeksskeegfor" → "geeksskeeg".

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: check all O(n²) substrings, each in O(n), for O(n³).
  2. DP insight: s[i..j] is a palindrome iff s[i]==s[j] and s[i+1..j-1] is one. That's O(n²) time and space.
  3. Centre insight: every palindrome mirrors around a centre. There are 2n−1 centres (each char, and each gap between chars for even lengths). Expand outward while the ends match. That's O(n²) time and O(1) space, and it's the usual interview answer.
  4. Expert: Manacher reuses the radius of a mirrored centre, for O(n).

docs.title: Approach — Expand around centre
docs.text:
1. For each c: odd = expand(c, c) and even = expand(c, c+1).
  2. expand moves l-- and r++ while s[l]==s[r], then returns r-l-1.
  3. If len beats the best, set start = c - (len-1)/2 and end = c + len/2.

docs.title: DP table ("cbbd", ✅ = palindrome)
docs.text: i \ j c b b d c ✅ b ✅ ✅ b ✅ d ✅

docs.title: Manacher in one paragraph
docs.text: Transform the string to ^#a#b#a#$ so every palindrome has odd length. Keep the right-most palindrome [center − p[center], right]. For i < right, the mirror 2·center − i already knows a radius, so p[i] = min(right − i, p[mirror]). Expand only beyond that, so right only ever moves forward, which gives O(n) in total.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

/** Longest palindromic substring ("babad" → "bab" or "aba"; we return the first found). */
public final class LongestPalindromicSubstring {
    private LongestPalindromicSubstring() {}

    /** Brute force: check all O(n^2) substrings, each in O(n). O(n^3). */
    public static String bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return "";
        String best = s.substring(0, 1);
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            for (int j = i + best.length(); j < s.length(); j++) {   // only longer candidates matter
                if (Palindrome.isPalindrome(s.substring(i, j + 1))) best = s.substring(i, j + 1);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Dynamic programming: dp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && dp[i+1][j-1]. O(n^2) time and space. */
    public static String dynamicProgramming(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return "";
        int n = s.length(), start = 0, len = 1;
        boolean[][] dp = new boolean[n][n];
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {                   // i goes down so dp[i+1] is ready
            for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
                dp[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j) && (j - i < 3 || dp[i + 1][j - 1]);
                if (dp[i][j] && j - i + 1 > len) {
                    start = i;
                    len = j - i + 1;
                }
            }
        }
        return s.substring(start, start + len);
    }

    /** Optimal in practice: expand around each of the 2n-1 centres. O(n^2) time, O(1) space. */
    public static String expandAroundCenter(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return "";
        int start = 0, end = 0;
        for (int c = 0; c < s.length(); c++) {
            int odd = expand(s, c, c), even = expand(s, c, c + 1);
            int len = Math.max(odd, even);
            if (len > end - start + 1) {
                start = c - (len - 1) / 2;
                end = c + len / 2;
            }
        }
        return s.substring(start, end + 1);
    }

    private static int expand(String s, int l, int r) {
        while (l >= 0 && r < s.length() && s.charAt(l) == s.charAt(r)) {
            l--;
            r++;
        }
        return r - l - 1;                                    // length of the palindrome found
    }

    /** Expert: Manacher's algorithm. O(n) time. Works on "^#a#b#a#$" to unify odd/even. */
    public static String manacher(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return "";
        StringBuilder t = new StringBuilder("^");
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) t.append('#').append(c);
        t.append("#$");
        int[] p = new int[t.length()];
        int center = 0, right = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < t.length() - 1; i++) {
            if (i < right) p[i] = Math.min(right - i, p[2 * center - i]);   // reuse mirror's radius
            while (t.charAt(i + 1 + p[i]) == t.charAt(i - 1 - p[i])) p[i]++;
            if (i + p[i] > right) {
                center = i;
                right = i + p[i];
            }
        }
        int bestLen = 0, bestCenter = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < p.length - 1; i++) {
            if (p[i] > bestLen) {
                bestLen = p[i];
                bestCenter = i;
            }
        }
        int start = (bestCenter - bestLen) / 2;              // map back to original indexes
        return s.substring(start, start + bestLen);
    }
}

docs.title: Longest substring without repeating characters
docs.text: Hard Sliding window Hashing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Return the length of the longest substring that has all distinct characters.

Input Output Why "abcabcbb" 3 "abc" "bbbbb" 1 "b" "pwwkew" 3 "wke" (not "pwke", which is a subsequence) "abba" 2 catches the "left must not move back" bug

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each start, extend while the chars stay unique. That's O(n²).
  2. Waste: when a duplicate appears at right, every window starting before the duplicate's previous position is also invalid, so restarting from start + 1 repeats work.
  3. Sliding window: keep [left, right] valid. Expand right, and when a duplicate appears, shrink from left.
  4. Better: store the last index of each char and jump left to last + 1 immediately. Use left = max(left, last + 1) so left never moves backwards (the "abba" case).

docs.title: Approach 1 — Brute force
docs.text: O(n²) time, O(k) space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Sliding window + Set
docs.text: Each char is added and removed at most once, so O(2n) = O(n).

docs.title: Approach 3 — Last-index jump (optimal)
docs.text:
1. lastSeen[c] stores index + 1 (0 means never seen).
  2. For each right: left = max(left, lastSeen[s[right]]).
  3. best = max(best, right - left + 1), then lastSeen[s[right]] = right + 1.

docs.title: Dry run ("abba")
docs.text: right char lastSeen before left window best 0 a 0 0 a 1 1 b 0 0 ab 2 2 b 2 2 b 2 3 a 1 max(2,1) = 2 ba 2

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Longest substring without repeating characters: "abba"
  1. Window [left, right] holds distinct characters. lastSeen stores index + 1, so 0 means "never seen".
  2. right = 0: a not seen before; left stays 0. Window = "a", best = 1.
  3. right = 1: b not seen before; left stays 0. Window = "ab", best = 2.
  4. right = 2: b was last at index 1, inside the window: jump left to 2. Window = "b", best = 2.
  5. right = 3: a was last at index 0, but that is before left (2). max(left, 1) keeps left at 2. Without max, left would move backwards: the classic bug. Window = "ba", best = 2.
  6. Done: the longest window had length 2 ("ab" or "ba"). Each character is visited once: O(n).

docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Length of the longest substring with all distinct characters ("abcabcbb" → 3, "abc"). */
public final class LongestSubstringWithoutRepeating {
    private LongestSubstringWithoutRepeating() {}

    /** Brute force: try every start, extend while unique. O(n^2) time. */
    public static int bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null) return 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            Set<Character> seen = new HashSet<>();
            for (int j = i; j < s.length() && seen.add(s.charAt(j)); j++) {
                best = Math.max(best, j - i + 1);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Sliding window with a set: grow right, shrink left while duplicate. O(n) — each char in/out once. */
    public static int slidingWindowSet(String s) {
        if (s == null) return 0;
        Set<Character> window = new HashSet<>();
        int best = 0, left = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            while (!window.add(s.charAt(right))) window.remove(s.charAt(left++));
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Optimal: remember last index of each char and JUMP left past it. O(n), O(1) fixed alphabet. */
    public static int optimal(String s) {
        if (s == null) return 0;
        int[] lastSeen = new int[Character.MAX_VALUE + 1];   // stores index + 1; 0 = never seen
        int best = 0, left = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            char c = s.charAt(right);
            left = Math.max(left, lastSeen[c]);              // never move left backwards
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
            lastSeen[c] = right + 1;
        }
        return best;
    }
}

docs.title: Minimum window substring
docs.text: Expert Sliding window Frequency counting

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every char of t, with multiplicity. s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC" → "BANC". Return "" if it's impossible.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each start, extend until the window covers t. That's O(n²).
  2. Observation: once [left, right] covers t, moving right further only makes the window longer. The improvement comes from moving left.
  3. Variable window: expand right until the window is valid, then shrink left while it stays valid, recording the minimum each time.
  4. O(1) validity check: keep need[c] (how many of c we still need) and one integer missing. When need[c] goes from positive to lower while expanding, missing--. When it goes from 0 to positive while shrinking, missing++.

docs.text: right char missing Action 0 A 2 useful 3 B 1 useful 5 C 0 valid ADOBEC (6). Shrink: drop A → missing 1 10 A 0 valid DOBECODEBA… shrink… 12 C 0 … shrink until BANC (4) ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

/**
 * Smallest substring of {@code s} containing every char of {@code t} (with multiplicity).
 * s="ADOBECODEBANC", t="ABC" → "BANC". Returns "" if impossible.
 */
public final class MinimumWindowSubstring {
    private MinimumWindowSubstring() {}

    /** Brute force: every substring, check coverage. O(n^2 · alphabet). Fine for teaching, not for prod. */
    public static String bruteForce(String s, String t) {
        if (s == null || t == null || t.isEmpty()) return "";
        String best = "";
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            int[] need = counts(t);
            int missing = t.length();
            for (int j = i; j < s.length(); j++) {
                if (need[s.charAt(j)]-- > 0) missing--;
                if (missing == 0) {
                    if (best.isEmpty() || j - i + 1 < best.length()) best = s.substring(i, j + 1);
                    break;                                   // longer j from same i can't be better
                }
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: variable sliding window. Expand right until window covers t, then shrink left while it
     * still covers, recording the minimum. Each index enters and leaves once → O(|s| + |t|).
     */
    public static String optimal(String s, String t) {
        if (s == null || t == null || t.isEmpty() || t.length() > s.length()) return "";
        int[] need = counts(t);                              // need[c] > 0 → still missing c
        int missing = t.length(), left = 0, bestStart = 0, bestLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            if (need[s.charAt(right)]-- > 0) missing--;      // this char was useful
            while (missing == 0) {                           // window valid → try to shrink
                if (right - left + 1 < bestLen) {
                    bestLen = right - left + 1;
                    bestStart = left;
                }
                if (++need[s.charAt(left++)] > 0) missing++; // removed a required char
            }
        }
        return bestLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? "" : s.substring(bestStart, bestStart + bestLen);
    }

    private static int[] counts(String t) {
        int[] need = new int[Character.MAX_VALUE + 1];
        for (char c : t.toCharArray()) need[c]++;
        return need;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(|s| + |t|) time, because each index enters and leaves the window once. O(1) space for the fixed alphabet.

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: Three things must be right at the same time: (1) multiplicity through need[] going negative for surplus chars, (2) the missing counter that avoids O(alphabet) checks, and (3) recording the answer inside the shrink loop.

docs.title: Palindrome check
docs.text: Easy Two pointers Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if s reads the same forwards and backwards. Variation: ignore case and every non-alphanumeric char (LeetCode 125).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Strict Ignore non-alnum "racecar" true true "Aba" false true "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" false true "" true true

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Case-sensitive? Ignore spaces and punctuation? What should null return? Here it returns false.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A palindrome means s[i] == s[n-1-i] for every i < n/2.
  2. Brute force: reverse and compare. That uses O(n) extra memory.
  3. Waste: we build a whole copy even when the first char already mismatches.
  4. Pattern: two pointers moving inward, with an early exit on the first mismatch. O(1) space.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Reverse and compare
docs.text: new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString().equals(s). O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Two pointers (optimal)
docs.text:
1. left = 0, right = n-1.
  2. While left < right: if s[left] != s[right], return false. Otherwise move both inward.
  3. Return true.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Recursive
docs.text: isPal(l, r) = l >= r || (s[l] == s[r] && isPal(l+1, r-1)). Pass indexes instead of substrings to avoid copies.

docs.title: Approach 4 — Streams
docs.text: IntStream.range(0, n/2).allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n-1-i)).

docs.title: Variation — Ignore non-alphanumerics
docs.text: Use the same two pointers, but skip junk with inner while loops and compare with Character.toLowerCase.

docs.title: Dry run ("abcba")
docs.text: left right s[left] s[right] Match? 0 4 a a ✅ 1 3 b b ✅ 2 2 stop true

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Two pointers: is "abcba" a palindrome?
  1. Start at both ends and walk inwards.
  2. s[0] = a and s[4] = a match. Move both pointers inwards.
  3. s[1] = b and s[3] = b match. Move both pointers inwards.
  4. left (2) is no longer < right (2): the middle character needs no partner. true after n/2 comparisons, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/**
 * Check whether a string is a palindrome.
 * {@link #isPalindrome} is a strict check; {@link #isValidPalindrome} ignores case and non-alphanumerics
 * ("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true). {@code null} is treated as not a palindrome.
 */
public final class Palindrome {
    private Palindrome() {}

    /** Brute force: reverse and compare. O(n) time, O(n) extra space. */
    public static boolean bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        return new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString().equals(s);
    }

    /** Optimal: two pointers moving inwards, stop at first mismatch. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        int left = 0, right = s.length() - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            if (s.charAt(left++) != s.charAt(right--)) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    /** Recursive: first == last && middle is a palindrome. O(n) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static boolean recursive(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        return recursive(s, 0, s.length() - 1);
    }

    private static boolean recursive(String s, int left, int right) {
        if (left >= right) return true;                       // base case: 0 or 1 char left
        if (s.charAt(left) != s.charAt(right)) return false;
        return recursive(s, left + 1, right - 1);
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: every i in the first half matches its mirror. */
    public static boolean streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        return IntStream.range(0, s.length() / 2)
                .allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(s.length() - 1 - i));
    }

    /** Variation: ignore case and anything that is not a letter or digit. */
    public static boolean isValidPalindrome(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        int left = 0, right = s.length() - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            while (left < right && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(left))) left++;   // skip junk
            while (left < right && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(right))) right--;
            if (Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(left)) != Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(right))) return false;
            left++;
            right--;
        }
        return true;
    }
}

docs.title: Reverse a string
docs.text: Easy Two pointers Recursion Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given a string s, return it reversed. null returns null.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output "hello" "olleh" "a" "a" "" ""

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text:
• Can I use StringBuilder.reverse()? (Usually "no, implement it yourself".)
  • Unicode emoji or surrogate pairs? A naive char swap breaks them, while StringBuilder.reverse() handles them.
  • Should I reverse in place? Java strings are immutable, so "in place" means on a char[].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Reversing means out[i] = s[n-1-i].
  2. Brute force: prepend each char to a result string. It's correct, but every + copies the whole string, so it's O(n²).
  3. Waste: the repeated copies. Use a mutable char[] instead.
  4. Pattern: two pointers at the ends, swap, move inward. That's n/2 swaps.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Brute force (prepend)
docs.text: Loop over the chars and do result = c + result. O(n²) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Optimal (two pointers on char[])
docs.text:
1. chars = s.toCharArray(), left = 0, right = n-1.
  2. While left < right: swap chars[left] and chars[right], then left++, right--.
  3. Return new String(chars).

O(n) time, O(n) space for the copy.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Recursive
docs.text:
• Base case: length ≤ 1, so return s.
  • Recursive case: reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0).

It is elegant but O(n²) (substring + concat at each level) and uses O(n) stack.

docs.title: Approach 4 — Java 8 Streams
docs.text: IntStream.range(0, n).map(i -> s.charAt(n-1-i)), then join the chars.

docs.title: Dry run (two pointers, "hello")
docs.text: Step left right chars 0 0 4 h e l l o 1 1 3 o e l l h 2 2 2 o l l e h. Stop: left == right

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Reverse a string — four ways. All methods return {@code null} for {@code null} input. */
public final class ReverseString {
    private ReverseString() {}

    /** Brute force: build a new string by prepending each char. O(n^2) because strings are immutable. */
    public static String bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        String result = "";
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            result = c + result;               // creates a new String every iteration
        }
        return result;
    }

    /** Optimal: two pointers swapping on a char[]. O(n) time, O(n) space for the array. */
    public static String optimal(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
        int left = 0, right = chars.length - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            char tmp = chars[left];
            chars[left++] = chars[right];
            chars[right--] = tmp;
        }
        return new String(chars);
    }

    /** Library: StringBuilder.reverse() — what you use in production (handles surrogate pairs). */
    public static String library(String s) {
        return s == null ? null : new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString();
    }

    /** Recursive: reverse(rest) + first char. Base case: length <= 1. O(n^2) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static String recursive(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.length() <= 1) return s;
        return recursive(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0);
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: walk indexes backwards and join. */
    public static String streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        return IntStream.range(0, s.length())
                .map(i -> s.charAt(s.length() - 1 - i))
                .mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char) c))
                .collect(Collectors.joining());
    }
}

docs.text: null, empty, a single char, an even/odd length, and surrogate pairs ("😀" is 2 chars).

docs.title: Reverse words in a sentence
docs.text: Medium Two pointers Parsing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse the order of the words. Trim the result and collapse multiple spaces into one. Variation: reverse the characters of each word but keep the word order.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output " the sky is blue " "blue is sky the" "I love Java" (variation) "I evol avaJ"

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Library way: trim().split("\\s+"), then reverse the list and join. That's correct and O(n), but the regex has overhead.
  2. Manual parse: scan from the end, skip spaces, mark the word end, find the word start, and append. Each char is touched about twice, so O(n), and it handles any spacing.
  3. In-place char[] trick (C-style): reverse the whole string, then reverse each word.

docs.title: Approach — Manual scan from the end (optimal)
docs.text:
1. i = n-1.
  2. Skip spaces (i--). Stop if i < 0.
  3. end = i. Move i left while s[i] != ' '.
  4. Append s[i+1..end], with a separating space if the builder isn't empty.

docs.title: Recursive
docs.text: reverse("the sky is") = reverse("sky is") + " " + "the". The base case is a single word.

docs.title: Streams
docs.text: reduce((acc, w) -> w + " " + acc) prepends each word.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/**
 * Reverse the order of words; collapse multiple spaces and trim ("  the sky  is blue " → "blue is sky the").
 * Also: reverse each word in place keeping word order ("I love Java" → "I evol avaJ").
 */
public final class ReverseWords {
    private ReverseWords() {}

    /** Library: split on whitespace, reverse list, join. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static String library(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        String trimmed = s.trim();
        if (trimmed.isEmpty()) return "";
        List<String> words = Arrays.asList(trimmed.split("\\s+"));
        Collections.reverse(words);
        return String.join(" ", words);
    }

    /** Optimal (manual parse): scan from the end, copy each word once. O(n) time, O(n) output. */
    public static String optimal(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        int i = s.length() - 1;
        while (i >= 0) {
            while (i >= 0 && s.charAt(i) == ' ') i--;        // skip spaces
            if (i < 0) break;
            int end = i;
            while (i >= 0 && s.charAt(i) != ' ') i--;        // find word start
            if (!sb.isEmpty()) sb.append(' ');
            sb.append(s, i + 1, end + 1);
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    /** Recursive: reverse(rest) + " " + firstWord. */
    public static String recursive(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        String t = s.trim();
        int space = t.indexOf(' ');
        if (space < 0) return t;                             // base case: single word (or empty)
        return recursive(t.substring(space + 1)) + " " + t.substring(0, space);
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: words reversed via a reducing join. */
    public static String streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        return Arrays.stream(s.trim().split("\\s+"))
                .filter(w -> !w.isEmpty())
                .reduce((acc, w) -> w + " " + acc)
                .orElse("");
    }

    /** Variation: reverse characters of each word, keep word order. */
    public static String reverseEachWord(String s) {
        if (s == null) return null;
        return Arrays.stream(s.split(" "))
                .map(w -> new StringBuilder(w).reverse().toString())
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) output for all but the recursive version (O(n²) from the substring copies).

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: All spaces → "". A single word. Leading and trailing spaces. Tabs (handled by \\s+ in the library version).

docs.title: String compression (run-length encoding)
docs.text: Medium Scanning Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Compress runs: "aaabbc" → "a3b2c1". The CTCI variant returns the original string if the compressed form isn't shorter. Also write decode, which must support multi-digit counts ("a12b3").

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Equal characters are adjacent, so you only ever compare with the previous char.
  2. Keep a run counter. When the char changes or the string ends, flush char + run.
  3. Trick: loop i up to n inclusive so the final run is flushed in the same branch.

docs.title: Approach — Single pass (optimal)
docs.text: i s[i-1] s[i] Action Output 1 a a run=2 2 a a run=3 3 a b flush a3 a3 4 b b run=2 a3 5 b c flush b2 a3b2 6 c end flush c1 a3b2c1

docs.title: Recursive
docs.text: Measure the first run, emit char + run, and recurse on s.substring(run).

docs.title: Decode
docs.text: Read a char, then read digits while isDigit (count = count*10 + d), then append c.repeat(count).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

/**
 * Run-length encoding: "aaabbc" → "a3b2c1". {@link #compressIfShorter} returns the original
 * when compression does not help (CTCI 1.6). {@link #decode} reverses it, supporting multi-digit counts.
 */
public final class StringCompression {
    private StringCompression() {}

    /** Optimal: single pass counting runs. O(n) time, O(n) output. */
    public static String compress(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return s;
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        int run = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++) {
            if (i < s.length() && s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(i - 1)) {
                run++;
            } else {                                         // run ended (or string ended)
                sb.append(s.charAt(i - 1)).append(run);
                run = 1;
            }
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    /** Recursive: encode the first run, recurse on the remainder. */
    public static String recursive(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return s;
        int run = 1;
        while (run < s.length() && s.charAt(run) == s.charAt(0)) run++;
        return "" + s.charAt(0) + run + recursive(s.substring(run));
    }

    public static String compressIfShorter(String s) {
        String c = compress(s);
        return c == null || c.length() >= s.length() ? s : c;
    }

    /** "a12b3" → 12 a's then 3 b's. */
    public static String decode(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) return s;
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        int i = 0;
        while (i < s.length()) {
            char c = s.charAt(i++);
            int count = 0;
            while (i < s.length() && Character.isDigit(s.charAt(i))) count = count * 10 + (s.charAt(i++) - '0');
            sb.append(String.valueOf(c).repeat(count));
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) output.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Using String += in the loop (O(n²)). Forgetting to flush the last run. Single-digit-only decoding.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: LeetCode 443: compress in place in a char[] with read/write pointers, and omit the count when it's 1.

docs.title: All permutations of a string
docs.text: Medium Recursion Backtracking

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return every arrangement of the characters. "abc" gives 6: abc acb bac bca cab cba. With duplicates ("aab"), return only the distinct ones.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. For the first position, try each character. Then solve the same problem for the remaining characters. That's recursion.
  2. Base case: no characters remain, so the prefix is a complete permutation.
  3. There are n choices, then n−1, and so on, which gives n! leaves. You can't beat O(n · n!) because that is the output size.
  4. To avoid creating substrings, swap in place on a char[] (choose → explore → un-choose).

docs.title: Recursion tree for "abc" (prefix | rest)
docs.text:
"" | abc
        /             |             \
    a | bc         b | ac         c | ab
    /    \         /    \         /    \
 ab|c   ac|b    ba|c   bc|a    ca|b   cb|a
   |      |       |      |       |      |
  abc    acb     bac    bca     cab    cba

docs.title: Approach 1 — Prefix + remaining (recursive)
docs.text: permute(prefix + rest[i], rest without i) for each i.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Swap backtracking
docs.text: For position k, swap each i ≥ k into slot k, recurse on k+1, then swap back. Collect into a TreeSet to dedupe.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Iterative (normal solution)
docs.text: Sort the chars, then repeatedly apply next permutation until it returns false. This naturally skips duplicates and produces lexicographic order.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/** All permutations of a string. "abc" → abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba. n! results. */
public final class StringPermutations {
    private StringPermutations() {}

    /** Recursive (prefix + remaining): pick each char as next, recurse on what is left. */
    public static List<String> recursive(String s) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (s != null) permute("", s, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void permute(String prefix, String rest, List<String> out) {
        if (rest.isEmpty()) {                                // base case: nothing left to place
            out.add(prefix);
            return;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < rest.length(); i++) {
            permute(prefix + rest.charAt(i), rest.substring(0, i) + rest.substring(i + 1), out);
        }
    }

    /** Backtracking with swaps on a char[] (no substring garbage). Distinct results via a sorted set. */
    public static Set<String> distinctBacktracking(String s) {
        Set<String> out = new TreeSet<>();
        if (s != null) swapPermute(s.toCharArray(), 0, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void swapPermute(char[] a, int k, Set<String> out) {
        if (k == a.length) {
            out.add(new String(a));
            return;
        }
        for (int i = k; i < a.length; i++) {
            swap(a, k, i);                                   // choose
            swapPermute(a, k + 1, out);                      // explore
            swap(a, k, i);                                   // un-choose (backtrack)
        }
    }

    /** Iterative "normal" solution: next lexicographic permutation, repeated (handles duplicates). */
    public static List<String> iterative(String s) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (s == null) return out;
        char[] a = s.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(a);
        do {
            out.add(new String(a));
        } while (nextPermutation(a));
        return out;
    }

    private static boolean nextPermutation(char[] a) {
        int i = a.length - 2;
        while (i >= 0 && a[i] >= a[i + 1]) i--;              // find first descent from the right
        if (i < 0) return false;                             // already the last permutation
        int j = a.length - 1;
        while (a[j] <= a[i]) j--;
        swap(a, i, j);
        for (int l = i + 1, r = a.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) swap(a, l, r);
        return true;
    }

    private static void swap(char[] a, int i, int j) {
        char t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.text: O(n · n!) time and O(n) recursion depth (plus the output).

  • Kth permutation without generating all of them. Factorial number system, O(n²).

docs.title: Valid parentheses
docs.text: Medium Stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given a string of ()[]{}, return true if every opener is closed by the same type in the correct order.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The most recent unmatched opener must be closed first, which is LIFO. So use a stack.
  2. Trick: push the expected closer instead of the opener. Then the check is just pop() == c.
  3. A mismatch, or a pop from an empty stack, means invalid. Leftovers at the end also mean invalid.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Brute force
docs.text: Repeatedly remove "()", "[]" and "{}" until nothing changes. Valid if the string ends up empty. That's O(n²).

docs.title: Approach 2 — Stack (optimal)
docs.text: char Action Stack (top on the right) { push } } [ push ] } ] ( push ) } ] ) ) pop ) ✅ } ] ] pop ] ✅ } } pop } ✅ empty → valid

docs.title: Approach 3 — Single bracket type
docs.text: With only ( and ), a counter is enough: it must never go negative and must end at 0. That's O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Brackets "()[]{}" are balanced if every opener is closed by the same type in the correct order. */
public final class ValidParentheses {
    private ValidParentheses() {}

    /** Brute force: repeatedly delete "()", "[]", "{}" until nothing changes. O(n^2). */
    public static boolean bruteForce(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        String prev;
        do {
            prev = s;
            s = s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "");
        } while (!s.equals(prev));
        return s.isEmpty();
    }

    /** Optimal: stack of expected closers. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean optimal(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            switch (c) {
                case '(' -> stack.push(')');                 // push what we EXPECT to see later
                case '[' -> stack.push(']');
                case '{' -> stack.push('}');
                default -> {
                    if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != c) return false;
                }
            }
        }
        return stack.isEmpty();                              // leftover openers → unbalanced
    }

    /** Only one bracket type? A counter is enough. O(1) space. */
    public static boolean singleTypeCounter(String s) {
        if (s == null) return false;
        int open = 0;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (c == '(') open++;
            else if (c == ')' && --open < 0) return false;   // closed more than opened
        }
        return open == 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Stack: O(n) time and O(n) space. Counter: O(n) time and O(1) space.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
• Minimum additions to make the string valid. Count the unmatched openers and closers.
  • Longest valid parentheses (Hard). Use a stack of indexes, or DP.
  • Generate all valid combinations of n pairs (backtracking).

docs.title: Count vowels & consonants
docs.text: Easy Classification Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the vowels (a e i o u) and consonants in s. Ignore digits, spaces and symbols. Return {vowels, consonants}.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: "Hello World 2026" → {3, 7} (e, o, o | h, l, l, w, r, l, d)

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Is y a vowel? (No, here.) Upper case? (Count it, case-insensitively.) Non-English letters? (Ignore them.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Each char falls into one of three buckets: vowel, consonant, or ignored.
  2. Lower-case once, check the range a..z, then test membership in "aeiou".
  3. One pass, so O(n). A 5-char lookup is effectively O(1).

docs.title: Approach 1 — Loop (optimal)
docs.text: For each char c in s.toLowerCase(): skip it if it's not in a..z. Otherwise increment vowels if "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0, else consonants.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Recursive
docs.text: Classify s[i], then recurse on i+1. Base case: i == length. Pass an index, not a substring.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Streams
docs.text: Count the vowels, then count the letters. Consonants = letters − vowels.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.strings;

/**
 * Count vowels and consonants (English letters only; digits, spaces and symbols are ignored).
 * Result is {@code int[]{vowels, consonants}}. {@code null}/empty → {0, 0}.
 */
public final class VowelConsonantCount {
    private VowelConsonantCount() {}

    /** Loop + {@code indexOf} lookup in a vowel string. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static int[] optimal(String s) {
        int vowels = 0, consonants = 0;
        if (s == null) return new int[]{0, 0};
        for (char c : s.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
            if (c < 'a' || c > 'z') continue;                // not an English letter
            if ("aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0) vowels++;
            else consonants++;
        }
        return new int[]{vowels, consonants};
    }

    /** Recursive: count first char, recurse on the rest by index (no substring copies). */
    public static int[] recursive(String s) {
        int[] acc = new int[2];
        if (s != null) recursive(s.toLowerCase(), 0, acc);
        return acc;
    }

    private static void recursive(String s, int i, int[] acc) {
        if (i == s.length()) return;                         // base case
        char c = s.charAt(i);
        if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') acc["aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0 ? 0 : 1]++;
        recursive(s, i + 1, acc);
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: filter letters, then count twice. */
    public static int[] streams(String s) {
        if (s == null) return new int[]{0, 0};
        String lower = s.toLowerCase();
        long vowels = lower.chars().filter(c -> "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0).count();
        long letters = lower.chars().filter(c -> c >= 'a' && c <= 'z').count();
        return new int[]{(int) vowels, (int) (letters - vowels)};
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: All approaches take O(n) time. The loop and streams use O(1) extra space; the recursive version uses O(n) stack.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Character.isLetter accepts é, ß and so on. Decide whether you want "English letters" or "any letter".

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• Contiguous memory gives O(1) index access. Inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n) because elements shift.
  • An "in place" answer usually means O(1) extra space, using read/write pointers or swaps.
  • Most array problems are one of: two pointers, prefix/suffix accumulation, Kadane, hashing, sorting first, reversal tricks, or a monotonic stack.

docs.title: Best time to buy & sell stock
docs.text: Medium Running minimum Greedy

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: prices[i] is the price on day i. Buy once and sell later to maximise profit, or return 0 if no profit is possible. [7,1,5,3,6,4] → 5 (buy at 1, sell at 6).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every (buy, sell) pair with buy < sell. That's O(n²).
  2. Insight: if you sell on day j, the best buy is the minimum price before j.
  3. So keep a running minSoFar, and each day compute price − minSoFar. That's O(n) and O(1).
  4. Unlimited transactions: collect every rise from one day to the next. Summing the up-moves equals buying at every valley and selling at every peak.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: day price minSoFar profit today best 0 7 7 0 0 1 1 1 0 0 2 5 1 4 4 4 6 1 5 5

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Stock prices by day. Max profit from ONE buy then a later sell (0 if no profit). Plus multi-transaction variant. */
public final class BuySellStock {
    private BuySellStock() {}

    /** Brute force: every buy/sell pair. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] prices) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < prices.length; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < prices.length; j++) best = Math.max(best, prices[j] - prices[i]);
        return best;
    }

    /** Optimal: track the minimum price so far; profit if sold today. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int optimal(int[] prices) {
        int minSoFar = Integer.MAX_VALUE, best = 0;
        for (int p : prices) {
            minSoFar = Math.min(minSoFar, p);
            best = Math.max(best, p - minSoFar);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Unlimited transactions (LeetCode 122): sum every positive day-to-day rise. Greedy, O(n). */
    public static int unlimitedTransactions(int[] prices) {
        int profit = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) profit += Math.max(0, prices[i] - prices[i - 1]);
        return profit;
    }
}

docs.title: The series
docs.text: I (one transaction) ✅ · II (unlimited) ✅ · III / IV (at most k transactions, a DP over states) · with cooldown · with a transaction fee. These are covered in DP.

docs.title: Find max & min of an array
docs.text: Easy Linear scan Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return {min, max} of a non-empty array. GfG asks for the version with the minimum number of comparisons.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sorting gives the min and max at the ends, but O(n log n) is overkill.
  2. One scan: update min and max per element. That's O(n) and about 2n comparisons.
  3. Pairwise trick: compare the two elements of a pair with each other first, then the smaller with min and the larger with max. That's 3 comparisons per 2 elements, about 1.5n.
  4. Divide & conquer: solve each half and combine. It also takes about 1.5n comparisons, and it's a nice recursion example.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.IntSummaryStatistics;

/** Find {min, max} of a non-empty int array. Throws IllegalArgumentException on null/empty. */
public final class MaxMin {
    private MaxMin() {}

    /** Sort then take ends. O(n log n) — mutates a copy only. */
    public static int[] sorting(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        return new int[]{c[0], c[c.length - 1]};
    }

    /** Optimal: one linear scan. O(n) time, O(1) space, ~2n comparisons. */
    public static int[] linear(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        int min = a[0], max = a[0];
        for (int x : a) {
            if (x < min) min = x;
            if (x > max) max = x;
        }
        return new int[]{min, max};
    }

    /** Pairwise comparison: ~1.5n comparisons (classic GfG "minimum comparisons" answer). */
    public static int[] pairwise(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        int i, min, max;
        if (a.length % 2 == 0) {
            min = Math.min(a[0], a[1]);
            max = Math.max(a[0], a[1]);
            i = 2;
        } else {
            min = max = a[0];
            i = 1;
        }
        for (; i < a.length; i += 2) {                       // compare the pair first, then 1 vs min, 1 vs max
            int small = Math.min(a[i], a[i + 1]), big = Math.max(a[i], a[i + 1]);
            if (small < min) min = small;
            if (big > max) max = big;
        }
        return new int[]{min, max};
    }

    /** Recursive (divide & conquer): min/max of halves. O(n) time, O(log n) stack. */
    public static int[] recursive(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        return dc(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int[] dc(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return new int[]{a[lo], a[lo]};
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        int[] l = dc(a, lo, mid), r = dc(a, mid + 1, hi);
        return new int[]{Math.min(l[0], r[0]), Math.max(l[1], r[1])};
    }

    /** Java 8: IntSummaryStatistics gives min, max, sum, avg, count in one pass. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        requireNonEmpty(a);
        IntSummaryStatistics s = Arrays.stream(a).summaryStatistics();
        return new int[]{s.getMin(), s.getMax()};
    }

    private static void requireNonEmpty(int[] a) {
        if (a == null || a.length == 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("array must be non-empty");
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Comparisons Space Sort O(n log n) — O(n) copy Linear O(n) ~2n O(1) Pairwise O(n) ~1.5n O(1) Recursive O(n) ~1.5n O(log n) stack IntSummaryStatistics O(n) ~2n O(1)
