docs.title: Maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm)
docs.text: Medium Kadane DP Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray. [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6 ([4,-1,2,1]).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every (i, j) with a running sum. That's O(n²).
  2. DP view: let best(i) = the best sum of a subarray ending at i. Then best(i) = max(a[i], best(i-1) + a[i]). In words: extend the previous run, or restart here.
  3. Restart exactly when the previous run is negative, because it can only hurt.
  4. The answer is max over i of best(i). Since you only need the previous value, space is O(1).

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: i a[i] current = max(a[i], current + a[i]) best 0 −2 −2 −2 1 1 max(1, −1) = 1 (restart) 1 2 −3 −2 1 3 4 max(4, 2) = 4 (restart) 4 4 −1 3 4 5 2 5 5 6 1 6 6 7 −5 1 6 8 4 5 6

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Kadane on [−2, 1, −3, 4, −1, 2, 1, −5, 4]
  1. Start with the first element: current = best = −2. The highlighted window is the best subarray ending here.
  2. i = 1: 1 beats -1 → restart here. New best = 1.
  3. i = 2: extend: current + a[i] = -2. best stays 1.
  4. i = 3: 4 beats 2 → restart here. New best = 4.
  5. i = 4: extend: current + a[i] = 3. best stays 4.
  6. i = 5: extend: current + a[i] = 5. New best = 5.
  7. i = 6: extend: current + a[i] = 6. New best = 6.
  8. i = 7: extend: current + a[i] = 1. best stays 6.
  9. i = 8: extend: current + a[i] = 5. best stays 6.
  10. Done. The best subarray is [4, −1, 2, 1] (indices 3–6), sum 6. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Maximum sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray (Kadane). [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6. */
public final class MaxSubarraySum {
    private MaxSubarraySum() {}

    /** Brute force: all subarrays with running sum. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            int sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                best = Math.max(best, sum);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Kadane: best subarray ending here = max(a[i], a[i] + best ending at i-1). O(n), O(1). */
    public static int kadane(int[] a) {
        int current = a[0], best = a[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            current = Math.max(a[i], current + a[i]);        // extend or restart
            best = Math.max(best, current);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Kadane returning the subarray bounds {sum, start, end}. */
    public static int[] kadaneWithIndices(int[] a) {
        int current = a[0], best = a[0], start = 0, bestStart = 0, bestEnd = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (a[i] > current + a[i]) {
                current = a[i];
                start = i;                                   // restart here
            } else {
                current += a[i];
            }
            if (current > best) {
                best = current;
                bestStart = start;
                bestEnd = i;
            }
        }
        return new int[]{best, bestStart, bestEnd};
    }

    /** Divide & conquer (recursive): max of left, right, crossing. O(n log n). */
    public static int divideAndConquer(int[] a) {
        return dc(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int dc(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return a[lo];
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        int leftBest = Integer.MIN_VALUE, sum = 0;
        for (int i = mid; i >= lo; i--) leftBest = Math.max(leftBest, sum += a[i]);
        int rightBest = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        sum = 0;
        for (int i = mid + 1; i <= hi; i++) rightBest = Math.max(rightBest, sum += a[i]);
        return Math.max(Math.max(dc(a, lo, mid), dc(a, mid + 1, hi)), leftBest + rightBest);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n²) O(1) Kadane O(n) O(1) Divide & conquer O(n log n) O(log n)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: For an all-negative array the answer is the largest single element, not 0. Initialise with a[0].

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text: Maximum product subarray (track both min and max). Circular max subarray (max(kadane, total − minSubarray)). Max sum of a submatrix (Kadane on column sums).

docs.title: Merge intervals
docs.text: Hard Sort + sweep

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge all overlapping intervals. [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]] → [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. Touching intervals ([1,4],[4,5]) merge.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Unsorted intervals can overlap anywhere, so comparing every pair is O(n²).
  2. Sort by start. Now an interval can only overlap the current merged block.
  3. Sweep: if next.start <= current.end, extend with current.end = max(current.end, next.end). Otherwise close the block and start a new one.
  4. Use max for the end because a later interval can sit entirely inside the current one ([1,10],[2,3]).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;

/** Merge overlapping intervals. [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]] → [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. Touching ([1,4],[4,5]) merges. */
public final class MergeIntervals {
    private MergeIntervals() {}

    /** Optimal: sort by start, then extend or append. O(n log n) time, O(n) output. */
    public static int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
        if (intervals == null || intervals.length == 0) return new int[0][];
        int[][] sorted = intervals.clone();
        Arrays.sort(sorted, Comparator.comparingInt(iv -> iv[0]));
        List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int[] current = sorted[0].clone();
        for (int i = 1; i < sorted.length; i++) {
            if (sorted[i][0] <= current[1]) {                // overlaps → extend
                current[1] = Math.max(current[1], sorted[i][1]);
            } else {                                          // gap → close current
                out.add(current);
                current = sorted[i].clone();
            }
        }
        out.add(current);
        return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }

    /** Follow-up: insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list. O(n). */
    public static int[][] insert(int[][] intervals, int[] add) {
        List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int i = 0, n = intervals.length;
        int[] merged = add.clone();
        while (i < n && intervals[i][1] < add[0]) out.add(intervals[i++]);          // fully left
        while (i < n && intervals[i][0] <= merged[1]) {                              // overlapping
            merged[0] = Math.min(merged[0], intervals[i][0]);
            merged[1] = Math.max(merged[1], intervals[i][1]);
            i++;
        }
        out.add(merged);
        while (i < n) out.add(intervals[i++]);                                       // fully right
        return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n log n) for the sort, plus an O(n) sweep. O(n) for the output.

docs.title: Interval family
docs.text: Insert interval ✅ · Meeting rooms (can one person attend all? sort, then check overlaps) · Meeting rooms II (minimum number of rooms: min-heap of end times, or a sweep line) · Non-overlapping intervals (greedy by end time).

docs.title: Missing number
docs.text: Easy Math XOR

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: An array holds n distinct numbers from 0..n, with exactly one missing. Find it. [3,0,1] → 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sort, then find the first i where a[i] != i. That's O(n log n).
  2. HashSet: insert everything, then check 0..n. That's O(n) time but O(n) space.
  3. Math: the expected sum is n(n+1)/2. Subtract the actual sum. That's O(1) space. Use long to avoid overflow.
  4. XOR: since x ^ x = 0, XOR-ing all the indexes 0..n and all the values leaves only the missing number. It can't overflow.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Array has n distinct numbers from 0..n; one is missing. Find it. [3,0,1] → 2. */
public final class MissingNumber {
    private MissingNumber() {}

    /** Sort and find the first index where a[i] != i. O(n log n). */
    public static int sorting(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        for (int i = 0; i < c.length; i++) if (c[i] != i) return i;
        return c.length;
    }

    /** Gauss sum: n(n+1)/2 − sum. Use long to avoid overflow. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int sumFormula(int[] a) {
        long n = a.length, expected = n * (n + 1) / 2, sum = 0;
        for (int x : a) sum += x;
        return (int) (expected - sum);
    }

    /** XOR trick: x ^ x = 0, so XOR of all indexes and values leaves the missing one. Overflow-free. */
    public static int xor(int[] a) {
        int x = a.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) x ^= i ^ a[i];
        return x;
    }

    /** Java 8. */
    public static int streams(int[] a) {
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(0, a.length).sum() - Arrays.stream(a).sum();
    }
}

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• 1..n with one missing and one duplicated: use sum and sum-of-squares equations, or XOR partitioning.
  • First missing positive (Hard): cyclic sort, putting each value v at index v−1.

docs.title: Move zeros to end
docs.text: Easy Two pointers In place

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Move all 0s to the end in place, keeping the order of the non-zero elements. [0,1,0,3,12] → [1,3,12,0,0].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Extra array: copy the non-zeros, and the remaining slots are zeros by default. That's O(n) space.
  2. In place: a write pointer marks where the next non-zero goes. A read pointer scans.
  3. When a[read] != 0, swap it into write and advance write. The relative order is preserved because write ≤ read.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Move all zeros to the end, keeping the relative order of non-zero elements. In place. */
public final class MoveZeros {
    private MoveZeros() {}

    /** Extra array: copy non-zeros, fill rest with zeros. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static int[] extraSpace(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        int k = 0;
        for (int x : a) if (x != 0) out[k++] = x;           // remaining slots are already 0
        return out;
    }

    /** Optimal: write pointer + swap. O(n) time, O(1) space, minimal writes. */
    public static void optimal(int[] a) {
        int write = 0;                                       // next position for a non-zero
        for (int read = 0; read < a.length; read++) {
            if (a[read] != 0) {
                int t = a[write];
                a[write++] = a[read];
                a[read] = t;
            }
        }
    }

    /** Java 8: concatenate non-zeros and zeros. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        return IntStream.concat(Arrays.stream(a).filter(x -> x != 0), Arrays.stream(a).filter(x -> x == 0)).toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text: Segregate 0s and 1s. Even before odd. Dutch National Flag (sort 0/1/2 with three pointers).

docs.title: Next permutation
docs.text: Hard Pivot · swap · reverse

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Rearrange the array, in place, into the next lexicographically greater permutation. If none exists, return the smallest. [1,2,3] → [1,3,2] · [3,2,1] → [1,2,3] · [1,1,5] → [1,5,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. To get the next bigger number, change the rightmost position you can.
  2. A suffix that is non-increasing is already at its maximum, and no rearrangement of it gets bigger.
  3. So find the pivot i: the first index from the right with a[i] < a[i+1].
  4. Swap a[i] with the smallest element in the suffix that is greater than it. Since the suffix is descending, that is the rightmost element > a[i].
  5. The suffix is still descending. Reverse it to make it ascending, which is the smallest possible arrangement.
  6. If there is no pivot, the whole array is descending. Reverse everything to get the smallest permutation.

docs.title: Dry run ([1,3,5,4,2])
docs.text:
pivot: from right, 2<4? no, 4<5? no, 5>3 → a[1] = 3 is the pivot (3 < 5)
swap 3 with the rightmost > 3 in [5,4,2] → 4  →  [1,4,5,3,2]
reverse suffix [5,3,2]                         →  [1,4,2,3,5] ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Rearrange to the next lexicographically greater permutation; if none, the smallest (sorted). In place. */
public final class NextPermutation {
    private NextPermutation() {}

    /**
     * 1. From the right, find the first i with a[i] < a[i+1] (the "pivot").
     * 2. If none → array is fully descending → reverse whole array.
     * 3. From the right, find first j with a[j] > a[i]; swap a[i], a[j].
     * 4. Reverse the suffix a[i+1..] (it was descending, now ascending = smallest).
     * O(n) time, O(1) space.
     */
    public static void next(int[] a) {
        int i = a.length - 2;
        while (i >= 0 && a[i] >= a[i + 1]) i--;
        if (i >= 0) {
            int j = a.length - 1;
            while (a[j] <= a[i]) j--;
            swap(a, i, j);
        }
        for (int l = i + 1, r = a.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) swap(a, l, r);
    }

    private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Product of array except self
docs.text: Hard Prefix / suffix

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return out[i] = the product of every element except a[i], without division, in O(n). [1,2,3,4] → [24,12,8,6].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: a nested loop, O(n²).
  2. Why not division? It fails on zeros, and the interviewer forbids it anyway.
  3. Insight: out[i] = (product of everything LEFT of i) × (product of everything RIGHT of i).
  4. Prefix/suffix arrays take O(n) space. Optimisation: store the prefix products in out, then sweep from the right with a single suffix variable, for O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** out[i] = product of all elements except a[i], WITHOUT division, in O(n). */
public final class ProductExceptSelf {
    private ProductExceptSelf() {}

    /** Brute force: nested loop. O(n^2). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            int p = 1;
            for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) if (i != j) p *= a[j];
            out[i] = p;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Prefix and suffix product arrays. O(n) time, O(n) extra. */
    public static int[] prefixSuffix(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] pre = new int[n], suf = new int[n], out = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) pre[i] = i == 0 ? 1 : pre[i - 1] * a[i - 1];
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) suf[i] = i == n - 1 ? 1 : suf[i + 1] * a[i + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = pre[i] * suf[i];
        return out;
    }

    /** Optimal: store prefix in output, multiply by a running suffix on the way back. O(n), O(1) extra. */
    public static int[] optimal(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        out[0] = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) out[i] = out[i - 1] * a[i - 1];   // product of everything left of i
        int suffix = 1;
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            out[i] *= suffix;                                         // × product of everything right of i
            suffix *= a[i];
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array
docs.text: Easy Slow/fast pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: In place, keep each value once and return the new length k. The first k slots hold the result. [0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,4] → k = 5, [0,1,2,3,4,…].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sorted means duplicates are adjacent, so you only need to compare with the last kept value.
  2. k = the length of the unique prefix. For each i, if a[i] != a[k-1], write it to a[k++].
  3. Generalisation: to allow at most m copies, compare with a[k-m].

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Remove duplicates from a SORTED array in place; return the new length k (first k slots hold uniques). */
public final class RemoveDuplicatesSorted {
    private RemoveDuplicatesSorted() {}

    /** Set-based (works unsorted too, but O(n) extra space). */
    public static int withSet(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) seen.add(x);
        int k = 0;
        for (int x : seen) a[k++] = x;
        return k;
    }

    /** Optimal: slow/fast pointers — sorted means duplicates are adjacent. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int optimal(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 0) return 0;
        int k = 1;                                           // a[0..k-1] are unique
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (a[i] != a[k - 1]) a[k++] = a[i];
        }
        return k;
    }

    /** Variation (LeetCode 80): allow each value at most twice. */
    public static int atMostTwice(int[] a) {
        int k = 0;
        for (int x : a) if (k < 2 || x != a[k - 2]) a[k++] = x;
        return k;
    }

    /** Java 8: returns a new array of distinct values. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        return Arrays.stream(a).distinct().toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Reverse an array
docs.text: Easy Two pointers Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse a in place. [1,2,3,4,5] → [5,4,3,2,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Element i belongs at n-1-i.
  2. Swapping the pair (l, r) fixes two positions at once, so you only need n/2 swaps.
  3. Stop when l >= r. The middle element of an odd-length array stays where it is.

docs.title: Approaches
docs.text:
• Iterative two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space.
  • Recursive: swap (l, r), then recurse on (l+1, r-1). Base case l >= r. O(n) stack.
  • Streams (new array): IntStream.range(0,n).map(i -> a[n-1-i]).toArray().

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Reverse an int array in place (and a copy-returning streams version). */
public final class ReverseArray {
    private ReverseArray() {}

    /** Optimal: two pointers swap. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static void inPlace(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return;
        for (int l = 0, r = a.length - 1; l < r; l++, r--) {
            int t = a[l];
            a[l] = a[r];
            a[r] = t;
        }
    }

    /** Recursive: swap ends, recurse inward. O(n) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static void recursive(int[] a) {
        if (a != null) recursive(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void recursive(int[] a, int l, int r) {
        if (l >= r) return;
        int t = a[l];
        a[l] = a[r];
        a[r] = t;
        recursive(a, l + 1, r - 1);
    }

    /** Java 8: new reversed array. */
    public static int[] streams(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return null;
        return IntStream.range(0, a.length).map(i -> a[a.length - 1 - i]).toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Rotate array by k
docs.text: Medium Reversal trick

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Rotate right by k in place. [1,2,3,4,5,6,7], k = 3 → [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. k may be larger than n.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Normalise: k %= n, because rotating n times gives back the original.
  2. Brute force: rotate by one, k times. That's O(n·k).
  3. Extra array: out[(i+k) % n] = a[i]. That's O(n) time and O(n) space.
  4. Reversal insight: the last k elements must come first. Reversing the whole array puts them at the front, but backwards. Reverse each part again to fix the order.

docs.title: Reversal, visualised
docs.text:
original      1 2 3 4 | 5 6 7
reverse all   7 6 5 | 4 3 2 1
reverse [0,k) 5 6 7 | 4 3 2 1
reverse [k,n) 5 6 7 | 1 2 3 4   ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

/** Rotate array to the RIGHT by k steps in place. [1..7], k=3 → [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. */
public final class RotateArray {
    private RotateArray() {}

    /** Brute force: rotate by one, k times. O(n·k). */
    public static void bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0) return;
        k %= a.length;
        for (int step = 0; step < k; step++) {
            int last = a[a.length - 1];
            System.arraycopy(a, 0, a, 1, a.length - 1);
            a[0] = last;
        }
    }

    /** Extra array: element i goes to (i+k) % n. O(n), O(n). */
    public static void extraArray(int[] a, int k) {
        int n = a.length;
        if (n == 0) return;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) out[(i + k) % n] = a[i];
        System.arraycopy(out, 0, a, 0, n);
    }

    /** Optimal: reverse all, reverse first k, reverse rest. O(n), O(1). */
    public static void reversal(int[] a, int k) {
        int n = a.length;
        if (n == 0) return;
        k %= n;                                              // k may exceed n
        reverse(a, 0, n - 1);
        reverse(a, 0, k - 1);
        reverse(a, k, n - 1);
    }

    /** Left rotation by d is right rotation by n - d. */
    public static void rotateLeft(int[] a, int d) {
        if (a.length == 0) return;
        reversal(a, a.length - d % a.length);
    }

    private static void reverse(int[] a, int l, int r) {
        while (l < r) {
            int t = a[l];
            a[l++] = a[r];
            a[r--] = t;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space One step at a time O(n·k) O(1) Extra array O(n) O(n) Three reversals O(n) O(1) Juggling (GCD cycles) O(n) O(1)

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: Left rotation by d is right rotation by n − d. Searching a rotated sorted array is a binary search variant.

docs.title: Second largest element
docs.text: Easy Linear scan

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the second-largest distinct value. [12, 35, 1, 10, 34, 1] → 34. [10, 5, 10] → 5. [10, 10] → none.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Distinct or not? (Here: distinct.) What should we return if there is none? (Here: OptionalInt.empty(), not −1, because −1 may be a valid value.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sort, then walk back from the end until a value differs from the max. That's O(n log n).
  2. One pass: keep first and second.
    • x > first: the old first becomes second, and first = x.
    • first > x > second: second = x. The strict < skips duplicates of the max.
  3. Use long sentinels so that an input containing Integer.MIN_VALUE still works.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.OptionalInt;

/** Second largest DISTINCT element. [10, 5, 10] → 5. Empty if it does not exist. */
public final class SecondLargest {
    private SecondLargest() {}

    /** Sort and walk back skipping duplicates of the max. O(n log n). */
    public static OptionalInt sorting(int[] a) {
        if (a == null || a.length < 2) return OptionalInt.empty();
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        for (int i = c.length - 2; i >= 0; i--) if (c[i] != c[c.length - 1]) return OptionalInt.of(c[i]);
        return OptionalInt.empty();
    }

    /** Optimal: track first and second in one pass. O(n), O(1). Uses long sentinels so MIN_VALUE works. */
    public static OptionalInt optimal(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return OptionalInt.empty();
        long first = Long.MIN_VALUE, second = Long.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int x : a) {
            if (x > first) {
                second = first;                              // old max becomes second
                first = x;
            } else if (x < first && x > second) {
                second = x;                                  // strictly less than max → candidate
            }
        }
        return second == Long.MIN_VALUE ? OptionalInt.empty() : OptionalInt.of((int) second);
    }

    /** Java 8: distinct, sort descending, skip 1. */
    public static OptionalInt streams(int[] a) {
        if (a == null) return OptionalInt.empty();
        return Arrays.stream(a).boxed().distinct().sorted((x, y) -> Integer.compare(y, x))
                .skip(1).mapToInt(Integer::intValue).findFirst();
    }
}

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: The Kth largest element is a heap of size k (O(n log k)) or Quickselect (O(n) on average).

docs.title: Trapping rain water
docs.text: Expert Two pointers Prefix max Monotonic stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given bar heights, compute how much water is trapped after rain. [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] → 6.

                 █
         █ ≈ ≈ ≈ █ █ ≈ █
     █ ≈ █ █ ≈ █ █ █ █ █ █
   ───────────────────────
h: 0 1 0 2 1 0 1 3 2 1 2 1      (≈ = water, total 6)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Key formula: water above bar i = min(maxLeft(i), maxRight(i)) − h[i].
  2. Brute force: compute maxLeft and maxRight by scanning for each i. That's O(n²).
  3. Waste: those maxima get recomputed every time. Precompute them as prefix-max and suffix-max arrays, for O(n) time and O(n) space.
  4. Two-pointer insight: if h[l] < h[r], then maxRight(l) ≥ h[r] > h[l], so the water at l depends only on leftMax. Process l and move it. Mirror the logic for r. That's O(n) time and O(1) space.
  5. Alternative view: a monotonic decreasing stack fills water layer by layer whenever a taller bar closes a basin.

docs.title: Dry run (two pointers, first steps)
docs.text: l r h[l] h[r] Side leftMax / rightMax +water 0 11 0 1 left L = 0 0 1 11 1 1 right R = 1 0 1 10 1 2 left L = 1 0 2 10 0 2 left L = 1 1 3 10 2 2 right R = 2 0 … … total 6

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Water trapped between bars. [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] → 6. */
public final class TrappingRainWater {
    private TrappingRainWater() {}

    /** Brute force: for each bar, scan left max and right max. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] h) {
        int water = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
            int leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0;
            for (int l = 0; l <= i; l++) leftMax = Math.max(leftMax, h[l]);
            for (int r = i; r < h.length; r++) rightMax = Math.max(rightMax, h[r]);
            water += Math.min(leftMax, rightMax) - h[i];
        }
        return water;
    }

    /** Precompute prefix-max and suffix-max arrays. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static int prefixMax(int[] h) {
        int n = h.length;
        if (n == 0) return 0;
        int[] left = new int[n], right = new int[n];
        left[0] = h[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) left[i] = Math.max(left[i - 1], h[i]);
        right[n - 1] = h[n - 1];
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) right[i] = Math.max(right[i + 1], h[i]);
        int water = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) water += Math.min(left[i], right[i]) - h[i];
        return water;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: two pointers. The side with the smaller max is the bottleneck — its water level is
     * already known, so process it and move inward. O(n) time, O(1) space.
     */
    public static int twoPointers(int[] h) {
        int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0, water = 0;
        while (l < r) {
            if (h[l] < h[r]) {
                leftMax = Math.max(leftMax, h[l]);
                water += leftMax - h[l++];
            } else {
                rightMax = Math.max(rightMax, h[r]);
                water += rightMax - h[r--];
            }
        }
        return water;
    }

    /** Monotonic decreasing stack: fill "layers" when a taller bar closes a basin. O(n). */
    public static int monotonicStack(int[] h) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int water = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && h[i] > h[stack.peek()]) {
                int bottom = stack.pop();
                if (stack.isEmpty()) break;                  // no left wall
                int left = stack.peek();
                int width = i - left - 1;
                int bounded = Math.min(h[left], h[i]) - h[bottom];
                water += width * bounded;
            }
            stack.push(i);
        }
        return water;
    }
}

docs.title: Two sum
docs.text: Medium Hashing Two pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target (exactly one solution). [2,7,11,15], 9 → [0,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: check every pair. That's O(n²).
  2. Waste: for each x, we search for target − x with a linear scan.
  3. Hashing: remember the values we've seen, mapped to their indices. Each lookup is then O(1), for O(n) total.
  4. Look up before inserting, so an element never pairs with itself ([3,3], 6 works, [3], 6 doesn't).
  5. If the array is sorted (or you're allowed to sort), use two pointers, which needs O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Dry run (hash map, [2,7,11,15], 9)
docs.text: i a[i] need seen Result 0 2 7 {} → 1 7 2 found 2 → idx 0 [0,1] ✅

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Two Sum with a hash map: [2, 7, 11, 15], target 26
  1. One pass. For each number, ask the map: have I already seen its complement?
  2. i = 0: need 26 − 2 = 24. Not in the map yet.
  3. Remember 2 → 0 for later numbers. Putting it after the lookup stops an element pairing with itself.
  4. i = 1: need 26 − 7 = 19. Not in the map yet.
  5. Remember 7 → 1 for later numbers. Putting it after the lookup stops an element pairing with itself.
  6. i = 2: need 26 − 11 = 15. Not in the map yet.
  7. Remember 11 → 2 for later numbers. Putting it after the lookup stops an element pairing with itself.
  8. i = 3: need 26 − 15 = 11. It's in the map at index 2: answer [2, 3].

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.arrays;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Indices of two numbers adding to target (exactly one solution assumed). Returns {} if none. */
public final class TwoSum {
    private TwoSum() {}

    /** Brute force: every pair. O(n^2), O(1). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a, int target) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++)
                if (a[i] + a[j] == target) return new int[]{i, j};
        return new int[0];
    }

    /** Optimal: one-pass hash map value → index; look up the complement first. O(n), O(n). */
    public static int[] optimal(int[] a, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            Integer j = seen.get(target - a[i]);
            if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
            seen.put(a[i], i);                               // insert AFTER lookup so we don't pair with self
        }
        return new int[0];
    }

    /** Sorted input variant: two pointers. O(n), O(1). Returns indices into the sorted array. */
    public static int[] sortedTwoPointers(int[] sorted, int target) {
        int l = 0, r = sorted.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int sum = sorted[l] + sorted[r];
            if (sum == target) return new int[]{l, r};
            if (sum < target) l++;                           // need bigger → move left up
            else r--;                                        // need smaller → move right down
        }
        return new int[0];
    }

    /** Unsorted + two pointers: sort index array by value (O(n log n)), keep original indices. */
    public static int[] sortThenTwoPointers(int[] a, int target) {
        Integer[] idx = new Integer[a.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) idx[i] = i;
        Arrays.sort(idx, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(a[x], a[y]));
        int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            int sum = a[idx[l]] + a[idx[r]];
            if (sum == target) return new int[]{Math.min(idx[l], idx[r]), Math.max(idx[l], idx[r])};
            if (sum < target) l++;
            else r--;
        }
        return new int[0];
    }
}

docs.title: Armstrong number
docs.text: Easy Digits Recursion Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: An Armstrong (narcissistic) number equals the sum of its digits, each raised to the number of digits. 153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³, 9474 = 9⁴ + 4⁴ + 7⁴ + 4⁴. Also: list every Armstrong number up to a limit.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Count the digits d once.
  2. Extract each digit with % 10 and / 10, and add digit^d.
  3. Compare the sum with the original. Keep a copy, because the loop destroys n.
  4. Pitfall: Math.pow returns a double. Use an integer power loop to avoid rounding errors.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Armstrong (narcissistic) number: sum of each digit^(number of digits) equals the number. 153 = 1³+5³+3³. */
public final class ArmstrongNumber {
    private ArmstrongNumber() {}

    /** Iterative: count digits, then sum powers. O(d). */
    public static boolean isArmstrong(int n) {
        if (n < 0) return false;
        int digits = String.valueOf(n).length();
        long sum = 0;
        for (int x = n; x > 0; x /= 10) sum += pow(x % 10, digits);
        return sum == n;
    }

    /** Recursive sum of digit powers. */
    public static boolean recursive(int n) {
        return n >= 0 && sumPowers(n, String.valueOf(n).length()) == n;
    }

    private static long sumPowers(int n, int p) {
        return n == 0 ? 0 : pow(n % 10, p) + sumPowers(n / 10, p);
    }

    /** Java 8: digits as chars → power sum. */
    public static boolean streams(int n) {
        if (n < 0) return false;
        String s = String.valueOf(n);
        return s.chars().mapToLong(c -> pow(c - '0', s.length())).sum() == n;
    }

    /** All Armstrong numbers in [1, limit]. */
    public static List<Integer> upTo(int limit) {
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, limit).filter(ArmstrongNumber::isArmstrong).boxed().collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new));
    }

    private static long pow(int base, int exp) {             // integer power — avoid Math.pow double rounding
        long r = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) r *= base;
        return r;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(d²) per number with the naive power, or O(d log d) with fast power. Since d ≤ 10, that's effectively O(1).

docs.title: Number base conversion
docs.text: Medium Division / Horner Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Convert integers between bases 2–36: decimal → binary (10 → 1010), hex → decimal (ff → 255), and any base → any base.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. To base b: n % b is the last digit, and n / b drops it. Repeat until n is 0. The digits come out least-significant first, so reverse them at the end.
  2. Recursive version, no reversal: convert n / b first (the higher digits), then append n % b.
  3. From base b, Horner's rule: read left to right with value = value × b + digit. "ff" → 0×16+15 = 15 → 15×16+15 = 255.
  4. Any → any: parse into a long, then format. Reject digits that are invalid for the base.
  5. Handle 0 and negative numbers explicitly.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

/** Convert integers between bases 2..36 (digits 0-9 then a-z), without Integer.toString(n, radix) as the main answer. */
public final class BaseConversion {
    private BaseConversion() {}

    private static final String DIGITS = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz";

    /** Repeated division: remainders are the digits from LEAST significant upward → reverse at the end. */
    public static String toBase(long n, int base) {
        check(base);
        if (n == 0) return "0";
        boolean negative = n < 0;
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        long x = Math.abs(n);                                // fine for |n| < 2^63
        while (x > 0) {
            sb.append(DIGITS.charAt((int) (x % base)));
            x /= base;
        }
        if (negative) sb.append('-');
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    /** Recursive: convert n / base first (the higher digits), then append the last digit — no reversal needed. */
    public static String toBaseRecursive(long n, int base) {
        check(base);
        if (n < 0) return "-" + toBaseRecursive(-n, base);
        if (n < base) return String.valueOf(DIGITS.charAt((int) n));
        return toBaseRecursive(n / base, base) + DIGITS.charAt((int) (n % base));
    }

    /** Parse: Horner's rule — value = value * base + digit, left to right. */
    public static long fromBase(String s, int base) {
        check(base);
        boolean negative = s.startsWith("-");
        long value = 0;
        for (char c : (negative ? s.substring(1) : s).toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
            int d = DIGITS.indexOf(c);
            if (d < 0 || d >= base) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad digit '" + c + "' for base " + base);
            value = value * base + d;
        }
        return negative ? -value : value;
    }

    /** Any base to any base via a long in the middle. */
    public static String convert(String s, int from, int to) {
        return toBase(fromBase(s, from), to);
    }

    private static void check(int base) {
        if (base < 2 || base > 36) throw new IllegalArgumentException("base must be 2..36");
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(log_b n) for both directions.

docs.title: FizzBuzz
docs.text: Easy Conditionals Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For 1..n: print "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, "FizzBuzz" for multiples of both, and the number otherwise.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The rules overlap, so check the most specific one (15) first or it will never fire.
  2. Senior touch: build the word by concatenation (Fizz + Buzz). Adding a new rule ("Bazz" for 7) is then one line instead of 2ᵏ branches. That shows you think about the Open/Closed principle.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** 1..n: "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for 5, "FizzBuzz" for both, else the number. */
public final class FizzBuzz {
    private FizzBuzz() {}

    /** Classic if/else — check 15 FIRST (the most specific rule). */
    public static List<String> classic(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            if (i % 15 == 0) out.add("FizzBuzz");
            else if (i % 3 == 0) out.add("Fizz");
            else if (i % 5 == 0) out.add("Buzz");
            else out.add(String.valueOf(i));
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Extensible: string concatenation — adding "Bazz for 7" is one line, no combinatorial branches. */
    public static List<String> extensible(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            String s = (i % 3 == 0 ? "Fizz" : "") + (i % 5 == 0 ? "Buzz" : "");
            out.add(s.isEmpty() ? String.valueOf(i) : s);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams. */
    public static List<String> streams(int n) {
        return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)
                .mapToObj(i -> i % 15 == 0 ? "FizzBuzz" : i % 3 == 0 ? "Fizz" : i % 5 == 0 ? "Buzz" : String.valueOf(i))
                .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) output.

docs.title: GCD & LCM
docs.text: Medium Euclid Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Compute gcd(a, b) and lcm(a, b). gcd(12, 18) = 6, lcm(12, 18) = 36. Also find the GCD of a whole array.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every d from min(a,b) down to 1. That's O(min(a, b)).
  2. Euclid's insight: any common divisor of a and b also divides a − b, and therefore a mod b. So gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), with base case gcd(a, 0) = a.
  3. The arguments shrink at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers, so the cost is O(log min(a,b)).
  4. LCM: a / gcd · b. Divide first to avoid overflow, and use long.
  5. Array: reduce(0, gcd), because gcd(0, x) = x.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Greatest common divisor and least common multiple. gcd(0, 0) is defined as 0 here. */
public final class GcdLcm {
    private GcdLcm() {}

    /** Brute force: largest d dividing both. O(min(a,b)). */
    public static int bruteForce(int a, int b) {
        a = Math.abs(a);
        b = Math.abs(b);
        if (a == 0 || b == 0) return a + b;
        for (int d = Math.min(a, b); d >= 1; d--) if (a % d == 0 && b % d == 0) return d;
        return 1;
    }

    /** Euclid recursive: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); gcd(a, 0) = a. O(log min(a,b)). */
    public static int recursive(int a, int b) {
        return b == 0 ? Math.abs(a) : recursive(b, a % b);
    }

    /** Euclid iterative. */
    public static int iterative(int a, int b) {
        while (b != 0) {
            int t = a % b;
            a = b;
            b = t;
        }
        return Math.abs(a);
    }

    /** lcm = a / gcd * b — divide FIRST to avoid overflow. */
    public static long lcm(int a, int b) {
        if (a == 0 || b == 0) return 0;
        return Math.abs((long) a / iterative(a, b) * b);
    }

    /** GCD of an array (Java 8 reduce). */
    public static int gcdOfArray(int[] a) {
        return Arrays.stream(a).reduce(0, GcdLcm::iterative);
    }
}

docs.title: LCM of 1..n (smallest multiple)
docs.text: Medium GCD/LCM Primes

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The smallest positive number divisible by every integer from 1 to n. n = 10 → 2520 · n = 20 → 232,792,560 (Project Euler 5).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: test multiples of n until every d ≤ n divides one. Fine for n ≤ 20, hopeless beyond that.
  2. Fold the LCM: lcm(1..n) = lcm(lcm(1..n−1), n), using lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) × b. Divide before multiplying to delay overflow. A long still overflows past n = 42.
  3. Prime-power insight: the answer must contain each prime p raised to the largest power ≤ n. For n = 10 that's 2³ · 3² · 5 · 7 = 2520. Combine this with the sieve and BigInteger and it's exact for any n.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.math.BigInteger;

/** Smallest positive number divisible by every integer 1..n (Project Euler 5: n=10 → 2520, n=20 → 232792560). */
public final class LcmOfRange {
    private LcmOfRange() {}

    /** Brute force: test multiples of n until one works. Fine for n ≤ ~20, hopeless beyond. */
    public static long bruteForce(int n) {
        for (long x = n; ; x += n) {
            boolean ok = true;
            for (int d = 1; d <= n && ok; d++) ok = x % d == 0;
            if (ok) return x;
        }
    }

    /** Fold lcm(acc, k) = acc / gcd(acc, k) * k across 1..n. O(n log). Overflows long beyond n = 42. */
    public static long iterative(int n) {
        long acc = 1;
        for (int k = 2; k <= n; k++) acc = acc / GcdLcm.iterative((int) (acc % k), k) * k;   // gcd(acc,k) = gcd(acc mod k, k)
        return acc;
    }

    /** Prime-power view: the answer is Π p^⌊log_p n⌋ over primes p ≤ n. Exact for any n with BigInteger. */
    public static BigInteger primePowers(int n) {
        BigInteger result = BigInteger.ONE;
        for (int p : PrimeNumbers.sieve(n)) {
            long power = p;
            while (power * p <= n) power *= p;               // largest power of p not exceeding n
            result = result.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(power));
        }
        return result;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Brute force: grows like the answer itself. LCM fold: O(n log n). Prime powers: O(n log log n) for the sieve, plus big-number multiplication.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The three methods are cross-checked for n ≤ 40, and the prime-power version is checked for n = 100 (a 41-digit answer).

docs.title: Leap year
docs.text: Easy Conditionals

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Is a year a Gregorian leap year? 2024 ✅ · 1900 ❌ · 2000 ✅.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The rule has three layers: divisible by 4 → leap; except centuries (÷100) → not leap; except ÷400 → leap.
  2. Check the most specific rule first (400, then 100, then 4), the same lesson as FizzBuzz.
  3. One expression: (y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0) || y % 400 == 0.
  4. In production, use java.time.Year.isLeap(y). Interviewers want to see that you know it exists and can derive the rule.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.time.Year;

/** Gregorian leap year: divisible by 4, except centuries, except centuries divisible by 400. */
public final class LeapYear {
    private LeapYear() {}

    /** Nested ifs — mirrors how the rule is usually stated. */
    public static boolean nested(int year) {
        if (year % 400 == 0) return true;
        if (year % 100 == 0) return false;
        return year % 4 == 0;
    }

    /** One boolean expression. */
    public static boolean expression(int year) {
        return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
    }

    /** Production: let the JDK decide (java.time). */
    public static boolean library(int year) {
        return Year.isLeap(year);
    }
}

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: Years 1–4000 are checked against java.time.

docs.title: Pattern printing
docs.text: Medium Nested loops Formulas

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The classic star and number patterns: right triangle, pyramid, diamond, Floyd's triangle, Pascal's triangle and a hollow square. 

pyramid(3)     diamond(3)    Floyd(4)     Pascal(5)
  *              *          1            1
 ***            ***         2 3          1 1
*****          *****        4 5 6        1 2 1
                ***         7 8 9 10     1 3 3 1
                 *                       1 4 6 4 1

docs.title: Thinking process (the method that solves every pattern)
docs.text:
1. Number the rows (i = 1..n).
  2. For row i, write down two formulas: the number of leading spaces, and what to print.
    • Pyramid: n − i spaces and 2i − 1 stars.
    • Diamond: a pyramid, then the same formulas with i going back down.
  3. Floyd's triangle: a single counter that keeps running across rows.
  4. Pascal: each entry is the sum of the two above it. A single row can also be built directly with C(k, j+1) = C(k, j) · (k − j) / (j + 1), without the earlier rows.
  5. Testable code: return the lines as a List<String> instead of calling System.out.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Classic pattern programs. They return lines (no System.out) so they can be tested; print with lines.forEach(System.out::println).
 * The trick to every pattern: for row i, work out (1) leading spaces and (2) what to print, as formulas of i and n.
 */
public final class PatternPrinting {
    private PatternPrinting() {}

    /** Right triangle of stars: row i has i stars. */
    public static List<String> rightTriangle(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) out.add("*".repeat(i));
        return out;
    }

    /** Centered pyramid: row i has (n - i) spaces and (2i - 1) stars. */
    public static List<String> pyramid(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) out.add(" ".repeat(n - i) + "*".repeat(2 * i - 1));
        return out;
    }

    /** Diamond: pyramid of n rows + inverted pyramid of n-1 rows. */
    public static List<String> diamond(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(pyramid(n));
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 1; i--) out.add(" ".repeat(n - i) + "*".repeat(2 * i - 1));
        return out;
    }

    /** Floyd's triangle: consecutive numbers, row i has i numbers. */
    public static List<String> floydsTriangle(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int next = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            StringBuilder row = new StringBuilder();
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) row.append(j == 0 ? "" : " ").append(next++);
            out.add(row.toString());
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Pascal's triangle values: each entry is the sum of the two above; edges are 1. */
    public static List<List<Long>> pascal(int n) {
        List<List<Long>> rows = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            List<Long> row = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++) {
                row.add(j == 0 || j == i ? 1L : rows.get(i - 1).get(j - 1) + rows.get(i - 1).get(j));
            }
            rows.add(row);
        }
        return rows;
    }

    /** Pascal row k directly with C(k, j+1) = C(k, j) * (k - j) / (j + 1) — O(k), no previous rows. */
    public static List<Long> pascalRow(int k) {
        List<Long> row = new ArrayList<>();
        long c = 1;
        for (int j = 0; j <= k; j++) {
            row.add(c);
            c = c * (k - j) / (j + 1);
        }
        return row;
    }

    /** Hollow square of side n. */
    public static List<String> hollowSquare(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (i == 0 || i == n - 1) out.add("*".repeat(n));
            else out.add(n == 1 ? "*" : "*" + " ".repeat(n - 2) + "*");
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n²) characters for every pattern (that's the output size). A Pascal row on its own is O(k).

docs.title: Perfect & strong numbers
docs.text: Easy Divisors Digits

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
• Perfect: n equals the sum of its proper divisors. 6 = 1+2+3, and 28, 496, 8128 are perfect.
  • Strong: n equals the sum of the factorials of its digits. 145 = 1! + 4! + 5!, and 40585 is strong.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Perfect, brute force: test every d from 1 to n−1. O(n).
  2. Divisor pairs: if d divides n, so does n/d, so you only scan to √n and add both d and n/d. Don't add √n twice for perfect squares. This makes it O(√n).
  3. Strong: digits only go up to 9, so precompute 0!…9! in a table once instead of recomputing factorials.
  4. Recursive strong: digitFactorialSum(n) = FACT[n % 10] + digitFactorialSum(n / 10).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/**
 * Perfect number: equals the sum of its proper divisors (6 = 1+2+3, 28, 496, 8128).
 * Strong number: equals the sum of the factorials of its digits (145 = 1! + 4! + 5!).
 */
public final class PerfectStrongNumbers {
    private PerfectStrongNumbers() {}

    /** Brute force: try every d in 1..n-1. O(n). */
    public static boolean isPerfectBrute(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        long sum = 0;
        for (int d = 1; d < n; d++) if (n % d == 0) sum += d;
        return sum == n;
    }

    /** Divisors come in pairs (d, n/d): only scan to √n. O(√n). */
    public static boolean isPerfect(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        long sum = 1;                                        // 1 is always a proper divisor
        for (long d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
            if (n % d == 0) {
                sum += d;
                long pair = n / d;
                if (pair != d) sum += pair;                  // don't count √n twice
            }
        }
        return sum == n;
    }

    /** Java 8 version of the brute force (readable, O(n)). */
    public static boolean isPerfectStreams(int n) {
        return n > 1 && IntStream.range(1, n).filter(d -> n % d == 0).sum() == n;
    }

    private static final int[] FACT = {1, 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, 720, 5040, 40320, 362880};   // 0!..9! precomputed

    /** Strong number: sum digit factorials with a lookup table. O(digits). */
    public static boolean isStrong(int n) {
        if (n <= 0) return false;
        int sum = 0;
        for (int x = n; x > 0; x /= 10) sum += FACT[x % 10];
        return sum == n;
    }

    /** Recursive digit-factorial sum. */
    public static boolean isStrongRecursive(int n) {
        return n > 0 && digitFactorialSum(n) == n;
    }

    private static int digitFactorialSum(int n) {
        return n == 0 ? 0 : FACT[n % 10] + digitFactorialSum(n / 10);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Perfect: O(n) brute force, O(√n) with pairs. Strong: O(digits).

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: Every n up to 10,000 is checked against the brute force. 33,550,336 (the fifth perfect number) is checked with the √n version.

docs.title: Prime check & Sieve of Eratosthenes
docs.text: Medium Math Sieve

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Is n prime?
  2. List every prime ≤ n.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every divisor from 2 to n−1. That's O(n).
  2. √n insight: if n = a·b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ √n. So you only need to test up to √n, which is O(√n). Loop with i * i <= n (using a long i) instead of calling Math.sqrt on every iteration.
  3. 6k ± 1: every prime above 3 has the form 6k−1 or 6k+1. Rule out 2 and 3, then test only i and i+2 with step 6. That's about 3× fewer checks.
  4. Many numbers: run the sieve once. For each prime p, mark p², p²+p, … as composite. Start at p² because smaller multiples were already marked by smaller primes.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Primality test and generating primes up to n. */
public final class PrimeNumbers {
    private PrimeNumbers() {}

    /** Brute force: try every divisor 2..n-1. O(n). */
    public static boolean bruteForce(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        for (int d = 2; d < n; d++) if (n % d == 0) return false;
        return true;
    }

    /** Optimal trial division: only up to √n, skip evens, then 6k±1. O(√n). */
    public static boolean isPrime(int n) {
        if (n < 2) return false;
        if (n < 4) return true;                              // 2 and 3
        if (n % 2 == 0 || n % 3 == 0) return false;
        for (long i = 5; i * i <= n; i += 6) {               // every prime > 3 is 6k-1 or 6k+1
            if (n % i == 0 || n % (i + 2) == 0) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

    /** Java 8. */
    public static boolean streams(int n) {
        return n >= 2 && IntStream.rangeClosed(2, (int) Math.sqrt(n)).noneMatch(d -> n % d == 0);
    }

    /** Sieve of Eratosthenes: all primes ≤ n. O(n log log n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static List<Integer> sieve(int n) {
        List<Integer> primes = new ArrayList<>();
        if (n < 2) return primes;
        boolean[] composite = new boolean[n + 1];
        for (long i = 2; i * i <= n; i++) {
            if (!composite[(int) i]) {
                for (long j = i * i; j <= n; j += i) composite[(int) j] = true;   // start at i², smaller multiples done
            }
        }
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) if (!composite[i]) primes.add(i);
        return primes;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n) O(1) √n / 6k±1 O(√n) O(1) Sieve (all ≤ n) O(n log log n) O(n)

docs.title: Reverse a number & palindrome number
docs.text: Easy Digit manipulation Overflow

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse the digits of a 32-bit int, keeping the sign. Return 0 if the result overflows. 123 → 321, -123 → −321, 120 → 21, 1534236469 → 0. Also check whether a number is a palindrome without converting it to a string.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Pop the last digit with d = x % 10 and drop it with x /= 10.
  2. Push it onto the result with r = r * 10 + d.
  3. Overflow: before multiplying, check r > MAX/10 or r < MIN/10.
  4. Negative numbers: Java's % keeps the dividend's sign (-123 % 10 == -3), so one loop handles both signs.
  5. Palindrome: reverse only half of the digits, stopping when x <= half, then compare. Overflow is impossible. Negatives and numbers ending in 0 (other than 0 itself) are never palindromes.

docs.title: Dry run (palindrome 1221)
docs.text: x half 1221 0 122 1 12 12 → stop, x == half ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.logical;

/** Reverse the digits of an int (sign kept). Returns 0 on overflow (LeetCode 7). Plus palindrome number. */
public final class ReverseNumber {
    private ReverseNumber() {}

    /** Optimal: pop last digit (x % 10), push onto result (r * 10 + d). Overflow-checked. O(log10 n). */
    public static int reverse(int x) {
        int r = 0;
        while (x != 0) {
            int d = x % 10;                                  // in Java, -123 % 10 == -3, so sign is preserved
            if (r > Integer.MAX_VALUE / 10 || r < Integer.MIN_VALUE / 10) return 0;   // r*10 would overflow
            r = r * 10 + d;
            x /= 10;
        }
        return r;
    }

    /** Recursive: carry the partially built reversed value. (No overflow check — teaching version, uses long.) */
    public static long recursive(long x) {
        return x < 0 ? -recursive(-x, 0) : recursive(x, 0);
    }

    private static long recursive(long x, long acc) {
        if (x == 0) return acc;                              // base case: no digits left
        return recursive(x / 10, acc * 10 + x % 10);
    }

    /** String version — easy to write, but allocates and must handle sign + overflow separately. */
    public static int viaString(int x) {
        try {
            String s = new StringBuilder(String.valueOf(Math.abs((long) x))).reverse().toString();
            return (int) Math.copySign(Integer.parseInt(s), x);
        } catch (NumberFormatException overflow) {
            return 0;
        }
    }

    /** Palindrome number: reverse only HALF the digits (no overflow possible). Negative → false. */
    public static boolean isPalindrome(int x) {
        if (x < 0 || (x % 10 == 0 && x != 0)) return false;
        int half = 0;
        while (x > half) {
            half = half * 10 + x % 10;
            x /= 10;
        }
        return x == half || x == half / 10;                  // /10 drops the middle digit for odd length
    }
}

void backtrack(State s, List<Answer> out) {
    if (isComplete(s)) { out.add(copyOf(s)); return; }   // base case
    for (Choice c : choices(s)) {
        if (!isValid(s, c)) continue;                     // prune
        apply(s, c);                                      // choose
        backtrack(s, out);                                // explore
        undo(s, c);                                       // un-choose
    }
}

docs.title: Combination sum I & II
docs.text: Hard Backtracking Duplicate skipping

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
• I: distinct candidates, each reusable. All combinations summing to target. [2,3,6,7], 7 → [2,2,3], [7].
  • II: candidates may repeat, each used at most once, and no duplicate combinations. [10,1,2,7,6,1,5], 8 → [1,1,6] [1,2,5] [1,7] [2,6].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. This uses the subsets template with a running remaining total. Record when it hits 0, and stop when it goes negative.
  2. Avoid permutations of the same combination ([2,3,2] vs [2,2,3]): pass a start index so you never pick an earlier candidate again. Combinations are then built in non-decreasing order.
  3. I, reuse allowed: recurse with i (the same index), not i + 1.
  4. Sort first, so you can break as soon as a candidate exceeds remaining. Every later one is bigger.
  5. II, the duplicate-skip rule: at the same depth, skip a value equal to the previous one (i > start && c[i] == c[i−1]). Equal values are still allowed at deeper levels, which is how [1,1,6] survives.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * I  (LeetCode 39): distinct candidates, each reusable, all combinations summing to target.
 * II (LeetCode 40): candidates may repeat, each used at most once, no duplicate combinations.
 * Combinations are non-decreasing lists; the result is in lexicographic order.
 */
public final class CombinationSum {
    private CombinationSum() {}

    public static List<List<Integer>> reusable(int[] candidates, int target) {
        int[] c = candidates.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);                                      // sorting enables the "break" prune below
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        reuse(c, 0, target, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void reuse(int[] c, int start, int remaining, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (remaining == 0) {
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur));
            return;
        }
        for (int i = start; i < c.length; i++) {
            if (c[i] > remaining) break;                     // sorted: every later candidate is too big as well
            cur.add(c[i]);
            reuse(c, i, remaining - c[i], cur, out);         // i, not i+1: the same number may be used again
            cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
        }
    }

    public static List<List<Integer>> onceEach(int[] candidates, int target) {
        int[] c = candidates.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        once(c, 0, target, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void once(int[] c, int start, int remaining, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (remaining == 0) {
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur));
            return;
        }
        for (int i = start; i < c.length; i++) {
            if (i > start && c[i] == c[i - 1]) continue;     // same value at the same depth → duplicate combination
            if (c[i] > remaining) break;
            cur.add(c[i]);
            once(c, i + 1, remaining - c[i], cur, out);      // i+1: each element at most once
            cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
        }
    }
}

docs.text: Easy Linear recursion Tail recursion BigInteger

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Compute n! for n ≥ 0. 5! = 120, 0! = 1.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Base case: 0! = 1! = 1.
  2. Recursive case: n! = n × (n−1)!.
  3. Stack: n frames. Java does not optimise tail calls, so the iterative loop is the production answer.
  4. Overflow: long holds up to 20!. Use BigInteger beyond that (100! has 158 digits).

docs.title: Call stack for fact(4)
docs.text:
fact(4) = 4 * fact(3)
              3 * fact(2)
                  2 * fact(1) = 1   ← base case
                  = 2
              = 6
        = 24

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.util.stream.LongStream;

/** n! for n ≥ 0. long overflows past 20!, so use BigInteger beyond that. Negative → IllegalArgumentException. */
public final class Factorial {
    private Factorial() {}

    /** Recursive: n! = n × (n-1)!, base 0! = 1. O(n) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static long recursive(int n) {
        check(n);
        return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * recursive(n - 1);
    }

    /** Tail-recursive form (Java does NOT optimise tail calls, but the shape converts to a loop easily). */
    public static long tailRecursive(int n) {
        check(n);
        return tail(n, 1);
    }

    private static long tail(int n, long acc) {
        return n <= 1 ? acc : tail(n - 1, acc * n);
    }

    /** Iterative "normal" solution. O(n), O(1). */
    public static long iterative(int n) {
        check(n);
        long r = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) r *= i;
        return r;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams. */
    public static long streams(int n) {
        check(n);
        return LongStream.rangeClosed(1, n).reduce(1, (a, b) -> a * b);
    }

    /** Arbitrary size. 100! has 158 digits. */
    public static BigInteger big(int n) {
        check(n);
        BigInteger r = BigInteger.ONE;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) r = r.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(i));
        return r;
    }

    private static void check(int n) {
        if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be >= 0");
    }
}

docs.title: Fibonacci: naive → memo → iterative → matrix
docs.text: Medium Tree recursion Memoization DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2). Compute F(n), and the first k terms.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Naive recursion is a direct translation of the definition. It makes two calls per level, which gives O(2ⁿ) (F(45) already takes seconds).
  2. Waste: the same subproblems are solved again and again (draw the tree on the mental model page).
  3. Memoization (top-down DP): cache each F(k). Every value is computed once, so O(n).
  4. Bottom-up (normal solution): you only ever need the last two values, so the cost is O(n) time and O(1) space.
  5. Expert: [[1,1],[1,0]]ⁿ = [[F(n+1),F(n)],[F(n),F(n−1)]]. Fast matrix power gives O(log n).

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

fib(5) with memoization: the call stack and the cache
  1. memo(5): not cached, so compute memo(4) + memo(3).
  2. memo(4): not cached, so compute memo(3) + memo(2).
  3. memo(3): not cached, so compute memo(2) + memo(1).
  4. memo(2): not cached, so compute memo(1) + memo(0).
  5. memo(1): base case, return 1.
  6. memo(0): base case, return 0.
  7. memo(2) = 1. Store it, so any later memo(2) is free.
  8. memo(1): base case, return 1.
  9. memo(3) = 2. Store it, so any later memo(3) is free.
  10. memo(2): cache hit, return 1 without recursing. This is the whole speed-up.
  11. memo(4) = 3. Store it, so any later memo(4) is free.
  12. memo(3): cache hit, return 2 without recursing. This is the whole speed-up.
  13. memo(5) = 5. Store it, so any later memo(5) is free.
  14. fib(5) = 5. Each n is computed once: O(n) calls instead of the naive O(2ⁿ).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

/** F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2). Shows how memoization turns exponential recursion into linear. */
public final class Fibonacci {
    private Fibonacci() {}

    /** Naive recursion: recomputes subproblems. O(2^n) time, O(n) stack. Fine for n ≤ ~35. */
    public static long naive(int n) {
        return n < 2 ? n : naive(n - 1) + naive(n - 2);
    }

    /** Top-down DP (memoization). O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static long memo(int n) {
        return memo(n, new HashMap<>());
    }

    private static long memo(int n, Map<Integer, Long> cache) {
        if (n < 2) return n;
        Long hit = cache.get(n);
        if (hit != null) return hit;
        long v = memo(n - 1, cache) + memo(n - 2, cache);
        cache.put(n, v);
        return v;
    }

    /** Bottom-up iterative "normal" solution: keep only the last two. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static long iterative(int n) {
        long a = 0, b = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            long next = a + b;
            a = b;
            b = next;
        }
        return a;
    }

    /** Expert: matrix exponentiation [[1,1],[1,0]]^n. O(log n). */
    public static long matrix(int n) {
        long[][] result = {{1, 0}, {0, 1}}, m = {{1, 1}, {1, 0}};
        for (int p = n; p > 0; p >>= 1) {
            if ((p & 1) == 1) result = mul(result, m);
            m = mul(m, m);
        }
        return result[0][1];
    }

    private static long[][] mul(long[][] x, long[][] y) {
        return new long[][]{
                {x[0][0] * y[0][0] + x[0][1] * y[1][0], x[0][0] * y[0][1] + x[0][1] * y[1][1]},
                {x[1][0] * y[0][0] + x[1][1] * y[1][0], x[1][0] * y[0][1] + x[1][1] * y[1][1]}};
    }

    /** Java 8: first n terms with Stream.iterate over pairs. */
    public static List<Long> series(int count) {
        return Stream.iterate(new long[]{0, 1}, f -> new long[]{f[1], f[0] + f[1]})
                .limit(count).map(f -> f[0]).collect(Collectors.toList());
    }
}

docs.title: Generate parentheses
docs.text: Medium Backtracking Pruning

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: All well-formed strings of n pairs of parentheses. n = 3 → ((())) (()()) (())() ()(()) ()()(). The count is the Catalan number: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42…

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: generate all 2^(2n) strings of ( and ), then keep the valid ones. Most of the work is wasted.
  2. Prune while building. A prefix can still become valid iff:
    • open ≤ n, so you may add ( while open < n;
    • close ≤ open, so you may add ) only while close < open.
  3. With those two rules, every leaf is valid. Nothing gets generated and then thrown away.
  4. Use a StringBuilder with append and delete (choose, explore, un-choose) instead of creating new strings.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** All well-formed strings of n pairs of parentheses, in lexicographic order ('(' < ')'). n=3 → 5 strings (Catalan). */
public final class GenerateParentheses {
    private GenerateParentheses() {}

    /** Brute force: generate all 2^(2n) strings, keep the valid ones. O(2^(2n) · n). */
    public static List<String> bruteForce(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        all(new char[2 * n], 0, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void all(char[] cur, int pos, List<String> out) {
        if (pos == cur.length) {
            if (valid(cur)) out.add(new String(cur));
            return;
        }
        cur[pos] = '(';
        all(cur, pos + 1, out);
        cur[pos] = ')';
        all(cur, pos + 1, out);
    }

    private static boolean valid(char[] s) {
        int bal = 0;
        for (char c : s) if ((bal += c == '(' ? 1 : -1) < 0) return false;
        return bal == 0;
    }

    /**
     * Backtracking with pruning: only add '(' while open < n, only add ')' while close < open.
     * Every leaf is valid — no wasted work. Generates exactly Catalan(n) strings.
     */
    public static List<String> backtracking(int n) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        build(new StringBuilder(), 0, 0, n, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void build(StringBuilder sb, int open, int close, int n, List<String> out) {
        if (sb.length() == 2 * n) {
            out.add(sb.toString());
            return;
        }
        if (open < n) {
            sb.append('(');
            build(sb, open + 1, close, n, out);
            sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1);                // backtrack
        }
        if (close < open) {
            sb.append(')');
            build(sb, open, close + 1, n, out);
            sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Backtracking: O(Catalan(n) · n) ≈ O(4ⁿ / √n). Brute force: O(4ⁿ · n).

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The counts match the Catalan numbers up to n = 8, and the output matches the brute force exactly up to n = 6.

docs.title: Letter combinations of a phone number
docs.text: Medium Backtracking Cartesian product

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Digits 2–9 map to phone keypad letters. Return every letter string the digits could spell. "23" → ad ae af bd be bf cd ce cf.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. It's a Cartesian product: one letter per digit. The recursion depth equals the number of digits.
  2. Recursive: at index i, loop over the letters of digits[i], append, recurse on i+1, then remove the letter.
  3. Iterative: start from [""], and for each digit extend every partial string with each of its letters. That's BFS over the choices.
  4. Empty input means an empty list (not [""]). Clarify this with the interviewer.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Phone keypad: all letter strings a digit string 2–9 could represent. "23" → [ad, ae, af, bd, …, cf]. */
public final class LetterCombinations {
    private LetterCombinations() {}

    private static final String[] KEYS = {"", "", "abc", "def", "ghi", "jkl", "mno", "pqrs", "tuv", "wxyz"};

    /** Recursive: pick a letter for the current digit, recurse on the next digit. O(4^n · n). */
    public static List<String> recursive(String digits) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (digits.isEmpty()) return out;
        go(digits, 0, new StringBuilder(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void go(String d, int i, StringBuilder sb, List<String> out) {
        if (i == d.length()) {
            out.add(sb.toString());
            return;
        }
        for (char c : KEYS[d.charAt(i) - '0'].toCharArray()) {
            sb.append(c);
            go(d, i + 1, sb, out);
            sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1);
        }
    }

    /** Iterative (BFS-like): extend every partial string by every letter of the next digit. */
    public static List<String> iterative(String digits) {
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (digits.isEmpty()) return out;
        out.add("");
        for (char digit : digits.toCharArray()) {
            List<String> next = new ArrayList<>();
            for (String prefix : out) for (char c : KEYS[digit - '0'].toCharArray()) next.add(prefix + c);
            out = next;
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(4ⁿ · n) for n digits (7 and 9 have four letters). That's the output size, so it can't be beaten.

docs.title: N-Queens
docs.text: Expert Backtracking Pruning Bitmask

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Place n queens on an n×n board so that no two share a row, column or diagonal. Return every board, and also the count. n = 4 has 2 solutions, and n = 8 has 92.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: choose n of the n² cells, which is C(n², n). Hopeless.
  2. One queen per row reduces the search to placing a column for each row, n at a time: nⁿ.
  3. One per column too reduces it to permutations: n!.
  4. Prune diagonals immediately: cells on the same \ diagonal share row − col, and cells on the same / diagonal share row + col. Keep three boolean arrays so each safety check is O(1).
  5. Backtrack: place a queen, recurse to the next row, then remove it.
  6. Expert speed-up: store columns and diagonals as bitmasks. free = ~(cols|diag|anti) & mask, and bit = free & −free picks the lowest free cell.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

/** Place n queens on an n×n board so none attack each other. Return all boards ("Q" / "."). */
public final class NQueens {
    private NQueens() {}

    /**
     * Backtracking row by row. Column / diagonal occupancy in boolean arrays gives O(1) safety checks:
     * diagonal id = row - col + n - 1, anti-diagonal id = row + col.
     */
    public static List<List<String>> solve(int n) {
        List<List<String>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        place(0, n, new int[n], new boolean[n], new boolean[2 * n - 1], new boolean[2 * n - 1], out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void place(int row, int n, int[] queenCol, boolean[] cols, boolean[] diag, boolean[] anti,
                              List<List<String>> out) {
        if (row == n) {                                      // all rows filled → record board
            out.add(render(queenCol));
            return;
        }
        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            int d = row - c + n - 1, ad = row + c;
            if (cols[c] || diag[d] || anti[ad]) continue;    // attacked → prune
            queenCol[row] = c;
            cols[c] = diag[d] = anti[ad] = true;
            place(row + 1, n, queenCol, cols, diag, anti, out);
            cols[c] = diag[d] = anti[ad] = false;            // backtrack
        }
    }

    /** Count only, using bitmasks (fastest form). */
    public static int count(int n) {
        return count(n, 0, 0, 0, 0);
    }

    private static int count(int n, int row, int cols, int diag, int anti) {
        if (row == n) return 1;
        int total = 0;
        int free = ~(cols | diag | anti) & ((1 << n) - 1);  // bits where a queen may go
        while (free != 0) {
            int bit = free & -free;                          // lowest free position
            free -= bit;
            total += count(n, row + 1, cols | bit, (diag | bit) << 1, (anti | bit) >> 1);
        }
        return total;
    }

    private static List<String> render(int[] queenCol) {
        List<String> board = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int c : queenCol) {
            char[] row = new char[queenCol.length];
            Arrays.fill(row, '.');
            row[c] = 'Q';
            board.add(new String(row));
        }
        return board;
    }
}
