docs.title: Permutations II (with duplicates)
docs.text: Hard Backtracking Pruning

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: All distinct permutations of an array that may contain duplicates. [1,1,2] → [1,1,2] [1,2,1] [2,1,1].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Generate everything and dedupe with a Set: correct, but [5,5,5,5,5,5] builds 720 lists to keep 1.
  2. Insight: duplicates appear because two equal values can swap roles. Force equal values to always be used in their original (sorted) order, and each arrangement is produced exactly once.
  3. Rule: after sorting, skip a[i] if a[i] == a[i−1] and a[i−1] is not currently used. That means its twin on the left must be placed first.
  4. A used[] array tracks which indexes are on the current path (choose, explore, un-choose).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

/** All DISTINCT permutations of an int array that may contain duplicates, in lexicographic order. [1,1,2] → 3. */
public final class PermutationsII {
    private PermutationsII() {}

    /** Generate all n! then dedupe with a set (wasteful: [1,1,1,1,1,1] builds 720 lists for 1 answer). */
    public static List<List<Integer>> withSet(int[] nums) {
        int[] a = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a);
        Set<List<Integer>> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        all(a, new boolean[a.length], new ArrayList<>(), seen);
        return new ArrayList<>(seen);
    }

    private static void all(int[] a, boolean[] used, List<Integer> cur, Set<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (cur.size() == a.length) {
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur));
            return;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (used[i]) continue;
            used[i] = true;
            cur.add(a[i]);
            all(a, used, cur, out);
            cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
            used[i] = false;
        }
    }

    /**
     * Pruned backtracking: sort, and at each position skip a value equal to its left neighbour unless that neighbour
     * is currently in use. Equal values are then always placed in their original order → each distinct permutation once.
     */
    public static List<List<Integer>> pruned(int[] nums) {
        int[] a = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a);
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        prune(a, new boolean[a.length], new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void prune(int[] a, boolean[] used, List<Integer> cur, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (cur.size() == a.length) {
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(cur));
            return;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (used[i]) continue;
            if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;   // the twin to the left must go first
            used[i] = true;
            cur.add(a[i]);
            prune(a, used, cur, out);
            cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
            used[i] = false;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n! · n) in the worst case (all distinct), but proportional to the number of distinct permutations when there are duplicates.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: The iterative next permutation also skips duplicates naturally, and is used by string permutations.

docs.text: Compared with the set-based version on 200 random arrays over a 3-value alphabet (lots of duplicates).

docs.title: Power: fast exponentiation
docs.text: Medium Divide & conquer Bit manipulation

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Compute xⁿ, where n can be negative (LeetCode 50). Also compute aᵇ mod m.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Naive: x · x^(n−1). That's O(n), and n = 2³¹ overflows the stack.
  2. Halving insight: xⁿ = (x^(n/2))², multiplied by x again if n is odd. That's O(log n).
  3. Compute half once. Calling pow(x, n/2) * pow(x, n/2) makes the cost O(n) again.
  4. Negative n: use x = 1/x and n = −n. Store n in a long, because −Integer.MIN_VALUE overflows an int.
  5. Iterative: walk the bits of n. Square x at every step, and multiply it into the result when the current bit is 1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

/** x^n for int n (may be negative). Shows linear vs logarithmic recursion ("fast exponentiation"). */
public final class Power {
    private Power() {}

    /** Naive recursion: x^n = x · x^(n-1). O(n) — stack overflow for large n. */
    public static double naive(double x, int n) {
        if (n < 0) return 1 / naive(x, -n);
        return n == 0 ? 1 : x * naive(x, n - 1);
    }

    /** Fast recursive: x^n = (x^(n/2))², times x if n odd. O(log n). */
    public static double fastRecursive(double x, int n) {
        long N = n;                                          // -Integer.MIN_VALUE overflows int → use long
        if (N < 0) {
            x = 1 / x;
            N = -N;
        }
        return fast(x, N);
    }

    private static double fast(double x, long n) {
        if (n == 0) return 1;
        double half = fast(x, n / 2);                        // compute ONCE, don't call twice
        return n % 2 == 0 ? half * half : half * half * x;
    }

    /** Fast iterative (binary exponentiation): walk bits of n. O(log n), O(1). */
    public static double fastIterative(double x, int n) {
        long N = n;
        if (N < 0) {
            x = 1 / x;
            N = -N;
        }
        double result = 1;
        while (N > 0) {
            if ((N & 1) == 1) result *= x;
            x *= x;
            N >>= 1;
        }
        return result;
    }

    /** Modular exponentiation (a^b mod m) — used in hashing / cryptography problems. */
    public static long modPow(long a, long b, long m) {
        long r = 1;
        a %= m;
        while (b > 0) {
            if ((b & 1) == 1) r = r * a % m;
            a = a * a % m;
            b >>= 1;
        }
        return r;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Naive O(n). Fast exponentiation O(log n), using O(log n) stack recursively or O(1) iteratively.

docs.title: Subsets / power set
docs.text: Hard Backtracking Bitmask

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return all 2ⁿ subsets of distinct integers. [1,2,3] → [], [1], [2], [3], [1,2], [1,3], [2,3], [1,2,3].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Each element is either in or out. That's a binary decision tree with depth n and 2ⁿ leaves.
  2. Pick/skip recursion: at index i, recurse without a[i], then with a[i], then backtrack.
  3. Start-index backtracking: every node is an answer. Loop i from start. This is the template for combinations.
  4. Iterative cascade: start with [[]]. For each x, copy every existing subset and add x to the copy.
  5. Bitmask: the numbers 0..2ⁿ−1 are the subsets. Bit j means "include a[j]".

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** All 2^n subsets (power set) of distinct ints. */
public final class Subsets {
    private Subsets() {}

    /** Recursive "pick / don't pick" — the binary recursion tree. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> pickOrSkip(int[] a) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        pick(a, 0, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void pick(int[] a, int i, List<Integer> current, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (i == a.length) {                                 // leaf: one decision made per element
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(current));
            return;
        }
        pick(a, i + 1, current, out);                        // skip a[i]
        current.add(a[i]);
        pick(a, i + 1, current, out);                        // pick a[i]
        current.remove(current.size() - 1);                  // backtrack
    }

    /** Backtracking with start index (every node is an answer) — the template reused for combinations. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> backtracking(int[] a) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        bt(a, 0, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void bt(int[] a, int start, List<Integer> current, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        out.add(new ArrayList<>(current));
        for (int i = start; i < a.length; i++) {
            current.add(a[i]);
            bt(a, i + 1, current, out);
            current.remove(current.size() - 1);
        }
    }

    /** Iterative cascading: start with [[]], for each x add x to every existing subset. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> iterative(int[] a) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        out.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int x : a) {
            int size = out.size();
            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
                List<Integer> copy = new ArrayList<>(out.get(i));
                copy.add(x);
                out.add(copy);
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Bitmask: number mask in [0, 2^n) — bit j set means include a[j]. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> bitmask(int[] a) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << a.length); mask++) {
            List<Integer> s = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) if ((mask & (1 << j)) != 0) s.add(a[j]);
            out.add(s);
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n · 2ⁿ) time, which is the output size. O(n) recursion depth.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text: Subsets II (with duplicates: sort, then skip a[i] == a[i−1] when i > start) · Combination sum · Subsets with a given sum · K-combinations.

docs.title: Sudoku solver
docs.text: Expert Backtracking Bitmasks Heuristics

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Fill a 9×9 Sudoku in place so that every row, column and 3×3 box contains 1–9 exactly once. Return false if that's impossible.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Plain backtracking: find an empty cell, try digits 1–9 that don't conflict, recurse, and undo on failure. Correct, but the conflict check scans 27 cells for every try.
  2. O(1) checks with bitmasks: keep rows[r], cols[c] and boxes[b] as 9-bit masks of the digits used. The candidates for a cell are ~(rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[b]) & 0x1FF. Placing or removing a digit is a single OR or AND.
  3. Most-constrained cell first (the MRV heuristic): always fill the empty cell with the fewest candidates. A cell with 0 candidates means a dead end, so backtrack immediately. A cell with 1 candidate is forced. This collapses the search tree from billions of nodes to thousands.
  4. Iterate over the candidates with free & −free (the lowest set bit), the same trick as in N-Queens and bit basics.
  5. Validate the givens up front: a puzzle that already breaks a rule has no solution.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

/**
 * Solve a 9×9 Sudoku in place ('.' = empty). Returns false if the puzzle has no solution.
 * Backtracking with O(1) validity checks (bitmasks per row/column/box) and the "most constrained cell first" heuristic.
 */
public final class SudokuSolver {
    private SudokuSolver() {}

    public static boolean solve(char[][] board) {
        int[] rows = new int[9], cols = new int[9], boxes = new int[9];   // bit d set = digit d+1 already used
        for (int r = 0; r < 9; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < 9; c++) {
                if (board[r][c] == '.') continue;
                int bit = 1 << (board[r][c] - '1'), b = box(r, c);
                if ((rows[r] & bit) != 0 || (cols[c] & bit) != 0 || (boxes[b] & bit) != 0) return false;   // invalid givens
                rows[r] |= bit;
                cols[c] |= bit;
                boxes[b] |= bit;
            }
        return backtrack(board, rows, cols, boxes);
    }

    private static boolean backtrack(char[][] board, int[] rows, int[] cols, int[] boxes) {
        int bestR = -1, bestC = -1, bestOptions = 10, bestMask = 0;
        for (int r = 0; r < 9; r++)                          // pick the empty cell with the FEWEST candidates
            for (int c = 0; c < 9; c++) {
                if (board[r][c] != '.') continue;
                int free = ~(rows[r] | cols[c] | boxes[box(r, c)]) & 0x1FF;
                int options = Integer.bitCount(free);
                if (options < bestOptions) {
                    bestR = r;
                    bestC = c;
                    bestOptions = options;
                    bestMask = free;
                    if (options == 0) return false;          // dead end: prune immediately
                }
            }
        if (bestR == -1) return true;                        // no empty cell left: solved
        int b = box(bestR, bestC);
        for (int free = bestMask; free != 0; free &= free - 1) {
            int bit = free & -free;
            board[bestR][bestC] = (char) ('1' + Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(bit));
            rows[bestR] |= bit;
            cols[bestC] |= bit;
            boxes[b] |= bit;
            if (backtrack(board, rows, cols, boxes)) return true;
            rows[bestR] &= ~bit;                             // undo
            cols[bestC] &= ~bit;
            boxes[b] &= ~bit;
        }
        board[bestR][bestC] = '.';
        return false;
    }

    private static int box(int r, int c) {
        return (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3;
    }

    /** Is a completely filled board a valid Sudoku? (used by tests) */
    public static boolean isValidSolution(char[][] board) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
            int row = 0, col = 0, bx = 0;
            for (int j = 0; j < 9; j++) {
                row |= 1 << (board[i][j] - '1');
                col |= 1 << (board[j][i] - '1');
                bx |= 1 << (board[(i / 3) * 3 + j / 3][(i % 3) * 3 + j % 3] - '1');
            }
            if (row != 0x1FF || col != 0x1FF || bx != 0x1FF) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Exponential in the worst case (Sudoku generalised to n×n is NP-complete). With bitmasks and MRV, real 9×9 puzzles take milliseconds, including Arto Inkala's "world's hardest Sudoku", which is in the tests.

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: It combines three ideas: backtracking, bitmask state, and a search-order heuristic. The same structure (constraint propagation plus MRV) powers real constraint solvers.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The solved grids are validated in full (every row, column and box), and the tests confirm the givens are unchanged. An invalid starting grid must return false.

docs.title: Sum of digits & digital root
docs.text: Easy Linear recursion Math

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Sum the digits of n (12345 → 15). The digital root repeats this until a single digit remains (12345 → 15 → 6).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Base case: n == 0 gives 0.
  2. Recursive case: n % 10 + sum(n / 10).
  3. Digital root: recurse on the sum until it's < 10.
  4. O(1) insight: n ≡ digitSum(n) (mod 9), so root = 1 + (n − 1) % 9 for n > 0.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

/** Sum of digits of a non-negative number, and digital root (repeat until one digit). */
public final class SumOfDigits {
    private SumOfDigits() {}

    /** Recursive: last digit + sum of the rest. Base: n == 0. O(d). */
    public static int recursive(long n) {
        return n == 0 ? 0 : (int) (n % 10) + recursive(n / 10);
    }

    /** Iterative. */
    public static int iterative(long n) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (; n > 0; n /= 10) sum += (int) (n % 10);
        return sum;
    }

    /** Java 8. */
    public static int streams(long n) {
        return String.valueOf(n).chars().map(c -> c - '0').sum();
    }

    /** Digital root, recursive: keep summing until one digit. */
    public static int digitalRoot(long n) {
        return n < 10 ? (int) n : digitalRoot(iterative(n));
    }

    /** Digital root in O(1): 1 + (n-1) % 9 (the "casting out nines" rule). */
    public static int digitalRootFormula(long n) {
        return n == 0 ? 0 : (int) (1 + (n - 1) % 9);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(d) for the digit sum and O(1) for the digital-root formula.

docs.title: Tower of Hanoi
docs.text: Medium Tree recursion Bit tricks

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Move n disks from peg A to peg C using B as a helper. Move one disk at a time, and never put a larger disk on a smaller one. List the moves.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Trust the recursion: assume you can move n−1 disks.
  2. To move n disks from A to C:
    1. Move n−1 disks from A to B, using C as the helper.
    2. Move disk n from A to C.
    3. Move n−1 disks from B to C, using A as the helper.
  3. Base case: n = 0, so do nothing.
  4. T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1, which solves to 2ⁿ − 1 moves. That is provably the minimum.

docs.title: n = 3 (7 moves)
docs.text: 1: A→C  2: A→B  1: C→B  3: A→C  1: B→A  2: B→C  1: A→C

docs.title: Iterative (normal) solution
docs.text: Move number m (1-based) moves disk trailingZeros(m) + 1, from peg (m & (m−1)) % 3 to peg ((m | (m−1)) + 1) % 3. The peg labels are A,B,C when n is odd and A,C,B when n is even.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Move n disks from A to C using B. Returns the moves as "disk k: X->Y". Always 2^n − 1 moves. */
public final class TowerOfHanoi {
    private TowerOfHanoi() {}

    /**
     * Recursive: (1) move n-1 from source to helper, (2) move disk n to target, (3) move n-1 helper → target.
     * T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 → 2^n − 1.
     */
    public static List<String> recursive(int n) {
        List<String> moves = new ArrayList<>();
        solve(n, 'A', 'C', 'B', moves);
        return moves;
    }

    private static void solve(int n, char from, char to, char via, List<String> moves) {
        if (n == 0) return;                                  // base case: nothing to move
        solve(n - 1, from, via, to, moves);
        moves.add("disk " + n + ": " + from + "->" + to);
        solve(n - 1, via, to, from, moves);
    }

    /**
     * Iterative: move number m (1-based) moves disk = trailing zeros of m + 1,
     * from peg (m & m-1) % 3 to peg ((m | m-1) + 1) % 3. Peg order (A,B,C) for odd n, (A,C,B) for even n.
     */
    public static List<String> iterative(int n) {
        List<String> moves = new ArrayList<>();
        char[] pegs = n % 2 == 1 ? new char[]{'A', 'B', 'C'} : new char[]{'A', 'C', 'B'};
        for (int m = 1; m < (1 << n); m++) {
            int disk = Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(m) + 1;
            int from = (m & (m - 1)) % 3, to = ((m | (m - 1)) + 1) % 3;
            moves.add("disk " + disk + ": " + pegs[from] + "->" + pegs[to]);
        }
        return moves;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(2ⁿ) time, which is the size of the output. Recursion depth is O(n).

docs.title: Word search
docs.text: Hard Grid backtracking

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Does a word exist in a letter grid as a path of up/down/left/right neighbours, with each cell used at most once? 

A B C E
S F C S      "ABCCED" ✅   "SEE" ✅   "ABCB" ❌ (would reuse B)
A D E E

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Try every cell as the start.
  2. From a cell matching word[k], look for word[k+1] in the four neighbours. That's DFS.
  3. "Each cell once" means marking cells on the current path. Temporarily overwrite the cell with '#', and restore it when backtracking, even on success, so the caller's grid is left intact.
  4. Prunes: the grid has fewer cells than the word is long → false. A mismatched character stops immediately. (Another common trick: if the last letter is rarer than the first, search the reversed word.)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.recursion;

/** Does `word` exist in the grid as a path of adjacent (4-dir) cells, each used at most once? (LeetCode 79) */
public final class WordSearch {
    private WordSearch() {}

    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

    /**
     * Backtracking from every cell: match word[k] here, mark the cell, try the 4 neighbours for word[k+1],
     * unmark on the way back. The grid is restored before returning. O(R·C·3^L) — after the first step there are
     * only 3 directions (we can't go back).
     */
    public static boolean exists(char[][] board, String word) {
        if (word.isEmpty()) return true;
        if ((long) board.length * board[0].length < word.length()) return false;   // cheap prune
        for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
                if (dfs(board, word, 0, r, c)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    private static boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int k, int r, int c) {
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length || b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;
        if (k == w.length() - 1) return true;
        char saved = b[r][c];
        b[r][c] = '#';                                       // visited on the current path
        boolean found = false;
        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
            if (dfs(b, w, k + 1, r + d[0], c + d[1])) {
                found = true;
                break;
            }
        }
        b[r][c] = saved;                                     // un-choose, even on success: leave the grid intact
        return found;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(R·C · 3^L): there are 4 directions at the first step and 3 after that, since you can't step back. O(L) recursion depth.

docs.title: Next level

docs.title: Question banks (Easy → Expert)
docs.text:
Bank Questions Level Numbers & lists 17 Easy → Medium Strings 15 Easy → Medium Employee dataset 17 Medium → Hard Optional deep-dive 8 Medium Custom collectors & teeing 6 Hard Parallel stream pitfalls 4 Expert

Pitfalls interviewers probe

  • Streams are single-use. Reusing one throws IllegalStateException.
  • toMap throws on duplicate keys unless you pass a merge function.
  • parallelStream() is not free. It uses the common ForkJoinPool, which hurts small inputs and anything with ordered or stateful lambdas.
  • Side effects inside map/filter (like the Set.add trick for duplicates) are acceptable only in sequential streams.
  • Stream.toList() (Java 16+) returns an unmodifiable list. Collectors.toList() makes no guarantee.

docs.title: Custom collectors & teeing
docs.text: Hard Collector.of teeing collectingAndThen

docs.title: How collect() actually works
docs.text:
A Collector<T, A, R> is four functions:

Function Role toList() equivalent supplier () → A create an empty mutable container ArrayList::new accumulator (A, T) → void fold one element in List::add combiner (A, A) → A merge two partial containers (parallel streams) addAll finisher A → R final transformation identity, or unmodifiableList

In a parallel stream, each chunk gets its own container from the supplier, which is why collect is thread-safe while forEach(list::add) isn't. See parallel pitfalls.

docs.title: Questions in this bank
docs.text: Q Collector Idea 1 toUnmodifiableList() the four functions, with an explicit finisher 2 averaging() a custom accumulation type (sum, count) and a combiner for parallel use 3 joiningLimited(2) → "a, b and 3 more" collectingAndThen(toList(), …) 4 min and max in one pass Collectors.teeing (Java 12) 5 sorted frequency map groupingBy(f, TreeMap::new, counting()) 6 chunked(n) → batches a stateful, order-dependent collector whose combiner refuses parallel use

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.java8;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collector;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/**
 * Writing your own Collector with Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher), plus teeing (Java 12)
 * and collectingAndThen. Knowing the 4 functions shows you understand how collect() really works.
 */
public final class CustomCollectors {
    private CustomCollectors() {}

    /** An unmodifiable list collector: accumulate into ArrayList, finish by wrapping. */
    public static <T> Collector<T, ?, List<T>> toUnmodifiableList() {
        return Collector.<T, List<T>, List<T>>of(          // explicit types: inference can't see T through ArrayList::new
                ArrayList::new,                              // supplier: a new mutable container per thread/segment
                List::add,                                   // accumulator: fold one element in
                (left, right) -> {                           // combiner: merge two partial containers (parallel)
                    left.addAll(right);
                    return left;
                },
                Collections::unmodifiableList);              // finisher: final transformation
    }

    /** Mutable result container for the average collector. */
    private static final class Avg {
        long sum, count;
    }

    /** Average of ints as a Collector — shows a custom accumulation type. Empty → 0.0. */
    public static Collector<Integer, ?, Double> averaging() {
        return Collector.of(Avg::new,
                (a, x) -> {
                    a.sum += x;
                    a.count++;
                },
                (a, b) -> {
                    a.sum += b.sum;
                    a.count += b.count;
                    return a;
                },
                a -> a.count == 0 ? 0.0 : (double) a.sum / a.count);
    }

    /** Joining with a custom separator and a LIMIT ("a, b, c and 2 more"). */
    public static Collector<String, ?, String> joiningLimited(int limit) {
        return Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.toList(), all -> {
            String head = String.join(", ", all.subList(0, Math.min(limit, all.size())));
            return all.size() > limit ? head + " and " + (all.size() - limit) + " more" : head;
        });
    }

    /** Collectors.teeing: two collectors over ONE pass, merged. Here: {min, max} of a list. */
    public static int[] minAndMax(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().collect(Collectors.teeing(
                Collectors.minBy(Integer::compare),
                Collectors.maxBy(Integer::compare),
                (min, max) -> new int[]{min.orElseThrow(), max.orElseThrow()}));
    }

    /** Frequency map sorted by key — groupingBy with a map factory and a downstream collector. */
    public static Map<Character, Long> sortedFrequency(String s) {
        return s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Partition into chunks of size n (e.g. batching DB writes) — a stateful custom collector. */
    public static <T> Collector<T, ?, List<List<T>>> chunked(int n) {
        if (n <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("n must be > 0");
        return Collector.of(
                () -> new ArrayList<List<T>>(),
                (chunks, x) -> {
                    if (chunks.isEmpty() || chunks.get(chunks.size() - 1).size() == n) chunks.add(new ArrayList<>());
                    chunks.get(chunks.size() - 1).add(x);
                },
                (a, b) -> {
                    throw new UnsupportedOperationException("chunking is order-dependent: sequential streams only");
                });
    }
}

docs.text: The toUnmodifiableList and averaging collectors are also run on parallel streams of 10,000 elements, which proves the combiners are correct and that encounter order is preserved.

docs.title: Employee dataset round
docs.text:
Medium → Hard groupingBy Comparator chains collectingAndThen

This is the most common Java 8 live-coding round. You get a list of employees and a series of questions.

package com.playbook.java8;

/** Sample domain used by {@link EmployeeStreamProblems}. Salary in whole rupees. */
public record Employee(int id, String name, int age, String gender, String department, int joinYear, long salary) {}
Q Question Key API Sample answer 1 Count by gender groupingBy(gender, counting()) {F=4, M=3} 2 Distinct departments map → distinct → sorted [Engineering, HR, Sales] 3 Average age by gender averagingInt F=33.25 4 Highest-paid employee max(comparingLong(salary)) Vikram 5 Highest paid per department groupingBy + collectingAndThen(maxBy, …) {Engineering=Vikram, HR=Meera, Sales=Karan} 6 Joined after 2015 filter → map → sorted [Neha, Priya, Ravi] 7 Count per department groupingBy(dept, counting()) 8 Average salary per department averagingLong 9 Youngest female filter → min Neha 10 Most experienced min(comparingInt(joinYear)) Vikram 11 Salary statistics summarizingDouble 12 Partition by age > 30 partitioningBy + mapping 13 Nth highest salary distinct → sorted(reverse) → skip(n−1) 3rd = 1,800,000 14 Sort by dept, salary desc, name comparing().thenComparing(…, reverseOrder()) 15 id → name map toMap(k, v, merge, TreeMap::new) 16 Department with the highest payroll summingLong, then max(comparingByValue()) Engineering 17 Names per department, comma-separated mapping(name, joining(", ")) HR=Meera, Priya

docs.title: Thinking process for "X per Y" questions
docs.text:
1. "per Y" means groupingBy(Y).
  2. "count / sum / average / max of X" is the downstream collector: counting(), summingLong, averagingX, maxBy.
  3. "only the name" means wrap it: collectingAndThen(maxBy(...), opt -> opt.map(Employee::name).orElseThrow()), or use mapping(Employee::name, …).
  4. "sorted output" means passing TreeMap::new as the map factory.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.java8;

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.DoubleSummaryStatistics;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** The classic "Employee dataset" Java 8 interview round (Medium → Hard). */
public final class EmployeeStreamProblems {
    private EmployeeStreamProblems() {}

    public static List<Employee> sample() {
        return List.of(
                new Employee(1, "Asha", 32, "F", "Engineering", 2015, 2_500_000),
                new Employee(2, "Ravi", 28, "M", "Engineering", 2019, 1_800_000),
                new Employee(3, "Meera", 45, "F", "HR", 2010, 1_500_000),
                new Employee(4, "Karan", 38, "M", "Sales", 2012, 1_200_000),
                new Employee(5, "Neha", 26, "F", "Sales", 2021, 900_000),
                new Employee(6, "Vikram", 50, "M", "Engineering", 2008, 3_500_000),
                new Employee(7, "Priya", 30, "F", "HR", 2018, 1_100_000));
    }

    /** Q1. Count by gender. */
    public static Map<String, Long> countByGender(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::gender, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Q2. Distinct department names (sorted). */
    public static List<String> departments(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().map(Employee::department).distinct().sorted().toList();
    }

    /** Q3. Average age by gender. */
    public static Map<String, Double> averageAgeByGender(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::gender, TreeMap::new, Collectors.averagingInt(Employee::age)));
    }

    /** Q4. Highest paid employee overall. */
    public static Optional<Employee> highestPaid(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().max(Comparator.comparingLong(Employee::salary));
    }

    /** Q5. Highest paid employee NAME per department. */
    public static Map<String, String> highestPaidPerDepartment(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department, TreeMap::new,
                Collectors.collectingAndThen(Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingLong(Employee::salary)),
                        e -> e.map(Employee::name).orElseThrow())));
    }

    /** Q6. Names of employees who joined after a year, sorted by name. */
    public static List<String> joinedAfter(List<Employee> es, int year) {
        return es.stream().filter(e -> e.joinYear() > year).map(Employee::name).sorted().toList();
    }

    /** Q7. Employee count per department. */
    public static Map<String, Long> countPerDepartment(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Q8. Average salary per department. */
    public static Map<String, Double> averageSalaryPerDepartment(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department, TreeMap::new, Collectors.averagingLong(Employee::salary)));
    }

    /** Q9. Youngest female employee. */
    public static Optional<Employee> youngestFemale(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().filter(e -> e.gender().equals("F")).min(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::age));
    }

    /** Q10. Most experienced (earliest join year). */
    public static Optional<Employee> mostExperienced(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().min(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::joinYear));
    }

    /** Q11. Salary statistics (count, min, max, avg, sum) in one pass. */
    public static DoubleSummaryStatistics salaryStats(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.summarizingDouble(Employee::salary));
    }

    /** Q12. Partition: age > 30 vs ≤ 30 (names). */
    public static Map<Boolean, List<String>> partitionByAge(List<Employee> es, int age) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(e -> e.age() > age,
                Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.toList())));
    }

    /** Q13. Nth highest salary (distinct). */
    public static Optional<Long> nthHighestSalary(List<Employee> es, int n) {
        return es.stream().map(Employee::salary).distinct().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(n - 1L).findFirst();
    }

    /** Q14. Sort by department, then salary descending, then name. */
    public static List<String> sortedByDeptSalaryName(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::department)
                        .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
                        .thenComparing(Employee::name))
                .map(Employee::name).toList();
    }

    /** Q15. id → name map (throws on duplicate key; provide a merge function if duplicates are possible). */
    public static Map<Integer, String> idToName(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Employee::id, Employee::name, (a, b) -> a, TreeMap::new));
    }

    /** Q16. Total salary per department, department with the highest total. */
    public static Optional<String> departmentWithHighestPayroll(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department, Collectors.summingLong(Employee::salary)))
                .entrySet().stream().max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).map(Map.Entry::getKey);
    }

    /** Q17. Comma-separated names per department. */
    public static Map<String, String> namesPerDepartment(List<Employee> es) {
        return es.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::department, TreeMap::new,
                Collectors.mapping(Employee::name, Collectors.joining(", "))));
    }
}

docs.title: Optional deep-dive
docs.text:
Medium Optional Null safety

Optional<T> is a return type that says "there may be no value", and forces the caller to deal with that.

Q Question Key API 1 Wrap a possibly-null lookup Optional.ofNullable(map.get(k)). Optional.of(null) throws NPE 2 Chain transformations safely map → filter → map, where any empty step short-circuits 3 The mapper itself returns an Optional flatMap, to avoid Optional<Optional<T>> 4 orElse vs orElseGet orElse always evaluates its argument, orElseGet is lazy 5 Fail with a meaningful error orElseThrow(() -> new …) instead of get() 6 Keep only present values from List<Optional<T>> flatMap(Optional::stream) (Java 9) 7 Fall back to another source lazily or(() -> otherOptional) (Java 9) 8 Handle both outcomes without isPresent() / get() ifPresentOrElse (Java 9)

docs.title: The orElse trap, demonstrated
docs.text:
present.orElse(expensiveCall());      // expensiveCall() RUNS even though a value is present
present.orElseGet(this::expensiveCall);  // runs only when empty
The tests count the calls: orElse → 1, orElseGet → 0.

Optional anti-patterns interviewers look for

  • opt.isPresent() ? opt.get() : x: that's just orElse(x).
  • Optional as a field or method parameter: it's not serializable, it adds overhead, and it was designed for return types.
  • Optional<List<T>>: return an empty list instead.
  • Optional.get() without a check is an NPE under a different name. Prefer orElseThrow().

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.java8;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.function.Supplier;

/** Optional interview questions: creation, transformation, defaults, and the anti-patterns to avoid. */
public final class OptionalProblems {
    private OptionalProblems() {}

    /** Q1. Wrap a possibly-null lookup (Map.get returns null for missing keys). */
    public static Optional<String> lookup(Map<String, String> m, String key) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(m.get(key));              // Optional.of(null) would throw NPE
    }

    /** Q2. Chain transformations; any empty step short-circuits. Length of a trimmed, non-blank city name. */
    public static Optional<Integer> cityNameLength(Map<String, String> userCity, String user) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(userCity.get(user))
                .map(String::trim)
                .filter(s -> !s.isEmpty())
                .map(String::length);
    }

    /** Q3. flatMap when the mapping function itself returns Optional (avoids Optional<Optional<T>>). */
    public static Optional<String> managerCity(Map<String, String> managerOf, Map<String, String> cityOf, String emp) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(managerOf.get(emp)).flatMap(m -> Optional.ofNullable(cityOf.get(m)));
    }

    /**
     * Q4. orElse vs orElseGet: orElse ALWAYS evaluates its argument (even when a value is present);
     * orElseGet only calls the supplier when empty. Returns how many times the expensive default ran.
     */
    public static int[] orElseVsOrElseGet(Optional<String> present, Supplier<String> expensive) {
        int[] calls = {0};
        Supplier<String> counted = () -> {
            calls[0]++;
            return expensive.get();
        };
        present.orElse(counted.get());                       // evaluated eagerly → counts 1 even though unused
        int afterOrElse = calls[0];
        present.orElseGet(counted);                          // lazy → not called when present
        return new int[]{afterOrElse, calls[0] - afterOrElse};
    }

    /** Q5. orElseThrow with a meaningful exception instead of get(). */
    public static String requireUser(Map<String, String> users, String id) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(users.get(id)).orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("no user " + id));
    }

    /** Q6. Optional.stream() (Java 9) — keep only present values from a list of Optionals. */
    public static List<String> presentValues(List<Optional<String>> list) {
        return list.stream().flatMap(Optional::stream).toList();
    }

    /** Q7. or() (Java 9): try a fallback Optional source lazily. */
    public static Optional<String> fromCacheOrDb(Map<String, String> cache, Map<String, String> db, String key) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(cache.get(key)).or(() -> Optional.ofNullable(db.get(key)));
    }

    /** Q8. ifPresentOrElse (Java 9): act on both outcomes without isPresent()/get(). */
    public static String describe(Optional<Integer> age) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        age.ifPresentOrElse(a -> sb.append("age ").append(a), () -> sb.append("unknown"));
        return sb.toString();
    }
}

docs.title: Parallel stream pitfalls
docs.text:
Expert parallelStream Thread safety reduce

parallelStream() splits the work across the common ForkJoinPool. It's one keyword away, and easy to get wrong. Each pitfall below has a wrong and a right method in the code.

docs.title: 1. Side effects into shared, non-thread-safe state
docs.text:
List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, n).parallel().forEach(out::add);   // ❌ race: lost elements or ArrayIndexOutOfBounds
List<Integer> out = IntStream.range(0, n).parallel().boxed().toList();   // ✅ let the stream collect

docs.title: 2. reduce with a non-neutral identity
docs.text: reduce(10, Integer::sum) adds 10 once per chunk in parallel, so the result depends on how the work was split. The identity must satisfy identity op x == x: 0 for +, 1 for ×, and the empty string for concatenation. Add constants outside the reduce.

docs.title: 3. reduce with a non-associative operation
docs.text: Subtraction: (a − b) − c ≠ a − (b − c). Parallel chunks combine in a different grouping, which gives a different answer. Only use associative operations (+, ×, min, max, string concatenation with a neutral identity).

docs.title: 4. Ordering
docs.text: forEach on a parallel stream runs in any order. forEachOrdered restores encounter order, but serialises the hand-off, so much of the parallel benefit is gone.

docs.title: When parallel streams do pay off
docs.text:
1. Large n (roughly 10⁴–10⁵ or more elements) with CPU-heavy per-element work.
  2. A splittable source: ArrayList, arrays and IntStream.range split well. LinkedList and Stream.iterate split badly.
  3. Stateless, non-blocking lambdas. I/O inside a parallel stream blocks the shared common pool for the whole JVM.
  4. Measure with JMH. Never assume.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.java8;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/**
 * Parallel streams: what goes wrong and the correct alternative. Each pitfall has a WRONG and a RIGHT method so the
 * difference can be demonstrated and tested.
 */
public final class ParallelStreamPitfalls {
    private ParallelStreamPitfalls() {}

    /** WRONG: side effects into a non-thread-safe ArrayList from a parallel stream → lost elements or exceptions. */
    public static int unsafeSideEffectSize(int n) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        try {
            IntStream.range(0, n).parallel().forEach(out::add);   // data race on ArrayList's size/elementData
        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException racedResize) {
            return -1;                                        // the race can also corrupt the array during a resize
        }
        return out.size();                                    // often < n
    }

    /** RIGHT: let the stream build the result — collect() gives each thread its own container and merges them. */
    public static List<Integer> safeCollect(int n) {
        return IntStream.range(0, n).parallel().boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());   // also keeps encounter order
    }

    /**
     * WRONG: reduce with an identity that is not neutral. reduce(10, Integer::sum) adds 10 ONCE sequentially but once
     * PER CHUNK in parallel → the answer depends on how the work was split.
     */
    public static int nonNeutralIdentity(List<Integer> list, boolean parallel) {
        return (parallel ? list.parallelStream() : list.stream()).reduce(10, Integer::sum);
    }

    /** RIGHT: neutral identity (0 for +), then add the constant once outside. */
    public static int neutralIdentity(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.parallelStream().reduce(0, Integer::sum) + 10;
    }

    /** WRONG: non-associative operation (subtraction) — sequential and parallel results differ. */
    public static int nonAssociative(List<Integer> list, boolean parallel) {
        return (parallel ? list.parallelStream() : list.stream()).reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b);
    }

    /** forEach on a parallel stream has NO order guarantee; forEachOrdered restores encounter order (at a cost). */
    public static List<Integer> forEachOrdered(int n) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        IntStream.range(0, n).parallel().forEachOrdered(out::add);   // sequential hand-off: safe for an ArrayList
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The "right" methods are asserted exactly. The racy method is asserted only loosely (it may lose elements or throw), because a test can't depend on a data race. The non-neutral-identity result is asserted to be ≥ the sequential one and to differ from it by a multiple of 10, which holds for any number of threads.

docs.title: Streams on numbers & lists
docs.text:
Easy → Medium filter/map/reduce Collectors

Sample input used in the tests: [10, 15, 8, 49, 25, 98, 98, 32, 15, 1]

Q Question Answer for the sample Key API 1 Even numbers [10, 8, 98, 98, 32] filter 2 Numbers starting with 1 [10, 15, 15, 1] map(String::valueOf) + startsWith 3 Duplicate elements [98, 15] filter(n -> !seen.add(n)) 4 First element 10 findFirst 5 Max 98 max(Integer::compare) 6 Sort descending [98, 98, 49, …] sorted(reverseOrder()) 7 Second highest distinct 49 distinct().sorted(reverse).skip(1) 8 Sum / average 351 / 35.1 reduce, mapToInt().average() 9 Average of squares > 100 mapToInt(n*n).filter(>100).average() 10 Frequency of each {98=2, 15=2, …} groupingBy(identity(), counting()) 11 Partition even/odd partitioningBy 12 Flatten list of lists flatMap(List::stream) 13 Merge two arrays, sorted & distinct IntStream.concat 14 All positive? true allMatch 15 Top 3 [98, 98, 49] sorted(reverse).limit(3) 16 Sum of digits chars().map(getNumericValue).sum() 17 Join as "[a, b]" joining(", ", "[", "]")

docs.title: How to think about any stream question
docs.text:
1. What is the source? A list.stream(), Arrays.stream(int[]) (primitive), or s.chars().
  2. Which elements? filter.
  3. What shape? map / mapToInt / flatMap.
  4. What order or uniqueness? distinct, sorted, limit, skip.
  5. What result? A single value (reduce, max, count) or a container (collect).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.java8;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Java 8 stream interview questions on numbers and lists (Easy → Medium). Each method = one question. */
public final class StreamBasics {
    private StreamBasics() {}

    /** Q1. Even numbers from a list. */
    public static List<Integer> evens(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).toList();
    }

    /** Q2. Numbers starting with digit 1 (e.g. 10, 15, 1). */
    public static List<Integer> startingWithOne(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().map(String::valueOf).filter(s -> s.startsWith("1")).map(Integer::valueOf).toList();
    }

    /** Q3. Duplicate elements (each reported once, in first-seen order). Set.add returns false on repeat. */
    public static Set<Integer> duplicates(List<Integer> list) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new java.util.HashSet<>();
        return list.stream().filter(n -> !seen.add(n)).collect(Collectors.toCollection(java.util.LinkedHashSet::new));
    }

    /** Q4. First element, or empty. */
    public static Optional<Integer> first(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().findFirst();
    }

    /** Q5. Max value (Optional because the list may be empty). */
    public static Optional<Integer> max(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().max(Integer::compare);
    }

    /** Q6. Sort descending. */
    public static List<Integer> sortDescending(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).toList();
    }

    /** Q7. Second highest distinct number. */
    public static Optional<Integer> secondHighest(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().distinct().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst();
    }

    /** Q8. Sum, average via reduce and IntStream. */
    public static int sum(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);
    }

    public static double average(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).average().orElse(0);
    }

    /** Q9. Square each, keep those > 100, average them. */
    public static double averageOfSquaresAbove100(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().mapToInt(n -> n * n).filter(sq -> sq > 100).average().orElse(0);
    }

    /** Q10. Frequency of each element. */
    public static Map<Integer, Long> frequency(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Q11. Partition into even / odd. */
    public static Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> partitionEvenOdd(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));
    }

    /** Q12. Flatten a list of lists. */
    public static List<Integer> flatten(List<List<Integer>> lists) {
        return lists.stream().flatMap(List::stream).toList();
    }

    /** Q13. Merge two arrays, sorted and distinct. */
    public static int[] mergeSortedDistinct(int[] a, int[] b) {
        return IntStream.concat(Arrays.stream(a), Arrays.stream(b)).sorted().distinct().toArray();
    }

    /** Q14. Check if any / all / none match. */
    public static boolean allPositive(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().allMatch(n -> n > 0);
    }

    /** Q15. Top-3 largest. */
    public static List<Integer> top3(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).limit(3).toList();
    }

    /** Q16. Sum of digits of a number via stream. */
    public static int sumOfDigits(int n) {
        return String.valueOf(Math.abs(n)).chars().map(Character::getNumericValue).sum();
    }

    /** Q17. Join numbers into "[1, 2, 3]" style string. */
    public static String join(List<Integer> list) {
        return list.stream().map(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));
    }
}

docs.title: Streams on strings
docs.text:
Easy → Medium chars() groupingBy

Q Question Example 1 Character frequency (ordered) "swiss" → {s=3, w=1, i=1} 2 First non-repeated character "swiss" → w 3 First repeated character "swiss" → s 4 Duplicate characters "swiss" → [s] 5 Reverse each word "Java Streams" → "avaJ smaertS" 6 Longest word 7 Word frequency (case-insensitive) "The cat, the hat!" → {the=2, cat=1, hat=1} 8 Most frequent character 9 Palindrome check IntStream.range(0, n/2).allMatch(...) 10 Sort by length, then alphabetically comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(naturalOrder()) 11 Group words by length groupingBy(String::length) 12 Remove duplicate characters "programming" → "progamin" 13 Count vowels 14 Anagram check compare chars().sorted().toArray() 15 Capitalise every word "hello jAVA world" → "Hello Java World"

chars() returns an IntStream

Use mapToObj(c -> (char) c) to get Character values for grouping, and mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char) c)) before joining().

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.java8;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;

/** Java 8 stream interview questions on strings (Easy → Hard). */
public final class StringStreamProblems {
    private StringStreamProblems() {}

    /** Q1. Character frequency (order preserved). */
    public static Map<Character, Long> charFrequency(String s) {
        return s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Q2. First non-repeated character. */
    public static Optional<Character> firstNonRepeated(String s) {
        return charFrequency(s).entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1).map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst();
    }

    /** Q3. First repeated character. */
    public static Optional<Character> firstRepeated(String s) {
        return charFrequency(s).entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1).map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst();
    }

    /** Q4. Duplicate characters. */
    public static List<Character> duplicateChars(String s) {
        return charFrequency(s).entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
    }

    /** Q5. Reverse each word. */
    public static String reverseEachWord(String s) {
        return Arrays.stream(s.split(" ")).map(w -> new StringBuilder(w).reverse()).collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
    }

    /** Q6. Longest word (first one on ties). */
    public static Optional<String> longestWord(String sentence) {
        return Arrays.stream(sentence.split("\\s+")).reduce((a, b) -> b.length() > a.length() ? b : a);
    }

    /** Q7. Word frequency (case-insensitive). */
    public static Map<String, Long> wordFrequency(String sentence) {
        return Arrays.stream(sentence.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")).filter(w -> !w.isEmpty())
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }

    /** Q8. Most frequent character. */
    public static Optional<Character> mostFrequentChar(String s) {
        return charFrequency(s).entrySet().stream().max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).map(Map.Entry::getKey);
    }

    /** Q9. Is palindrome (IntStream over the first half). */
    public static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        return IntStream.range(0, s.length() / 2).allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(s.length() - 1 - i));
    }

    /** Q10. Sort strings by length, then alphabetically. */
    public static List<String> sortByLengthThenAlpha(List<String> words) {
        return words.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())).toList();
    }

    /** Q11. Group words by length. */
    public static Map<Integer, List<String>> groupByLength(List<String> words) {
        return words.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(String::length));
    }

    /** Q12. Remove duplicate characters, keep first occurrence. */
    public static String removeDuplicateChars(String s) {
        return s.chars().distinct().mapToObj(c -> String.valueOf((char) c)).collect(Collectors.joining());
    }

    /** Q13. Count vowels. */
    public static long countVowels(String s) {
        return s.toLowerCase().chars().filter(c -> "aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0).count();
    }

    /** Q14. Are two strings anagrams? */
    public static boolean areAnagrams(String a, String b) {
        return Arrays.equals(a.chars().sorted().toArray(), b.chars().sorted().toArray());
    }

    /** Q15. Capitalise the first letter of every word. */
    public static String capitalize(String s) {
        return Arrays.stream(s.split(" "))
                .map(w -> w.isEmpty() ? w : Character.toUpperCase(w.charAt(0)) + w.substring(1).toLowerCase())
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
    }
}

See the full step-by-step versions in Strings. Every problem there also has a streams approach.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• A node holds a value and a next reference. There is no index access: reaching node k takes O(k).
  • Inserting or deleting at a node you already hold is O(1). That's the reason to use a list over an array.
  • Every problem is about rewiring references safely. Draw boxes and arrows, and save next before you overwrite it.
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Singly linked list node used by every problem in this package, plus test/demo helpers. */
public final class ListNode {
    public int val;
    public ListNode next;

    public ListNode(int val) {
        this.val = val;
    }

    public ListNode(int val, ListNode next) {
        this.val = val;
        this.next = next;
    }

    /** Build a list from values; empty array → null. */
    public static ListNode of(int... values) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
        for (int v : values) tail = tail.next = new ListNode(v);
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Values from head to tail. Stops after 10_000 nodes so an accidental cycle can't hang a test. */
    public static List<Integer> toList(ListNode head) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null && out.size() < 10_000; n = n.next) out.add(n.val);
        return out;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return toList(this).toString();
    }
}

docs.title: Add two numbers
docs.text: Hard Carry Dummy head Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Two non-negative numbers are stored as digit lists in reverse order (342 is 2→4→3). Return their sum in the same form. 2→4→3 + 5→6→4 → 7→0→8 (342 + 465 = 807). Follow-up (LeetCode 445): the digits are in forward order.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Can the lists have different lengths? (Yes.) Leading zeros? (No, except for the number 0 itself.) Could the numbers exceed long? (Yes, which is why converting to a number is wrong.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Tempting but wrong: convert to long, add, and convert back. It overflows after 19 digits.
  2. Reverse order is a gift: the head is the ones digit, exactly where grade-school addition starts.
  3. At each step, sum = carry + digitA + digitB. Emit sum % 10 and carry sum / 10.
  4. Loop while either list has digits or the carry is non-zero. That last condition produces the extra leading digit (99 + 1 = 100).
  5. Forward-order follow-up: reverse both lists, add, and reverse the result. A stack-based version also works.

docs.title: Dry run (342 + 465)
docs.text: a b carry in sum digit carry out 2 5 0 7 7 0 4 6 0 10 0 1 3 4 1 8 8 0

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Numbers stored as digit lists in REVERSE order (342 = 2→4→3). Return their sum in the same form. */
public final class AddTwoNumbers {
    private AddTwoNumbers() {}

    /** Iterative: grade-school addition with a carry. O(max(m,n)). Works for any length — no overflow. */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
        int carry = 0;
        while (a != null || b != null || carry != 0) {       // carry != 0 emits the final extra digit
            int sum = carry + (a != null ? a.val : 0) + (b != null ? b.val : 0);
            tail = tail.next = new ListNode(sum % 10);
            carry = sum / 10;
            if (a != null) a = a.next;
            if (b != null) b = b.next;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Recursive: add this digit pair plus carry, recurse on the rest with the new carry. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        return add(a, b, 0);
    }

    private static ListNode add(ListNode a, ListNode b, int carry) {
        if (a == null && b == null && carry == 0) return null;
        int sum = carry + (a != null ? a.val : 0) + (b != null ? b.val : 0);
        return new ListNode(sum % 10, add(a != null ? a.next : null, b != null ? b.next : null, sum / 10));
    }

    /** Follow-up (LeetCode 445): digits in FORWARD order. Reverse both, add, reverse the result. */
    public static ListNode forwardOrder(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        return ReverseLinkedList.iterative(iterative(ReverseLinkedList.iterative(a), ReverseLinkedList.iterative(b)));
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(max(m, n)) time. O(max(m, n)) for the output, plus O(max(m, n)) stack in the recursive version.

docs.title: Copy list with random pointer
docs.text: Hard Hashing Interleaving

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Each node has next and a random pointer to any node or null. Return a deep copy. No pointer in the copy may reference an original node.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Copying next is easy. The trouble is that random may point forward to a node you haven't copied yet.
  2. Two passes with a map: pass 1 creates every copy (original → copy). Pass 2 sets copy.next = map.get(orig.next) and copy.random = map.get(orig.random). O(n) space.
  3. O(1) space insight: the map exists only to find "the copy of X". Put each copy right after its original (A → A' → B → B'). Then the copy of X is simply X.next.
  4. Three passes: insert the copies, set copy.random = orig.random.next, then unweave the two lists, restoring the original.

docs.title: Interleaving, visualised
docs.text:
original:     A → B → C
interleaved:  A → A' → B → B' → C → C'
random:       A'.random = A.random.next
split:        A → B → C      A' → B' → C'

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Deep-copy a list whose nodes also have a {@code random} pointer to any node (or null). */
public final class CopyRandomList {
    private CopyRandomList() {}

    /** Node with an extra random pointer. */
    public static final class Node {
        public int val;
        public Node next, random;

        public Node(int val) {
            this.val = val;
        }
    }

    /** HashMap original → copy, then wire next/random in a second pass. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static Node withMap(Node head) {
        Map<Node, Node> copy = new HashMap<>();
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) copy.put(n, new Node(n.val));
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {
            copy.get(n).next = copy.get(n.next);             // get(null) → null, which is exactly right
            copy.get(n).random = copy.get(n.random);
        }
        return copy.get(head);
    }

    /**
     * Interleave: A→A'→B→B'→… so every copy sits right after its original (original.next IS the map).
     * Then set randoms, then unweave. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
     */
    public static Node interleave(Node head) {
        if (head == null) return null;
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next.next) {    // 1. insert copies
            Node c = new Node(n.val);
            c.next = n.next;
            n.next = c;
        }
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next.next) {    // 2. copy.random = original.random's copy
            if (n.random != null) n.next.random = n.random.next;
        }
        Node copyHead = head.next;
        for (Node n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {         // 3. split the two lists, restoring the original
            Node c = n.next;
            n.next = c.next;
            c.next = c.next != null ? c.next.next : null;
        }
        return copyHead;
    }
}

docs.title: Intersection of two linked lists
docs.text: Medium Two pointers Hashing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Two lists may merge into a shared tail (the same nodes, not just equal values). Return the first shared node, or null.

A:      4 → 1 ↘
                8 → 4 → 5
B:  5 → 6 → 1 ↗

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each node of A, scan B. That's O(m·n).
  2. HashSet: store A's nodes, then walk B. O(m + n) time, O(m) space.
  3. Length insight: after the merge point both lists are identical, so the only difference is the head part. Skip the extra |m − n| nodes of the longer list, then walk both together.
  4. Elegant version: walk A then B with one pointer, and B then A with the other. Both travel m + n, so they meet at the intersection, or reach null at the same moment if there isn't one. You never need to count lengths.

docs.title: Why switching heads works
docs.text: Pointer p travels a + c + b and pointer q travels b + c + a, where c is the shared tail. The totals are equal, so they arrive at the start of c together.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Return the node where two lists merge (by identity), or null. Lists are not modified. */
public final class IntersectionOfTwoLists {
    private IntersectionOfTwoLists() {}

    /** Store every node of A, walk B until one is found. O(m+n) time, O(m) space. */
    public static ListNode withSet(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        Set<ListNode> seen = new HashSet<>();
        for (ListNode x = a; x != null; x = x.next) seen.add(x);
        for (ListNode y = b; y != null; y = y.next) if (seen.contains(y)) return y;
        return null;
    }

    /** Align by length: skip the longer list's extra head, then walk together. O(m+n), O(1). */
    public static ListNode lengthDiff(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        int la = length(a), lb = length(b);
        for (; la > lb; la--) a = a.next;
        for (; lb > la; lb--) b = b.next;
        while (a != b) {
            a = a.next;
            b = b.next;
        }
        return a;
    }

    /**
     * Switch heads: each pointer walks its list then the other one. Both travel m+n, so they arrive at the
     * intersection together — or at null together when there is none. O(m+n), O(1), no length counting.
     */
    public static ListNode switchHeads(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode p = a, q = b;
        while (p != q) {
            p = p == null ? b : p.next;
            q = q == null ? a : q.next;
        }
        return p;
    }

    private static int length(ListNode n) {
        int len = 0;
        for (; n != null; n = n.next) len++;
        return len;
    }
}

docs.title: Detect a cycle & find its start
docs.text: Medium Floyd's tortoise & hare Hashing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Does the list contain a cycle?
  2. If so, which node does the cycle start at (LeetCode 142)?
  3. How long is the cycle?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: remember every node you visit in a HashSet. The first repeat is the cycle start. O(n) space.
  2. O(1) insight: on a circular track, a runner going 2 steps per tick gains 1 step per tick on a runner going 1, so it must land on it. It can't jump over, because the gap shrinks by exactly 1.
  3. Finding the start: let F = distance from head to the start, and a = distance from the start to the meeting point. Slow walked F + a and fast walked 2(F + a). The difference F + a is a whole number of loops, so F ≡ −a (mod loop). A pointer from the head and a pointer from the meeting point, both moving 1 step, therefore meet exactly at the start.

docs.title: Picture
docs.text:
head → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
               ↑       ↓
               7 ← 6 ← 5        F = 2 (head..3), loop length 5

docs.title: Approach 1 — HashSet
docs.text: O(n) time, O(n) space. The first node that add rejects is the start.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Floyd (optimal)
docs.text:
1. slow and fast both start at head. Loop while fast and fast.next exist.
  2. If slow == fast, there's a cycle.
  3. To find the start, set p = head and step p and slow together until they meet.
  4. For the length, walk around once from the start.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Floyd's tortoise and hare on a list whose tail loops back to node 3
  1. Both pointers start at the head. slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2.
  2. slow → node 2, fast → node 3. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  3. slow → node 3, fast → node 5. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  4. slow → node 4, fast → node 7. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  5. slow → node 5, fast → node 4. Once both are inside the loop, fast gains one step per round.
  6. slow → node 6, fast → node 6. They meet: inside a loop the faster runner must land on the slower one, because the gap shrinks by exactly 1 each round.
  7. Phase 2: put p at the head and keep slow at the meeting point (node 6). Both now move 1 step at a time.
  8. p → node 2, slow → node 7.
  9. p → node 3, slow → node 3. Same node!
  10. They meet exactly at the start of the cycle, node 3: the distance from the head equals the distance from the meeting point, modulo the loop length. O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Does the list loop back on itself? If so, where does the loop start, and how long is it? */
public final class LinkedListCycle {
    private LinkedListCycle() {}

    /** HashSet of visited nodes (identity, not value). O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean hasCycleWithSet(ListNode head) {
        Set<ListNode> seen = new HashSet<>();                // ListNode has no equals(): identity semantics
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {
            if (!seen.add(n)) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    /** Floyd: fast gains one step per round on slow; inside a loop it must land on slow. O(n), O(1). */
    public static boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
            if (slow == fast) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    /**
     * Start of the cycle. After slow and fast meet, a pointer from head and a pointer from the meeting
     * point, both moving 1 step, meet exactly at the cycle start (distance head→start = meet→start mod loop).
     */
    public static ListNode cycleStart(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
            if (slow == fast) {
                ListNode p = head;
                while (p != slow) {
                    p = p.next;
                    slow = slow.next;
                }
                return p;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

    /** Length of the cycle (0 if none): from the meeting point walk once around. */
    public static int cycleLength(ListNode head) {
        ListNode start = cycleStart(head);
        if (start == null) return 0;
        int len = 1;
        for (ListNode n = start.next; n != start; n = n.next) len++;
        return len;
    }
}

docs.title: LRU cache
docs.text: Expert HashMap Doubly linked list Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Design a cache of fixed capacity with O(1) get(key) and put(key, value). When it's full, put evicts the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a use.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: What does get return for a missing key? (−1.) Does updating an existing key count as a use? (Yes.) Thread safety? (Not required here. Mention synchronized or a ConcurrentHashMap + lock as a follow-up.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. O(1) lookup needs a HashMap.
  2. O(1) "who is the oldest?" needs an order. An array costs O(n) to shift, so use a list.
  3. O(1) "move this entry to the front" means you must unlink a node from the middle in O(1), which needs a doubly linked list (you need prev).
  4. The map stores key → node, so the node is found instantly and moved in O(1).
  5. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove every null check.
  6. Each node must store its key too: on eviction you have the tail node and must remove its key from the map.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
map: { 1 → ●, 3 → ●, 4 → ● }
head ⇄ [4] ⇄ [3] ⇄ [1] ⇄ tail
       most recent      least recent (evicted next)

docs.title: Operation trace (capacity 2)
docs.text: Op List (MRU → LRU) Result put(1,1) 1 put(2,2) 2, 1 get(1) 1, 2 1 put(3,3) 3, 1 (evict 2) get(2) 3, 1 −1

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Least-Recently-Used cache with O(1) get and put. When full, put evicts the key used longest ago.
 * {@code get} returns -1 for a missing key.
 */
public final class LruCache {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<Integer, Entry> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Entry head = new Entry(0, 0), tail = new Entry(0, 0);   // sentinels: no null checks

    /** Doubly linked node: most recent right after head, least recent right before tail. */
    private static final class Entry {
        final int key;
        int value;
        Entry prev, next;

        Entry(int key, int value) {
            this.key = key;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    public LruCache(int capacity) {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("capacity must be > 0");
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    public int get(int key) {
        Entry e = map.get(key);
        if (e == null) return -1;
        moveToFront(e);                                      // reading counts as "use"
        return e.value;
    }

    public void put(int key, int value) {
        Entry e = map.get(key);
        if (e != null) {
            e.value = value;
            moveToFront(e);
            return;
        }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {                        // evict least recently used
            Entry lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru);
            map.remove(lru.key);                             // that's why Entry stores its key
        }
        e = new Entry(key, value);
        map.put(key, e);
        addFront(e);
    }

    public int size() {
        return map.size();
    }

    private void moveToFront(Entry e) {
        unlink(e);
        addFront(e);
    }

    private void unlink(Entry e) {
        e.prev.next = e.next;
        e.next.prev = e.prev;
    }

    private void addFront(Entry e) {
        e.next = head.next;
        e.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = e;
        head.next = e;
    }

    /** Production shortcut: LinkedHashMap in access order + removeEldestEntry. Know it, but expect to hand-roll. */
    public static <K, V> Map<K, V> withLinkedHashMap(int capacity) {
        return new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
            @Override
            protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
                return size() > capacity;
            }
        };
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(1) for get and put. O(capacity) space.

docs.text: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) (access order) plus removeEldestEntry is a two-line LRU, and the class shows it. Interviewers usually ask you to build the structure yourself, so know both.

docs.title: Merge K sorted lists
docs.text: Expert Min-heap Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list. [1→4→5, 1→3→4, 2→6] → 1→1→2→3→4→4→5→6. Let N be the total number of nodes.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Collect and sort: O(N log N). It ignores the fact that the input is already sorted.
  2. Merge one by one: merge list 1 with 2, the result with 3, and so on. The growing result is re-walked k times, which gives O(k·N).
  3. Heap insight: at any moment the next output node is the smallest of the k current heads. A min-heap of size k gives that in O(log k), so the total is O(N log k).
  4. Divide & conquer: merge lists in pairs, like merge sort. There are log k rounds and each touches every node once, so it's also O(N log k), with no heap.

docs.title: Heap trace (first steps)
docs.text: Heap (heads) Pop Push 1a, 1b, 2 1a 4a 1b, 2, 4a 1b 3b 2, 3b, 4a 2 6 3b, 4a, 6 3b 4b

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list. N = total nodes. */
public final class MergeKSortedLists {
    private MergeKSortedLists() {}

    /** Brute force: collect all values, sort, rebuild. O(N log N) time, O(N) space. */
    public static ListNode collectAndSort(ListNode[] lists) {
        List<Integer> all = new ArrayList<>();
        for (ListNode l : lists) all.addAll(ListNode.toList(l));
        Collections.sort(all);
        return ListNode.of(all.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray());
    }

    /** Sequential: merge list 1 into 2, result into 3, … O(k·N) — the first list is re-walked k times. */
    public static ListNode sequential(ListNode[] lists) {
        ListNode result = null;
        for (ListNode l : lists) result = MergeTwoSortedLists.iterative(result, l);
        return result;
    }

    /** Min-heap of the k current heads: pop smallest, push its successor. O(N log k) time, O(k) space. */
    public static ListNode heap(ListNode[] lists) {
        PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Integer.compare(x.val, y.val));
        for (ListNode l : lists) if (l != null) pq.offer(l);
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            ListNode smallest = pq.poll();
            tail = tail.next = smallest;
            if (smallest.next != null) pq.offer(smallest.next);
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Divide & conquer: merge pairs like merge sort. log k rounds, each O(N) → O(N log k), O(log k) stack. */
    public static ListNode divideAndConquer(ListNode[] lists) {
        if (lists.length == 0) return null;
        return merge(lists, 0, lists.length - 1);
    }

    private static ListNode merge(ListNode[] lists, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return lists[lo];
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        return MergeTwoSortedLists.iterative(merge(lists, lo, mid), merge(lists, mid + 1, hi));
    }
}
