docs.title: Merge two sorted lists
docs.text: Easy Dummy head Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge two sorted lists into one sorted list by splicing the existing nodes. 1→2→4 + 1→3→4 → 1→1→2→3→4→4.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. The smallest overall node is one of the two heads, so take it and repeat. This is the merge step of merge sort.
  2. Dummy head: start with a fake node, so "append to result" is always tail.next = x, with no special case for the first node.
  3. When one list runs out, the rest of the other is already sorted, so attach it in one assignment.
  4. Use <= to take from a on ties. That keeps the merge stable.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Iterative with a dummy head (optimal)
docs.text: O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Recursive
docs.text: merge(a, b): whichever head is smaller becomes the answer, and its next = merge(rest, other). The base case is when either list is empty. It's elegant, but uses O(n + m) stack.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Merge two sorted lists by splicing nodes (no new nodes). 1→3→5 + 2→4 = 1→2→3→4→5. */
public final class MergeTwoSortedLists {
    private MergeTwoSortedLists() {}

    /** Iterative with a dummy head: always attach the smaller front node. O(n+m), O(1). */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;      // dummy removes the "is result empty?" special case
        while (a != null && b != null) {
            if (a.val <= b.val) {                            // <= keeps the merge stable
                tail.next = a;
                a = a.next;
            } else {
                tail.next = b;
                b = b.next;
            }
            tail = tail.next;
        }
        tail.next = a != null ? a : b;                       // append whatever is left in one go
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** Recursive: the smaller head wins, its next is the merge of the rest. O(n+m) time and stack. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
        if (a == null) return b;
        if (b == null) return a;
        if (a.val <= b.val) {
            a.next = recursive(a.next, b);
            return a;
        }
        b.next = recursive(a, b.next);
        return b;
    }
}

docs.title: Middle of the linked list
docs.text: Easy Slow / fast pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the middle node. For an even length, return the second middle: 1→2→3→4→5 → 3, 1→2→3→4→5→6 → 4.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: For an even length, which middle? Merge sort's split needs the first middle, so the code has both.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Two passes: count n, then walk n/2 steps. That's O(n) and simple.
  2. One pass: if fast moves twice as fast as slow, then when fast reaches the end slow has gone half as far.
  3. The loop condition fast != null && fast.next != null decides which middle you get. Starting fast at head.next instead shifts the answer to the first middle.

docs.title: Dry run (1→2→3→4→5→6)
docs.text: Step slow fast 0 1 1 1 2 3 2 3 5 3 4 null → stop

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Middle node; for even length return the SECOND middle (1→2→3→4 gives 3). */
public final class MiddleNode {
    private MiddleNode() {}

    /** Two passes: count, then walk n/2. O(n). */
    public static ListNode twoPass(ListNode head) {
        int n = 0;
        for (ListNode x = head; x != null; x = x.next) n++;
        ListNode x = head;
        for (int i = 0; i < n / 2; i++) x = x.next;
        return x;
    }

    /** Optimal: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast falls off, slow is in the middle. One pass, O(1). */
    public static ListNode slowFast(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }
        return slow;
    }

    /** Variant: FIRST middle for even length (needed when splitting a list for merge sort). */
    public static ListNode firstMiddle(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null) return null;
        ListNode slow = head, fast = head.next;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }
        return slow;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time and O(1) space for both approaches. The slow/fast version takes a single pass.

docs.title: Palindrome linked list
docs.text: Medium Slow / fast In-place reversal Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if the values read the same forwards and backwards. 1→2→2→1 ✅, 1→2→3→1 ❌. Can you do it in O(1) space?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: copy the values into an ArrayList and use two pointers. O(n) space.
  2. The problem: a singly linked list can't walk backwards.
  3. Insight: make the second half walk "forwards" by reversing it. Find the first middle, reverse everything after it, and compare it node by node with the first half.
  4. Senior touch: reverse the second half back afterwards. A check function shouldn't mutate its input.
  5. Recursive trick: the recursion visits nodes from the tail backwards while a shared front pointer moves forwards, so you compare the outermost pair first.

docs.title: Picture (1→2→3→2→1)
docs.text:
first half: 1 → 2 → 3          second half reversed: 1 → 2
            ↑ compare ↑                              ↑   ↑

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Is the list a palindrome? 1→2→2→1 yes, 1→2 no. */
public final class PalindromeLinkedList {
    private PalindromeLinkedList() {}

    /** Copy values into a list, then two pointers. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static boolean copyToList(ListNode head) {
        List<Integer> v = ListNode.toList(head);
        for (int l = 0, r = v.size() - 1; l < r; l++, r--) if (!v.get(l).equals(v.get(r))) return false;
        return true;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: find the middle, reverse the second half, compare, then reverse it back so the caller's
     * list is unchanged. O(n) time, O(1) space.
     */
    public static boolean reverseHalf(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return true;
        ListNode firstEnd = MiddleNode.firstMiddle(head);
        ListNode second = ReverseLinkedList.iterative(firstEnd.next);
        boolean ok = true;
        for (ListNode p = head, q = second; ok && q != null; p = p.next, q = q.next) ok = p.val == q.val;
        firstEnd.next = ReverseLinkedList.iterative(second); // restore input
        return ok;
    }

    /** Recursive: recursion unwinds from the tail while a "front" pointer walks forward. O(n) stack. */
    public static boolean recursive(ListNode head) {
        ListNode[] front = {head};
        return check(head, front);
    }

    private static boolean check(ListNode node, ListNode[] front) {
        if (node == null) return true;
        if (!check(node.next, front)) return false;          // compare deepest (tail) first
        boolean same = node.val == front[0].val;
        front[0] = front[0].next;
        return same;
    }
}

docs.title: Remove Nth node from end
docs.text: Medium Two pointers with a gap Dummy head

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Delete the n-th node from the end and return the head. 1→2→3→4→5, n = 2 → 1→2→3→5. n is always valid.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. To delete a node, you need the node before it.
  2. Two passes: count L, and the target's predecessor is node L − n counting from a dummy. O(n), but two passes.
  3. One pass: move fast n + 1 steps ahead of slow, then advance both together. When fast falls off the end, slow sits right before the target.
  4. Dummy head handles n == L (removing the head) without a special case.

docs.title: Dry run (n = 2)
docs.text: slow fast after the gap of 3 dummy 3 step 1 4 step 2 5 step 3 null → unlink 3.next (4)

docs.title: Recursive
docs.text: Count positions on the way back up the recursion. When the count equals n, return node.next to skip yourself.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Remove the n-th node from the end (1-based; n is valid). 1→2→3→4→5, n=2 gives 1→2→3→5. */
public final class RemoveNthFromEnd {
    private RemoveNthFromEnd() {}

    /** Two passes: length L, then delete node number L-n (0-based) from the front. */
    public static ListNode twoPass(ListNode head, int n) {
        int len = 0;
        for (ListNode x = head; x != null; x = x.next) len++;
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), prev = dummy;
        for (int i = 0; i < len - n; i++) prev = prev.next;
        prev.next = prev.next.next;
        return dummy.next;
    }

    /** One pass: keep a gap of n nodes between fast and slow; when fast hits the end, slow is before the target. */
    public static ListNode onePass(ListNode head, int n) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), slow = dummy, fast = dummy;
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) fast = fast.next;       // gap of n+1 so slow stops BEFORE the target
        while (fast != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next;
        }
        slow.next = slow.next.next;
        return dummy.next;                                   // dummy handles "remove the head" too
    }

    /** Recursive: count positions on the way back up; unlink when the count equals n. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode head, int n) {
        int[] fromEnd = {0};
        return remove(head, n, fromEnd);
    }

    private static ListNode remove(ListNode node, int n, int[] fromEnd) {
        if (node == null) return null;
        node.next = remove(node.next, n, fromEnd);
        return ++fromEnd[0] == n ? node.next : node;         // skip myself if I am the n-th from the end
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: All versions take O(n) time. The iterative ones use O(1) space; the recursive one uses O(n) stack.

docs.title: Reverse nodes in k-group
docs.text: Hard In-place reversal Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse the list k nodes at a time. A final group shorter than k stays as it is. 1→2→3→4→5: k = 2 gives 2→1→4→3→5, and k = 3 gives 3→2→1→4→5.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. It's reverse a list, repeated on segments, so the hard part is the stitching.
  2. Check first: before reversing, make sure k nodes exist. Otherwise, leave the group alone.
  3. Recursive view: solve the rest of the list first, then reverse my k nodes so the last of them points at that solved remainder. Start prev at the remainder instead of null, and the stitch happens automatically.
  4. Iterative view: keep groupPrev, the node before the current group (initially a dummy). Reverse the group with prev starting at groupNext, point groupPrev.next at the old k-th node, and move groupPrev to the old first node, which is now the group's tail.

docs.title: Picture (k = 2, one group)
docs.text:
dummy → [1 → 2] → 3 → 4 → 5        groupPrev = dummy, kth = 2, groupNext = 3
dummy → [2 → 1] → 3 → 4 → 5        groupPrev = 1 (old first, now the tail)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

/** Reverse nodes k at a time; a final group shorter than k stays as is. 1..5, k=2 gives 2→1→4→3→5. */
public final class ReverseKGroup {
    private ReverseKGroup() {}

    /** Recursive: check k nodes exist, reverse them, attach the recursively solved rest. O(n), O(n/k) stack. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode head, int k) {
        ListNode probe = head;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            if (probe == null) return head;                  // fewer than k left: leave untouched
            probe = probe.next;
        }
        ListNode prev = recursive(probe, k), curr = head;    // prev starts as the solved remainder
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            ListNode next = curr.next;
            curr.next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = next;
        }
        return prev;
    }

    /** Iterative: for each full group, reverse in place and stitch between groupPrev and the next group. O(1) space. */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode head, int k) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), groupPrev = dummy;
        while (true) {
            ListNode kth = groupPrev;
            for (int i = 0; i < k && kth != null; i++) kth = kth.next;
            if (kth == null) break;                          // not a full group
            ListNode groupNext = kth.next, prev = groupNext, curr = groupPrev.next;
            while (curr != groupNext) {                      // reverse, pointing the first node at groupNext
                ListNode next = curr.next;
                curr.next = prev;
                prev = curr;
                curr = next;
            }
            ListNode oldFirst = groupPrev.next;              // becomes the group's tail
            groupPrev.next = kth;
            groupPrev = oldFirst;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time, since each node is reversed once. O(1) extra space iteratively, or O(n/k) stack recursively.

docs.title: Edge cases
docs.text: k = 1 (no change). k = n (a full reversal). k > n (no change). The length is an exact multiple of k.

docs.title: Reverse a linked list
docs.text: Easy In-place reversal Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head. 1→2→3→4→5 → 5→4→3→2→1. Follow-up: reverse only positions left..right (LeetCode 92).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Input Output 1→2→3→4→5 5→4→3→2→1 1 1 empty empty

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: May I modify the input, or should I build a new list? (In place is expected.) Is the list possibly cyclic? (Assume not.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Reversing means every arrow a → b becomes b → a, and the old tail becomes the head.
  2. Brute force: push every node on a stack and pop them to relink. That's correct but uses O(n) memory.
  3. Insight: you only need the previous node to flip the current arrow. The danger is losing the rest of the list when you overwrite curr.next, so save it first.
  4. Pattern: three pointers prev, curr and next, flipping one arrow per step.

docs.title: Approach 1 — Stack
docs.text: Push all nodes, then pop to rebuild the chain. Remember tail.next = null, or the old head still points forward and you get a cycle. O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Approach 2 — Iterative three pointers (optimal)
docs.text:
1. prev = null, curr = head.
  2. While curr != null: next = curr.next, curr.next = prev, prev = curr, curr = next.
  3. Return prev.

docs.title: Approach 3 — Recursive
docs.text:
• Base case: 0 or 1 node, so return it.
  • Trust the call: newHead = reverse(head.next) reverses everything after me. My old next is now the tail of that reversed part.
  • My job: head.next.next = head (that tail points back to me), then head.next = null.

docs.title: Dry run (iterative, 1→2→3)
docs.text: Step prev curr Links after the step 0 null 1 1→2→3 1 1 2 null←1  2→3 2 2 3 null←1←2  3 3 3 null null←1←2←3 → return 3

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Reverse 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 with three pointers
  1. prev = null (nothing reversed yet), curr = head.
  2. Save next = curr.next (node 2) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  3. Flip: node 1 now points to null.
  4. Advance both: prev = node 1, curr = node 2.
  5. Save next = curr.next (node 3) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  6. Flip: node 2 now points to node 1.
  7. Advance both: prev = node 2, curr = node 3.
  8. Save next = curr.next (node 4) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  9. Flip: node 3 now points to node 2.
  10. Advance both: prev = node 3, curr = node 4.
  11. Save next = curr.next (node null) before we overwrite the arrow, or the rest of the list is lost.
  12. Flip: node 4 now points to node 3.
  13. Advance both: prev = node 4, curr = null.
  14. curr is null, so every arrow is flipped. prev (node 4) is the new head: 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. O(n) time, O(1) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.linkedlist;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head. 1→2→3 becomes 3→2→1. */
public final class ReverseLinkedList {
    private ReverseLinkedList() {}

    /** Brute force: push nodes on a stack, pop to relink. O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static ListNode withStack(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null) return null;
        Deque<ListNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) stack.push(n);
        ListNode newHead = stack.pop(), tail = newHead;
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) tail = tail.next = stack.pop();
        tail.next = null;                                    // old head must now point nowhere
        return newHead;
    }

    /** Optimal: three pointers (prev, curr, next). Flip one arrow per step. O(n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static ListNode iterative(ListNode head) {
        ListNode prev = null, curr = head;
        while (curr != null) {
            ListNode next = curr.next;                       // 1. save the rest
            curr.next = prev;                                // 2. flip the arrow
            prev = curr;                                     // 3. advance prev
            curr = next;                                     // 4. advance curr
        }
        return prev;
    }

    /** Recursive: reverse the rest, then hook the old next back to me. O(n) time, O(n) stack. */
    public static ListNode recursive(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return head; // base case: 0 or 1 node
        ListNode newHead = recursive(head.next);
        head.next.next = head;                               // the node after me now points back to me
        head.next = null;
        return newHead;
    }

    /** Follow-up: reverse only positions left..right (1-based). One pass. */
    public static ListNode reverseBetween(ListNode head, int left, int right) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head), before = dummy;
        for (int i = 1; i < left; i++) before = before.next;
        ListNode curr = before.next;
        for (int i = 0; i < right - left; i++) {             // move curr.next to the front of the segment
            ListNode moved = curr.next;
            curr.next = moved.next;
            moved.next = before.next;
            before.next = moved;
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }
}

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
Stack (LIFO) Queue (FIFO) Deque Order last in, first out first in, first out both ends Java type ArrayDeque (push/pop/peek) ArrayDeque (offer/poll/peek) ArrayDeque (offerFirst/pollLast…) Typical use undo, recursion, matching brackets, "most recent unresolved" BFS, scheduling, buffering sliding window, monotonic queue

Don't use java.util.Stack

It extends Vector, so every call is synchronised and it allows index access, which breaks the abstraction. Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>() is the modern choice.

docs.title: When should you think "stack"?
docs.text:
1. Something must be matched with the most recent unmatched thing: brackets, tags, operators.
  2. You need the nearest greater or smaller element to the left or right. That's a monotonic stack.
  3. You're converting recursion to iteration. The call stack becomes an explicit stack.
  4. You're evaluating or parsing expressions: postfix, infix, calculators.

docs.title: The monotonic stack template (memorise it)
docs.text:
Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();        // indexes; values kept monotonic
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    while (!st.isEmpty() && a[st.peek()] < a[i]) {   // a[i] resolves everyone smaller
        int j = st.pop();
        // a[i] is the NEXT GREATER of a[j]; st.peek() (if any) is the PREVIOUS GREATER-OR-EQUAL of a[j]
    }
    st.push(i);
}
// every index is pushed once and popped at most once → O(n) total, despite the nested while

docs.title: Implement a stack with an array
docs.text: Easy Design Amortised analysis

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Build an int stack with push, pop, peek, isEmpty and size, each in O(1). Variant (GfG): implement two stacks in one array without wasting space.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Fixed capacity or growable? What should pop on an empty stack do (throw, or return a sentinel)? Generic or int only?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A stack only ever touches one end, and the end of an array is O(1) to read and write.
  2. Keep top = the index of the top element, with -1 meaning empty. push is data[++top] = x, and pop is data[top--].
  3. Growing: when the array is full, copy it into one twice as big. A single resize costs O(n), but n pushes cost at most n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n copies in total, so push is amortised O(1). Growing by a constant (+10) would make it O(n).
  4. Two stacks in one array: grow stack 1 from the left and stack 2 from the right. Overflow happens only when the two tops meet, so no slot is wasted. Splitting the array in half would waste space whenever one stack is much smaller.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/**
 * Stack backed by a growable int array. push/pop/peek are O(1) (push is amortised O(1) because of doubling).
 * Also shows the classic "two stacks in one array" variant.
 */
public final class ArrayStack {
    private int[] data;
    private int top = -1;                                    // index of the top element; -1 = empty

    public ArrayStack() {
        this(8);
    }

    public ArrayStack(int initialCapacity) {
        data = new int[Math.max(1, initialCapacity)];
    }

    public void push(int x) {
        if (top + 1 == data.length) data = Arrays.copyOf(data, data.length * 2);   // double: amortised O(1)
        data[++top] = x;
    }

    public int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack underflow");
        return data[top--];
    }

    public int peek() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
        return data[top];
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return top == -1;
    }

    public int size() {
        return top + 1;
    }

    /** Two stacks sharing one fixed array: stack 1 grows from the left, stack 2 from the right. */
    public static final class TwoStacks {
        private final int[] arr;
        private int top1, top2;

        public TwoStacks(int capacity) {
            arr = new int[capacity];
            top1 = -1;
            top2 = capacity;
        }

        public void push1(int x) {
            if (top1 + 1 == top2) throw new IllegalStateException("overflow");   // the two tops met
            arr[++top1] = x;
        }

        public void push2(int x) {
            if (top1 + 1 == top2) throw new IllegalStateException("overflow");
            arr[--top2] = x;
        }

        public int pop1() {
            if (top1 < 0) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return arr[top1--];
        }

        public int pop2() {
            if (top2 == arr.length) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return arr[top2++];
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Operation Time push O(1) amortised (O(n) on a resize) pop / peek / isEmpty / size O(1)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Underflow (pop on empty) must be handled explicitly. With object stacks, null out the popped slot (data[top--] = null) or the garbage collector can't free it. This is a classic memory leak from Effective Java.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: A linked-list stack (push and pop at the head) never needs a resize, but each node carries a pointer, so it uses more memory.

docs.text: Expert Recursive descent Two stacks Parsing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Evaluate a string expression with non-negative integers, + - * /, parentheses, spaces and unary minus. Do not use eval or a script engine. "2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)" = 21, "-(2+3)" = −5.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Integer division truncating toward zero? (Yes.) Unary minus allowed? (Yes.) Is the input always valid? (Still, report errors cleanly.) Overflow? (Compute in long.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Only +, − and parentheses (LeetCode 224): keep a running result and the current sign. At (, push (result, sign) and start fresh. At ), combine with outerSign × inner + outerResult. This is one pass with one stack.

  2. With * and /: precedence matters. The cleanest senior answer is to write the grammar, so precedence falls out of the structure:

    • expr := term (('+'|'-') term)*
    • term := factor (('*'|'/') factor)*
    • factor := number | '(' expr ')' | '-' factor

    Each rule becomes one method. This is recursive descent, which is how real compilers parse. 3. Two stacks (Dijkstra): one for operands and one for operators. Apply an operator whenever the one on top has ≥ precedence. It's equivalent to shunting-yard and evaluating in the same pass.

docs.title: How recursive descent handles 2+3*4
docs.text:
expr
├── term → factor 2
├── '+'
└── term
    ├── factor 3
    ├── '*'
    └── factor 4        → 3*4 is computed inside term before expr adds it: 2 + 12 = 14

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Evaluate an infix string with non-negative integers, + - * /, parentheses, unary minus and spaces.
 * "2*(5+5*2)/3+(6/2+8)" = 21. Division truncates toward zero. Arithmetic is done in long, result cast to int.
 */
public final class BasicCalculator {
    private BasicCalculator() {}

    /**
     * Calculator I (only + - and parentheses, LeetCode 224): one running result, a sign, and a stack that saves
     * (result, sign) when entering a parenthesis. O(n).
     */
    public static int plusMinusParens(String s) {
        Deque<Long> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        long result = 0, number = 0;
        int sign = 1;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                number = number * 10 + (c - '0');
            } else if (c == '+' || c == '-') {
                result += sign * number;
                number = 0;
                sign = c == '+' ? 1 : -1;
            } else if (c == '(') {
                stack.push(result);                          // save the outer state
                stack.push((long) sign);
                result = 0;
                sign = 1;
            } else if (c == ')') {
                result += sign * number;
                number = 0;
                result = stack.pop() * result + stack.pop(); // outerSign * inner + outerResult
            }
        }
        return (int) (result + sign * number);
    }

    /**
     * Full calculator (LeetCode 772) by recursive descent — the grammar IS the precedence:
     *   expr   := term (('+'|'-') term)*
     *   term   := factor (('*'|'/') factor)*
     *   factor := number | '(' expr ')' | '-' factor
     */
    public static int evaluate(String s) {
        Parser p = new Parser(s.replace(" ", ""));
        long v = p.expr();
        if (p.pos != p.s.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected '" + p.s.charAt(p.pos) + "'");
        return (int) v;
    }

    private static final class Parser {
        final String s;
        int pos;

        Parser(String s) {
            this.s = s;
        }

        long expr() {
            long v = term();
            while (pos < s.length() && (peek() == '+' || peek() == '-')) {
                v = s.charAt(pos++) == '+' ? v + term() : v - term();
            }
            return v;
        }

        long term() {
            long v = factor();
            while (pos < s.length() && (peek() == '*' || peek() == '/')) {
                v = s.charAt(pos++) == '*' ? v * factor() : v / factor();
            }
            return v;
        }

        long factor() {
            if (pos >= s.length()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected end");
            char c = peek();
            if (c == '-') {
                pos++;
                return -factor();                            // unary minus
            }
            if (c == '(') {
                pos++;
                long v = expr();
                if (pos >= s.length() || s.charAt(pos++) != ')') throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing )");
                return v;
            }
            if (!Character.isDigit(c)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unexpected '" + c + "'");
            long n = 0;
            while (pos < s.length() && Character.isDigit(peek())) n = n * 10 + (s.charAt(pos++) - '0');
            return n;
        }

        char peek() {
            return s.charAt(pos);
        }
    }

    /**
     * Two-stack version (operands + operators), the classic Dijkstra approach: apply an operator whenever the one
     * on the stack has ≥ precedence. Handles + - * / and parentheses (binary operators only).
     */
    public static int twoStacks(String s) {
        Deque<Long> nums = new ArrayDeque<>();
        Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
        String e = s.replace(" ", "");
        for (int i = 0; i < e.length(); i++) {
            char c = e.charAt(i);
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                long n = 0;
                while (i < e.length() && Character.isDigit(e.charAt(i))) n = n * 10 + (e.charAt(i++) - '0');
                i--;
                nums.push(n);
            } else if (c == '(') {
                ops.push(c);
            } else if (c == ')') {
                while (ops.peek() != '(') apply(nums, ops.pop());
                ops.pop();
            } else {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '(' && prec(ops.peek()) >= prec(c)) apply(nums, ops.pop());
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) apply(nums, ops.pop());
        return (int) (long) nums.pop();
    }

    private static void apply(Deque<Long> nums, char op) {
        long b = nums.pop(), a = nums.pop();
        nums.push(switch (op) {
            case '+' -> a + b;
            case '-' -> a - b;
            case '*' -> a * b;
            default -> a / b;
        });
    }

    private static int prec(char op) {
        return op == '+' || op == '-' ? 1 : 2;
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time for all three approaches. Space is O(n) in the worst case (the nesting depth).

docs.text: You have to handle precedence, associativity, unary minus, multi-digit numbers, whitespace and error reporting at the same time, and explain your choice of design. Being able to state the grammar is the clearest sign of seniority here.

docs.title: Daily temperatures
docs.text: Medium Monotonic stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For each day, return how many days you wait for a warmer temperature, or 0 if none comes. [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73] → [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. This is next greater element, except the answer is a distance. So the stack stores indexes, not values.
  2. Keep days that are still waiting on the stack. Their temperatures are decreasing from bottom to top, because a warmer day would already have resolved them.
  3. When today is warmer than the top, pop it and record today − thatDay. Repeat, then push today.
  4. O(1) extra space trick: walk from right to left. To find day i's answer, start at j = i + 1 and, while t[j] ≤ t[i], jump j += out[j], which skips days already known to be colder.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature (0 if never). [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73] → [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0]. */
public final class DailyTemperatures {
    private DailyTemperatures() {}

    /** Brute force: scan forward for each day. O(n^2). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] t) {
        int[] out = new int[t.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
            for (int j = i + 1; j < t.length; j++) {
                if (t[j] > t[i]) {
                    out[i] = j - i;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Monotonic stack of INDEXES (we need distances, not values). Each index pushed/popped once → O(n). */
    public static int[] monotonicStack(int[] t) {
        int[] out = new int[t.length];
        Deque<Integer> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();         // indexes with decreasing temperatures
        for (int i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && t[waiting.peek()] < t[i]) {
                int day = waiting.pop();
                out[day] = i - day;                          // today is the first warmer day for `day`
            }
            waiting.push(i);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * O(1) extra space: walk right to left and jump using answers already computed
     * (if day j is not warmer, the next candidate is j + out[j]).
     */
    public static int[] backwardJumps(int[] t) {
        int n = t.length;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        for (int i = n - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
            int j = i + 1;
            while (t[j] <= t[i] && out[j] != 0) j += out[j];
            out[i] = t[j] > t[i] ? j - i : 0;
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Evaluate postfix (Reverse Polish Notation)
docs.text: Medium Stack Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Evaluate a postfix expression of integers with + - * / (division truncates toward zero). ["2","1","+","3","*"] = (2 + 1) × 3 = 9 · ["4","13","5","/","+"] = 4 + 13/5 = 6.

docs.title: Why postfix exists
docs.text: Postfix needs no parentheses and no precedence rules: the order of the tokens is the order of evaluation. Compilers and HP calculators use it, and infix → postfix is how you get there.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. When you read an operator, its operands are the two most recent results. "Most recent" means a stack.
  2. Push a number. For an operator, pop right first, then left, and push left op right. The order matters for − and /.
  3. At the end, exactly one value must remain. Anything else means the expression is malformed.
  4. Recursive view: read the expression backwards. An operator's right operand is the sub-expression just before it, and its left operand is the one before that.

docs.title: Dry run (2 1 + 3 *)
docs.text: Token Stack (top on the right) 2 2 1 2 1 + 3 3 3 3 * 9

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Evaluate a postfix (Reverse Polish) expression of integers with + - * /. Division truncates toward zero.
 * ["2","1","+","3","*"] = (2 + 1) * 3 = 9. Invalid input throws IllegalArgumentException.
 */
public final class EvaluateRpn {
    private EvaluateRpn() {}

    /** Operand stack: numbers are pushed; an operator pops two, applies, pushes the result. O(n). */
    public static int evaluate(String[] tokens) {
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (String t : tokens) {
            if (t.length() == 1 && "+-*/".contains(t)) {
                if (stack.size() < 2) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not enough operands for " + t);
                int right = stack.pop(), left = stack.pop();    // order matters for - and /
                stack.push(switch (t.charAt(0)) {
                    case '+' -> left + right;
                    case '-' -> left - right;
                    case '*' -> left * right;
                    default -> left / right;
                });
            } else {
                stack.push(Integer.parseInt(t));             // handles negatives like "-11"
            }
        }
        if (stack.size() != 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed expression");
        return stack.pop();
    }

    /** Recursive: read the expression from the END — an operator's operands are the two sub-expressions before it. */
    public static int recursive(String[] tokens) {
        int[] pos = {tokens.length - 1};
        int result = eval(tokens, pos);
        if (pos[0] != -1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("malformed expression");
        return result;
    }

    private static int eval(String[] t, int[] pos) {
        if (pos[0] < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not enough operands");
        String tok = t[pos[0]--];
        if (tok.length() == 1 && "+-*/".contains(tok)) {
            int right = eval(t, pos), left = eval(t, pos);   // right operand is nearer the operator
            return switch (tok.charAt(0)) {
                case '+' -> left + right;
                case '-' -> left - right;
                case '*' -> left * right;
                default -> left / right;
            };
        }
        return Integer.parseInt(tok);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) space, both with the explicit stack and recursively.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: "-11" is a number, not an operator, so check length() == 1 before treating a token as an operator. Popping the operands in the wrong order gives 1 − 2 instead of 2 − 1.

docs.title: Infix to postfix (shunting-yard)
docs.text: Hard Stack Parsing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Convert an infix expression (single-character operands, + - * / ^, parentheses) to postfix. a+b*(c^d-e)^(f+g*h)-i → abcd^e-fgh*+^*+i-. Bonus: convert to prefix.

docs.title: Rules you must state
docs.text: Operator Precedence Associativity ^ 3 right (a^b^c = a^(b^c)) * / 2 left + - 1 left

docs.title: Thinking process (Dijkstra's shunting-yard)
docs.text:
1. Operands go straight to the output, because their order never changes between infix and postfix.
  2. Operators wait on a stack until we know nothing with higher priority still needs to be applied first.
  3. When a new operator c arrives, pop to the output every operator on the stack that must run before it: higher precedence, or equal precedence and c is left-associative. Then push c.
  4. ( is pushed as a wall. ) pops to the output until the matching (, then discards both.
  5. At the end, pop everything that's left. A stray ( means the parentheses were unbalanced.

docs.title: Dry run (a+b*c-d)
docs.text: Token Output Operator stack a a + a + b ab + * ab + * (higher, so it waits on top) c abc + * - abc*+ − (pops * and +: higher and equal-left) d abc*+d − end *abc+d-

docs.title: Infix → prefix
docs.text: Reverse the string, swap ( and ), run the same algorithm with associativity flipped, then reverse the output. (A-B/C)*(A/K-L) → *-A/BC-/AKL.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Convert an infix expression with single-letter/digit operands, + - * / ^ and parentheses to postfix.
 * "a+b*(c^d-e)^(f+g*h)-i" → "abcd^e-fgh*+^*+i-". ^ is right-associative. Spaces are ignored.
 */
public final class InfixToPostfix {
    private InfixToPostfix() {}

    /** Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm with an operator stack. O(n). */
    public static String convert(String infix) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : infix.toCharArray()) {
            if (c == ' ') continue;
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) {
                out.append(c);                               // operands go straight to the output
            } else if (c == '(') {
                ops.push(c);
            } else if (c == ')') {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '(') out.append(ops.pop());
                if (ops.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unbalanced )");
                ops.pop();                                   // discard '('
            } else {
                // pop operators that must be applied BEFORE c: higher precedence, or equal and left-associative
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '('
                        && (prec(ops.peek()) > prec(c) || (prec(ops.peek()) == prec(c) && c != '^'))) {
                    out.append(ops.pop());
                }
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) {
            char op = ops.pop();
            if (op == '(') throw new IllegalArgumentException("unbalanced (");
            out.append(op);
        }
        return out.toString();
    }

    /** Bonus: infix → prefix = reverse, swap parentheses, convert (treating ^ carefully), reverse. */
    public static String toPrefix(String infix) {
        StringBuilder rev = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = infix.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            char c = infix.charAt(i);
            rev.append(c == '(' ? ')' : c == ')' ? '(' : c);
        }
        // On the reversed string, + - * / become right-associative and ^ left-associative.
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        Deque<Character> ops = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (char c : rev.toString().toCharArray()) {
            if (c == ' ') continue;
            if (Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)) out.append(c);
            else if (c == '(') ops.push(c);
            else if (c == ')') {
                while (ops.peek() != '(') out.append(ops.pop());
                ops.pop();
            } else {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && ops.peek() != '('
                        && (prec(ops.peek()) > prec(c) || (prec(ops.peek()) == prec(c) && c == '^'))) {
                    out.append(ops.pop());
                }
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) out.append(ops.pop());
        return out.reverse().toString();
    }

    private static int prec(char op) {
        return switch (op) {
            case '+', '-' -> 1;
            case '*', '/' -> 2;
            case '^' -> 3;
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown operator " + op);
        };
    }
}

docs.title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
docs.text: Expert Monotonic stack Previous / next smaller

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given bar heights (each 1 wide), return the area of the largest rectangle under the histogram. [2,1,5,6,2,3] → 10 (height 5 across the bars 5 and 6).

        █
      █ █
      █ █   █
      █ █ █ █
  █   █ █ █ █
  █ █ █ █ █ █
  2 1 5 6 2 3

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Every optimal rectangle is limited by its shortest bar. So for each bar i, ask: "what is the widest rectangle in which bar i is the shortest?"
  2. That rectangle extends left until the previous smaller bar and right until the next smaller bar. Its area is h[i] × (nextSmaller − prevSmaller − 1).
  3. Brute force: expand left and right for each bar. That's O(n²).
  4. Two monotonic stacks compute every previous-smaller and next-smaller index in O(n). See next greater element.
  5. One pass: keep a stack of indexes with increasing heights. When a lower bar arrives at i, every taller bar popped has just found its right boundary (i), and its left boundary is the element below it on the stack. A sentinel bar of height 0 at the end flushes the stack.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Largest rectangle in a histogram of bar heights (width 1 each). [2,1,5,6,2,3] → 10 (bars 5,6). */
public final class LargestRectangleHistogram {
    private LargestRectangleHistogram() {}

    /** Brute force: for every bar as the shortest, expand left and right. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] h) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < h.length; i++) {
            int l = i, r = i;
            while (l > 0 && h[l - 1] >= h[i]) l--;
            while (r < h.length - 1 && h[r + 1] >= h[i]) r++;
            best = Math.max(best, h[i] * (r - l + 1));
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Two passes of "previous/next smaller index" (monotonic stacks), then one pass for areas. O(n). */
    public static int nearestSmaller(int[] h) {
        int n = h.length;
        int[] left = new int[n], right = new int[n];         // first smaller index on each side (exclusive)
        Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] >= h[i]) st.pop();
            left[i] = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
            st.push(i);
        }
        st.clear();
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] >= h[i]) st.pop();
            right[i] = st.isEmpty() ? n : st.peek();
            st.push(i);
        }
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) best = Math.max(best, h[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1));
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal one pass: stack of indexes with increasing heights. When a lower bar arrives, every taller bar
     * on the stack has found its right boundary (i) and its left boundary is the element below it.
     * A sentinel height 0 at i == n flushes the stack. O(n).
     */
    public static int onePass(int[] h) {
        Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i <= h.length; i++) {
            int cur = i == h.length ? 0 : h[i];
            while (!st.isEmpty() && h[st.peek()] > cur) {
                int height = h[st.pop()];
                int leftBoundary = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek();
                best = Math.max(best, height * (i - leftBoundary - 1));
            }
            st.push(i);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Follow-up: maximal rectangle of 1s in a binary matrix — each row is a histogram of column heights. */
    public static int maximalRectangle(char[][] grid) {
        if (grid.length == 0) return 0;
        int[] heights = new int[grid[0].length];
        int best = 0;
        for (char[] row : grid) {
            for (int c = 0; c < row.length; c++) heights[c] = row[c] == '1' ? heights[c] + 1 : 0;
            best = Math.max(best, onePass(heights));
        }
        return best;
    }
}

docs.title: Min stack in O(1)
docs.text: Medium Stack Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top and getMin, all in O(1).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Naive: scan the stack in getMin. That's O(n).
  2. Tempting but wrong: keep a single min variable. After you pop the minimum, you don't know the previous minimum.
  3. Insight: a stack only changes at the top, so the minimum below any entry never changes while that entry exists. Store minSoFar alongside each value. getMin is then peek().minSoFar.
  4. Expert, O(1) extra space: keep one min field. When pushing a new minimum x, store the encoded value 2x − oldMin, which is always below x. On pop, a stored value below min means "this was a minimum push", and oldMin = 2·min − stored recovers the previous minimum. Use long so 2x − min can't overflow.

docs.title: Trace (pairs version)
docs.text: Op Stack (value, minSoFar), top on the right getMin push 5 (5,5) 5 push 3 (5,5) (3,3) 3 push 7 (5,5) (3,3) (7,3) 3 pop (5,5) (3,3) 3 pop (5,5) 5, recovered automatically

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/** Stack with push, pop, top and getMin — all O(1). */
public final class MinStack {
    /** Each entry remembers the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed. */
    private record Entry(int value, int minSoFar) {}

    private final Deque<Entry> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void push(int x) {
        int min = stack.isEmpty() ? x : Math.min(x, stack.peek().minSoFar());
        stack.push(new Entry(x, min));
    }

    public int pop() {
        if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return stack.pop().value();                          // the entry below already knows its own min
    }

    public int top() {
        if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return stack.peek().value();
    }

    public int getMin() {
        if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return stack.peek().minSoFar();
    }

    /**
     * Expert variant: O(1) EXTRA space (one long for the min). When x is a new minimum we store an encoded
     * value 2x - oldMin (always < x), which lets pop recover the previous minimum.
     */
    public static final class Encoded {
        private final Deque<Long> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private long min;

        public void push(int x) {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) {
                stack.push((long) x);
                min = x;
            } else if (x < min) {
                stack.push(2L * x - min);                    // encoded flag: value < current min
                min = x;
            } else {
                stack.push((long) x);
            }
        }

        public int pop() {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            long y = stack.pop();
            if (y < min) {                                   // this slot held the min → restore the previous min
                int popped = (int) min;
                min = 2 * min - y;
                return popped;
            }
            return (int) y;
        }

        public int top() {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            long y = stack.peek();
            return (int) (y < min ? min : y);
        }

        public int getMin() {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return (int) min;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Next greater element
docs.text: Medium Monotonic stack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: For every element, find the first element to its right that is strictly greater, or −1. [4, 5, 2, 25, 7, 8] → [5, 25, 25, −1, 8, −1]. Variants: circular array (LeetCode 503), and previous smaller element.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each i, scan to the right. That's O(n²).
  2. Waste: scanning right from i, you pass elements that can never be anyone's answer. In … 3, 9 …, the 3 is hidden behind the 9 for every element to the left of both.
  3. Monotonic stack (right to left): keep only the useful candidates, which form a decreasing sequence. For a[i], pop every candidate ≤ a[i] (now useless), and the top is the answer. Then push a[i].
  4. Equivalent left-to-right view: the stack holds indexes still waiting for an answer. A new bigger value resolves every smaller waiting index.
  5. Circular: loop 2n times using i % n, and push only in the first lap.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Next greater element with a monotonic stack (right to left)
  1. Walk from the right. The stack holds candidates in decreasing order: anything smaller than a newcomer can never be anyone's answer again.
  2. i = 5: the stack is empty, so nothing to the right is bigger: out[5] = −1.
  3. Push 8: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  4. i = 4: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[4] = 8.
  5. Push 7: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  6. i = 3, a[i] = 25: pop 7, 8 (≤ 25). 25 is closer and at least as big, so they're useless from here on.
  7. i = 3: the stack is empty, so nothing to the right is bigger: out[3] = −1.
  8. Push 25: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  9. i = 2: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[2] = 25.
  10. Push 2: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  11. i = 1, a[i] = 5: pop 2 (≤ 5). 5 is closer and at least as big, so they're useless from here on.
  12. i = 1: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[1] = 25.
  13. Push 5: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  14. i = 0: the top of the stack is the next greater element: out[0] = 5.
  15. Push 4: it's a candidate for everything further left.
  16. Done: [5, 25, 25, −1, 8, −1]. Every value is pushed once and popped at most once: O(n).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Deque;

/** For each element, the first element to its RIGHT that is strictly greater; -1 if none. */
public final class NextGreaterElement {
    private NextGreaterElement() {}

    /** Brute force: scan right for every index. O(n^2). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            out[i] = -1;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) {
                if (a[j] > a[i]) {
                    out[i] = a[j];
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Monotonic stack, right to left: keep a stack of candidates in decreasing order. Pop everything
     * ≤ a[i] (it can never be the answer for anything further left, because a[i] is closer and bigger).
     * Each index is pushed and popped once → O(n).
     */
    public static int[] monotonicStack(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();           // values, decreasing from bottom to top
        for (int i = a.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() <= a[i]) stack.pop();
            out[i] = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek();
            stack.push(a[i]);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Left-to-right form: stack holds indexes still WAITING for their answer; a bigger value resolves them. */
    public static int[] leftToRight(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        Arrays.fill(out, -1);
        Deque<Integer> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && a[waiting.peek()] < a[i]) out[waiting.pop()] = a[i];
            waiting.push(i);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Circular array (LeetCode 503): walk the array twice, only push during the first lap. */
    public static int[] circular(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] out = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(out, -1);
        Deque<Integer> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 2 * n; i++) {
            int v = a[i % n];
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && a[waiting.peek()] < v) out[waiting.pop()] = v;
            if (i < n) waiting.push(i);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Mirror problem: previous smaller element (nearest strictly smaller to the LEFT). */
    public static int[] previousSmaller(int[] a) {
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() >= a[i]) stack.pop();
            out[i] = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek();
            stack.push(a[i]);
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Queue using two stacks
docs.text: Easy Design Amortised O(1)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a FIFO queue (enqueue, dequeue, peek, isEmpty) using only stacks. Reverse variant: a LIFO stack using only a queue.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A stack reverses order. Two reversals cancel out, so pouring stack A into stack B puts the oldest element on top of B.
  2. Use in for every new element and out to serve the oldest.
  3. The key rule: refill out only when it is empty. If you pour while out still holds elements, newer elements land on top of older ones and FIFO order breaks.
  4. Each element is pushed to in once, moved once, and popped from out once. That's 3 operations, so dequeue is amortised O(1), even though a single dequeue can cost O(n).

docs.title: Stack using one queue
docs.text: After offer(x), rotate the queue size − 1 times (poll and re-offer) so x moves to the front. Push is O(n) and pop is O(1).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/**
 * FIFO queue built from two LIFO stacks. Every element is moved from {@code in} to {@code out} at most once,
 * so enqueue/dequeue are amortised O(1). Also: a stack built from one queue.
 */
public final class QueueUsingStacks {
    private final Deque<Integer> in = new ArrayDeque<>();    // receives new elements
    private final Deque<Integer> out = new ArrayDeque<>();   // serves the oldest element on top

    public void enqueue(int x) {
        in.push(x);
    }

    public int dequeue() {
        shiftIfNeeded();
        if (out.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("queue is empty");
        return out.pop();
    }

    public int peek() {
        shiftIfNeeded();
        if (out.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException("queue is empty");
        return out.peek();
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return in.isEmpty() && out.isEmpty();
    }

    /** Only refill out when it is EMPTY — refilling earlier would bury older elements under newer ones. */
    private void shiftIfNeeded() {
        if (out.isEmpty()) while (!in.isEmpty()) out.push(in.pop());
    }

    /** Reverse direction: LIFO stack from ONE FIFO queue — rotate the queue after each push. push O(n), pop O(1). */
    public static final class StackUsingQueue {
        private final Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();

        public void push(int x) {
            q.offer(x);
            for (int i = 1; i < q.size(); i++) q.offer(q.poll());   // move older elements behind x
        }

        public int pop() {
            if (q.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return q.poll();
        }

        public int top() {
            if (q.isEmpty()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            return q.peek();
        }

        public boolean isEmpty() {
            return q.isEmpty();
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Sliding window maximum
docs.text: Hard Monotonic deque Heap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the maximum of every contiguous window of size k. [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3 → [3,3,5,5,6,7].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: compute the max of each window. That's O(n·k).
  2. Heap: a max-heap of (value, index). Leave expired elements in the heap and discard the top only when its index has left the window (lazy deletion). That's O(n log n).
  3. Insight: when a new element x arrives, every older element smaller than x can never be a maximum again. x is bigger and stays in the window longer. Throw them away.
  4. What's left is decreasing from front to back, so the front is the max. Keep it in a deque of indexes:
    • pop the front if it slid out of the window (index ≤ i − k);
    • pop from the back while a[back] ≤ x;
    • push x at the back; once i ≥ k − 1, record a[front].

docs.title: Dry run (k = 3), deque shown as values
Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.stackqueue;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Maximum of every window of size k. [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k=3 → [3,3,5,5,6,7]. */
public final class SlidingWindowMaximum {
    private SlidingWindowMaximum() {}

    /** Brute force: max of each window. O(n·k). */
    public static int[] bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0 || k <= 0) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i + k <= a.length; i++) {
            int max = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
            for (int j = i; j < i + k; j++) max = Math.max(max, a[j]);
            out[i] = max;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Max-heap of (value, index); lazily discard tops that slid out. O(n log n). */
    public static int[] heap(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0 || k <= 0) return new int[0];
        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Integer.compare(y[0], x[0]));
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            pq.offer(new int[]{a[i], i});
            if (i >= k - 1) {
                while (pq.peek()[1] <= i - k) pq.poll();     // stale: index left the window
                out[i - k + 1] = pq.peek()[0];
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: monotonic deque of indexes with DECREASING values. Front = current max.
     * Pop back while smaller than the new element (they can never be a max again), pop front if it slid out.
     * Each index enters and leaves once → O(n), O(k) space.
     */
    public static int[] monotonicDeque(int[] a, int k) {
        if (a.length == 0 || k <= 0) return new int[0];
        int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1];
        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();   // front fell out of the window
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) dq.pollLast(); // dominated by a[i]
            dq.offerLast(i);
            if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• A hash table turns a key into an array index (hash(key) & (capacity − 1)), so put, get and contains are O(1) on average. Collisions share a bucket. Java chains them in a list and turns a long chain into a red-black tree (8+ nodes), which caps the worst case at O(log n).
  • The trade: you pay O(n) memory to turn "search" from O(n) into O(1). Most "brute force O(n²) → optimal O(n)" improvements in interviews are exactly this trade.
  • Contract: if a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). Break it, and HashMap silently loses entries.

docs.title: Intersection of two arrays
docs.text: Easy HashSet Count map Two pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Unique (LeetCode 349): each common value once. [4,9,5] ∩ [9,4,9,8,4] → [4,9].
  2. With counts (LeetCode 350): each value as many times as it appears in both. [1,2,2,1] ∩ [2,2] → [2,2].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each value of a, search b. O(n·m).
  2. Unique: put a in a HashSet, then keep the values of b that are in it, collecting them in another set to remove repeats. O(n + m). Set.retainAll is the library version.
  3. With counts: a set loses the counts, so use a count map for a. While walking b, take a value only if its count is still > 0, then decrement.
  4. Both arrays sorted: two pointers, advancing the smaller side and taking the value when they're equal. O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * Intersection of two arrays.
 * {@link #unique}: each common value once (LeetCode 349). {@link #withCounts}: as many times as it appears in BOTH (LeetCode 350).
 * Results are sorted so they are easy to compare.
 */
public final class ArrayIntersection {
    private ArrayIntersection() {}

    /** Brute force: for each value of a, linear search in b. O(n·m). */
    public static int[] bruteForceUnique(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> out = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a)
            for (int y : b)
                if (x == y) {
                    out.add(x);
                    break;
                }
        return sorted(out);
    }

    /** Set of a, then keep values of b that are in it. O(n + m). */
    public static int[] unique(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> setA = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) setA.add(x);
        Set<Integer> out = new HashSet<>();
        for (int y : b) if (setA.contains(y)) out.add(y);
        return sorted(out);
    }

    /** Library: Set.retainAll does exactly "keep only what is also in the other collection". */
    public static int[] retainAll(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Set<Integer> setA = new HashSet<>(Arrays.stream(a).boxed().toList());
        setA.retainAll(Arrays.stream(b).boxed().toList());
        return sorted(setA);
    }

    /** With multiplicity: count a, then consume counts while walking b. O(n + m). */
    public static int[] withCounts(int[] a, int[] b) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) count.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int y : b) {
            int c = count.getOrDefault(y, 0);
            if (c > 0) {
                out.add(y);
                count.put(y, c - 1);                         // each copy in a can be used once
            }
        }
        return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sorted().toArray();
    }

    /** Both arrays already sorted: two pointers, O(1) extra space. Follow-up interviewers love. */
    public static int[] sortedTwoPointers(int[] a, int[] b) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int i = 0, j = 0;
        while (i < a.length && j < b.length) {
            if (a[i] < b[j]) i++;
            else if (a[i] > b[j]) j++;
            else {
                out.add(a[i]);
                i++;
                j++;
            }
        }
        return out.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    private static int[] sorted(Set<Integer> s) {
        return s.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sorted().toArray();
    }
}

docs.title: Contains duplicate
docs.text: Easy HashSet Sorting Streams

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if any value appears at least twice. [1,2,3,1] → true, [1,2,3,4] → false. Variant (LeetCode 219): two equal values whose indexes are at most k apart.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Can I modify the array (sorting in place saves memory)? How large is n? Do I need the duplicate itself or just yes/no?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: compare every pair. O(n²) time, O(1) space.
  2. Sort: equal values become neighbours, so one scan is enough. O(n log n) time, and O(1) extra if sorting in place is allowed.
  3. HashSet: remember what you've seen. Set.add already returns false for a repeat, so there's no separate contains call. O(n) time, O(n) space, and it exits early on the first duplicate.
  4. Within distance k: store the last index of each value. map.put returns the previous index, so you get it for free.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

/** Does any value appear at least twice? Plus the "within distance k" variant (LeetCode 219). */
public final class ContainsDuplicate {
    private ContainsDuplicate() {}

    /** Brute force: compare every pair. O(n^2), O(1). */
    public static boolean bruteForce(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++)
                if (a[i] == a[j]) return true;
        return false;
    }

    /** Sort a copy: duplicates become neighbours. O(n log n), O(n) for the copy (O(1) if mutation is allowed). */
    public static boolean sorting(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        for (int i = 1; i < c.length; i++) if (c[i] == c[i - 1]) return true;
        return false;
    }

    /** Optimal: HashSet.add returns false when the value is already present. O(n), O(n). */
    public static boolean hashSet(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) if (!seen.add(x)) return true;      // early exit on the first repeat
        return false;
    }

    /** Java 8 streams: distinct count smaller than total count. Always scans everything. */
    public static boolean streams(int[] a) {
        return Arrays.stream(a).distinct().count() < a.length;
    }

    /** Variant: two equal values whose indexes differ by at most k. Map value → last index. O(n). */
    public static boolean withinDistance(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> lastIndex = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            Integer prev = lastIndex.put(a[i], i);           // put returns the previous mapping
            if (prev != null && i - prev <= k) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }
}

docs.text: Hard Meet in the middle HashMap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given four arrays of length n, count the tuples (i,j,k,l) with a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] = 0. a=[1,2] b=[−2,−1] c=[−1,2] d=[0,2] → 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: four nested loops. O(n⁴). With n = 200 that's 1.6 billion iterations, which is too slow.
  2. Hash one array: three loops plus a lookup of −(x+y+z) in a count map of d. O(n³).
  3. Meet in the middle: split the four arrays into two pairs. Count every sum a[i] + b[j] in a map (n² entries). Then for every c[k] + d[l], add map[−(c[k] + d[l])]. O(n²) time and space.
  4. General principle: when you combine m independent choices, hash half of them and enumerate the other half. That turns O(Nᵐ) into O(N^(m/2)).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Count tuples (i, j, k, l) with a[i] + b[j] + c[k] + d[l] == 0 across four equal-length arrays (LeetCode 454). */
public final class FourSumCount {
    private FourSumCount() {}

    /** Brute force: four nested loops. O(n^4). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c, int[] d) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int x : a) for (int y : b) for (int z : c) for (int w : d) if ((long) x + y + z + w == 0) count++;
        return count;
    }

    /** Hash one array: three loops + lookup. O(n^3). A useful middle step when explaining. */
    public static int threeLoops(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c, int[] d) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> dCount = new HashMap<>();
        for (int w : d) dCount.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);
        int count = 0;
        for (int x : a) for (int y : b) for (int z : c) count += dCount.getOrDefault(-(x + y + z), 0);
        return count;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal meet-in-the-middle: count every pair sum of (a, b), then for each pair sum of (c, d) look up its
     * negation. O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space.
     */
    public static int meetInTheMiddle(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c, int[] d) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> abSums = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) for (int y : b) abSums.merge(x + y, 1, Integer::sum);
        int count = 0;
        for (int z : c) for (int w : d) count += abSums.getOrDefault(-(z + w), 0);
        return count;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Four loops O(n⁴) O(1) Three loops + map O(n³) O(n) Meet in the middle O(n²) O(n²)

docs.title: Contrast with 4Sum (one array, list the unique quadruplets)
docs.text: That variant asks for distinct value tuples from a single array. Sort it, fix two indexes, and run two pointers, for O(n³) with duplicate skipping. The hashing trick above fits counting across separate arrays.

docs.title: Longest consecutive sequence
docs.text: Medium HashSet

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array, in O(n). [100,4,200,1,3,2] → 4 (1,2,3,4). Duplicates don't break or extend a run.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each x, look for x+1, x+2, … with a linear search each time. O(n³) in the worst case.
  2. Sort: runs become contiguous. Skip duplicates, extend when c[i] == c[i−1] + 1, otherwise reset. O(n log n). That's good, but the problem asks for O(n).
  3. HashSet makes "is x+1 present?" O(1). But counting upward from every x is still O(n²) on 1..n, because each run is re-walked from each of its elements.
  4. Key insight: only start counting at a sequence start, an x where x − 1 is absent. Each run is then walked exactly once, so the total work is O(n), even though the loop looks nested.

docs.title: Dry run ({100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2})
docs.text: x x−1 present? Action Length 100 no count 100 1 4 yes (3) skip 200 no count 200 1 1 no count 1,2,3,4 4 3, 2 yes skip

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Length of the longest run of consecutive integers (any order, duplicates allowed). [100,4,200,1,3,2] → 4 (1..4). */
public final class LongestConsecutiveSequence {
    private LongestConsecutiveSequence() {}

    /** Brute force: for each x, count x+1, x+2, … with a linear search each time. O(n^3) worst case. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int len = 1;
            long next = (long) x + 1;
            while (contains(a, next)) {
                len++;
                next++;
            }
            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** Sort, then count runs, skipping duplicates. O(n log n). */
    public static int sorting(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 0) return 0;
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        int best = 1, run = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i < c.length; i++) {
            if (c[i] == c[i - 1]) continue;                  // duplicate: neither extends nor breaks
            run = (long) c[i] == (long) c[i - 1] + 1 ? run + 1 : 1;
            best = Math.max(best, run);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: put everything in a HashSet. Only start counting at a sequence START (x-1 not present),
     * so every element is walked at most once overall. O(n) time, O(n) space.
     */
    public static int hashSet(int[] a) {
        Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : a) set.add(x);
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : set) {                                  // iterate the set: duplicates already removed
            if (x != Integer.MIN_VALUE && set.contains(x - 1)) continue;   // not a start
            int len = 1;
            for (int y = x; y != Integer.MAX_VALUE && set.contains(y + 1); y++) len++;
            best = Math.max(best, len);
        }
        return best;
    }

    private static boolean contains(int[] a, long v) {
        for (int x : a) if (x == v) return true;
        return false;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force O(n³) O(1) Sort O(n log n) O(n) copy HashSet (starts only) O(n) O(n)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: x − 1 and y + 1 overflow at Integer.MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE, so the code guards them. Iterating the original array instead of the set re-processes duplicates, which is still correct but wasteful.

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text: Union-Find also solves it in near-O(n): union x with x+1 when both exist, and the answer is the largest component.

docs.title: Longest subarray with sum 0 / equal 0s and 1s
docs.text: Hard Prefix sum First-index map

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Longest subarray with sum 0 (GfG): [15,−2,2,−8,1,7,10,23] → 5 (−2,2,−8,1,7).
  2. Equal 0s and 1s (LeetCode 525): [0,1,1,1,1,1,0,0,0] → 6.

The code solves the general case, the longest subarray with sum k, which covers both.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: every start with a running sum. O(n²).
  2. Prefix-sum view: a[i+1..j] sums to k ⇔ prefix[j] − prefix[i] = k.
  3. To make that subarray longest for a fixed j, you want the smallest i, so store the first index at which each prefix value appears, and never overwrite it (putIfAbsent).
  4. Seed {0: −1}, so a subarray starting at index 0 has length j − (−1) = j + 1.
  5. Equal 0s and 1s: replace 0 with −1. Equal counts then means the sum is 0, so it's the same problem.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Longest subarray with sum 0 (GfG) and its twin: longest subarray with equal numbers of 0s and 1s
 * (LeetCode 525 — map 0 → -1 and it becomes the same problem). Generalised to sum k.
 */
public final class LongestZeroSumSubarray {
    private LongestZeroSumSubarray() {}

    /** Brute force: every start, running sum. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                if (sum == k) best = Math.max(best, j - i + 1);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: prefix sums with the FIRST index each prefix was seen. If prefix[j] - k was first seen at i,
     * a[i+1..j] sums to k and is the longest such subarray ending at j. Never overwrite → keeps it longest. O(n).
     */
    public static int longestWithSum(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Long, Integer> firstIndex = new HashMap<>();
        firstIndex.put(0L, -1);                              // empty prefix "ends" before index 0
        long prefix = 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) {
            prefix += a[j];
            Integer i = firstIndex.get(prefix - k);
            if (i != null) best = Math.max(best, j - i);
            firstIndex.putIfAbsent(prefix, j);               // FIRST occurrence only
        }
        return best;
    }

    public static int longestZeroSum(int[] a) {
        return longestWithSum(a, 0);
    }

    /** Equal 0s and 1s: treat 0 as -1, then it is "longest subarray with sum 0". */
    public static int longestEqualZerosOnes(int[] bits) {
        int[] mapped = new int[bits.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < bits.length; i++) mapped[i] = bits[i] == 0 ? -1 : 1;
        return longestZeroSum(mapped);
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) space with the map, versus O(n²) and O(1) for brute force.
