docs.title: Design a HashMap from scratch
docs.text: Expert Design Separate chaining Resizing

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement put, get, remove, containsKey and size with average O(1) operations, without using any built-in hash table. Support any key type, including null.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Generic keys or only int? Must it grow? (Yes.) Null keys? Thread safety? (No. Mention ConcurrentHashMap as a follow-up.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Array of buckets: the index is derived from key.hashCode(). Different keys can land in the same bucket, a collision, so each bucket holds a small linked list of entries (separate chaining).
  2. Index: hash & (capacity − 1). With a power-of-two capacity this equals hash mod capacity, is never negative, and costs one CPU instruction.
  3. Spread the bits: h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes the high bits into the low bits. Without it, hash codes that differ only in their high bits would all collide, because the mask only keeps the low bits. This is the same trick java.util.HashMap uses.
  4. Lookup: walk the chain comparing the stored hash first (a cheap int comparison), then Objects.equals (which is null-safe and possibly expensive).
  5. Load factor 0.75: once size > capacity × 0.75, chains start growing. Double the table and re-bucket. A single resize is O(n), but doubling makes put amortised O(1), for the same reason as an array stack.
  6. Store the hash in each node, so a resize never calls hashCode() again.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
table (capacity 8)
[0] → null
[1] → ("b", 2) → ("j", 9) → null      ← collision chain
[2] → null
[3] → ("d", 4) → null

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.Objects;

/**
 * A HashMap from scratch: array of buckets with separate chaining, hash spreading, load-factor resize.
 * Supports null keys like java.util.HashMap. Not thread-safe.
 */
public final class MyHashMap<K, V> {
    private static final int DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 16;          // always a power of two
    private static final float LOAD_FACTOR = 0.75f;

    /** One entry in a bucket's singly linked chain. */
    private static final class Node<K, V> {
        final int hash;
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K, V> next;

        Node(int hash, K key, V value, Node<K, V> next) {
            this.hash = hash;
            this.key = key;
            this.value = value;
            this.next = next;
        }
    }

    private Node<K, V>[] table;
    private int size;

    public MyHashMap() {
        this(DEFAULT_CAPACITY);
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public MyHashMap(int initialCapacity) {
        int cap = 1;
        while (cap < Math.max(1, initialCapacity)) cap <<= 1; // round up to a power of two
        table = (Node<K, V>[]) new Node[cap];
    }

    /**
     * Spread the high bits into the low bits (same trick as java.util.HashMap): the index uses only the low bits,
     * so without this, hashCodes differing only in high bits would all collide.
     */
    static int hash(Object key) {
        int h = key == null ? 0 : key.hashCode();
        return h ^ (h >>> 16);
    }

    /** index = hash mod capacity; with a power-of-two capacity that is a cheap bit mask, and never negative. */
    private static int indexFor(int hash, int capacity) {
        return hash & (capacity - 1);
    }

    /** Insert or replace. Returns the previous value or null. Average O(1). */
    public V put(K key, V value) {
        int h = hash(key);
        int i = indexFor(h, table.length);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[i]; n != null; n = n.next) {
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) { // cheap hash check first, then equals
                V old = n.value;
                n.value = value;
                return old;
            }
        }
        table[i] = new Node<>(h, key, value, table[i]);      // prepend to the chain
        if (++size > table.length * LOAD_FACTOR) resize();
        return null;
    }

    public V get(K key) {
        Node<K, V> n = find(key);
        return n == null ? null : n.value;
    }

    public boolean containsKey(K key) {
        return find(key) != null;                            // distinguishes "absent" from "mapped to null"
    }

    /** Remove the mapping; returns the old value or null. Average O(1). */
    public V remove(K key) {
        int h = hash(key);
        int i = indexFor(h, table.length);
        Node<K, V> prev = null;
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[i]; n != null; prev = n, n = n.next) {
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) {
                if (prev == null) table[i] = n.next;
                else prev.next = n.next;
                size--;
                return n.value;
            }
        }
        return null;
    }

    public int size() {
        return size;
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    /** Current bucket count (exposed for tests and teaching). */
    int capacity() {
        return table.length;
    }

    private Node<K, V> find(K key) {
        int h = hash(key);
        for (Node<K, V> n = table[indexFor(h, table.length)]; n != null; n = n.next) {
            if (n.hash == h && Objects.equals(n.key, key)) return n;
        }
        return null;
    }

    /** Double the table and re-bucket every node. O(n), but happens rarely enough to be amortised O(1) per put. */
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    private void resize() {
        Node<K, V>[] old = table;
        table = (Node<K, V>[]) new Node[old.length * 2];
        for (Node<K, V> head : old) {
            for (Node<K, V> n = head; n != null; ) {
                Node<K, V> next = n.next;
                int i = indexFor(n.hash, table.length);      // stored hash: no need to call hashCode() again
                n.next = table[i];
                table[i] = n;
                n = next;
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Operation Average Worst case (everything collides) put / get / remove O(1) O(n). Java 8 caps this at O(log n) by turning long chains into trees resize O(n), amortised O(1) per put

docs.title: How it's tested
docs.text: The test runs a differential check: 20,000 random put/remove/get calls applied to both MyHashMap and java.util.HashMap, asserting identical results and sizes through many resizes. It also uses a key class whose hashCode() always returns 7, to stress the collision chains.

docs.title: What java.util.HashMap adds on top
docs.text:
• Treeification: a chain with 8 or more nodes becomes a red-black tree, when the table has 64 or more buckets.
  • Resize splitting: after doubling, each node either keeps its index or moves to index + oldCapacity, decided by one bit.
  • Fail-fast iterators using modCount.

docs.title: Alternative: open addressing
docs.text: Store the entries in the array itself, and on a collision probe the next slot (linear or quadratic probing). It's cache-friendly, but deletion needs tombstones, and performance drops sharply above about 70% load. ThreadLocal and Python's dict use variants of it.

docs.title: Subarray sum equals K
docs.text: Medium Prefix sum HashMap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values can be negative. [1,1,1], k = 2 → 2 · [3,4,7,2,−3,1,4,2], k = 7 → 4.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Negative numbers? (Yes, which rules out a plain sliding window.) Count or list them? Overflow? (Use long sums.)

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: every start i, extending j with a running sum. O(n²).
  2. Why not a sliding window? A window works only if growing it always increases the sum. With negative numbers, shrinking might increase the sum, so the window logic breaks.
  3. Prefix-sum insight: sum(i+1..j) = prefix[j] − prefix[i]. So a subarray ending at j sums to k exactly when an earlier prefix equals prefix[j] − k.
  4. Keep a map prefix value → how many times seen. At each j, add map[prefix − k] to the count, then record prefix.
  5. Seed the map with {0: 1} (the empty prefix), so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values may be negative. [1,1,1], k=2 → 2. */
public final class SubarraySumEqualsK {
    private SubarraySumEqualsK() {}

    /** Brute force: every (start, end) with a running sum. O(n^2), O(1). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int j = i; j < a.length; j++) {
                sum += a[j];
                if (sum == k) count++;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal: prefix sums + hash map. sum(i+1..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i], so a subarray ending at j sums to k
     * exactly when an EARLIER prefix equals prefix[j] - k. Count those with a map prefix → occurrences. O(n), O(n).
     */
    public static int prefixSumMap(int[] a, int k) {
        Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        seen.put(0L, 1);                                     // empty prefix: lets subarrays starting at index 0 count
        long prefix = 0;
        int count = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            prefix += x;
            count += seen.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0);       // look up BEFORE inserting the current prefix
            seen.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        return count;
    }

    /** Only valid for NON-NEGATIVE values: sliding window (shrink while sum > k). O(n), O(1). */
    public static int slidingWindowNonNegative(int[] a, int k) {
        int count = 0, left = 0;
        long sum = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < a.length; right++) {
            sum += a[right];
            while (sum > k && left <= right) sum -= a[left++];
            if (sum == k && left <= right) {                // left > right means an EMPTY window (k == 0)
                count++;
                // zeros at the left edge give extra windows with the same sum
                for (int l = left; l < right && a[l] == 0; l++) count++;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }
}

docs.text: Approach Time Space Works with negatives? Brute force O(n²) O(1) ✅ Prefix sum + map O(n) O(n) ✅ Sliding window O(n) O(1) ❌ (non-negative only)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: Inserting the current prefix before the lookup counts the empty subarray when k = 0. Forgetting the {0: 1} seed. int prefix overflow on large inputs.

docs.title: Same pattern
docs.text: Longest subarray with sum k · Subarray sums divisible by k (key = prefix mod k, normalised to be non-negative) · Count of subarrays with XOR = k (prefix XOR).

docs.title: Top K frequent elements
docs.text: Medium HashMap Heap Bucket sort

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the k most frequent values. [1,1,1,2,2,3], k = 2 → [1,2]. (Here ties go to the smaller value, so results are deterministic and testable.) Can you beat O(n log n)?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Step 1 is always counting: map.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum). O(n). Let d = the number of distinct values.
  2. Sort the entries by frequency, descending. O(d log d), which is fine but sorts more than needed.
  3. Min-heap of size k: push each entry and pop the weakest whenever the size exceeds k. The heap keeps the k strongest seen so far. O(d log k), which is much better when k ≪ d.
  4. Bucket sort: a frequency is between 1 and n. Use bucket[f] = the values that occur f times, and read buckets from n down until you have k values. O(n).

docs.title: Bucket sort for [1,1,1,2,2,3]
docs.text:
Frequency 6 5 4 3 2 1 Values 1 2 3

Reading from the right gives 1, then 2, so k = 2 is satisfied.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.hashing;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/**
 * The k most frequent values. Ties broken by smaller value first so results are deterministic.
 * [1,1,1,2,2,3], k=2 → [1,2]. Output ordered from most to least frequent.
 */
public final class TopKFrequent {
    private TopKFrequent() {}

    private static final Comparator<Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>> BY_FREQ_DESC_THEN_VALUE =
            Map.Entry.<Integer, Integer>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey());

    /** Count, then sort all distinct values by frequency. O(n + d log d). */
    public static List<Integer> sorting(int[] a, int k) {
        return counts(a).entrySet().stream().sorted(BY_FREQ_DESC_THEN_VALUE).limit(k).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
    }

    /** Min-heap of size k: the root is the weakest of the current top k. O(n + d log k), O(d + k). */
    public static List<Integer> heap(int[] a, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(BY_FREQ_DESC_THEN_VALUE.reversed());
        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : counts(a).entrySet()) {
            pq.offer(e);
            if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();                    // evict the weakest — heap never exceeds k
        }
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) out.add(0, pq.poll().getKey()); // weakest comes out first → prepend
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Bucket sort: frequency is at most n, so bucket[f] = values occurring f times. Walk buckets from high to low.
     * O(n) time, O(n) space — beats O(n log n).
     */
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public static List<Integer> bucketSort(int[] a, int k) {
        List<Integer>[] buckets = new List[a.length + 1];
        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : counts(a).entrySet()) {
            int f = e.getValue();
            if (buckets[f] == null) buckets[f] = new ArrayList<>();
            buckets[f].add(e.getKey());
        }
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int f = a.length; f > 0 && out.size() < k; f--) {
            if (buckets[f] == null) continue;
            buckets[f].sort(null);                           // tie-break: smaller value first
            for (int v : buckets[f]) {
                if (out.size() == k) break;
                out.add(v);
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    private static Map<Integer, Integer> counts(int[] a) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) m.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
        return m;
    }
}

docs.title: Why a min-heap for the top k largest?
docs.text: You want to evict the weakest candidate quickly, and the weakest of the current top k sits at the root of a min-heap.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• Binary search works on anything monotone, not just sorted arrays: a rotated array, a slope, or a yes/no function of the answer ("can we do it with limit L?"). If you can discard half the candidates with one check, use it.
  • Sorting is often step 1 of a better algorithm: duplicates become neighbours, intervals can be swept, and two pointers work.

docs.title: The two binary-search templates (pick one and never mix them)
docs.text:
// Closed [lo, hi] — "find an exact match"
int lo = 0, hi = n - 1;
while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1; if (ok) return mid; if (tooSmall) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1; }

// Half-open [lo, hi) — "find the first index where condition becomes true" (lower bound)
int lo = 0, hi = n;
while (lo < hi)  { int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1; if (condition(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1; }
return lo;   // first true, or n if none

The classic bug

(lo + hi) / 2 overflows when lo + hi > Integer.MAX_VALUE. That bug sat in the JDK's own Arrays.binarySearch for nine years. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2 or (lo + hi) >>> 1.

docs.title: Linear & binary search
docs.text: Easy Binary search Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the index of target in a sorted array, or −1. [−5,−1,0,3,8,13,21], 8 → 4. Bonus: integer square root (the largest r with r² ≤ x) using binary search on the answer.

docs.title: Clarifying questions
docs.text: Sorted ascending? Duplicates (which index do they want)? See first & last occurrence. Empty array?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Linear search checks every element. O(n), and it's the only option for unsorted data.
  2. Sorted insight: comparing with the middle element tells you which half cannot contain the target. Discard it.
  3. Halving gives about log₂ n steps. For a million elements that's about 20 comparisons.
  4. Invariant: "if the target exists, it is inside [lo, hi]". Every update must keep that true, which is why it's mid + 1 / mid − 1 (mid has already been checked).
  5. Recursive form: the same logic, with the range passed as parameters. The base case is an empty range.

docs.title: Dry run (target 8)
docs.text: lo hi mid a[mid] Action 0 6 3 3 3 < 8, go right 4 6 5 13 13 > 8, go left 4 4 4 8 found ✅

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Binary search for 8 in [−5, −1, 0, 3, 8, 13, 21]
  1. The target can be anywhere in [lo, hi] = [0, 6]. target = 8.
  2. mid = 0 + (6 − 0) / 2 = 3, a[mid] = 3.
  3. 3 < 8, so the target is strictly right of mid: discard the left half, lo = 4.
  4. mid = 4 + (6 − 4) / 2 = 5, a[mid] = 13.
  5. 13 > 8, so the target is left of mid: discard the right half, hi = 4.
  6. mid = 4 + (4 − 4) / 2 = 4, a[mid] = 8.
  7. a[4] = 8: found at index 4 after 3 probes instead of 5.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** Find the index of target in a SORTED array, or -1. */
public final class BinarySearch {
    private BinarySearch() {}

    /** Linear search: works on unsorted data too. O(n). */
    public static int linear(int[] a, int target) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] == target) return i;
        return -1;
    }

    /**
     * Iterative binary search on the closed range [lo, hi]. Each step discards half → O(log n), O(1).
     * Invariant: if target exists, it is inside [lo, hi].
     */
    public static int iterative(int[] a, int target) {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
        while (lo <= hi) {                                   // <= because [lo, hi] is closed: one element left still counts
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;                    // never (lo + hi) / 2 — it can overflow
            if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
            if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;               // target is strictly right of mid
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
        return -1;
    }

    /** Recursive form of the same idea. O(log n) time, O(log n) stack. */
    public static int recursive(int[] a, int target) {
        return recursive(a, target, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int recursive(int[] a, int target, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo > hi) return -1;                              // base case: empty range
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;                           // unsigned shift: also overflow-safe
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        return a[mid] < target ? recursive(a, target, mid + 1, hi) : recursive(a, target, lo, mid - 1);
    }

    /** Integer square root by binary search on the answer: largest r with r*r <= x. */
    public static int sqrt(int x) {
        if (x < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative");
        long lo = 0, hi = x;
        while (lo < hi) {
            long mid = (lo + hi + 1) / 2;                    // upper mid, because lo = mid below
            if (mid * mid <= x) lo = mid;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
        return (int) lo;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Linear O(n) O(1) Binary, iterative O(log n) O(1) Binary, recursive O(log n) O(log n) stack

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text: while (lo < hi) with closed bounds misses a single remaining element. (lo + hi) / 2 overflows. Setting lo = mid with a lower mid loops forever. That's why sqrt uses the upper mid.

docs.title: Count inversions
docs.text: Hard Merge sort Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]. This measures how far the array is from sorted. [8,4,2,1] → 6 (every pair). [1,20,6,4,5] → 5.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: check every pair. O(n²).
  2. Divide & conquer: inversions = (inside the left half) + (inside the right half) + (crossing: left element > right element).
  3. The crossing ones are the hard part, until both halves are sorted. Then, during the merge, whenever a right element R[j] is taken before the left element L[i], R[j] is smaller than L[i] and every element after it in the left half. That's mid − i + 1 inversions counted in one step.
  4. So it's merge sort plus one line of counting, for O(n log n).

docs.title: Merge step counting
docs.text:
left  = [2, 4, 8]      right = [1, 3]
take 1 (right) → beats 2, 4, 8  → +3
take 2 (left)
take 3 (right) → beats 4, 8     → +2
take 4, 8
crossing inversions = 5

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** Number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j] — "how far from sorted" an array is. [8,4,2,1] → 6. */
public final class CountInversions {
    private CountInversions() {}

    /** Brute force: check every pair. O(n^2). */
    public static long bruteForce(int[] a) {
        long count = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a[i] > a[j]) count++;
        return count;
    }

    /**
     * Merge sort, counting while merging: when a right-half element is taken before left[i..mid],
     * it is smaller than ALL remaining left elements → it forms (mid - i + 1) inversions at once. O(n log n).
     * Works on a copy so the input is untouched. Result is long: up to n(n-1)/2.
     */
    public static long mergeSort(int[] a) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        return sortCount(c, new int[c.length], 0, c.length - 1);
    }

    private static long sortCount(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return 0;
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        long count = sortCount(a, tmp, lo, mid) + sortCount(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi);
        System.arraycopy(a, lo, tmp, lo, hi - lo + 1);
        int i = lo, j = mid + 1;
        for (int k = lo; k <= hi; k++) {
            if (i > mid) a[k] = tmp[j++];
            else if (j > hi) a[k] = tmp[i++];
            else if (tmp[j] < tmp[i]) {
                count += mid - i + 1;                        // tmp[j] beats every remaining left element
                a[k] = tmp[j++];
            } else a[k] = tmp[i++];
        }
        return count;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Return a long, since n = 100,000 reversed gives about 5·10⁹ inversions, which overflows an int. The tests check exactly this.

docs.title: Bubble, selection, insertion & counting sort
docs.text: Easy Sorting Stability

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement the classic simple sorts, and be able to explain each one's invariant, stability and best case.

docs.title: The invariant behind each sort
docs.text: Sort After pass i… Inner action Bubble the last i elements are the largest, in final position swap adjacent pairs that are out of order Selection the first i elements are the smallest, in final position find the min of the rest and swap it to the front Insertion the first i elements are sorted among themselves shift bigger ones right and drop the key in

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Bubble: after each pass the largest remaining element is at the end. If a pass makes no swaps, the array is sorted, so stop. That makes the best case O(n).
  2. Selection: always exactly n − 1 swaps, which is useful when writes are expensive. It is not stable, because the long-distance swap can jump an element over its equal twin.
  3. Insertion: like sorting playing cards in your hand. Shift instead of swapping, which means fewer writes. On nearly sorted data it's nearly O(n). TimSort uses it for small runs.
  4. Counting sort: if values are small integers in [0, k], don't compare at all. Count them, take prefix sums to get each value's final position, and place elements right to left to keep it stable. That's O(n + k).

docs.title: Stability, illustrated
docs.text: Sort [(3,a), (1,b), (3,c)] by number. A stable sort gives (1,b) (3,a) (3,c). An unstable one may give (3,c) (3,a). Stability matters when you sort by one key after another (for example, by name, then by department).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** The O(n^2) sorts every interview expects you to write and compare. All sort in place, ascending. */
public final class ElementarySorts {
    private ElementarySorts() {}

    /** Bubble sort: repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; the largest "bubbles" to the end each pass. Stable. */
    public static void bubble(int[] a) {
        for (int end = a.length - 1; end > 0; end--) {
            boolean swapped = false;
            for (int i = 0; i < end; i++) {
                if (a[i] > a[i + 1]) {                       // strict > keeps equal elements in order → stable
                    swap(a, i, i + 1);
                    swapped = true;
                }
            }
            if (!swapped) return;                            // already sorted: best case O(n)
        }
    }

    /** Selection sort: pick the minimum of the unsorted part, put it at the front. Exactly n-1 swaps. NOT stable. */
    public static void selection(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
            int min = i;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a[j] < a[min]) min = j;
            swap(a, i, min);
        }
    }

    /** Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix, shifting bigger elements right. Stable, adaptive, great for small/nearly sorted input. */
    public static void insertion(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {
            int key = a[i], j = i - 1;
            while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {
                a[j + 1] = a[j];                             // shift, don't swap: fewer writes
                j--;
            }
            a[j + 1] = key;
        }
    }

    /** Recursive insertion sort: sort the first n-1, then insert the last. */
    public static void insertionRecursive(int[] a) {
        insertionRecursive(a, a.length);
    }

    private static void insertionRecursive(int[] a, int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return;
        insertionRecursive(a, n - 1);
        int key = a[n - 1], j = n - 2;
        while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) {
            a[j + 1] = a[j];
            j--;
        }
        a[j + 1] = key;
    }

    /** Counting sort for values in [0, maxValue]: O(n + k), not comparison-based. Stable when done via prefix sums. */
    public static int[] counting(int[] a, int maxValue) {
        int[] count = new int[maxValue + 1];
        for (int x : a) count[x]++;
        for (int v = 1; v <= maxValue; v++) count[v] += count[v - 1];   // count[v] = number of elements <= v
        int[] out = new int[a.length];
        for (int i = a.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) out[--count[a[i]]] = a[i];   // right-to-left keeps stability
        return out;
    }

    private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.title: Find a peak element
docs.text: Hard Binary search on a slope

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A peak is strictly greater than its neighbours. Treat out-of-bounds neighbours as −∞, and adjacent values are never equal. Return the index of any peak in O(log n). [1,2,1,3,5,6,4] → 1 or 5.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Linear: the first i with a[i] > a[i+1] is a peak, because everything before it was climbing. O(n).
  2. Why binary search works on an unsorted array: look at the slope at mid.
    • If a[mid] < a[mid+1], you're going uphill. Keep walking right: either it keeps rising to the end (then the last element is a peak, since a[n] = −∞) or it turns down somewhere, and that turn is a peak. A peak must exist to the right.
    • Otherwise you're going downhill or standing on a peak, so a peak exists at mid or to its left.
  3. Every step keeps a half that is guaranteed to contain a peak. That guarantee is all binary search needs. Being sorted is just one way to get it.

docs.title: Picture
docs.text:
6
      5   4        mid at 3 (value 3): a[3] < a[4] → uphill → go right
  2     3
1   1

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/**
 * A peak is strictly greater than its neighbours (a[-1] = a[n] = -∞). Neighbours are never equal.
 * Return the index of ANY peak. [1,2,1,3,5,6,4] → 1 or 5.
 */
public final class FindPeakElement {
    private FindPeakElement() {}

    /** Linear: the first i with a[i] > a[i+1] is a peak (everything before it was rising). O(n). */
    public static int linear(int[] a) {
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) if (a[i] > a[i + 1]) return i;
        return a.length - 1;
    }

    /**
     * Binary search on the slope: if a[mid] < a[mid+1] we are on an upward slope and a peak MUST exist to the right
     * (the array eventually drops to -∞). Otherwise a peak exists at mid or to its left. O(log n).
     */
    public static int binary(int[] a) {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (a[mid] < a[mid + 1]) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        return lo;
    }

    /** Recursive version of the same idea. */
    public static int recursive(int[] a) {
        return recursive(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int recursive(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return lo;
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        return a[mid] < a[mid + 1] ? recursive(a, mid + 1, hi) : recursive(a, lo, mid);
    }

    public static boolean isPeak(int[] a, int i) {
        boolean left = i == 0 || a[i] > a[i - 1], right = i == a.length - 1 || a[i] > a[i + 1];
        return left && right;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Linear O(n). Binary O(log n), with O(1) space iteratively or O(log n) stack recursively.

docs.title: First & last occurrence (lower / upper bound)
docs.text: Medium Binary search

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: In a sorted array with duplicates, return the first and last index of target, or [−1, −1]. [5,7,7,8,8,10], 8 → [3, 4]. Bonus: count the occurrences in O(log n).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Linear scan: O(n). Binary search, then expand left and right: O(n) in the worst case ([8,8,8,…,8]).
  2. Insight: don't search for the target. Search for a boundary:
    • lower bound = the first index with a[i] ≥ target;
    • upper bound = the first index with a[i] > target.
  3. Both are "find the first index where a condition becomes true", which is the half-open template. When the condition holds at mid, keep mid as a candidate (hi = mid). Otherwise discard it (lo = mid + 1).
  4. first = lower bound (if a[first] == target), last = upper bound − 1, and count = upper bound − lower bound.

docs.title: Dry run (lower bound of 8 in [5,7,7,8,8,10])
docs.text: lo hi mid a[mid] ≥ 8? Action 0 6 3 yes hi = 3 0 3 1 no lo = 2 2 3 2 no lo = 3 3 3 stop 3

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** First and last index of target in a sorted array with duplicates; {-1, -1} if absent. [5,7,7,8,8,10], 8 → {3, 4}. */
public final class FirstLastOccurrence {
    private FirstLastOccurrence() {}

    /** Linear scan. O(n). */
    public static int[] linear(int[] a, int target) {
        int first = -1, last = -1;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (a[i] == target) {
                if (first == -1) first = i;
                last = i;
            }
        }
        return new int[]{first, last};
    }

    /** Two binary searches: lower bound and upper bound. O(log n). */
    public static int[] binary(int[] a, int target) {
        int first = lowerBound(a, target);
        if (first == a.length || a[first] != target) return new int[]{-1, -1};
        return new int[]{first, upperBound(a, target) - 1};
    }

    /** First index with a[i] >= target (a.length if none). Half-open [lo, hi) template. */
    public static int lowerBound(int[] a, int target) {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (a[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;               // mid is too small: answer is to the right
            else hi = mid;                                   // mid might be the answer: keep it
        }
        return lo;
    }

    /** First index with a[i] > target (a.length if none). */
    public static int upperBound(int[] a, int target) {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (a[mid] <= target) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        return lo;
    }

    /** Count of target = upperBound - lowerBound. O(log n). */
    public static int count(int[] a, int target) {
        return upperBound(a, target) - lowerBound(a, target);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(log n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n) for the linear or "find and expand" approaches.

docs.title: Java equivalents
docs.text: Arrays.binarySearch returns some matching index, not necessarily the first. For bounds on collections, use TreeMap.ceilingKey / higherKey. C++ users know these as lower_bound / upper_bound.

docs.title: Kth smallest element (Quickselect)
docs.text: Hard Quickselect Heap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the k-th smallest element (1-based) of an unsorted array. [7,10,4,3,20,15], k = 3 → 7. Twin: the k-th largest is the (n − k + 1)-th smallest.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sort: O(n log n). Simple, but it sorts far more than needed.
  2. Max-heap of size k: keep the k smallest seen so far, with the largest of them on top. The top is the answer. That's O(n log k), and it works on a stream where you can't hold everything.

  3. Quickselect: partition around a pivot, exactly like quicksort. The pivot lands at its final sorted index p.

    • p == k − 1: done.
    • p < k − 1: the answer is on the right. Ignore the left completely.
    • p > k − 1: the answer is on the left.

    Since only one side is ever processed, the expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n = O(n). 4. Use a random pivot. A fixed one makes sorted input O(n²).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

/** k-th smallest element (1-based) of an unsorted array. [7,10,4,3,20,15], k=3 → 7. */
public final class KthSmallest {
    private KthSmallest() {}

    /** Sort a copy. O(n log n). */
    public static int sorting(int[] a, int k) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        return c[k - 1];
    }

    /** Max-heap of size k: its root is the k-th smallest seen so far. O(n log k), O(k). Works on streams. */
    public static int maxHeap(int[] a, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
        for (int x : a) {
            pq.offer(x);
            if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();                    // drop the largest: it can't be among the k smallest
        }
        return pq.peek();
    }

    /**
     * Quickselect (Hoare's selection): partition like quicksort, then recurse into ONE side only.
     * n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n) expected with a random pivot; O(n^2) worst case. Works on a copy.
     */
    public static int quickselect(int[] a, int k) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        int lo = 0, hi = c.length - 1, target = k - 1;
        while (true) {
            int p = partition(c, lo, hi);
            if (p == target) return c[p];
            if (p < target) lo = p + 1;
            else hi = p - 1;
        }
    }

    private static int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        MergeQuickSort.swap(a, lo + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(hi - lo + 1), hi);
        int pivot = a[hi], i = lo;
        for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) if (a[j] < pivot) MergeQuickSort.swap(a, i++, j);
        MergeQuickSort.swap(a, i, hi);
        return i;
    }

    /** Kth LARGEST is the (n - k + 1)-th smallest. */
    public static int kthLargest(int[] a, int k) {
        return quickselect(a, a.length - k + 1);
    }
}

docs.title: Median of two sorted arrays
docs.text: Expert Binary search on a partition

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Two sorted arrays of sizes m and n. Return the median of their union in O(log(min(m, n))). [1,3] + [2] → 2.0 · [1,2] + [3,4] → 2.5.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Merge everything, then pick the middle: O(m + n) time and space.
  2. Merge only to the middle: O(m + n) time, O(1) space. That's a good answer, but not the target.
  3. Reframe the question: the median splits the combined data into a left half and a right half of equal size, where everything on the left ≤ everything on the right.
  4. Cut array a after i elements. Then b must be cut after j = half − i elements. Only i is free, so binary search i over the shorter array.
  5. The cut is valid when aLeft ≤ bRight and bLeft ≤ aRight. If aLeft > bRight, you took too many from a, so move i left. Otherwise move it right.
  6. Median = max(leftSide) for an odd total, or (max(leftSide) + min(rightSide)) / 2 for an even total. Use ±∞ sentinels for empty sides.

docs.title: Picture
docs.text:
a:  1  3  | 8  9          i = 2
b:  2  4  5 | 7  10       j = half − i = 3
left = {1,3,2,4,5}  right = {8,9,7,10}
check: 3 ≤ 7 ✅  5 ≤ 8 ✅  → odd total, median = max(3,5) = 5

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** Median of two sorted arrays (not both empty). [1,3] + [2] → 2.0; [1,2] + [3,4] → 2.5. Target O(log(min(m,n))). */
public final class MedianTwoSortedArrays {
    private MedianTwoSortedArrays() {}

    /** Merge until the middle (like merge sort's merge). O(m + n) time, O(1) space. */
    public static double merge(int[] a, int[] b) {
        int total = a.length + b.length, i = 0, j = 0, prev = 0, curr = 0;
        for (int step = 0; step <= total / 2; step++) {
            prev = curr;
            curr = (j >= b.length || (i < a.length && a[i] <= b[j])) ? a[i++] : b[j++];
        }
        return total % 2 == 1 ? curr : (prev + (double) curr) / 2;
    }

    /**
     * Partition binary search on the SHORTER array. Cut a at i and b at j = half - i so the left side holds
     * half the elements. The cut is correct when aLeft <= bRight and bLeft <= aRight; then the median comes from
     * the max of the left side and the min of the right side. O(log(min(m, n))).
     */
    public static double partition(int[] a, int[] b) {
        if (a.length > b.length) return partition(b, a);     // binary search the smaller array
        int m = a.length, n = b.length, half = (m + n + 1) / 2;
        int lo = 0, hi = m;
        while (lo <= hi) {
            int i = (lo + hi) >>> 1, j = half - i;
            int aLeft = i == 0 ? Integer.MIN_VALUE : a[i - 1];
            int aRight = i == m ? Integer.MAX_VALUE : a[i];
            int bLeft = j == 0 ? Integer.MIN_VALUE : b[j - 1];
            int bRight = j == n ? Integer.MAX_VALUE : b[j];
            if (aLeft <= bRight && bLeft <= aRight) {        // valid cut
                int leftMax = Math.max(aLeft, bLeft);
                if ((m + n) % 2 == 1) return leftMax;
                return (leftMax + (double) Math.min(aRight, bRight)) / 2;
            }
            if (aLeft > bRight) hi = i - 1;                  // took too many from a
            else lo = i + 1;                                 // took too few from a
        }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("arrays must be sorted");
    }
}

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: The jump from "search for a value" to "search for a cut" is the whole insight, and the boundary handling (empty sides, odd/even totals, searching the shorter array) has to be exactly right. The tests compare it with a full merge on 500 random cases, including empty arrays.

docs.title: Merge sort & quick sort
docs.text: Medium Divide & conquer Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement both O(n log n) divide-and-conquer sorts, and explain when you'd choose each.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Divide & conquer: split the problem, solve the parts recursively, and combine.
  2. Merge sort splits blindly (at the middle) and does its work in the combine step, merging two sorted halves with two pointers. It's always O(n log n), stable, and needs an O(n) buffer.
  3. Quick sort does its work in the split step: partition around a pivot so the smaller elements go left and the larger ones right. Then there's nothing to combine. It sorts in place and is very fast in practice, but a bad pivot gives O(n²).
  4. Defending quick sort:
    • Random pivot makes the worst case astronomically unlikely, even on sorted input.
    • Recurse on the smaller side and loop on the larger keeps the stack at O(log n).
    • Hoare partition (two pointers moving inward) handles many duplicates gracefully, where Lomuto degrades to O(n²).
  5. Bottom-up merge sort merges runs of width 1, 2, 4, … with no recursion at all.

docs.title: Lomuto partition (pivot = last element)
docs.text: i marks the end of the "< pivot" zone. Scan with j, and when a[j] < pivot, swap it into the zone. At the end, swap the pivot to i, which is its final position.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

/** The O(n log n) divide-and-conquer sorts: merge sort (recursive + bottom-up) and quicksort (Lomuto + Hoare). */
public final class MergeQuickSort {
    private MergeQuickSort() {}

    /** Merge sort, top-down recursive. O(n log n) always, O(n) extra, STABLE. */
    public static void mergeSort(int[] a) {
        if (a.length < 2) return;
        mergeSort(a, new int[a.length], 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void mergeSort(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return;                                // base case: 0 or 1 element is sorted
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        mergeSort(a, tmp, lo, mid);
        mergeSort(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi);
        if (a[mid] <= a[mid + 1]) return;                    // halves already in order: skip the merge
        merge(a, tmp, lo, mid, hi);
    }

    static void merge(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int mid, int hi) {
        System.arraycopy(a, lo, tmp, lo, hi - lo + 1);
        int i = lo, j = mid + 1;
        for (int k = lo; k <= hi; k++) {
            if (i > mid) a[k] = tmp[j++];
            else if (j > hi) a[k] = tmp[i++];
            else if (tmp[j] < tmp[i]) a[k] = tmp[j++];       // strict < : take from the LEFT on ties → stable
            else a[k] = tmp[i++];
        }
    }

    /** Merge sort, bottom-up iterative: merge runs of width 1, 2, 4, … No recursion. */
    public static void mergeSortBottomUp(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        int[] tmp = new int[n];
        for (int width = 1; width < n; width *= 2) {
            for (int lo = 0; lo < n - width; lo += 2 * width) {
                merge(a, tmp, lo, lo + width - 1, Math.min(lo + 2 * width - 1, n - 1));
            }
        }
    }

    /** Quicksort with Lomuto partition and a RANDOM pivot. O(n log n) expected, O(n^2) worst, in place, NOT stable. */
    public static void quickSortLomuto(int[] a) {
        quickLomuto(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void quickLomuto(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        while (lo < hi) {
            int p = lomuto(a, lo, hi);
            if (p - lo < hi - p) {                           // recurse on the SMALLER side, loop on the larger:
                quickLomuto(a, lo, p - 1);                   // keeps the stack O(log n) even in bad cases
                lo = p + 1;
            } else {
                quickLomuto(a, p + 1, hi);
                hi = p - 1;
            }
        }
    }

    /** Lomuto: pivot at hi; everything < pivot is moved left of index i. Returns the pivot's final index. */
    static int lomuto(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        swap(a, lo + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(hi - lo + 1), hi);   // random pivot defeats sorted input
        int pivot = a[hi], i = lo;
        for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) if (a[j] < pivot) swap(a, i++, j);
        swap(a, i, hi);
        return i;
    }

    /** Quicksort with Hoare partition: two pointers moving inward, ~3x fewer swaps than Lomuto, handles duplicates well. */
    public static void quickSortHoare(int[] a) {
        quickHoare(a, 0, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static void quickHoare(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo >= hi) return;
        int pivot = a[lo + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(hi - lo + 1)];
        int i = lo - 1, j = hi + 1;
        while (true) {
            do i++; while (a[i] < pivot);
            do j--; while (a[j] > pivot);
            if (i >= j) break;
            swap(a, i, j);
        }
        quickHoare(a, lo, j);                                // Hoare returns a split point, not the pivot's index
        quickHoare(a, j + 1, hi);
    }

    static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.title: Search in a rotated sorted array
docs.text: Medium Binary search

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot: [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] → [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. Find target in O(log n). 0 → 4, 3 → −1. Bonus: find the minimum (the rotation point).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A linear search is O(n), and the problem explicitly asks for O(log n).
  2. Key observation: cut the range at mid, and at least one half is perfectly sorted. If a[lo] ≤ a[mid], the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is.
  3. In the sorted half, a simple range check (a[lo] ≤ target < a[mid]) tells you whether the target is there. If it is, go there. If not, it must be in the other half.
  4. Minimum: compare a[mid] with a[hi]. If a[mid] > a[hi], the drop (the minimum) is strictly to the right. Otherwise mid could be the minimum, so keep it.
  5. Alternative: find the pivot, then run a normal binary search with indexes shifted by the pivot ((mid + pivot) % n).

docs.title: Dry run (target 0 in [4,5,6,7,0,1,2])
docs.text: lo hi mid a[mid] Sorted half Target inside? Action 0 6 3 7 left [4..7] no lo = 4 4 6 5 1 left [0..1] yes hi = 4 4 4 4 0 found ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** A sorted array of DISTINCT values rotated at an unknown pivot: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. Search it and find its minimum in O(log n). */
public final class RotatedSortedArray {
    private RotatedSortedArray() {}

    /**
     * One binary search: at least one half of [lo, hi] is always sorted. Check whether target lies in the
     * sorted half; if yes go there, otherwise go to the other half.
     */
    public static int search(int[] a, int target) {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
        while (lo <= hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
            if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {                           // left half [lo, mid] is sorted
                if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
                else lo = mid + 1;
            } else {                                         // right half [mid, hi] is sorted
                if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
                else hi = mid - 1;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }

    /** Index of the minimum (= rotation count). Compare mid with the RIGHT end. */
    public static int minIndex(int[] a) {
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (a[mid] > a[hi]) lo = mid + 1;                // min is strictly right of mid
            else hi = mid;                                   // mid could be the min
        }
        return lo;
    }

    /** Alternative: find the pivot, then a normal binary search in the correct sorted part. */
    public static int searchViaPivot(int[] a, int target) {
        if (a.length == 0) return -1;
        int pivot = minIndex(a), n = a.length;
        int lo = 0, hi = n - 1;
        while (lo <= hi) {                                   // search in "virtual" sorted index space
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1, real = (mid + pivot) % n;
            if (a[real] == target) return real;
            if (a[real] < target) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

docs.text: With [1,0,1,1,1], a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] and you can't tell which half is sorted. Shrink both ends by one (lo++, hi--). The worst case degrades to O(n), and you should say so.

docs.title: Sort 0s, 1s and 2s (Dutch National Flag)
docs.text: Medium Three pointers In place

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2, in place, in one pass. [2,0,2,1,1,0] → [0,0,1,1,2,2].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A general sort is O(n log n), which is overkill with only three distinct values.
  2. Counting: count the 0s, 1s and 2s, then overwrite. O(n), but it takes two passes.
  3. One pass: keep four regions with three pointers: [0, low) = 0s · [low, mid) = 1s · [mid, high] = unknown · (high, n) = 2s.
  4. Look at a[mid]:
    • 0: swap it to low. The value coming back from low is a known 1, so advance both low and mid.
    • 1: it's already in the right region, so mid++.
    • 2: swap it to high and high--. The value coming back is unknown, so don't advance mid.
  5. Stop when mid > high, because the unknown region is empty.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Dutch national flag: sort [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] in one pass
  1. Regions: [0, low) are 0s · [low, mid) are 1s · [mid, high] unknown · (high, end] are 2s.
  2. a[mid] = 2: swap it to high and shrink high. Don't advance mid: the value that came back is still unknown.
  3. a[mid] = 0: swap it to low, then advance both (what came from low is a known 1, or the same cell).
  4. a[mid] = 0: swap it to low, then advance both (what came from low is a known 1, or the same cell).
  5. a[mid] = 2: swap it to high and shrink high. Don't advance mid: the value that came back is still unknown.
  6. a[mid] = 1: already in the middle zone, just advance mid.
  7. a[mid] = 1: already in the middle zone, just advance mid.
  8. mid (4) > high (3): nothing unknown is left. Sorted in one pass, O(1) extra space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/** Sort an array containing only 0, 1, 2 in place (Dutch National Flag). [2,0,2,1,1,0] → [0,0,1,1,2,2]. */
public final class SortColors {
    private SortColors() {}

    /** Two passes: count each colour, then overwrite. O(n), O(1). Simple but not one-pass. */
    public static void counting(int[] a) {
        int[] c = new int[3];
        for (int x : a) c[x]++;
        int k = 0;
        for (int colour = 0; colour < 3; colour++) for (int i = 0; i < c[colour]; i++) a[k++] = colour;
    }

    /**
     * Dijkstra's Dutch National Flag, one pass, three pointers:
     *   [0, low) = 0s · [low, mid) = 1s · [mid, high] = unknown · (high, n) = 2s.
     */
    public static void dutchFlag(int[] a) {
        int low = 0, mid = 0, high = a.length - 1;
        while (mid <= high) {
            switch (a[mid]) {
                case 0 -> swap(a, low++, mid++);             // swapped-in value from low is a known 1 → mid can advance
                case 1 -> mid++;
                default -> swap(a, mid, high--);             // swapped-in value from high is UNKNOWN → don't advance mid
            }
        }
    }

    private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.text: O(n) time in one pass, O(1) space.

docs.title: Where else
docs.text: This is quicksort's 3-way partition (< pivot, = pivot, > pivot), which makes quicksort fast on many duplicates. The same technique segregates negatives and positives, or even and odd numbers.

docs.title: Split array largest sum / allocate minimum pages
docs.text: Expert Binary search on the answer Greedy check

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Split a non-negative array into k contiguous non-empty parts so that the largest part sum is as small as possible. [7,2,5,10,8], k = 2 → 18 ([7,2,5] | [10,8]). The same problem appears as Allocate minimum pages (GfG, books → students), Painter's partition, and Capacity to ship within D days.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every position for the first cut and recurse on the rest. Exponential.
  2. Flip the question: instead of "what is the best split?", ask "can it be done with every part ≤ L?"
  3. The check is greedy and O(n): fill the current part until adding the next element would exceed L, then start a new part. If the number of parts needed is ≤ k, then L is feasible.
  4. Feasibility is monotone: if L works, every larger L also works. Monotone yes/no means you can binary search for the smallest feasible L.
  5. Bounds: L ≥ the max element (a part must hold it) and L ≤ the total sum (everything in one part).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.searchsort;

/**
 * Split non-negative array into k contiguous non-empty parts minimising the largest part sum.
 * Same as GfG "Allocate minimum pages" / "Painter's partition". [7,2,5,10,8], k=2 → 18 ([7,2,5] | [10,8]).
 */
public final class SplitArrayLargestSum {
    private SplitArrayLargestSum() {}

    /** Brute force recursion: try every position for the first cut. Exponential. */
    public static long bruteForce(int[] a, int k) {
        return best(a, 0, k);
    }

    private static long best(int[] a, int start, int k) {
        if (k == 1) {
            long s = 0;
            for (int i = start; i < a.length; i++) s += a[i];
            return s;
        }
        long result = Long.MAX_VALUE, first = 0;
        for (int end = start; end <= a.length - k; end++) {  // leave at least one element per remaining part
            first += a[end];
            result = Math.min(result, Math.max(first, best(a, end + 1, k - 1)));
        }
        return result;
    }

    /**
     * Binary search on the ANSWER: for a candidate limit L, greedily count how many parts are needed
     * (start a new part when adding would exceed L). parts(L) is monotone in L, so binary search
     * the smallest L with parts(L) <= k. Range: [max element, total sum]. O(n log(sum)).
     */
    public static long binarySearchOnAnswer(int[] a, int k) {
        long lo = 0, hi = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            lo = Math.max(lo, x);                            // a part must hold the biggest element
            hi += x;                                         // one part holding everything
        }
        while (lo < hi) {
            long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (partsNeeded(a, mid) <= k) hi = mid;          // feasible: try smaller
            else lo = mid + 1;
        }
        return lo;
    }

    static int partsNeeded(int[] a, long limit) {
        int parts = 1;
        long sum = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            if (sum + x > limit) {
                parts++;
                sum = 0;
            }
            sum += x;
        }
        return parts;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n · log(sum)) time and O(1) space, versus exponential for brute force. A DP alternative takes O(k·n²).

docs.title: Spot the pattern
docs.text: "Minimise the maximum" or "maximise the minimum", with a monotone feasibility check, means binary search on the answer. Other examples: Koko eating bananas · Aggressive cows (maximise the minimum distance) · Minimum days to make m bouquets.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• A binary tree node has at most two children. Height h ranges from log n (balanced) to n (a skewed "linked list"). Recursive solutions use O(h) stack, so state that explicitly.
  • BST property: every node in the left subtree < node < every node in the right subtree. That makes an in-order traversal sorted, and a balanced BST gives O(log n) search. Java's TreeMap is a red-black BST.
  • Almost every tree problem is a traversal plus one decision: what each node returns to its parent, and what it records globally.
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/** Binary tree node + helpers to build/print trees in LeetCode level-order form, e.g. [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]. */
public final class TreeNode {
    public int val;
    public TreeNode left, right;

    public TreeNode(int val) {
        this.val = val;
    }

    public TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) {
        this.val = val;
        this.left = left;
        this.right = right;
    }

    /** Build from level order; null marks a missing child. Empty / leading null → null tree. */
    public static TreeNode of(Integer... levelOrder) {
        if (levelOrder.length == 0 || levelOrder[0] == null) return null;
        TreeNode root = new TreeNode(levelOrder[0]);
        Deque<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(root);
        int i = 1;
        while (!queue.isEmpty() && i < levelOrder.length) {
            TreeNode node = queue.poll();
            if (i < levelOrder.length && levelOrder[i] != null) queue.offer(node.left = new TreeNode(levelOrder[i]));
            i++;
            if (i < levelOrder.length && levelOrder[i] != null) queue.offer(node.right = new TreeNode(levelOrder[i]));
            i++;
        }
        return root;
    }

    /** Level order with nulls, trailing nulls trimmed — the inverse of {@link #of}. */
    public static List<Integer> toLevelOrder(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        List<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayList<>();
        queue.add(root);
        for (int i = 0; i < queue.size(); i++) {
            TreeNode n = queue.get(i);
            out.add(n == null ? null : n.val);
            if (n != null) {
                queue.add(n.left);
                queue.add(n.right);
            }
        }
        while (!out.isEmpty() && out.get(out.size() - 1) == null) out.remove(out.size() - 1);
        return out;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return toLevelOrder(this).toString();
    }
}

docs.title: The universal recursive template
docs.text:
ReturnType solve(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return BASE;                 // 1. base case
    ReturnType l = solve(node.left);               // 2. trust the recursion
    ReturnType r = solve(node.right);
    updateGlobalAnswer(node, l, r);                // 3. answer that "bends" at this node (optional)
    return combineForParent(node, l, r);           // 4. what the parent can use
}
Diameter, balanced check, LCA and max path sum are all this template.

docs.title: Build a tree from pre-order & in-order
docs.text: Hard Divide & conquer HashMap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given the pre-order and in-order traversals of a tree with distinct values, rebuild the tree. pre [3,9,20,15,7], in [9,3,15,20,7] → [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]. Variant: post-order + in-order.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. In pre-order the first value is always the root: 3.
  2. Find 3 in the in-order array. Everything to its left is the left subtree ([9]) and everything to its right is the right subtree ([15,20,7]).
  3. The left subtree's size (1) tells you where it ends in pre-order: pre[1..1] is the left subtree and pre[2..4] is the right.
  4. Recurse on both parts with index ranges, not array copies.
  5. Speed-up: searching in-order for the root at every step is O(n), which makes the whole thing O(n²) on a skewed tree. Pre-build a value → index map so each lookup is O(1), and the total is O(n).
  6. Post + in: the root is the last element of the post-order array. Everything else is the same.

docs.text:
pre:  [3] [9] [20 15 7]          in:  [9] [3] [15 20 7]
       ↑   ↑      ↑                    ↑   ↑      ↑
     root left  right                left root  right

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/** Rebuild a binary tree (distinct values) from its pre-order and in-order traversals. Also from post + in. */
public final class BuildTree {
    private BuildTree() {}

    /**
     * Pre-order's first value is the root. Its position in in-order splits left subtree | right subtree, and the
     * left size tells where the right subtree starts in pre-order. Index map → O(n) total instead of O(n^2).
     */
    public static TreeNode fromPreIn(int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> pos = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) pos.put(inorder[i], i);
        return preIn(preorder, 0, preorder.length - 1, 0, pos);
    }

    private static TreeNode preIn(int[] pre, int preLo, int preHi, int inLo, Map<Integer, Integer> pos) {
        if (preLo > preHi) return null;
        TreeNode root = new TreeNode(pre[preLo]);
        int inRoot = pos.get(root.val), leftSize = inRoot - inLo;
        root.left = preIn(pre, preLo + 1, preLo + leftSize, inLo, pos);
        root.right = preIn(pre, preLo + leftSize + 1, preHi, inRoot + 1, pos);
        return root;
    }

    /** Post-order's LAST value is the root; otherwise identical. */
    public static TreeNode fromPostIn(int[] postorder, int[] inorder) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> pos = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) pos.put(inorder[i], i);
        return postIn(postorder, 0, postorder.length - 1, 0, pos);
    }

    private static TreeNode postIn(int[] post, int lo, int hi, int inLo, Map<Integer, Integer> pos) {
        if (lo > hi) return null;
        TreeNode root = new TreeNode(post[hi]);
        int inRoot = pos.get(root.val), leftSize = inRoot - inLo;
        root.left = postIn(post, lo, lo + leftSize - 1, inLo, pos);
        root.right = postIn(post, lo + leftSize, hi - 1, inRoot + 1, pos);
        return root;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time with the index map (O(n²) without it), O(n) space.

docs.title: Why do you need the in-order array?
docs.text: Pre-order and post-order together can't distinguish a node with only a left child from one with only a right child. In-order is the traversal that separates left from right. This is a frequent follow-up question.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The tests take 200 random tree shapes, relabel them with distinct values, generate their traversals, rebuild, and compare the structure.

docs.title: Diameter of a binary tree
docs.text: Medium Post-order Global best

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path does not have to pass through the root. [1,2,3,4,5] → 3 (4→2→1→3 or 5→2→1→3).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Every path has a single highest node, where it "bends". Through that node, the length is height(left) + height(right).
  2. Brute force: try each node as the bend and compute both heights from scratch. O(n²) on a skewed tree.
  3. Waste: the heights are recomputed over and over. A post-order traversal already computes every height once.
  4. Pattern: the recursion returns the height (what the parent needs) and records l + r in a global best (the answer that can't be extended upward). It's one pass, O(n).

docs.title: Picture
docs.text:
1
        /   \
       2     3        at node 2: l = 1, r = 1 → path 2 (4-2-5)
      / \             at node 1: l = 2, r = 1 → path 3 ✅
     4   5

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

/** Diameter = number of EDGES on the longest path between any two nodes (may not pass through the root). */
public final class Diameter {
    private Diameter() {}

    /** Brute force: at every node, leftHeight + rightHeight, recomputing heights each time. O(n^2) on a skewed tree. */
    public static int bruteForce(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) return 0;
        int through = TreeHeight.maxDepthRecursive(root.left) + TreeHeight.maxDepthRecursive(root.right);
        return Math.max(through, Math.max(bruteForce(root.left), bruteForce(root.right)));
    }

    /** Optimal: one post-order pass returns height AND updates the best "through this node" path. O(n). */
    public static int optimal(TreeNode root) {
        int[] best = {0};
        height(root, best);
        return best[0];
    }

    private static int height(TreeNode n, int[] best) {
        if (n == null) return 0;
        int l = height(n.left, best), r = height(n.right, best);
        best[0] = Math.max(best[0], l + r);                  // longest path that bends at n
        return 1 + Math.max(l, r);                           // what the parent can extend
    }
}

docs.title: Level-order traversal
docs.text: Easy BFS DFS with depth

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the values grouped by level, left to right. [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] → [[3],[9,20],[15,7]].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. "Level by level" means BFS with a queue.
  2. Knowing where a level ends: at the start of each round, size = queue.size() is exactly the number of nodes on the current level. Poll that many, and push their children for the next round.
  3. DFS alternative: pre-order carrying depth. The first time you reach a new depth, open a new list. Left is visited before right, so the order within a level is still left to right.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: Round Queue at start size Level output 1 3 1 [3] 2 9, 20 2 [9, 20] 3 15, 7 2 [15, 7]

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;

/** Level-order traversal grouped by level: [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]. Plus zig-zag order. */
public final class LevelOrder {
    private LevelOrder() {}

    /** BFS with a queue; snapshot the queue size to know where a level ends. O(n). */
    public static List<List<Integer>> bfs(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
                TreeNode n = q.poll();
                level.add(n.val);
                if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
            }
            out.add(level);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** DFS with depth: pre-order puts each value into the list for its depth. Same result, O(h) stack. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> dfs(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        dfs(root, 0, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void dfs(TreeNode n, int depth, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (n == null) return;
        if (depth == out.size()) out.add(new ArrayList<>());   // first time we reach this depth
        out.get(depth).add(n.val);
        dfs(n.left, depth + 1, out);
        dfs(n.right, depth + 1, out);
    }

    /** Zig-zag: alternate direction per level; add to the front of the level list on odd levels. O(n). */
    public static List<List<Integer>> zigzag(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        boolean leftToRight = true;
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            LinkedList<Integer> level = new LinkedList<>();
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
                TreeNode n = q.poll();
                if (leftToRight) level.addLast(n.val);
                else level.addFirst(n.val);                  // reverse without reversing the traversal
                if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
            }
            out.add(level);
            leftToRight = !leftToRight;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Zig-zag with two stacks (the classic GfG approach): children pushed in alternating order. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> zigzagTwoStacks(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> current = new ArrayDeque<>(), next = new ArrayDeque<>();
        current.push(root);
        boolean leftToRight = true;
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!current.isEmpty()) {
            TreeNode n = current.pop();
            level.add(n.val);
            TreeNode first = leftToRight ? n.left : n.right, second = leftToRight ? n.right : n.left;
            if (first != null) next.push(first);
            if (second != null) next.push(second);
            if (current.isEmpty()) {
                out.add(level);
                level = new ArrayList<>();
                Deque<TreeNode> t = current;
                current = next;
                next = t;
                leftToRight = !leftToRight;
            }
        }
        return out;
    }
}
(The same class also contains zig-zag order.)

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time. O(width) queue space for BFS (up to n/2 for the last level), O(h) stack for DFS.

docs.title: Lowest common ancestor
docs.text: Medium Post-order BST

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Return the deepest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant).

            3
          /   \
         5     1          LCA(5, 1) = 3
        / \   / \         LCA(5, 4) = 5   (a node can be its own ancestor)
       6   2 0   8        LCA(7, 4) = 2
          / \
         7   4

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Path approach: record root → p and root → q with backtracking DFS. The LCA is the last node the two paths share. It takes two traversals and O(h) memory.
  2. One-pass insight: ask each subtree "did you find p or q?"
    • If the current node is p or q, return it. Anything below it can't be lower than it.
    • If the left subtree found one and the right subtree found the other, this node is where the paths split, so it's the LCA.
    • If only one side found something, pass that result upward.
  3. BST: values tell you the direction. If both are smaller, go left. If both are larger, go right. Otherwise you're at the split point. That's O(h) with no recursion.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Lowest common ancestor of two values that exist in the tree (a node may be its own ancestor). */
public final class LowestCommonAncestor {
    private LowestCommonAncestor() {}

    /** Path comparison: record root→p and root→q paths, the last common node is the LCA. O(n), O(h). */
    public static TreeNode viaPaths(TreeNode root, int p, int q) {
        List<TreeNode> a = new ArrayList<>(), b = new ArrayList<>();
        if (!path(root, p, a) || !path(root, q, b)) return null;
        TreeNode lca = null;
        for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(a.size(), b.size()) && a.get(i) == b.get(i); i++) lca = a.get(i);
        return lca;
    }

    private static boolean path(TreeNode n, int target, List<TreeNode> out) {
        if (n == null) return false;
        out.add(n);
        if (n.val == target || path(n.left, target, out) || path(n.right, target, out)) return true;
        out.remove(out.size() - 1);                          // backtrack: target not under n
        return false;
    }

    /**
     * Optimal single pass: return the node if it is p or q; otherwise ask both subtrees.
     * Both non-null → this node is where the paths split → LCA. One non-null → pass it up. O(n), O(h).
     */
    public static TreeNode recursive(TreeNode root, int p, int q) {
        if (root == null || root.val == p || root.val == q) return root;
        TreeNode left = recursive(root.left, p, q), right = recursive(root.right, p, q);
        if (left != null && right != null) return root;
        return left != null ? left : right;
    }

    /** BST: walk down; both smaller → go left, both bigger → go right, otherwise we're at the split. O(h), O(1). */
    public static TreeNode bst(TreeNode root, int p, int q) {
        TreeNode n = root;
        while (n != null) {
            if (p < n.val && q < n.val) n = n.left;
            else if (p > n.val && q > n.val) n = n.right;
            else return n;
        }
        return null;
    }
}

docs.title: Binary tree maximum path sum
docs.text: Expert Post-order Gain function

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A path is any sequence of connected nodes, with no node repeated and at least one node. Return the maximum sum. Values can be negative. [−10,9,20,null,null,15,7] → 42 (15 → 20 → 7).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. As in the diameter problem, every path has one highest node where it bends. At that node the sum is node + (best chain going down-left) + (best chain going down-right).
  2. Define gain(n) = the best sum of a chain that starts at n and goes down one side: n.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)).
  3. Drop negative chains with max(0, …): a chain is only worth taking if it adds something.
  4. At each node, record the bending path in a global best. But return only one side to the parent, because a path that goes up can't use both children.
  5. Initialise the best to Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0. An all-negative tree must return its largest (least negative) node.

docs.title: Trace on [−10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]
