docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

/** Maximum sum of any path (any node to any node, at least one node, no node repeated). Values may be negative. */
public final class MaxPathSum {
    private MaxPathSum() {}

    /** Brute force: treat every node as the "bend" and compute the best downward chains from scratch. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("empty tree");
        int here = root.val + Math.max(0, bestDown(root.left)) + Math.max(0, bestDown(root.right));
        int best = here;
        if (root.left != null) best = Math.max(best, bruteForce(root.left));
        if (root.right != null) best = Math.max(best, bruteForce(root.right));
        return best;
    }

    private static int bestDown(TreeNode n) {
        if (n == null) return 0;
        return n.val + Math.max(0, Math.max(bestDown(n.left), bestDown(n.right)));
    }

    /**
     * Optimal post-order: gain(n) = best downward chain starting at n = n.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)).
     * At each node also try the path that bends here: n.val + max(0, gainL) + max(0, gainR). O(n).
     * Negative gains are dropped (max with 0): a chain only helps if it adds something.
     */
    public static int optimal(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("empty tree");
        int[] best = {Integer.MIN_VALUE};                    // MIN, not 0: an all-negative tree must return its max node
        gain(root, best);
        return best[0];
    }

    private static int gain(TreeNode n, int[] best) {
        if (n == null) return 0;
        int l = Math.max(0, gain(n.left, best)), r = Math.max(0, gain(n.right, best));
        best[0] = Math.max(best[0], n.val + l + r);          // path bending at n (can't be extended upward)
        return n.val + Math.max(l, r);                       // parent may extend only ONE side
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Brute force (recompute chains at each bend) O(n²) O(h) Gain function O(n) O(h)

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: Two values flow differently: the bending sum (recorded, but never returned) and the one-sided gain (returned). Mixing them up, or initialising the best to 0, are the classic failures. The tests check both against brute force on 300 random trees with negative values.

docs.title: Serialize & deserialize a binary tree
docs.text: Expert Pre-order BFS Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Design serialize(root) → String and deserialize(String) → root so that the round trip produces an identical tree. Values can be negative and repeated.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A single traversal without markers is ambiguous: pre-order 1,2 could mean 2 is the left child or the right child.
  2. Add null markers (#). Now pre-order fully determines the shape: 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#.
  3. Decoding mirrors encoding: read a token. If it's #, return null. Otherwise create the node, then recursively build the left subtree, then the right. An iterator over the tokens keeps track of the position automatically.
  4. Level-order format (what LeetCode displays): BFS writing # for missing children, with the trailing #s trimmed. Decode with a queue, assigning two tokens as the children of each dequeued node.
  5. Because markers encode the shape, duplicates and negatives just work. You never search for values.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.List;

/** Encode a tree to a string and decode it back to an identical tree. Works for duplicates and negatives. */
public final class SerializeTree {
    private SerializeTree() {}

    private static final String NULL = "#", SEP = ",";

    /** Pre-order with null markers: "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#". Markers make the shape unambiguous. O(n). */
    public static String serializePreorder(TreeNode root) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        pre(root, sb);
        return sb.substring(0, sb.length() - 1);            // drop trailing separator
    }

    private static void pre(TreeNode n, StringBuilder sb) {
        if (n == null) {
            sb.append(NULL).append(SEP);
            return;
        }
        sb.append(n.val).append(SEP);
        pre(n.left, sb);
        pre(n.right, sb);
    }

    /** Recursive decode: read a token; "#" → null, else build node and recursively read left then right. */
    public static TreeNode deserializePreorder(String data) {
        return build(Arrays.asList(data.split(SEP)).iterator());
    }

    private static TreeNode build(Iterator<String> tokens) {
        String t = tokens.next();
        if (t.equals(NULL)) return null;
        TreeNode n = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t));
        n.left = build(tokens);
        n.right = build(tokens);
        return n;
    }

    /**
     * BFS level order with markers (LeetCode's format), trailing markers trimmed. ArrayDeque rejects null, so the
     * queue is an ArrayList walked by index — it holds null children naturally. O(n).
     */
    public static String serializeLevelOrder(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) return "";
        List<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayList<>();
        queue.add(root);
        List<String> tokens = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < queue.size(); i++) {
            TreeNode n = queue.get(i);
            if (n == null) {
                tokens.add(NULL);
                continue;
            }
            tokens.add(String.valueOf(n.val));
            queue.add(n.left);
            queue.add(n.right);
        }
        while (tokens.get(tokens.size() - 1).equals(NULL)) tokens.remove(tokens.size() - 1);
        return String.join(SEP, tokens);
    }

    public static TreeNode deserializeLevelOrder(String data) {
        if (data.isEmpty()) return null;
        String[] t = data.split(SEP);
        TreeNode root = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t[0]));
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        int i = 1;
        while (!q.isEmpty() && i < t.length) {
            TreeNode n = q.poll();
            if (!t[i].equals(NULL)) q.offer(n.left = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t[i])));
            i++;
            if (i < t.length && !t[i].equals(NULL)) q.offer(n.right = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t[i])));
            i++;
        }
        return root;
    }

    /** Structural equality (used by tests). */
    public static boolean sameTree(TreeNode a, TreeNode b) {
        if (a == null || b == null) return a == b;
        return a.val == b.val && sameTree(a.left, b.left) && sameTree(a.right, b.right);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) time and O(n) space for both formats in both directions.

docs.title: Design discussion (what makes it "Expert")
docs.text:
• Separator choice: , is fine for ints. For strings you need escaping or length prefixes (3:abc).
  • Size: about 2n tokens because of the markers. A BST can be serialized with no markers (pre-order plus the BST bounds rebuild it), a classic follow-up.
  • Recursion depth: a skewed tree with 10⁵ nodes overflows the recursive decoder. The BFS version is iterative.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The tests round-trip 300 random trees (including negative values and duplicates) through both formats and compare the structure.

docs.title: Pre-, in-, post-order traversals
docs.text: Easy DFS Explicit stack Morris

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Return the node values in pre-order (root, left, right), in-order (left, root, right) and post-order (left, right, root), recursively and iteratively. Expert bonus: in-order with O(1) extra space.

        1
      /   \
     2     3          pre:  1 2 4 5 3 6
    / \     \         in:   4 2 5 1 3 6
   4   5     6        post: 4 5 2 6 3 1

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Recursive: the position of the "visit" line relative to the two recursive calls is the traversal. That's three lines each.
  2. Iterative pre-order: pop and visit, then push right before left, because a stack is LIFO and left must come out first.
  3. Iterative in-order: you can't visit a node until its whole left subtree is done. Run down the left spine pushing nodes; pop one, visit it, then move to its right child and repeat.
  4. Iterative post-order trick: root → right → left is just pre-order with the pushes swapped. Reverse that and you get left → right → root.
  5. Morris (O(1) space): before going left, make the in-order predecessor (the rightmost node of the left subtree) point back to the current node. That temporary "thread" replaces the stack. On the second arrival, remove the thread and visit.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/** Pre-, in- and post-order, each recursively and iteratively (explicit stack), plus Morris in-order in O(1) space. */
public final class Traversals {
    private Traversals() {}

    // ---------- recursive: the order of the three lines IS the traversal ----------
    public static List<Integer> preorderRecursive(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        pre(root, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void pre(TreeNode n, List<Integer> out) {
        if (n == null) return;
        out.add(n.val);                                      // root
        pre(n.left, out);                                    // left
        pre(n.right, out);                                   // right
    }

    public static List<Integer> inorderRecursive(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        in(root, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void in(TreeNode n, List<Integer> out) {
        if (n == null) return;
        in(n.left, out);
        out.add(n.val);
        in(n.right, out);
    }

    public static List<Integer> postorderRecursive(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        post(root, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void post(TreeNode n, List<Integer> out) {
        if (n == null) return;
        post(n.left, out);
        post(n.right, out);
        out.add(n.val);
    }

    // ---------- iterative ----------
    /** Pre-order: pop, visit, push RIGHT then LEFT (so left is processed first). */
    public static List<Integer> preorderIterative(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        if (root != null) stack.push(root);
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            TreeNode n = stack.pop();
            out.add(n.val);
            if (n.right != null) stack.push(n.right);
            if (n.left != null) stack.push(n.left);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** In-order: go left as far as possible pushing nodes; pop, visit, then turn right. */
    public static List<Integer> inorderIterative(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        TreeNode curr = root;
        while (curr != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
            while (curr != null) {
                stack.push(curr);
                curr = curr.left;
            }
            curr = stack.pop();
            out.add(curr.val);
            curr = curr.right;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Post-order trick: root-RIGHT-left pre-order, reversed, is left-right-root. */
    public static List<Integer> postorderIterative(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        if (root != null) stack.push(root);
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            TreeNode n = stack.pop();
            out.add(n.val);
            if (n.left != null) stack.push(n.left);
            if (n.right != null) stack.push(n.right);
        }
        Collections.reverse(out);
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * Morris in-order: O(1) extra space. Temporarily thread each node's in-order predecessor's right pointer back to it,
     * so we can return without a stack; the thread is removed on the second visit, restoring the tree.
     */
    public static List<Integer> inorderMorris(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        TreeNode curr = root;
        while (curr != null) {
            if (curr.left == null) {
                out.add(curr.val);
                curr = curr.right;
            } else {
                TreeNode pred = curr.left;
                while (pred.right != null && pred.right != curr) pred = pred.right;
                if (pred.right == null) {                    // first visit: create the thread, go left
                    pred.right = curr;
                    curr = curr.left;
                } else {                                     // second visit: remove the thread, visit, go right
                    pred.right = null;
                    out.add(curr.val);
                    curr = curr.right;
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Height, minimum depth & balanced check
docs.text: Easy Post-order BFS

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Max depth: the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] → 3.
  2. Min depth: the nearest leaf.
  3. Balanced: at every node, the subtree heights differ by at most 1.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Max depth, recursively: 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), with an empty tree at 0. It's post-order, because the children answer first.
  2. Max depth, iteratively: BFS and count the levels. Snapshot queue.size() to know where each level ends.
  3. Min depth pitfall: 1 + min(left, right) is wrong for a node with one child. The null side returns 0, but a null side isn't a leaf. If one child is missing, recurse only into the other.
  4. Balanced, naive: compute heights at every node, which is O(n²) on a skewed tree. Better: one post-order pass that returns the height, or −1 meaning unbalanced, and stops early. That's O(n).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Maximum depth (number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path) and minimum depth. Empty tree → 0. */
public final class TreeHeight {
    private TreeHeight() {}

    /** Recursive (post-order): 1 + max(left, right). O(n) time, O(h) stack. */
    public static int maxDepthRecursive(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) return 0;
        return 1 + Math.max(maxDepthRecursive(root.left), maxDepthRecursive(root.right));
    }

    /** Iterative BFS: count levels. O(n) time, O(width) space. */
    public static int maxDepthBfs(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) return 0;
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        int depth = 0;
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            depth++;
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {    // process exactly one level
                TreeNode n = q.poll();
                if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
            }
        }
        return depth;
    }

    /** Minimum depth to a LEAF. Pitfall: a node with one child is not a leaf, so don't take min with the null side. */
    public static int minDepth(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) return 0;
        if (root.left == null) return 1 + minDepth(root.right);
        if (root.right == null) return 1 + minDepth(root.left);
        return 1 + Math.min(minDepth(root.left), minDepth(root.right));
    }

    /** Balanced: every node's subtree heights differ by ≤ 1. One pass returning -1 for "unbalanced". O(n). */
    public static boolean isBalanced(TreeNode root) {
        return checkedHeight(root) != -1;
    }

    private static int checkedHeight(TreeNode n) {
        if (n == null) return 0;
        int l = checkedHeight(n.left);
        if (l == -1) return -1;
        int r = checkedHeight(n.right);
        if (r == -1 || Math.abs(l - r) > 1) return -1;
        return 1 + Math.max(l, r);
    }
}

docs.title: Left, right, top & bottom view
docs.text: Medium BFS Horizontal distance

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Return the nodes visible when looking at the tree from each side.

            1                hd: −2 −1  0  1  2
          /   \
         2     3             left:   1 2 4 8
        / \   / \            right:  1 3 7 8
       4   5 6   7           top:    4 2 1 3 7
        \                    bottom: 4 8 6 3 7   (GfG rule: on a tie, the later/right node wins)
         8

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Left and right views are per-level questions, so use BFS: the first node of each level is the left view and the last is the right view.
  2. Recursive right view: DFS visiting right before left. The first node you reach at each new depth is visible.
  3. Top and bottom views are per-column questions. Give each node a horizontal distance (root 0, left child −1, right child +1).
    • Top: the first node BFS meets in each column (putIfAbsent). BFS meets shallower nodes first.
    • Bottom: the last node BFS meets in each column (put overwrites).
  4. A TreeMap<hd, value> returns the columns sorted from left to right with no extra sort.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;

/** What you see from the left, right, top and bottom of a binary tree. */
public final class TreeViews {
    private TreeViews() {}

    /** Left view: first node of every level (BFS). */
    public static List<Integer> left(TreeNode root) {
        return levelEdge(root, true);
    }

    /** Right view: last node of every level (BFS). */
    public static List<Integer> right(TreeNode root) {
        return levelEdge(root, false);
    }

    private static List<Integer> levelEdge(TreeNode root, boolean first) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int size = q.size();
            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
                TreeNode n = q.poll();
                if (first ? i == 0 : i == size - 1) out.add(n.val);
                if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Right view, recursive: visit right child first; the first node seen at each depth is visible. */
    public static List<Integer> rightRecursive(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        rightDfs(root, 0, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void rightDfs(TreeNode n, int depth, List<Integer> out) {
        if (n == null) return;
        if (depth == out.size()) out.add(n.val);
        rightDfs(n.right, depth + 1, out);
        rightDfs(n.left, depth + 1, out);
    }

    /**
     * Top view: horizontal distance hd (root 0, left -1, right +1). BFS guarantees the FIRST node met at each hd is
     * the topmost (ties at the same depth go to the left one). TreeMap keeps hd sorted.
     */
    public static List<Integer> top(TreeNode root) {
        return byColumn(root, true);
    }

    /** Bottom view: the LAST node met at each hd in BFS (later = deeper; same depth → the right one, as GfG specifies). */
    public static List<Integer> bottom(TreeNode root) {
        return byColumn(root, false);
    }

    private static List<Integer> byColumn(TreeNode root, boolean keepFirst) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> column = new TreeMap<>();
        if (root == null) return new ArrayList<>();
        Deque<Object[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(new Object[]{root, 0});
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            Object[] e = q.poll();
            TreeNode n = (TreeNode) e[0];
            int hd = (int) e[1];
            if (keepFirst) column.putIfAbsent(hd, n.val);
            else column.put(hd, n.val);
            if (n.left != null) q.offer(new Object[]{n.left, hd - 1});
            if (n.right != null) q.offer(new Object[]{n.right, hd + 1});
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(column.values());
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n) for the left and right views. O(n log n) for the top and bottom views because of the TreeMap. Tracking the min and max hd in a HashMap would make it O(n).

docs.title: Why BFS and not DFS for the top view?
docs.text: A DFS can reach a deep node in a column before a shallower one in the same column, so it would need depth comparisons. BFS guarantees level order for free.

docs.title: Validate a binary search tree
docs.text: Medium Range bounds In-order

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if every node is strictly greater than all nodes in its left subtree and strictly less than all nodes in its right subtree.

docs.title: The trap
docs.text:
5
       / \
      1   6
         / \
        3   7       every parent/child pair looks fine, but 3 < 5 sits in 5's RIGHT subtree ❌
Comparing a node only with its children passes this tree. The code keeps that wrong version (naiveChildrenOnly), and the test shows it being fooled.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Range idea: each node must fall inside an allowed interval inherited from its ancestors. The root gets (−∞, +∞). Going left, the upper bound becomes the parent's value. Going right, the lower bound becomes the parent's value.
  2. Use long bounds, or nullable bounds, so nodes holding Integer.MIN_VALUE / MAX_VALUE are still valid.
  3. In-order idea: a BST's in-order traversal is strictly increasing. Traverse and compare each value with the previous one. Stop at the first violation.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Is the tree a valid BST (left subtree < node < right subtree, strictly, at EVERY level)? */
public final class ValidateBst {
    private ValidateBst() {}

    /** Wrong-but-tempting: only compares with direct children. Kept to show the bug in the docs and tests. */
    public static boolean naiveChildrenOnly(TreeNode n) {
        if (n == null) return true;
        if (n.left != null && n.left.val >= n.val) return false;
        if (n.right != null && n.right.val <= n.val) return false;
        return naiveChildrenOnly(n.left) && naiveChildrenOnly(n.right);
    }

    /** Correct: pass the allowed (low, high) range down. long bounds so Integer.MIN/MAX values work. O(n). */
    public static boolean range(TreeNode root) {
        return range(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    private static boolean range(TreeNode n, long low, long high) {
        if (n == null) return true;
        if (n.val <= low || n.val >= high) return false;
        return range(n.left, low, n.val) && range(n.right, n.val, high);
    }

    /** In-order of a BST is strictly increasing: iterate and compare with the previous value. O(n). */
    public static boolean inorder(TreeNode root) {
        Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        TreeNode curr = root;
        Long prev = null;
        while (curr != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
            while (curr != null) {
                stack.push(curr);
                curr = curr.left;
            }
            curr = stack.pop();
            if (prev != null && curr.val <= prev) return false;
            prev = (long) curr.val;
            curr = curr.right;
        }
        return true;
    }

    /** BST insert (used by tests to build valid trees). */
    public static TreeNode insert(TreeNode root, int val) {
        if (root == null) return new TreeNode(val);
        if (val < root.val) root.left = insert(root.left, val);
        else if (val > root.val) root.right = insert(root.right, val);
        return root;
    }
}

docs.title: Zig-zag level order
docs.text: Hard BFS Deque Two stacks

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Level order, but alternate the direction: left to right, then right to left, and so on. [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] → [[3],[20,9],[15,7]].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Simplest correct idea: a normal level order, reversing every odd level. O(n), but it does extra work.
  2. Cleaner: keep the BFS order unchanged, but build each level with a deque. On left-to-right levels use addLast, and on right-to-left levels use addFirst. No reversal needed.
  3. Two stacks (classic GfG): pop from the current stack and push children onto next, left then right on left-to-right levels and right then left otherwise. The LIFO order produces the zig-zag naturally. Swap the stacks at the end of each level.

docs.title: Two stacks, traced
docs.text: Level current (pop order) Children pushed onto next Output 0 → 3 9, 20 [3] 1 ← 20, 9 20: 7, 15 · 9: none [20, 9] 2 → 15, 7 [15, 7]

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The deque version (zigzag) and the two-stack version (zigzagTwoStacks) are both in LevelOrder: 

package com.playbook.trees;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.List;

/** Level-order traversal grouped by level: [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]. Plus zig-zag order. */
public final class LevelOrder {
    private LevelOrder() {}

    /** BFS with a queue; snapshot the queue size to know where a level ends. O(n). */
    public static List<List<Integer>> bfs(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
                TreeNode n = q.poll();
                level.add(n.val);
                if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
            }
            out.add(level);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** DFS with depth: pre-order puts each value into the list for its depth. Same result, O(h) stack. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> dfs(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        dfs(root, 0, out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void dfs(TreeNode n, int depth, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (n == null) return;
        if (depth == out.size()) out.add(new ArrayList<>());   // first time we reach this depth
        out.get(depth).add(n.val);
        dfs(n.left, depth + 1, out);
        dfs(n.right, depth + 1, out);
    }

    /** Zig-zag: alternate direction per level; add to the front of the level list on odd levels. O(n). */
    public static List<List<Integer>> zigzag(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);
        boolean leftToRight = true;
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            LinkedList<Integer> level = new LinkedList<>();
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
                TreeNode n = q.poll();
                if (leftToRight) level.addLast(n.val);
                else level.addFirst(n.val);                  // reverse without reversing the traversal
                if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
                if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
            }
            out.add(level);
            leftToRight = !leftToRight;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Zig-zag with two stacks (the classic GfG approach): children pushed in alternating order. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> zigzagTwoStacks(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;
        Deque<TreeNode> current = new ArrayDeque<>(), next = new ArrayDeque<>();
        current.push(root);
        boolean leftToRight = true;
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!current.isEmpty()) {
            TreeNode n = current.pop();
            level.add(n.val);
            TreeNode first = leftToRight ? n.left : n.right, second = leftToRight ? n.right : n.left;
            if (first != null) next.push(first);
            if (second != null) next.push(second);
            if (current.isEmpty()) {
                out.add(level);
                level = new ArrayList<>();
                Deque<TreeNode> t = current;
                current = next;
                next = t;
                leftToRight = !leftToRight;
            }
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array (children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2). In a min-heap every parent ≤ its children, so the minimum is always at index 0.
  • peek is O(1), offer/poll are O(log n), and building a heap from n items is O(n). Searching for an arbitrary element is still O(n), because a heap is only partially ordered.
  • Java: PriorityQueue<>() is a min-heap. Pass Comparator.reverseOrder() for a max-heap.

docs.title: When to reach for a heap
docs.text:
The problem says… Heap pattern "k largest / k smallest / top k" heap of size k holding the opposite extreme: a min-heap for the k largest "kth largest in a stream" the root of a size-k min-heap "merge k sorted …" heap of the k current heads "median of a stream" two heaps (max-heap for the low half, min-heap for the high half) "always process the most/least urgent next" scheduling, Dijkstra

Why a min-heap for the k largest?

You need to evict the weakest of your current top-k quickly, and that's the minimum. Keeping the heap at size k makes every operation O(log k) instead of O(log n).

docs.text: Expert Design Sift up / down Heapsort

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Implement a min-heap with push, pop, peek and size, without PriorityQueue. Then show O(n) heapify and in-place heapsort.

docs.title: Array layout
docs.text:
index:   0  1  2  3  4  5
value:   1  3  2  7  4  5            parent(i) = (i−1)/2
                                     left(i)   = 2i+1
tree:        1                       right(i)  = 2i+2
           /   \
          3     2
         / \   /
        7   4 5
The tree is complete (every level is full except the last, which fills from the left), so an array stores it with no gaps and no pointers.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. push: put the new value in the only free slot, the end, which may break the heap property with its parent. Sift up: while it's smaller than its parent, swap them. Height is log n, so O(log n).
  2. pop: the minimum is at the root. Move the last element to the root (to keep the tree complete), then sift down: swap with the smaller child while that child is smaller. O(log n).
  3. heapify in O(n): don't push n times (O(n log n)). Sift down every non-leaf, starting from the bottom (n/2 − 1 down to 0). Most nodes are near the bottom and barely move, so the total sums to O(n).
  4. Heapsort: build a max-heap in place, then repeatedly swap the root (the maximum) with the last element and sift down within the shrinking prefix. That's O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space, but it's not stable.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.NoSuchElementException;

/**
 * Min-heap from scratch on an int array. Node i has children 2i+1, 2i+2 and parent (i-1)/2.
 * Heap property: every parent ≤ its children → the minimum is at index 0. Also: O(n) heapify and in-place heapsort.
 */
public final class BinaryHeap {
    private int[] heap = new int[16];
    private int size;

    /** Append at the end, then sift UP while smaller than the parent. O(log n). */
    public void push(int x) {
        if (size == heap.length) heap = Arrays.copyOf(heap, size * 2);
        heap[size] = x;
        siftUp(heap, size++);
    }

    /** Take the root, move the LAST element to the root, sift it DOWN. O(log n). */
    public int pop() {
        if (size == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException("heap is empty");
        int min = heap[0];
        heap[0] = heap[--size];
        siftDown(heap, 0, size);
        return min;
    }

    public int peek() {
        if (size == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException("heap is empty");
        return heap[0];
    }

    public int size() {
        return size;
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    /** Build a heap from an array in O(n): sift down every non-leaf, bottom-up (NOT n pushes, which is O(n log n)). */
    public static BinaryHeap heapify(int[] values) {
        BinaryHeap h = new BinaryHeap();
        h.heap = Arrays.copyOf(values, Math.max(16, values.length));
        h.size = values.length;
        for (int i = h.size / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--) siftDown(h.heap, i, h.size);
        return h;
    }

    private static void siftUp(int[] h, int i) {
        while (i > 0) {
            int parent = (i - 1) / 2;
            if (h[parent] <= h[i]) return;                   // heap property restored
            swap(h, parent, i);
            i = parent;
        }
    }

    /** Min-heap sift-down within h[0..n). */
    private static void siftDown(int[] h, int i, int n) {
        while (true) {
            int smallest = i, l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
            if (l < n && h[l] < h[smallest]) smallest = l;
            if (r < n && h[r] < h[smallest]) smallest = r;
            if (smallest == i) return;
            swap(h, i, smallest);
            i = smallest;
        }
    }

    /**
     * Heapsort ascending, in place, O(n log n), O(1) extra: build a MAX-heap, then repeatedly swap the max to the end
     * and shrink the heap. Not stable.
     */
    public static void heapSort(int[] a) {
        int n = a.length;
        for (int i = n / 2 - 1; i >= 0; i--) maxSiftDown(a, i, n);
        for (int end = n - 1; end > 0; end--) {
            swap(a, 0, end);                                 // largest goes to its final position
            maxSiftDown(a, 0, end);
        }
    }

    private static void maxSiftDown(int[] h, int i, int n) {
        while (true) {
            int largest = i, l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
            if (l < n && h[l] > h[largest]) largest = l;
            if (r < n && h[r] > h[largest]) largest = r;
            if (largest == i) return;
            swap(h, i, largest);
            i = largest;
        }
    }

    private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        int t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.title: K closest points to the origin
docs.text: Medium Max-heap of size k Quickselect

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the k points closest to (0, 0), in any order. [[3,3],[5,−1],[−2,4]], k = 2 → [[3,3],[−2,4]].

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Compare squared distances (x² + y²). Taking the square root costs time and brings floating point in, and it doesn't change the order. Use long, because squares of large coordinates overflow an int.
  2. Sort by distance and take k. O(n log n).
  3. Max-heap of size k: to keep the k closest, evict the farthest, which is the root of a max-heap. O(n log k).
  4. Quickselect on distance: partition until the pivot lands at index k − 1. The first k are then the answer, unordered. O(n) expected.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;

/** The k points closest to the origin (any order). Compare SQUARED distances — no sqrt, no floating point. */
public final class KClosestPoints {
    private KClosestPoints() {}

    static long dist2(int[] p) {
        return (long) p[0] * p[0] + (long) p[1] * p[1];     // long: 2 * (4.6e4)^2 can overflow int for large coords
    }

    /** Sort all by distance. O(n log n). */
    public static int[][] sorting(int[][] points, int k) {
        int[][] c = points.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c, Comparator.comparingLong(KClosestPoints::dist2));
        return Arrays.copyOf(c, k);
    }

    /** MAX-heap of size k: root = farthest of the current k, evicted when a closer point arrives. O(n log k). */
    public static int[][] maxHeap(int[][] points, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingLong(KClosestPoints::dist2).reversed());
        for (int[] p : points) {
            pq.offer(p);
            if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();
        }
        return pq.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }

    /** Quickselect on distance: partition so the first k are the closest. O(n) expected. */
    public static int[][] quickselect(int[][] points, int k) {
        int[][] c = points.clone();
        int lo = 0, hi = c.length - 1;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int p = partition(c, lo, hi);
            if (p == k - 1) break;
            if (p < k - 1) lo = p + 1;
            else hi = p - 1;
        }
        return Arrays.copyOf(c, k);
    }

    private static int partition(int[][] a, int lo, int hi) {
        swap(a, lo + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(hi - lo + 1), hi);
        long pivot = dist2(a[hi]);
        int i = lo;
        for (int j = lo; j < hi; j++) if (dist2(a[j]) < pivot) swap(a, i++, j);
        swap(a, i, hi);
        return i;
    }

    private static void swap(int[][] a, int i, int j) {
        int[] t = a[i];
        a[i] = a[j];
        a[j] = t;
    }
}

docs.title: Kth largest element (array & stream)
docs.text: Easy Min-heap of size k

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Kth largest in an array: [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2 → 5.
  2. Stream (LeetCode 703): KthLargest(k, initial), then each add(x) returns the current kth largest.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sort: O(n log n). That's fine once, but in a stream you'd re-sort after every add.
  2. Insight: you only care about the k largest values seen so far. Of those, the kth largest is the smallest, which is exactly what a min-heap's root gives you.
  3. Push each value. If the size goes above k, pop the root, which is the smallest and can't be in the top k.
  4. Each add is O(log k), and the answer is just peek().

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/**
 * Kth largest element in a STREAM (LeetCode 703): constructor gets k and initial numbers, add(x) returns the current
 * kth largest. Plus the one-shot array version.
 */
public final class KthLargest {
    private final int k;
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();   // holds the k largest seen so far

    public KthLargest(int k, int[] nums) {
        if (k <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("k must be > 0");
        this.k = k;
        for (int x : nums) {                                 // don't call add(): it throws while size < k
            minHeap.offer(x);
            if (minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.poll();
        }
    }

    /** O(log k): push, and if we exceed k evict the smallest — the root is then exactly the kth largest. */
    public int add(int x) {
        minHeap.offer(x);
        if (minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.poll();
        if (minHeap.size() < k) throw new IllegalStateException("fewer than k elements so far");
        return minHeap.peek();
    }

    /** Brute force for one array: sort descending, pick index k-1. O(n log n). */
    public static int sorting(int[] a, int k) {
        int[] c = a.clone();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        return c[c.length - k];
    }

    /** Min-heap of size k. O(n log k) time, O(k) space. */
    public static int minHeap(int[] a, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
        for (int x : a) {
            pq.offer(x);
            if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();
        }
        return pq.peek();
    }
}

docs.title: Median of a data stream
docs.text: Expert Two heaps Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Support addNum(x) and findMedian() over a stream that keeps growing. After 1, 2 the median is 1.5. After 1, 2, 3 it's 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Sorted list: binary-search the insert position. addNum is O(n), because the elements shift, and findMedian is O(1).

  2. Insight: the median only needs the middle. Split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half:

    • lower half in a max-heap, so its largest element is on top;
    • upper half in a min-heap, so its smallest element is on top.

    The median is one of the two tops, or their average. 3. Two invariants: - order: max(lower) ≤ min(upper); - size: lower.size() == upper.size() or upper.size() + 1. 4. Insert recipe: push x into lower, move lower's top to upper (this restores order), and if upper became bigger, move its top back to lower (this restores size). That's three heap operations, so O(log n).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** addNum(x) and findMedian() over a growing stream (LeetCode 295). */
public final class MedianOfStream {

    /** Two heaps: lower half in a MAX-heap, upper half in a MIN-heap; sizes differ by at most 1 (lower may have +1). */
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> lower = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> upper = new PriorityQueue<>();

    /** O(log n). Always route through lower then rebalance, so the ordering invariant (max(lower) ≤ min(upper)) holds. */
    public void addNum(int x) {
        lower.offer(x);
        upper.offer(lower.poll());                           // the largest of the lower half moves up
        if (upper.size() > lower.size()) lower.offer(upper.poll());   // keep lower.size() ∈ {upper.size(), upper.size()+1}
    }

    /** O(1). */
    public double findMedian() {
        if (lower.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("no numbers yet");
        if (lower.size() > upper.size()) return lower.peek();
        return (lower.peek() + (double) upper.peek()) / 2;
    }

    /** Brute force reference: keep a sorted list (binary-search insert). add O(n), median O(1). */
    public static final class SortedList {
        private final List<Integer> data = new ArrayList<>();

        public void addNum(int x) {
            int i = Collections.binarySearch(data, x);
            data.add(i < 0 ? -i - 1 : i, x);                 // insertion point; ArrayList shift makes this O(n)
        }

        public double findMedian() {
            int n = data.size();
            if (n == 0) throw new IllegalStateException("no numbers yet");
            return n % 2 == 1 ? data.get(n / 2) : (data.get(n / 2 - 1) + (double) data.get(n / 2)) / 2;
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Merge K sorted arrays
docs.text: Hard Min-heap Divide & conquer

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Merge k sorted arrays into one sorted array. [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[0,9]] → [0,1,2,4,5,7,8,9]. N = the total number of elements.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Concatenate and sort: O(N log N). It ignores the fact that the inputs are already sorted.
  2. Heap of heads: the next output element is always the smallest of the k current heads. Put the heads in a min-heap as {value, whichArray, indexInArray}. Poll the smallest, output it, and push the next element from the same array. The heap never holds more than k entries, so each step is O(log k).
  3. Divide & conquer: merge the arrays in pairs (k → k/2 → … → 1). Each round touches all N elements, and there are log k rounds.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Merge k sorted int arrays into one sorted array. N = total elements. */
public final class MergeKSortedArrays {
    private MergeKSortedArrays() {}

    /** Concatenate and sort. O(N log N). */
    public static int[] concatAndSort(int[][] arrays) {
        int[] all = Arrays.stream(arrays).flatMapToInt(Arrays::stream).toArray();
        Arrays.sort(all);
        return all;
    }

    /**
     * Min-heap of entries {value, arrayIndex, elementIndex}: always output the smallest current head, then push that
     * array's next element. Heap never exceeds k. O(N log k) time, O(k) extra.
     */
    public static int[] heap(int[][] arrays) {
        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[0], y[0]));
        int total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < arrays.length; i++) {
            total += arrays[i].length;
            if (arrays[i].length > 0) pq.offer(new int[]{arrays[i][0], i, 0});
        }
        int[] out = new int[total];
        int w = 0;
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            int[] e = pq.poll();
            out[w++] = e[0];
            int next = e[2] + 1;
            if (next < arrays[e[1]].length) pq.offer(new int[]{arrays[e[1]][next], e[1], next});
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Divide & conquer pairwise merging. O(N log k), no heap. */
    public static int[] divideAndConquer(int[][] arrays) {
        if (arrays.length == 0) return new int[0];
        return dc(arrays, 0, arrays.length - 1);
    }

    private static int[] dc(int[][] a, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) return a[lo];
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        return mergeTwo(dc(a, lo, mid), dc(a, mid + 1, hi));
    }

    static int[] mergeTwo(int[] x, int[] y) {
        int[] out = new int[x.length + y.length];
        int i = 0, j = 0, k = 0;
        while (i < x.length && j < y.length) out[k++] = x[i] <= y[j] ? x[i++] : y[j++];
        while (i < x.length) out[k++] = x[i++];
        while (j < y.length) out[k++] = y[j++];
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Task scheduler
docs.text: Hard Greedy Max-heap Math

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Tasks are letters, and each takes one time unit. Two runs of the same task need at least n units in between, and the CPU may idle. Return the minimum total time. [A,A,A,B,B,B], n = 2 → 8 (A B _ A B _ A B).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Greedy choice: at every time unit, run the available task with the most remaining copies. It's the hardest one to fit, and postponing it only creates idle time later. "Most remaining" means a max-heap.
  2. A task that just ran goes into a cooldown queue with the time it becomes available again (now + n). When that time comes, it returns to the heap.
  3. Simulation: one loop per time unit. O(T log 26), which is effectively O(T).
  4. Formula insight: the most frequent task (count maxF) dictates a skeleton of maxF − 1 frames of length n + 1, plus a final frame containing every task that ties for maxF: (maxF − 1) × (n + 1) + tiedAtMax. If there are more tasks than slots, the frames just stretch and nobody idles, so the answer is max(that, tasks.length).

docs.title: Skeleton for A×3, B×3, n = 2
docs.text:
| A B _ | A B _ | A B |
  frame   frame   last frame (A and B tie at maxF)
(3 − 1) × (2 + 1) + 2 = 8

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/**
 * CPU tasks (letters A–Z), each takes 1 unit; the same task needs n idle units between runs.
 * Minimum total units (LeetCode 621). [A,A,A,B,B,B], n=2 → 8: A B idle A B idle A B.
 */
public final class TaskScheduler {
    private TaskScheduler() {}

    /**
     * Simulation: max-heap of remaining counts (always run the most-remaining task — it is the hardest to fit),
     * plus a cooldown queue of {count, readyTime}. O(T log 26).
     */
    public static int simulate(char[] tasks, int n) {
        int[] freq = new int[26];
        for (char c : tasks) freq[c - 'A']++;
        PriorityQueue<Integer> ready = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
        for (int f : freq) if (f > 0) ready.offer(f);
        Deque<int[]> cooling = new ArrayDeque<>();           // {remainingCount, timeWhenReady}
        int time = 0;
        while (!ready.isEmpty() || !cooling.isEmpty()) {
            time++;
            if (!ready.isEmpty()) {
                int left = ready.poll() - 1;
                if (left > 0) cooling.offer(new int[]{left, time + n});
            }                                                // else: CPU idles this unit
            if (!cooling.isEmpty() && cooling.peek()[1] == time) ready.offer(cooling.poll()[0]);
        }
        return time;
    }

    /**
     * Formula: the most frequent task (count maxF) forms maxF-1 full "frames" of length n+1, plus a final frame
     * holding every task that ties for maxF. If there are more tasks than slots, no idling is needed → tasks.length.
     * O(T).
     */
    public static int formula(char[] tasks, int n) {
        int[] freq = new int[26];
        for (char c : tasks) freq[c - 'A']++;
        int maxF = 0, tiedAtMax = 0;
        for (int f : freq) {
            if (f > maxF) {
                maxF = f;
                tiedAtMax = 1;
            } else if (f == maxF) tiedAtMax++;
        }
        return Math.max(tasks.length, (maxF - 1) * (n + 1) + tiedAtMax);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(T) for both (the heap holds at most 26 entries). O(1) space.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The formula and the simulation are compared on 300 random task lists. The simulation explains the result, and the formula is what you'd present as the optimised answer.

docs.title: Top K frequent words
docs.text: Medium HashMap Heap Comparator

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the k most frequent words, sorted by frequency and then alphabetically. ["i","love","leetcode","i","love","coding"], k = 2 → ["i","love"] (both appear twice, and "i" < "love").

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Count with a HashMap. Let d = the number of distinct words.
  2. Sort all entries with the "better" order: count descending, then word ascending. O(d log d).
  3. Heap of size k: the heap must evict the worst candidate, so it's ordered by the reverse of "better": lower count first, and on equal counts the alphabetically later word first. Getting this tie-break backwards is the main bug.
  4. Popping returns the worst first, so reverse at the end.

docs.title: Comparator, spelled out
docs.text:
Comparator<Entry<String, Long>> better =
    Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()      // higher count first
         .thenComparing(Entry.comparingByKey());           // then a, b, c…
PriorityQueue<…> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(better.reversed());   // root = worst

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.heap;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

/** k most frequent words; ties broken ALPHABETICALLY (LeetCode 692). ["i","love","leetcode","i","love","coding"], 2 → [i, love]. */
public final class TopKFrequentWords {
    private TopKFrequentWords() {}

    /** "Better" order: higher count first, then alphabetical. */
    private static Comparator<Map.Entry<String, Long>> better() {
        return Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey());
    }

    /** Count, sort all distinct words. O(n + d log d). */
    public static List<String> sorting(String[] words, int k) {
        return count(words).entrySet().stream().sorted(better()).limit(k).map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
    }

    /**
     * Heap of size k ordered WORST-first (lower count, or alphabetically LATER on a tie) so the root is the one to evict.
     * O(n + d log k). Pop gives worst → best, so reverse at the end.
     */
    public static List<String> heap(String[] words, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(better().reversed());
        for (Map.Entry<String, Long> e : count(words).entrySet()) {
            pq.offer(e);
            if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();
        }
        List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) out.add(pq.poll().getKey());
        Collections.reverse(out);
        return out;
    }

    private static Map<String, Long> count(String[] words) {
        return java.util.Arrays.stream(words).collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), HashMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
    }
}

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• A graph is V vertices and E edges. It can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and may contain cycles.
  • Representation: an adjacency list (List<List<Integer>>) takes O(V + E) space and is the default. An adjacency matrix takes O(V²) and suits dense graphs or Floyd-Warshall.
  • Grids are graphs too: every cell is a vertex, and its up/down/left/right neighbours are its edges.
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Helpers to turn an edge list into an adjacency list (the representation most problems want). */
public final class Graph {
    private Graph() {}

    /** Undirected adjacency list for nodes 0..n-1. O(V + E) space. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> undirected(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = empty(n);
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
            adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]);
        }
        return adj;
    }

    /** Directed adjacency list: edge {u, v} means u → v. */
    public static List<List<Integer>> directed(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = empty(n);
        for (int[] e : edges) adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        return adj;
    }

    private static List<List<Integer>> empty(int n) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        return adj;
    }
}

Always mark visited

Without a visited set, any cycle loops forever. In BFS, mark when enqueuing, not when dequeuing, or the same node gets queued many times.

docs.title: Bellman-Ford & Floyd-Warshall
docs.text: Expert Negative weights DP All pairs

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Bellman-Ford: shortest paths from one source when edges can be negative. Report a negative cycle if one is reachable.
  2. Floyd-Warshall: shortest paths between every pair of nodes.

docs.title: Thinking process: Bellman-Ford
docs.text:
1. A shortest path without cycles has at most V − 1 edges.
  2. Relax every edge, V − 1 times. After round k, every shortest path that uses ≤ k edges is correct, by induction.
  3. Negative cycle check: run one more round. If anything still improves, a reachable negative cycle exists, and "shortest" is undefined (you could loop forever), so return null.
  4. Early exit: if a round changes nothing, the distances are final.

docs.title: Thinking process: Floyd-Warshall
docs.text:
1. DP over intermediate nodes: d[i][j] = the shortest path from i to j using only nodes 0..k in the middle.
  2. Adding node k as a possible stop gives d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]).
  3. k must be the outer loop. Putting it inside is a classic bug, because then d[i][k] isn't final yet.
  4. If d[i][i] < 0 for some i, there's a negative cycle.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.Arrays;

/**
 * Shortest paths that allow NEGATIVE weights. edges[i] = {u, v, w}, directed.
 * Bellman-Ford: single source, detects negative cycles. Floyd-Warshall: all pairs.
 */
public final class BellmanFordFloydWarshall {
    private BellmanFordFloydWarshall() {}

    public static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4;       // headroom so INF + w never overflows

    /**
     * Bellman-Ford: relax EVERY edge V-1 times (a shortest path has at most V-1 edges). If a V-th round still improves
     * something, a negative cycle is reachable → return null. O(V·E).
     */
    public static long[] bellmanFord(int n, int[][] edges, int src) {
        long[] dist = new long[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
        dist[src] = 0;
        for (int round = 0; round < n - 1; round++) {
            boolean changed = false;
            for (int[] e : edges) {
                if (dist[e[0]] != INF && dist[e[0]] + e[2] < dist[e[1]]) {
                    dist[e[1]] = dist[e[0]] + e[2];
                    changed = true;
                }
            }
            if (!changed) break;                             // early exit: already optimal
        }
        for (int[] e : edges) if (dist[e[0]] != INF && dist[e[0]] + e[2] < dist[e[1]]) return null;
        return dist;
    }

    /**
     * Floyd-Warshall: dist[i][j] using intermediate nodes {0..k}. For each k, try going i → k → j.
     * O(V^3) time, O(V^2) space. A negative dist[i][i] reveals a negative cycle → return null.
     */
    public static long[][] floydWarshall(int n, int[][] edges) {
        long[][] d = new long[n][n];
        for (long[] row : d) Arrays.fill(row, INF);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) d[i][i] = 0;
        for (int[] e : edges) d[e[0]][e[1]] = Math.min(d[e[0]][e[1]], e[2]);   // keep the cheapest parallel edge
        for (int k = 0; k < n; k++)                          // k MUST be the outer loop
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                if (d[i][k] == INF) continue;
                for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
                    if (d[k][j] != INF && d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]) d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j];
            }
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (d[i][i] < 0) return null;
        return d;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity & choice
docs.text: Algorithm Time Space Negative edges Detects negative cycles Dijkstra O((V+E) log V) O(V) ❌ ❌ Bellman-Ford O(V·E) O(V) ✅ ✅ Floyd-Warshall O(V³) O(V²) ✅ ✅

docs.title: Implementation detail worth mentioning
docs.text: INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4 instead of MAX_VALUE, so INF + weight can never overflow and wrap into a negative "shortcut". Always skip relaxing from an unreachable node.
