docs.title: BFS & DFS
docs.text: Easy Queue Stack Recursion

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Traverse a graph from a start node with breadth-first and depth-first search (recursive and iterative). Also compute the fewest-edges distance to every node and count the connected components.

0 — 1
|   |       BFS from 0: 0 1 2 3 4      (by distance: 0 | 1 2 | 3 | 4)
2 — 3 — 4   DFS from 0: 0 1 3 2 4      (as deep as possible first)
            5 is isolated → 2 components

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. BFS explores in rings of distance: all nodes 1 edge away, then 2, and so on. Use a FIFO queue. Because nodes are reached in distance order, BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs for free.
  2. DFS follows one path as deep as it can, then backtracks. Use recursion or a LIFO stack.
  3. Visited prevents infinite loops on cycles. In BFS, mark nodes when enqueuing.
  4. Iterative DFS matching the recursive order: push neighbours in reverse and mark nodes when popping. A node may sit on the stack more than once, and the visited check skips the extra copies.
  5. Components: start a new traversal from every node that is still unvisited, and count the starts.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/** Breadth-first and depth-first traversal of an adjacency list, plus unweighted shortest distances. */
public final class BfsDfs {
    private BfsDfs() {}

    /** BFS: visit by distance from start, using a queue. Mark visited WHEN ENQUEUING so nothing is queued twice. O(V+E). */
    public static List<Integer> bfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[adj.size()];
        Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(start);
        seen[start] = true;
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int u = q.poll();
            order.add(u);
            for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
                if (!seen[v]) {
                    seen[v] = true;
                    q.offer(v);
                }
            }
        }
        return order;
    }

    /** DFS, recursive: go as deep as possible before backtracking. O(V+E), O(V) stack. */
    public static List<Integer> dfsRecursive(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
        dfs(adj, start, new boolean[adj.size()], order);
        return order;
    }

    private static void dfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, boolean[] seen, List<Integer> order) {
        seen[u] = true;
        order.add(u);
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) if (!seen[v]) dfs(adj, v, seen, order);
    }

    /**
     * DFS, iterative with an explicit stack. Push neighbours in REVERSE so the first neighbour is explored first,
     * and mark visited when POPPING — this reproduces the recursive order exactly.
     */
    public static List<Integer> dfsIterative(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
        List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[adj.size()];
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
        stack.push(start);
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            int u = stack.pop();
            if (seen[u]) continue;                           // a node can be pushed several times; process once
            seen[u] = true;
            order.add(u);
            List<Integer> nbrs = adj.get(u);
            for (int i = nbrs.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) if (!seen[nbrs.get(i)]) stack.push(nbrs.get(i));
        }
        return order;
    }

    /** Fewest edges from start to every node (-1 if unreachable): BFS reaches each node first by a shortest path. */
    public static int[] shortestDistances(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start) {
        int[] dist = new int[adj.size()];
        Arrays.fill(dist, -1);
        dist[start] = 0;
        Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(start);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int u = q.poll();
            for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
                if (dist[v] == -1) {
                    dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                    q.offer(v);
                }
            }
        }
        return dist;
    }

    /** Number of connected components (undirected): start a traversal from every unvisited node. */
    public static int components(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[adj.size()];
        int count = 0;
        for (int s = 0; s < adj.size(); s++) {
            if (!seen[s]) {
                count++;
                dfs(adj, s, seen, new ArrayList<>());
            }
        }
        return count;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(V + E) time for every method. Space is O(V) for the visited array plus the queue or stack.

docs.title: BFS or DFS?
docs.text: Prefer BFS Prefer DFS shortest path (unweighted) detecting cycles, topological order level-by-level answers exploring every path (backtracking) a very deep graph (no recursion limit) less memory on wide graphs

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The iterative DFS must produce exactly the recursive order on 200 random graphs, and BFS and DFS must reach the same set of nodes.

docs.title: Course schedule (can finish? / find an order)
docs.text: Hard Topological sort Cycle detection

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
There are numCourses courses. prerequisites[i] = {a, b} means you must take b before a. 1. Can you finish them all? (LeetCode 207) 2. Return a valid order, or an empty array. (LeetCode 210)

2, [[1,0]] → true, order [0,1] · 2, [[1,0],[0,1]] → false.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Model it: courses are nodes and prerequisites are directed edges. Watch the direction: {a, b} means b must come first, so the edge is b → a. Getting this backwards is the most common bug.
  2. "Can finish everything" ⇔ there's no cycle, because a cycle means courses waiting on each other forever.
  3. "Find an order" is a topological sort. Kahn's algorithm gives the order and cycle detection in one pass: if fewer than n courses come out, return [].

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

/**
 * numCourses courses; prerequisites[i] = {course, prereq} means prereq must be taken first (LeetCode 207 / 210).
 * Note the edge direction: prereq → course.
 */
public final class CourseSchedule {
    private CourseSchedule() {}

    /** Can all courses be finished? ⇔ the prerequisite graph has no cycle. */
    public static boolean canFinish(int numCourses, int[][] prerequisites) {
        return findOrder(numCourses, prerequisites).length == numCourses;
    }

    /** A valid order, or an empty array if impossible. Kahn's algorithm on edges prereq → course. */
    public static int[] findOrder(int numCourses, int[][] prerequisites) {
        int[][] edges = new int[prerequisites.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < prerequisites.length; i++) edges[i] = new int[]{prerequisites[i][1], prerequisites[i][0]};
        int[] order = TopologicalSort.kahn(numCourses, edges);
        return order.length == numCourses ? order : new int[0];
    }
}
(It reuses TopologicalSort.kahn, so the interview answer is "reverse the edges, run Kahn, check the count".)

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(V + E) time and space.

docs.title: Why it's rated "Hard" here
docs.text: The algorithm is standard. The difficulty is modelling: spotting that it's a graph problem, choosing the edge direction, and connecting "impossible" with "cycle". Interviewers often follow up with "what's the minimum number of semesters?" (the number of BFS levels in Kahn's algorithm).

docs.title: Detect a cycle (undirected & directed)
docs.text: Medium DFS Three colours Union-Find

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return true if the graph contains a cycle. The answer and the algorithm differ for undirected and directed graphs.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Undirected, DFS: every edge appears twice (u→v and v→u). Going back to the node you came from isn't a cycle, so ignore the parent once. Any other already-visited neighbour closes a loop. (Ignoring the parent only once means a parallel edge u–v counts as a cycle, which is correct.)
  2. Undirected, Union-Find: process the edges one at a time. If an edge joins two nodes that are already connected, it closes a cycle.
  3. Directed, the trap: a plain "visited" flag gives false positives. In the diamond 0→1, 0→2, 1→2, node 2 is reached twice, but there's no cycle.
  4. Directed, three colours: WHITE = unvisited, GREY = on the current DFS path, BLACK = finished. Only an edge to a GREY node (a back edge) means a cycle.
  5. Directed, Kahn: topological sort outputs every node iff the graph has no cycle.

docs.title: Diamond vs. cycle
docs.text:
0 → 1          0 → 1
  ↓   ↓          ↑   ↓
  2 ←─┘          └─ 2
 no cycle         cycle (2 is GREY when 1 → 2 → 0 → … )

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.List;

/** Does a graph contain a cycle? Undirected and directed graphs need DIFFERENT logic. */
public final class CycleDetection {
    private CycleDetection() {}

    /** Undirected, DFS: a visited neighbour that is NOT the node we came from closes a cycle. O(V+E). */
    public static boolean undirectedDfs(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = Graph.undirected(n, edges);
        boolean[] seen = new boolean[n];
        for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) if (!seen[s] && dfsUndirected(adj, s, -1, seen)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    private static boolean dfsUndirected(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, int parent, boolean[] seen) {
        seen[u] = true;
        boolean skippedParent = false;
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (v == parent && !skippedParent) {             // skip the tree edge back ONCE (a parallel edge is a cycle)
                skippedParent = true;
                continue;
            }
            if (seen[v] || dfsUndirected(adj, v, u, seen)) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    /** Undirected, Union-Find: an edge whose endpoints are already connected closes a cycle. O(E·α). */
    public static boolean undirectedUnionFind(int n, int[][] edges) {
        UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(n);
        for (int[] e : edges) if (!uf.union(e[0], e[1])) return true;
        return false;
    }

    private static final int WHITE = 0, GREY = 1, BLACK = 2;

    /**
     * Directed, DFS with three colours: WHITE unvisited, GREY on the current recursion path, BLACK finished.
     * An edge to a GREY node is a back edge → cycle. (Plain "visited" is wrong for directed graphs: reaching a
     * finished node through another path is not a cycle.) O(V+E).
     */
    public static boolean directedDfs(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = Graph.directed(n, edges);
        int[] colour = new int[n];
        for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) if (colour[s] == WHITE && dfsDirected(adj, s, colour)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    private static boolean dfsDirected(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, int[] colour) {
        colour[u] = GREY;
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (colour[v] == GREY) return true;
            if (colour[v] == WHITE && dfsDirected(adj, v, colour)) return true;
        }
        colour[u] = BLACK;
        return false;
    }

    /** Directed, Kahn's algorithm: a cycle exists iff topological sort cannot output every node. */
    public static boolean directedKahn(int n, int[][] edges) {
        return TopologicalSort.kahn(n, edges).length < n;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(V + E) for the DFS and Kahn approaches, and O(E·α(V)) for Union-Find.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: On 300 random graphs (including self-loops and parallel edges), DFS and Union-Find must agree for undirected graphs, and the three-colour DFS and Kahn must agree for directed graphs.

docs.title: Dijkstra's shortest path
docs.text: Hard Min-heap Greedy Relaxation

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Shortest distance from src to every node in a directed graph with non-negative weights. Unreachable nodes report ∞. | Edge | Weight | |------|--------| | 0 → 1 | 4 | | 0 → 2 | 1 | | 2 → 1 | 2 | | 1 → 3 | 1 | | 2 → 3 | 5 |

Distances from 0: [0, 3, 1, 4]. The cheapest way to 1 is 0 → 2 → 1 (cost 3), not the direct edge (cost 4).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. BFS fails here: fewest edges isn't the same as the smallest weight.
  2. Greedy insight: the unfinished node with the smallest tentative distance is final, because every other route to it goes through nodes that are already farther away, and weights can't be negative.
  3. Relaxation: once u is final, for each edge u → v with weight w, try dist[u] + w < dist[v].
  4. Picking the closest node: a linear scan costs O(V) per pick (O(V²) total, good for dense graphs). A min-heap costs O(log V) per operation.
  5. Lazy deletion: PriorityQueue can't decrease a key. Push a new entry instead, and skip popped entries whose distance is stale (d > dist[u]).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/**
 * Single-source shortest paths with NON-NEGATIVE weights. edges[i] = {u, v, w}, directed.
 * Unreachable nodes get Long.MAX_VALUE.
 */
public final class Dijkstra {
    private Dijkstra() {}

    public static final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE;

    /** Array version: pick the closest unfinished node by linear scan. O(V^2) — best for dense graphs. */
    public static long[] arrayScan(int n, int[][] edges, int src) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = weighted(n, edges);
        long[] dist = new long[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
        dist[src] = 0;
        boolean[] done = new boolean[n];
        for (int iter = 0; iter < n; iter++) {
            int u = -1;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (!done[i] && dist[i] != INF && (u == -1 || dist[i] < dist[u])) u = i;
            if (u == -1) break;                              // the rest is unreachable
            done[u] = true;
            for (int[] e : adj.get(u)) if (dist[u] + e[1] < dist[e[0]]) dist[e[0]] = dist[u] + e[1];
        }
        return dist;
    }

    /**
     * Heap version: min-heap of {dist, node}; pop the closest, relax its edges. Stale entries (a shorter distance was
     * found after pushing) are skipped instead of deleted ("lazy deletion"). O((V + E) log V).
     */
    public static long[] heap(int n, int[][] edges, int src) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = weighted(n, edges);
        long[] dist = new long[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, INF);
        dist[src] = 0;
        PriorityQueue<long[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(a[0], b[0]));
        pq.offer(new long[]{0, src});
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            long[] top = pq.poll();
            int u = (int) top[1];
            if (top[0] > dist[u]) continue;                  // stale entry
            for (int[] e : adj.get(u)) {
                int v = e[0];
                long nd = dist[u] + e[1];
                if (nd < dist[v]) {                          // relaxation
                    dist[v] = nd;
                    pq.offer(new long[]{nd, v});
                }
            }
        }
        return dist;
    }

    static List<List<int[]>> weighted(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<int[]>> adj = new ArrayList<>(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            if (e[2] < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Dijkstra needs non-negative weights");
            adj.get(e[0]).add(new int[]{e[1], e[2]});
        }
        return adj;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Version Time Best for Array scan O(V²) dense graphs (E ≈ V²) Binary heap O((V + E) log V) sparse graphs (most interviews)

docs.title: Why negative weights break it
docs.text: A node marked final could become cheaper later through a negative edge. The code rejects negative weights with an exception. For those graphs, use Bellman-Ford.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: On 300 random graphs, both Dijkstra versions, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall must produce identical distances.

docs.title: Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal & Prim)
docs.text: Expert Greedy Union-Find Min-heap

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
In a connected, undirected, weighted graph, choose V − 1 edges that connect every vertex with the minimum total weight. Return −1 if the graph is disconnected. 

   0 ──10── 1
   | \      |
   6   5    15        MST = (2–3: 4) + (0–3: 5) + (0–1: 10) = 19
   |     \  |
   2 ──4─── 3

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Cut property (why the greedy choice works): for any split of the vertices into two groups, the cheapest edge crossing the split belongs to some MST.
  2. Kruskal (edge-centric): sort all edges by weight. Take each edge unless it would make a cycle, which Union-Find checks in about O(1). Stop at V − 1 edges.
  3. Prim (vertex-centric): grow a single tree from any vertex. A min-heap holds the edges leaving the tree, and you always add the cheapest one that reaches a new vertex. Skip stale heap entries whose target is already in the tree.
  4. Disconnected graph: fewer than V − 1 edges get used (Kruskal), or fewer than V vertices are reached (Prim).

docs.title: Kruskal trace
docs.text: Edge (w) Union? Total 2–3 (4) ✅ 4 0–3 (5) ✅ 9 0–2 (6) ❌ 0 and 2 are already connected 9 0–1 (10) ✅ 19 (3 edges, done)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/**
 * Minimum spanning tree weight of a connected, undirected, weighted graph. edges[i] = {u, v, w}.
 * Returns -1 if the graph is not connected.
 */
public final class MinimumSpanningTree {
    private MinimumSpanningTree() {}

    /** Kruskal: sort edges by weight, add each edge that joins two different components (Union-Find). O(E log E). */
    public static long kruskal(int n, int[][] edges) {
        int[][] sorted = edges.clone();
        Arrays.sort(sorted, Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e[2]));
        UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(n);
        long total = 0;
        int used = 0;
        for (int[] e : sorted) {
            if (uf.union(e[0], e[1])) {                      // skip edges that would form a cycle
                total += e[2];
                if (++used == n - 1) break;
            }
        }
        return used == n - 1 || n <= 1 ? total : -1;
    }

    /** Prim: grow one tree from node 0, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (min-heap). O(E log V). */
    public static long prim(int n, int[][] edges) {
        if (n <= 1) return 0;
        List<List<int[]>> adj = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new java.util.ArrayList<>());
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            adj.get(e[0]).add(new int[]{e[1], e[2]});
            adj.get(e[1]).add(new int[]{e[0], e[2]});
        }
        boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(x -> x[1]));   // {node, weight}
        pq.offer(new int[]{0, 0});
        long total = 0;
        int added = 0;
        while (!pq.isEmpty() && added < n) {
            int[] top = pq.poll();
            if (inTree[top[0]]) continue;                    // stale: already connected more cheaply
            inTree[top[0]] = true;
            total += top[1];
            added++;
            for (int[] e : adj.get(top[0])) if (!inTree[e[0]]) pq.offer(new int[]{e[0], e[1]});
        }
        return added == n ? total : -1;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Algorithm Time Best for Kruskal O(E log E) sparse graphs, edges given as a list Prim (binary heap) O(E log V) dense graphs, adjacency lists

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: On 300 random multigraphs (parallel edges, self-loops, sometimes disconnected), Kruskal and Prim must return the same total.

docs.title: Real-world uses
docs.text: Network cabling, clustering (stop Kruskal early to get k clusters), approximating the travelling salesman problem.

docs.title: Number of islands
docs.text: Medium Grid DFS/BFS Union-Find

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Count the groups of '1' cells connected up/down/left/right. 

1 1 0 0 0
1 1 0 0 0      → 3 islands
0 0 1 0 0
0 0 0 1 1

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A grid is a graph: cells are nodes, and the four neighbours are edges. An island is a connected component of land.
  2. Scan every cell. When you hit unvisited land, count one island and flood-fill it, marking the whole island visited so it's never counted again.
  3. DFS flood fill is the shortest code. BFS avoids stack overflow on huge islands (a 1000×1000 all-land grid is 10⁶ frames deep).
  4. Union-Find: start with count = land cells. Each union that merges two different sets decrements the count. It suits the follow-up where land is added over time (LeetCode 305, Number of Islands II).
  5. Don't destroy the input: "sink" visited land on a copy, or keep a visited array. Mutating a caller's grid is a code-review red flag.

docs.title: Step through it
docs.text:
Play the trace, or step with ← →. The highlighted line is the code that just ran.

Number of islands: DFS flood fill
  1. Scan cell by cell. Each '1' that hasn't been visited starts a new island.
  2. (0,0) is unvisited land: island #1. Sink all of it.
  3. Visit (0,0): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  4. Visit (1,0): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  5. Visit (1,1): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  6. Visit (0,1): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  7. (2,2) is unvisited land: island #2. Sink all of it.
  8. Visit (2,2): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  9. (3,3) is unvisited land: island #3. Sink all of it.
  10. Visit (3,3): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  11. Visit (3,4): mark it so it's never counted again, then try its 4 neighbours.
  12. Every cell scanned: 3 islands. Each cell is visited a constant number of times: O(R·C). (The real code sinks a copy, so the caller's grid is untouched.)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/** Count islands of '1' (4-directionally connected) in a grid of '1'/'0'. The input grid is NOT modified. */
public final class NumberOfIslands {
    private NumberOfIslands() {}

    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

    /** DFS flood fill: every unvisited land cell starts a new island; sink the whole island. O(R·C). */
    public static int dfs(char[][] grid) {
        char[][] g = copy(grid);
        int count = 0;
        for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
                if (g[r][c] == '1') {
                    count++;
                    sink(g, r, c);
                }
        return count;
    }

    private static void sink(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] != '1') return;
        g[r][c] = '0';                                       // mark visited by sinking (on our copy)
        for (int[] d : DIRS) sink(g, r + d[0], c + d[1]);
    }

    /** BFS flood fill: same idea, explicit queue — no recursion depth risk on huge islands. */
    public static int bfs(char[][] grid) {
        char[][] g = copy(grid);
        int count = 0, rows = g.length, cols = rows == 0 ? 0 : g[0].length;
        for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
                if (g[r][c] != '1') continue;
                count++;
                g[r][c] = '0';
                Deque<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
                q.offer(new int[]{r, c});
                while (!q.isEmpty()) {
                    int[] cell = q.poll();
                    for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                        int nr = cell[0] + d[0], nc = cell[1] + d[1];
                        if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < rows && nc < cols && g[nr][nc] == '1') {
                            g[nr][nc] = '0';                 // mark when enqueuing
                            q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        return count;
    }

    /** Union-Find: every land cell is a set; union with land neighbours; answer = number of land sets. */
    public static int unionFind(char[][] grid) {
        int rows = grid.length, cols = rows == 0 ? 0 : grid[0].length;
        UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(rows * cols);
        int land = 0;
        for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
                if (grid[r][c] != '1') continue;
                land++;
                if (r + 1 < rows && grid[r + 1][c] == '1' && uf.union(r * cols + c, (r + 1) * cols + c)) land--;
                if (c + 1 < cols && grid[r][c + 1] == '1' && uf.union(r * cols + c, r * cols + c + 1)) land--;
            }
        return land;                                         // each successful union merged two islands into one
    }

    private static char[][] copy(char[][] g) {
        char[][] c = new char[g.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < g.length; i++) c[i] = g[i].clone();
        return c;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(R·C) time for all three. Space is O(R·C) in the worst case for the recursion, queue or DSU.

docs.title: Family
docs.text: Max area of an island · Surrounded regions (flood fill from the border) · Pacific Atlantic water flow · Number of distinct islands (encode each island's shape) · Rotting oranges.

docs.title: Rotting oranges
docs.text: Medium Multi-source BFS

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
In a grid, 0 = empty, 1 = fresh and 2 = rotten. Every minute, rotten oranges rot their four neighbours. Return the minutes until nothing fresh is left, or −1 if some orange can never rot. 

2 1 1      minute 0 → 4
1 1 0      answer 4
0 1 1

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Simulation: each minute, scan the whole grid and rot the neighbours of rotten cells. Correct, but O((R·C)²).
  2. Rot spreads outward in rings, one ring per minute. That's BFS levels.
  3. Multi-source: put every initially rotten orange in the queue at time 0. BFS then expands from all of them at once, and each level is exactly one minute.
  4. Count the fresh oranges first. Decrement as they rot, and if any remain at the end, return −1.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

/**
 * Grid: 0 empty, 1 fresh, 2 rotten. Each minute rotten oranges rot their 4 neighbours.
 * Minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if some never rot (LeetCode 994).
 */
public final class RottingOranges {
    private RottingOranges() {}

    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

    /** Brute force: simulate minute by minute, scanning the whole grid each time. O((R·C)^2). */
    public static int simulate(int[][] grid) {
        int[][] g = copy(grid);
        int minutes = 0;
        while (true) {
            int[][] next = copy(g);
            boolean changed = false;
            for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
                for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
                    if (g[r][c] == 2)
                        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                            int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                            if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < g.length && nc < g[0].length && g[nr][nc] == 1) {
                                next[nr][nc] = 2;
                                changed = true;
                            }
                        }
            if (!changed) break;
            g = next;
            minutes++;
        }
        for (int[] row : g) for (int v : row) if (v == 1) return -1;
        return minutes;
    }

    /**
     * Multi-source BFS: put ALL rotten oranges in the queue at time 0; each BFS level is one minute.
     * Every cell is processed once → O(R·C).
     */
    public static int multiSourceBfs(int[][] grid) {
        int[][] g = copy(grid);
        int rows = g.length, cols = rows == 0 ? 0 : g[0].length, fresh = 0;
        Deque<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
                if (g[r][c] == 2) q.offer(new int[]{r, c});
                else if (g[r][c] == 1) fresh++;
            }
        int minutes = 0;
        while (!q.isEmpty() && fresh > 0) {
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {    // one level = one minute
                int[] cell = q.poll();
                for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                    int nr = cell[0] + d[0], nc = cell[1] + d[1];
                    if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < rows && nc < cols && g[nr][nc] == 1) {
                        g[nr][nc] = 2;
                        fresh--;
                        q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
                    }
                }
            }
            minutes++;
        }
        return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;
    }

    private static int[][] copy(int[][] g) {
        int[][] c = new int[g.length][];
        for (int i = 0; i < g.length; i++) c[i] = g[i].clone();
        return c;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Simulation O((R·C)²) O(R·C) Multi-source BFS O(R·C) O(R·C)

docs.title: Same pattern
docs.text: Walls and gates (distance to the nearest gate) · 01-matrix (distance to the nearest 0) · Shortest bridge. Whenever you have many starting points and want the distance from the nearest one, seed the BFS with all of them.

docs.title: Topological sort
docs.text: Medium Kahn's algorithm DFS

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Order the nodes of a directed graph so that every edge u → v puts u before v. This only exists if there is no cycle (a DAG). Edges 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1 → one valid order is 4 5 2 3 1 0.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A node with in-degree 0 has no prerequisites, so it can go first.
  2. Kahn (BFS): queue every in-degree-0 node. Pop one, output it, and "delete" its outgoing edges by decrementing its neighbours' in-degrees. Any neighbour that reaches 0 joins the queue.
  3. If the output has fewer than V nodes, the rest are stuck in a cycle. Kahn detects cycles for free.
  4. DFS: a node finishes only after everything reachable from it. Push each node to the front of a list when it finishes, which reverses the finishing order. Use the three-colour state to detect cycles along the way.

docs.title: Kahn trace
docs.text: Ready queue Output In-degrees after 4, 5 4 0: 1, 1: 1 5 5 2: 0 → ready, 0: 0 → ready 2, 0 2 3: 0 → ready 0, 3 0 3 3 1: 0 → ready 1 1 done (6 = V ✅)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Order the nodes of a DAG so every edge u → v has u before v. If there is a cycle, no order exists:
 * both methods then return an array SHORTER than n (Kahn) or an empty array (DFS).
 */
public final class TopologicalSort {
    private TopologicalSort() {}

    /** Kahn (BFS): repeatedly output a node with in-degree 0 and remove its outgoing edges. O(V+E). */
    public static int[] kahn(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = Graph.directed(n, edges);
        int[] indegree = new int[n];
        for (int[] e : edges) indegree[e[1]]++;
        Deque<Integer> ready = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indegree[i] == 0) ready.offer(i);
        int[] order = new int[n];
        int k = 0;
        while (!ready.isEmpty()) {
            int u = ready.poll();
            order[k++] = u;
            for (int v : adj.get(u)) if (--indegree[v] == 0) ready.offer(v);   // last prerequisite done
        }
        return java.util.Arrays.copyOf(order, k);            // k < n means a cycle blocked some nodes
    }

    /** DFS: a node is finished only after all its descendants; reverse finishing order is a topological order. */
    public static int[] dfs(int n, int[][] edges) {
        List<List<Integer>> adj = Graph.directed(n, edges);
        int[] state = new int[n];                            // 0 new, 1 in progress, 2 done
        Deque<Integer> finished = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) if (state[s] == 0 && !visit(adj, s, state, finished)) return new int[0];
        return finished.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    private static boolean visit(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, int[] state, Deque<Integer> finished) {
        state[u] = 1;
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (state[v] == 1) return false;                 // back edge: cycle
            if (state[v] == 0 && !visit(adj, v, state, finished)) return false;
        }
        state[u] = 2;
        finished.push(u);                                    // push to FRONT → reversed finishing order
        return true;
    }

    /** Validate an order: a permutation of 0..n-1 that respects every edge (used by tests). */
    public static boolean isValidOrder(int n, int[][] edges, int[] order) {
        if (order.length != n) return false;
        int[] pos = new int[n];
        java.util.Arrays.fill(pos, -1);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (order[i] < 0 || order[i] >= n || pos[order[i]] != -1) return false;
            pos[order[i]] = i;
        }
        for (int[] e : edges) if (pos[e[0]] >= pos[e[1]]) return false;
        return true;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(V + E) time and O(V) space for both.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: Orders aren't unique, so the tests don't compare with a fixed answer. They validate the result instead: it must be a permutation, and every edge must point forward. On cyclic graphs, both methods must refuse.

docs.title: Used by
docs.text: Course schedule · build systems (Gradle task graph) · spreadsheet recalculation · alien dictionary.

docs.title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) / number of provinces
docs.text: Hard DSU Path compression Union by rank

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Maintain a collection of disjoint sets with two operations: find(x) (which set is x in?) and union(a, b) (merge two sets). Then count the provinces (connected groups of cities) from an adjacency matrix (LeetCode 547).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Represent each set as a tree, where every element points to a parent and the root names the set.
  2. find follows parents up to the root. union hangs one root under the other.
  3. Problem: trees can degenerate into long chains, making find O(n).
  4. Fix 1: union by rank: hang the shorter tree under the taller one, so height stays O(log n).
  5. Fix 2: path compression: while finding, point nodes closer to the root (path halving: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]). Together these give amortised O(α(n)) per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function (≤ 4 for any realistic n).
  6. Have union return false when both elements are already in the same set. That one boolean powers cycle detection and Kruskal's MST.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

/**
 * Disjoint Set Union with path compression + union by rank: find/union in amortised O(α(n)) — effectively constant.
 */
public final class UnionFind {
    private final int[] parent, rank;
    private int sets;

    public UnionFind(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        rank = new int[n];
        sets = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;          // every element starts as its own root
    }

    /** Root of x's set; path compression points every node on the way directly at the root. */
    public int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];                   // path halving: cheap, iterative form of compression
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    /** Merge the sets of a and b. Returns false if they were already together (useful for cycle detection). */
    public boolean union(int a, int b) {
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;
        if (rank[ra] < rank[rb]) {                           // attach the shorter tree under the taller one
            int t = ra;
            ra = rb;
            rb = t;
        }
        parent[rb] = ra;
        if (rank[ra] == rank[rb]) rank[ra]++;
        sets--;
        return true;
    }

    public boolean connected(int a, int b) {
        return find(a) == find(b);
    }

    public int sets() {
        return sets;
    }

    /** Number of provinces (LeetCode 547) from an adjacency MATRIX, using DSU. */
    public static int provinces(int[][] isConnected) {
        int n = isConnected.length;
        UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(n);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) if (isConnected[i][j] == 1) uf.union(i, j);
        return uf.sets();
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Operation Naive With rank + compression find / union O(n) O(α(n)), effectively O(1)

docs.title: When DSU beats BFS/DFS
docs.text: When edges arrive over time and you're asked "are a and b connected now?" between arrivals. A BFS per query would be O(V + E) each. Examples: number of islands II, accounts merge, redundant connection, Kruskal.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: On 200 random graphs, the number of DSU sets must equal the number of BFS components.

docs.title: Word ladder
docs.text: Expert BFS Implicit graph Bidirectional BFS

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Transform begin into end by changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the dictionary. Return the number of words in the shortest sequence, or 0. hit → hot → dot → dog → cog = 5.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Model: words are nodes, and two words are connected if they differ in exactly one letter. You want the fewest steps in an unweighted graph, so use BFS.
  2. Don't build the graph: comparing every pair of words is O(N²·L). Instead, generate each word's neighbours on the fly: try all 26 letters at each of its L positions and keep the candidates that are in the dictionary set. That's O(26·L) per word.
  3. Visited = remove the word from the dictionary set when you enqueue it.
  4. Expert speed-up, bidirectional BFS: grow one frontier from begin and one from end, always expanding the smaller frontier, and stop as soon as a generated word is in the other frontier. With branching factor b and distance d, the work drops from about b^d to about 2·b^(d/2).

docs.title: BFS levels
docs.text: Level Words 1 hit 2 hot 3 dot, lot 4 dog, log 5 cog ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.graphs;

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;

/**
 * Fewest words in a transformation begin → end, changing one letter at a time, every intermediate word in the
 * dictionary (LeetCode 127). hit → hot → dot → dog → cog = 5. Returns 0 if impossible.
 */
public final class WordLadder {
    private WordLadder() {}

    /** BFS over an IMPLICIT graph: neighbours are generated by trying all 26 letters at each position. O(N·L·26). */
    public static int bfs(String begin, String end, List<String> dictionary) {
        Set<String> unvisited = new HashSet<>(dictionary);
        if (!unvisited.contains(end)) return 0;
        Deque<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(begin);
        unvisited.remove(begin);
        for (int length = 1; !q.isEmpty(); length++) {
            for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
                String word = q.poll();
                if (word.equals(end)) return length;
                for (String next : neighbours(word, unvisited)) {
                    unvisited.remove(next);                  // mark when enqueuing
                    q.offer(next);
                }
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }

    /**
     * Bidirectional BFS: expand from both ends, always growing the SMALLER frontier; stop when they touch.
     * Explores roughly 2·b^(d/2) words instead of b^d.
     */
    public static int bidirectional(String begin, String end, List<String> dictionary) {
        Set<String> dict = new HashSet<>(dictionary);
        if (!dict.contains(end)) return 0;
        if (begin.equals(end)) return 1;
        Set<String> front = new HashSet<>(Set.of(begin)), back = new HashSet<>(Set.of(end));
        dict.remove(begin);
        dict.remove(end);
        for (int length = 2; !front.isEmpty() && !back.isEmpty(); length++) {
            if (front.size() > back.size()) {
                Set<String> t = front;
                front = back;
                back = t;
            }
            Set<String> next = new HashSet<>();
            for (String word : front) {
                char[] w = word.toCharArray();
                for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) {
                    char original = w[i];
                    for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; c++) {
                        if (c == original) continue;
                        w[i] = c;
                        String cand = new String(w);
                        if (back.contains(cand)) return length;   // frontiers meet
                        if (dict.remove(cand)) next.add(cand);
                    }
                    w[i] = original;
                }
            }
            front = next;
        }
        return 0;
    }

    private static List<String> neighbours(String word, Set<String> unvisited) {
        List<String> out = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
        char[] w = word.toCharArray();
        for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) {
            char original = w[i];
            for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; c++) {
                if (c == original) continue;
                w[i] = c;
                String cand = new String(w);
                if (unvisited.contains(cand)) out.add(cand);
            }
            w[i] = original;
        }
        return out;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(N · L · 26) time and O(N · L) space, where N = dictionary size and L = word length. The bidirectional version has the same worst case but is much faster in practice.

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: You have to see that it's a graph problem with no graph given, choose implicit neighbour generation over pairwise comparison, and optionally reach for bidirectional BFS. Word Ladder II (return all shortest paths) adds parent tracking and backtracking on top.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: 200 random small dictionaries: plain BFS and bidirectional BFS must agree.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
DP is recursion plus never solving the same subproblem twice. A problem is a DP problem when it has:

  1. Optimal substructure: the answer is built from answers to smaller versions of the same problem.
  2. Overlapping subproblems: plain recursion would solve the same smaller version many times.

docs.title: The 4-step ladder (every page in this topic follows it)
docs.text:
1. Recursion: write the brute-force recurrence. Ask: "what is the last decision?" (last step, last coin, last item, last character).
  2. Memoization (top-down): cache results by the recursion's changing parameters. That parameter list is your DP state.
  3. Tabulation (bottom-up): fill a table in an order where every dependency is already computed. No recursion, so no stack overflow.
  4. Space optimisation: if row i only reads row i − 1, keep one or two rows.

Finding the state

The state is the smallest set of facts that fully determines the remaining sub-problem: an index (i), a remaining capacity (w), two prefix lengths (i, j) or an interval (i, j). Count the states and the work per state to get the complexity: states × transitions.

docs.title: The DP families
docs.text: Family State Examples here 1D linear dp[i] Climbing stairs, House robber, LIS, Word break Unbounded knapsack dp[amount] Coin change 0/1 knapsack dp[i][w] → dp[w] (iterate w down) 0/1 Knapsack, Partition equal subset Grid dp[r][c] Unique paths Two strings dp[i][j] over prefixes LCS, Edit distance Interval dp[i][j] over a range, by increasing length Matrix chain, Burst balloons

docs.title: Problems (Easy → Expert)
docs.text:
# Problem Level Recurrence in one line 1 Climbing stairs Easy f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) 2 House robber Easy f(i) = max(f(i−1), a[i] + f(i−2)) 3 Coin change: min coins & ways Medium f(a) = 1 + min f(a − c) 4 Longest increasing subsequence Medium f(i) = 1 + max f(j), j < i, a[j] < a[i] 5 Unique paths Medium f(r,c) = f(r−1,c) + f(r,c−1) 6 0/1 knapsack Medium f(i,w) = max(skip, take) 7 Longest common subsequence Hard match: 1 + f(i−1,j−1); else max(f(i−1,j), f(i,j−1)) 8 Edit distance Hard 1 + min(replace, delete, insert) 9 Partition equal subset sum Hard subset sum to total/2 10 Word break Expert f(i) = ∃ j: f(j) ∧ s[j..i) ∈ dict 11 Matrix chain multiplication Expert min over split k 12 Burst balloons Expert choose the last balloon to burst

Also DP elsewhere: Fibonacci · Kadane · Longest palindromic substring · Buy & sell stock.

docs.title: Burst balloons
docs.text: Expert Interval DP Think backwards

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Burst balloons one at a time. Bursting balloon i earns left × nums[i] × right, where left and right are its current neighbours (1 beyond the ends). Maximise the total. [3,1,5,8] → 167.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every order, n! of them. The tests use this as the reference for small n.
  2. Why "first to burst" fails as a DP state: bursting balloon k first makes its neighbours adjacent, so the left and right sides aren't independent anymore.
  3. The flip: choose the balloon to burst last in an interval. While everything else inside (i, j) bursts, k is still standing, so the left part and right part never touch each other. When k finally bursts, its neighbours are exactly the interval boundaries i and j.
  4. So dp[i][j] = max over k in (i, j) of dp[i][k] + a[i]·a[k]·a[j] + dp[k][j], over an array padded with a 1 at each end.
  5. Fill by increasing interval length, the interval-DP pattern again. That's O(n³).

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: The algorithm is ordinary interval DP. The insight, reverse the time direction to make subproblems independent, is not. Spotting when "first" breaks independence and "last" restores it is a reusable senior-level trick. It also appears in "minimum cost to cut a stick".

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Burst balloon i to earn left·nums[i]·right (neighbours at that moment; outside = 1). Max total coins.
 * [3,1,5,8] → 167. (LeetCode 312)
 */
public final class BurstBalloons {
    private BurstBalloons() {}

    /** Brute force: try every balloon as the NEXT one to burst, recursively. O(n!). Only for tiny inputs. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] nums) {
        List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int x : nums) list.add(x);
        return brute(list);
    }

    private static int brute(List<Integer> b) {
        if (b.isEmpty()) return 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < b.size(); i++) {
            int left = i == 0 ? 1 : b.get(i - 1), right = i == b.size() - 1 ? 1 : b.get(i + 1);
            int coins = left * b.get(i) * right;
            Integer removed = b.remove(i);
            best = Math.max(best, coins + brute(b));
            b.add(i, removed);                               // backtrack
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Interval DP, thinking BACKWARDS: choose k = the LAST balloon to burst inside the open interval (i, j).
     * When k bursts last, its neighbours are exactly the interval boundaries i and j — fixed, independent of the order
     * inside. So dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + a[i]·a[k]·a[j] + dp[k][j]. O(n^3).
     */
    public static int intervalDp(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] a = new int[n + 2];
        a[0] = a[n + 1] = 1;                                 // virtual boundary balloons
        System.arraycopy(nums, 0, a, 1, n);
        int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2];
        for (int len = 2; len <= n + 1; len++)               // len = j - i
            for (int i = 0; i + len <= n + 1; i++) {
                int j = i + len;
                for (int k = i + 1; k < j; k++)
                    dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + a[i] * a[k] * a[j] + dp[k][j]);
            }
        return dp[0][n + 1];
    }
}

docs.text: Brute force O(n!) · interval DP O(n³) time, O(n²) space.

docs.title: Climbing stairs
docs.text: Easy 1D DP Recursion → memo → table → O(1)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to reach step n? n = 3 → 3 (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1). Generalisation: any set of allowed step sizes.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Last decision: the final move onto step n was a 1-step (from n−1) or a 2-step (from n−2). Those two groups don't overlap and together cover every way, so f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) with f(0) = f(1) = 1. It's Fibonacci.
  2. Recursion recomputes the same values exponentially often, so cache them (memo), which is O(n).
  3. Table: dp[i] only needs dp[i−1] and dp[i−2], so fill it left to right.
  4. O(1) space: keep just the two previous values.
  5. Any step set {s₁…sₖ}: dp[i] = Σ dp[i − s], for O(n·k).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps (n ≥ 0; 0 stairs → 1 way). The "hello world" of DP. */
public final class ClimbingStairs {
    private ClimbingStairs() {}

    /** 1. Plain recursion: last move was 1 or 2 steps → f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2). O(2^n). */
    public static long recursive(int n) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;
        return recursive(n - 1) + recursive(n - 2);
    }

    /** 2. Memoization (top-down): cache each f(k). O(n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static long memo(int n) {
        long[] cache = new long[n + 1];
        Arrays.fill(cache, -1);
        return memo(n, cache);
    }

    private static long memo(int n, long[] cache) {
        if (n <= 1) return 1;
        if (cache[n] != -1) return cache[n];
        return cache[n] = memo(n - 1, cache) + memo(n - 2, cache);
    }

    /** 3. Tabulation (bottom-up): fill dp[0..n] in order. O(n), O(n). */
    public static long table(int n) {
        long[] dp = new long[Math.max(2, n + 1)];
        dp[0] = dp[1] = 1;
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2];
        return dp[n];
    }

    /** 4. Space-optimised: only the last two values matter. O(n), O(1). */
    public static long optimal(int n) {
        long prev2 = 1, prev1 = 1;                           // f(0), f(1)
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            long cur = prev1 + prev2;
            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = cur;
        }
        return prev1;
    }

    /** Generalisation: allowed step sizes are given (e.g. {1, 3, 5}). dp[i] = Σ dp[i - s]. O(n·k). */
    public static long withSteps(int n, int[] steps) {
        long[] dp = new long[n + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) for (int s : steps) if (i >= s) dp[i] += dp[i - s];
        return dp[n];
    }
}

docs.title: Coin change: fewest coins & number of ways
docs.text: Medium Unbounded knapsack

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Each coin denomination can be used any number of times. 1. Fewest coins to make amount, or −1 (LeetCode 322): [1,2,5], 11 → 3 (5 + 5 + 1). 2. Number of combinations (LeetCode 518): [1,2,5], 5 → 4.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Why greedy fails: with [1,3,4] and 6, "largest coin first" gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 = 2. You have to try every option.
  2. Last decision: the last coin used was some c, so f(a) = 1 + min over c of f(a − c), with f(0) = 0.
  3. State = the remaining amount alone, giving amount + 1 states × #coins transitions.
  4. Table: fill dp[1..amount] upward. Use amount + 1 as "infinity", since no answer can use more coins than the amount.
  5. Counting ways, the loop-order subtlety:
    • coins outer, amounts inner: each coin is added in a fixed order, so {1,2} and {2,1} count once. Those are combinations.
    • amounts outer, coins inner: every ordering is counted. Those are permutations (5 → 9).

  3. a = 2: try every coin as the last one: dp[1]+1 = 2, dp[0]+1 = 1. Best is coin 2 → dp[2] = 1.
  4. a = 3: try every coin as the last one: dp[2]+1 = 2, dp[1]+1 = 2. Best is coin 1 → dp[3] = 2.
  5. a = 4: try every coin as the last one: dp[3]+1 = 3, dp[2]+1 = 2. Best is coin 2 → dp[4] = 2.

  8. a = 7: try every coin as the last one: dp[6]+1 = 3, dp[5]+1 = 2, dp[2]+1 = 2. Best is coin 2 → dp[7] = 2.
  9. a = 8: try every coin as the last one: dp[7]+1 = 3, dp[6]+1 = 3, dp[3]+1 = 3. Best is coin 1 → dp[8] = 3.
  10. a = 9: try every coin as the last one: dp[8]+1 = 4, dp[7]+1 = 3, dp[4]+1 = 3. Best is coin 2 → dp[9] = 3.
  11. a = 10: try every coin as the last one: dp[9]+1 = 4, dp[8]+1 = 4, dp[5]+1 = 2. Best is coin 5 → dp[10] = 2.
  12. a = 11: try every coin as the last one: dp[10]+1 = 3, dp[9]+1 = 4, dp[6]+1 = 3. Best is coin 1 → dp[11] = 3.
  13. dp[11] = 3 (5 + 5 + 1). O(amount × coins) time, O(amount) space.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Unlimited coins of each denomination. (1) fewest coins for amount, -1 if impossible. (2) number of combinations. */
public final class CoinChange {
    private CoinChange() {}

    /** Recursion: try every coin as the last one. Exponential. */
    public static int minCoinsRecursive(int[] coins, int amount) {
        if (amount == 0) return 0;
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int c : coins) {
            if (c > amount) continue;
            int sub = minCoinsRecursive(coins, amount - c);
            if (sub != -1) best = Math.min(best, sub + 1);
        }
        return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : best;
    }

    /** Memoized: cache by remaining amount. O(amount · coins). */
    public static int minCoinsMemo(int[] coins, int amount) {
        int[] cache = new int[amount + 1];
        Arrays.fill(cache, -2);                              // -2 = not computed, -1 = impossible
        return memo(coins, amount, cache);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] coins, int amount, int[] cache) {
        if (amount == 0) return 0;
        if (cache[amount] != -2) return cache[amount];
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int c : coins) {
            if (c > amount) continue;
            int sub = memo(coins, amount - c, cache);
            if (sub != -1) best = Math.min(best, sub + 1);
        }
        return cache[amount] = best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : best;
    }

    /** Bottom-up: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]). "amount + 1" acts as infinity (can never be reached). O(amount · coins). */
    public static int minCoins(int[] coins, int amount) {
        int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
        Arrays.fill(dp, amount + 1);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
            for (int c : coins) if (c <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);
        return dp[amount] > amount ? -1 : dp[amount];
    }

    /**
     * Number of COMBINATIONS (order doesn't matter, LeetCode 518). Coins in the OUTER loop: each coin is "unlocked" once,
     * so {1,2} and {2,1} are counted once. Swapping the loops counts permutations instead.
     */
    public static long combinations(int[] coins, int amount) {
        long[] dp = new long[amount + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (int c : coins) for (int a = c; a <= amount; a++) dp[a] += dp[a - c];
        return dp[amount];
    }

    /** Number of ordered sequences (permutations) — loops swapped. */
    public static long permutations(int[] coins, int amount) {
        long[] dp = new long[amount + 1];
        dp[0] = 1;
        for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++) for (int c : coins) if (c <= a) dp[a] += dp[a - c];
        return dp[amount];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(amount × coins) time and O(amount) space for the memo and table versions. The plain recursion is exponential.

docs.title: Edit distance (Levenshtein)
docs.text: Hard Two-string DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The minimum number of single-character inserts, deletes and replacements to turn a into b. "horse" → "ros" = 3 (replace h→r, delete r, delete e).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. State = prefixes (i, j). Base cases: turning i characters into an empty string takes i deletes, and turning an empty string into j characters takes j inserts.
  2. Last characters equal cost nothing: f(i−1, j−1).
  3. Different: try all three operations on the last position and take the cheapest:
    • replace a's last character with b's: 1 + f(i−1, j−1);
    • delete a's last character: 1 + f(i−1, j);
    • insert b's last character at the end of a: 1 + f(i, j−1).
  4. One row: each cell needs its left, upper and upper-left neighbours. Save the upper-left value in a diag variable before it's overwritten.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** Minimum insert/delete/replace operations to turn a into b ("horse" → "ros" = 3). Levenshtein distance. */
public final class EditDistance {
    private EditDistance() {}

    /** Recursion on prefixes. O(3^(m+n)). */
    public static int recursive(String a, String b) {
        return rec(a, b, a.length(), b.length());
    }

    private static int rec(String a, String b, int i, int j) {
        if (i == 0) return j;                                // insert the remaining j chars
        if (j == 0) return i;                                // delete the remaining i chars
        if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) return rec(a, b, i - 1, j - 1);   // free match
        return 1 + Math.min(rec(a, b, i - 1, j - 1),        // replace
                Math.min(rec(a, b, i - 1, j),                // delete from a
                        rec(a, b, i, j - 1)));               // insert into a
    }

    /** Table dp[i][j] = distance between a[0..i) and b[0..j). O(m·n). */
    public static int table(String a, String b) {
        int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
        int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;
        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
                dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1]
                        : 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1], Math.min(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]));
        return dp[m][n];
    }

    /** One row + a saved diagonal. O(m·n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static int oneRow(String a, String b) {
        int n = b.length();
        int[] row = new int[n + 1];
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) row[j] = j;
        for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
            int diag = row[0];                               // dp[i-1][j-1]
            row[0] = i;
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
                int above = row[j];                          // dp[i-1][j], about to be overwritten
                row[j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? diag : 1 + Math.min(diag, Math.min(above, row[j - 1]));
                diag = above;
            }
        }
        return row[n];
    }
}

docs.text: Recursion O(3^(m+n)) · table O(m·n) time and space · one row O(m·n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: House robber
docs.text: Easy 1D DP Take / skip

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Houses in a row hold money, and you can't rob two adjacent houses. Maximise the total. [2,7,9,3,1] → 12 (2 + 9 + 1). Variant: the houses are in a circle (LeetCode 213).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Last decision at house i: skip it (best up to i−1), or take it (a[i] plus the best up to i−2, since i−1 is now forbidden). f(i) = max(f(i−1), a[i] + f(i−2)).
  2. Recursion → memo → table, then only two values are needed, so use O(1) space.
  3. Circle: the first and last houses are now adjacent, so you can't take both. Solve two straight-line problems, without the last and without the first, and take the larger.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Max money robbing houses in a row without robbing two adjacent ones. [2,7,9,3,1] → 12 (2 + 9 + 1). */
public final class HouseRobber {
    private HouseRobber() {}

    /** Recursion from the end: rob house i (skip i-1) or skip it. O(2^n). */
    public static int recursive(int[] a) {
        return rob(a, a.length - 1);
    }

    private static int rob(int[] a, int i) {
        if (i < 0) return 0;
        return Math.max(rob(a, i - 1), a[i] + rob(a, i - 2));
    }

    /** Memoized. O(n). */
    public static int memo(int[] a) {
        int[] cache = new int[a.length];
        Arrays.fill(cache, -1);
        return memo(a, a.length - 1, cache);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] a, int i, int[] cache) {
        if (i < 0) return 0;
        if (cache[i] != -1) return cache[i];
        return cache[i] = Math.max(memo(a, i - 1, cache), a[i] + memo(a, i - 2, cache));
    }

    /** Tabulation with O(1) space: best including up to previous house, and up to the one before. */
    public static int optimal(int[] a) {
        int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int cur = Math.max(prev1, prev2 + x);            // skip x, or take x on top of best two back
            prev2 = prev1;
            prev1 = cur;
        }
        return prev1;
    }

    /** Circular street (LeetCode 213): first and last are neighbours → max(rob without last, rob without first). */
    public static int circular(int[] a) {
        if (a.length == 1) return a[0];
        return Math.max(optimal(Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 0, a.length - 1)), optimal(Arrays.copyOfRange(a, 1, a.length)));
    }
}

docs.text: Recursive O(2ⁿ) · memo O(n)/O(n) · optimal O(n)/O(1).

docs.title: 0/1 knapsack
docs.text: Medium Knapsack 2D → 1D

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Items have a weight and a value, and each can be used at most once. Maximise the value with total weight ≤ capacity. weights [10,20,30], values [60,100,120], capacity 50 → 220 (items 2 and 3).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Greedy by value/weight ratio fails for 0/1 (it works for the fractional knapsack in the Greedy topic).
  2. Decision per item: skip it, giving f(i−1, w), or take it if it fits, giving val[i] + f(i−1, w − wt[i]).
  3. State = (item index, remaining capacity), so there are n × W states with O(1) work each: O(n·W). That's pseudo-polynomial, since it depends on the value of W.
  4. 2D table: dp[i][w] uses only row i−1, so one row is enough.
  5. The direction trick: in the 1D version, iterate w downward. That way dp[w − wt] is still the previous item's value, and each item is used once. Iterating upward lets an item be reused, which turns it into the unbounded knapsack.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** 0/1 knapsack: each item once; maximise value with total weight ≤ capacity. */
public final class Knapsack01 {
    private Knapsack01() {}

    /** Recursion: for item i, skip it or take it (if it fits). O(2^n). */
    public static int recursive(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        return rec(wt, val, wt.length - 1, cap);
    }

    private static int rec(int[] wt, int[] val, int i, int cap) {
        if (i < 0 || cap == 0) return 0;
        int skip = rec(wt, val, i - 1, cap);
        if (wt[i] > cap) return skip;
        return Math.max(skip, val[i] + rec(wt, val, i - 1, cap - wt[i]));
    }

    /** Memoized on (item, capacity). O(n·W). */
    public static int memo(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        Integer[][] cache = new Integer[wt.length][cap + 1];
        return memo(wt, val, wt.length - 1, cap, cache);
    }

    private static int memo(int[] wt, int[] val, int i, int cap, Integer[][] cache) {
        if (i < 0 || cap == 0) return 0;
        if (cache[i][cap] != null) return cache[i][cap];
        int skip = memo(wt, val, i - 1, cap, cache);
        int best = wt[i] > cap ? skip : Math.max(skip, val[i] + memo(wt, val, i - 1, cap - wt[i], cache));
        return cache[i][cap] = best;
    }

    /** 2D table: dp[i][w] = best using the first i items with capacity w. O(n·W) time and space. */
    public static int table(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        int n = wt.length;
        int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][cap + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
            for (int w = 0; w <= cap; w++) {
                dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w];
                if (wt[i - 1] <= w) dp[i][w] = Math.max(dp[i][w], val[i - 1] + dp[i - 1][w - wt[i - 1]]);
            }
        return dp[n][cap];
    }

    /**
     * 1D: one row, capacity iterated DOWNWARD so dp[w - wt] still holds the previous item's row
     * (iterating upward would let an item be reused = unbounded knapsack). O(n·W) time, O(W) space.
     */
    public static int optimal(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++)
            for (int w = cap; w >= wt[i]; w--) dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]]);
        return dp[cap];
    }

    /** Unbounded knapsack (items reusable): the same loop, capacity iterated UPWARD. */
    public static int unbounded(int[] wt, int[] val, int cap) {
        int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < wt.length; i++)
            for (int w = wt[i]; w <= cap; w++) dp[w] = Math.max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w - wt[i]]);
        return dp[cap];
    }
}

docs.title: Longest common subsequence
docs.text: Hard Two-string DP Reconstruction

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The length of the longest sequence that appears, in order, in both strings, and the sequence itself. "abcde", "ace" → 3, "ace".

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. State = two prefix lengths (i, j): a[0..i) and b[0..j).
  2. Compare the last characters:
    • equal: they can both end the LCS, giving 1 + f(i−1, j−1);
    • different: at least one of them isn't in the LCS, giving max(f(i−1, j), f(i, j−1)).
  3. The base case is an empty prefix, giving 0. That's (m+1)(n+1) states with O(1) work each, so O(m·n).
  4. Reconstruction: walk back from dp[m][n]. On equal characters, take the character and move diagonally. Otherwise move toward the larger neighbour.
  5. Space: for the length only, keep two rows, and make the shorter string the columns.

LCS table for "abcde" and "ace"

  2. dp[1][1]: a = a: take the diagonal + 1 → 1.
  3. dp[1][2]: a ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 0, left 1) = 1.
  4. dp[1][3]: a ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 0, left 1) = 1.
  5. dp[2][1]: b ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  6. dp[2][2]: b ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 1) = 1.
  7. dp[2][3]: b ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 1) = 1.
  8. dp[3][1]: c ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  9. dp[3][2]: c = c: take the diagonal + 1 → 2.
  10. dp[3][3]: c ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 2) = 2.
  11. dp[4][1]: d ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  12. dp[4][2]: d ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 2, left 1) = 2.
  13. dp[4][3]: d ≠ e: drop one character from either string, max(up 2, left 2) = 2.
  14. dp[5][1]: e ≠ a: drop one character from either string, max(up 1, left 0) = 1.
  15. dp[5][2]: e ≠ c: drop one character from either string, max(up 2, left 1) = 2.
  16. dp[5][3]: e = e: take the diagonal + 1 → 3.
  17. Answer: dp[5][3] = 3. Walking back from the corner (diagonal on a match) spells the LCS "ace". O(m·n) time and space.

docs.title: Code

package com.playbook.dp;

/** Longest common subsequence of two strings ("abcde", "ace" → 3, "ace"). */
public final class LongestCommonSubsequence {
    private LongestCommonSubsequence() {}

    /** Recursion on prefixes: last chars equal → 1 + lcs(both shorter); else max(drop one from either). O(2^(m+n)). */
    public static int recursive(String a, String b) {
        return rec(a, b, a.length(), b.length());
    }

    private static int rec(String a, String b, int i, int j) {
        if (i == 0 || j == 0) return 0;
        if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) return 1 + rec(a, b, i - 1, j - 1);
        return Math.max(rec(a, b, i - 1, j), rec(a, b, i, j - 1));
    }

    /** Memoized. O(m·n). */
    public static int memo(String a, String b) {
        Integer[][] cache = new Integer[a.length() + 1][b.length() + 1];
        return memo(a, b, a.length(), b.length(), cache);
    }

    private static int memo(String a, String b, int i, int j, Integer[][] cache) {
        if (i == 0 || j == 0) return 0;
        if (cache[i][j] != null) return cache[i][j];
        int r = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? 1 + memo(a, b, i - 1, j - 1, cache)
                : Math.max(memo(a, b, i - 1, j, cache), memo(a, b, i, j - 1, cache));
        return cache[i][j] = r;
    }

    /** Table dp[i][j] = LCS of a[0..i) and b[0..j). O(m·n). */
    public static int[][] table(String a, String b) {
        int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
        int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
                dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
        return dp;
    }

    public static int length(String a, String b) {
        return table(a, b)[a.length()][b.length()];
    }

    /** Reconstruct one LCS by walking the table back from the bottom-right corner. */
    public static String sequence(String a, String b) {
        int[][] dp = table(a, b);
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = a.length(), j = b.length(); i > 0 && j > 0; ) {
            if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) {
                sb.append(a.charAt(i - 1));
                i--;
                j--;
            } else if (dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]) i--;
            else j--;
        }
        return sb.reverse().toString();
    }

    /** Two rows instead of a full table: O(min(m,n)) space when only the length is needed. */
    public static int twoRows(String a, String b) {
        if (b.length() > a.length()) return twoRows(b, a);
        int[] prev = new int[b.length() + 1], cur = new int[b.length() + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= b.length(); j++)
                cur[j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? prev[j - 1] + 1 : Math.max(prev[j], cur[j - 1]);
            int[] t = prev;
            prev = cur;
            cur = t;
        }
        return prev[b.length()];
    }
}

docs.title: Longest increasing subsequence
docs.text: Medium 1D DP Binary search Patience sorting

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (not necessarily contiguous). [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] → 4 (2,3,7,18).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Recursion: for each element, skip it or take it (if it's bigger than the last one taken). O(2ⁿ).
  2. DP O(n²): dp[i] = the length of the LIS ending exactly at i = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with a[j] < a[i]. The answer is max(dp).
  3. O(n log n) insight: for each length k, only the smallest possible tail matters, because a smaller tail is easier to extend. Keep tails[k], which is always sorted. For each x, binary-search the first tail ≥ x and replace it with x. If x is bigger than every tail, append it.
  4. Careful: tails is not an actual LIS. Only its length is the answer. (Rebuilding the sequence needs parent pointers.)

docs.title: Patience trace
docs.text: x tails 10 [10] 9 [9] replace 2 [2] replace 5 [2, 5] append 3 [2, 3] replace 7 [2, 3, 7] append 101 [2, 3, 7, 101] append 18 [2, 3, 7, 18] replace → length 4

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Length of the longest STRICTLY increasing subsequence. [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] → 4 (2,3,7,18). */
public final class LongestIncreasingSubsequence {
    private LongestIncreasingSubsequence() {}

    /** Recursion: take or skip each element, remembering the last taken value. O(2^n). */
    public static int recursive(int[] a) {
        return rec(a, 0, -1);
    }

    private static int rec(int[] a, int i, int prevIdx) {
        if (i == a.length) return 0;
        int skip = rec(a, i + 1, prevIdx);
        int take = prevIdx == -1 || a[i] > a[prevIdx] ? 1 + rec(a, i + 1, i) : 0;
        return Math.max(skip, take);
    }

    /** DP O(n^2): dp[i] = LIS ending exactly at i = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with a[j] < a[i]. */
    public static int quadratic(int[] a) {
        int[] dp = new int[a.length];
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            dp[i] = 1;
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j] < a[i]) dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Patience sorting O(n log n): tails[k] = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.
     * tails is sorted, so binary-search where each element goes (replace the first tail ≥ x, or extend).
     */
    public static int patience(int[] a) {
        int[] tails = new int[a.length];
        int len = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int pos = Arrays.binarySearch(tails, 0, len, x);
            if (pos < 0) pos = -pos - 1;                     // insertion point = first tail >= x (strictly increasing)
            tails[pos] = x;
            if (pos == len) len++;
        }
        return len;
    }
}

docs.title: Matrix chain multiplication
docs.text: Expert Interval DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Matrices A₁…Aₙ, where Aᵢ has dimensions dims[i−1] × dims[i]. Multiplication is associative, so choose the parenthesisation that minimises scalar multiplications. dims = [10,30,5,60] → 4500, from (A₁A₂)A₃, versus 27,000 for A₁(A₂A₃).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Multiplying a p×q matrix by a q×r one costs p·q·r.
  2. Last decision: the final multiplication splits the chain i..j at some k: (Aᵢ…Aₖ)(Aₖ₊₁…Aⱼ). The cost is f(i,k) + f(k+1,j) + dims[i−1]·dims[k]·dims[j]. Try every k.
  3. State = the interval (i, j): O(n²) states with O(n) choices of k each, so O(n³).
  4. Fill order: a chain needs shorter chains first, so loop over length, then the start. That's the signature of interval DP.

docs.title: Interval DP fill order
docs.text:
len 2: (1,2) (2,3) …          ← pairs first
len 3: (1,3) (2,4) …          ← uses len-2 results
…
len n: (1,n)                  ← the answer

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/**
 * Matrices A1..An where Ai has dims[i-1] × dims[i]. Minimum scalar multiplications to compute the product
 * (choosing the parenthesisation). dims = [10, 30, 5, 60] → 4500: (A1·A2)·A3.
 */
public final class MatrixChainMultiplication {
    private MatrixChainMultiplication() {}

    /** Recursion: try every split point k for the chain i..j. Exponential (Catalan number of orders). */
    public static long recursive(int[] dims) {
        return rec(dims, 1, dims.length - 1);
    }

    private static long rec(int[] d, int i, int j) {
        if (i >= j) return 0;                                // one matrix: no multiplication
        long best = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int k = i; k < j; k++)
            best = Math.min(best, rec(d, i, k) + rec(d, k + 1, j) + (long) d[i - 1] * d[k] * d[j]);
        return best;
    }

    /** Memoized on (i, j). O(n^3). */
    public static long memo(int[] dims) {
        int n = dims.length;
        return memo(dims, 1, n - 1, new long[n][n]);
    }

    private static long memo(int[] d, int i, int j, long[][] cache) {
        if (i >= j) return 0;
        if (cache[i][j] != 0) return cache[i][j];
        long best = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int k = i; k < j; k++)
            best = Math.min(best, memo(d, i, k, cache) + memo(d, k + 1, j, cache) + (long) d[i - 1] * d[k] * d[j]);
        return cache[i][j] = best;
    }

    /** Interval DP: solve chains by increasing LENGTH so sub-chains are always ready. O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space. */
    public static long table(int[] dims) {
        int n = dims.length - 1;                             // number of matrices
        long[][] dp = new long[n + 1][n + 1];
        for (int len = 2; len <= n; len++)
            for (int i = 1; i + len - 1 <= n; i++) {
                int j = i + len - 1;
                dp[i][j] = Long.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int k = i; k < j; k++)
                    dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + (long) dims[i - 1] * dims[k] * dims[j]);
            }
        return dp[1][n];
    }
}
