docs.title: Partition equal subset sum
docs.text: Hard Subset sum 0/1 knapsack Bitset

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Can positive integers be split into two subsets with equal sums? [1,5,11,5] → true ([11] and [1,5,5]). [1,2,3,5] → false.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Reduce it: an odd total can't be split. Otherwise the question becomes: is there a subset summing to total/2? That's the subset-sum problem.
  2. Recursion: for each number, take it or skip it. O(2ⁿ).
  3. DP: can[s] = "some subset seen so far sums to s". For each x, can[s] |= can[s − x]. Iterate s downward so each number is used at most once, exactly as in the 0/1 knapsack.
  4. Bitset: represent can as bits, so adding x becomes bits |= bits << x. That handles 64 sums per machine word, a constant-factor speed-up worth mentioning.

docs.title: DP trace ([1,5,11,5], target 11)
docs.text: After Reachable sums start 0 1 0 1 5 0 1 5 6 11 0 1 5 6 11 ✅

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.BitSet;

/** Can the positive numbers be split into two subsets of equal sum? [1,5,11,5] → true (11 | 1+5+5). */
public final class PartitionEqualSubset {
    private PartitionEqualSubset() {}

    /** Reduce to subset-sum: is there a subset summing to total/2? Recursive take/skip. O(2^n). */
    public static boolean recursive(int[] a) {
        int total = sum(a);
        return total % 2 == 0 && subset(a, a.length - 1, total / 2);
    }

    private static boolean subset(int[] a, int i, int target) {
        if (target == 0) return true;
        if (i < 0 || target < 0) return false;
        return subset(a, i - 1, target - a[i]) || subset(a, i - 1, target);
    }

    /** 1D boolean DP, sums iterated DOWNWARD (each number used once, like 0/1 knapsack). O(n · sum). */
    public static boolean dp(int[] a) {
        int total = sum(a);
        if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
        int target = total / 2;
        boolean[] can = new boolean[target + 1];
        can[0] = true;
        for (int x : a)
            for (int s = target; s >= x; s--) can[s] |= can[s - x];
        return can[target];
    }

    /** Bitset trick: bit s set = sum s reachable. Adding x is (bits | bits << x) — 64 sums per machine word. */
    public static boolean bitset(int[] a) {
        int total = sum(a);
        if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
        BitSet reachable = new BitSet(total + 1);
        reachable.set(0);
        for (int x : a) {
            BitSet shifted = new BitSet(total + 1);
            for (int s = reachable.nextSetBit(0); s >= 0 && s + x <= total; s = reachable.nextSetBit(s + 1)) shifted.set(s + x);
            reachable.or(shifted);
        }
        return reachable.get(total / 2);
    }

    private static int sum(int[] a) {
        int s = 0;
        for (int x : a) s += x;
        return s;
    }
}

docs.text: Recursion O(2ⁿ) · DP O(n · sum) time, O(sum) space · bitset O(n · sum / 64).

docs.title: Unique paths in a grid
docs.text: Medium Grid DP Combinatorics

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A robot at the top-left of an m×n grid moves only right or down. How many paths reach the bottom-right? 3×7 → 28. Variant: some cells are blocked.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Last move into (r, c) came from above or from the left, so f(r,c) = f(r−1,c) + f(r,c−1). The first row and first column are 1.
  2. Recursion → memo → 2D table, filled row by row.
  3. 1D rolling row: before you update row[c], it still holds the value from the row above. Add row[c−1] (from the left, already updated). That's O(n) space.
  4. Maths shortcut: every path is a sequence of (m−1) downs and (n−1) rights, so the count is C(m+n−2, m−1). Compute it incrementally so it stays an integer at every step.
  5. Obstacles: a blocked cell has 0 paths. The same rolling row handles it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

/** Robot moves only right/down in an m×n grid from top-left to bottom-right. Count paths; variant with obstacles. */
public final class UniquePaths {
    private UniquePaths() {}

    /** Recursion: paths(r, c) = paths(r-1, c) + paths(r, c-1). O(2^(m+n)). */
    public static long recursive(int m, int n) {
        if (m == 1 || n == 1) return 1;
        return recursive(m - 1, n) + recursive(m, n - 1);
    }

    /** Memoized. O(m·n). */
    public static long memo(int m, int n) {
        return memo(m, n, new long[m + 1][n + 1]);
    }

    private static long memo(int m, int n, long[][] cache) {
        if (m == 1 || n == 1) return 1;
        if (cache[m][n] != 0) return cache[m][n];
        return cache[m][n] = memo(m - 1, n, cache) + memo(m, n - 1, cache);
    }

    /** 2D table. O(m·n) time and space. */
    public static long table(int m, int n) {
        long[][] dp = new long[m][n];
        for (int r = 0; r < m; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) dp[r][c] = (r == 0 || c == 0) ? 1 : dp[r - 1][c] + dp[r][c - 1];
        return dp[m - 1][n - 1];
    }

    /** 1D rolling row: row[c] already holds "from above"; add "from the left". O(m·n) time, O(n) space. */
    public static long rolling(int m, int n) {
        long[] row = new long[n];
        java.util.Arrays.fill(row, 1);
        for (int r = 1; r < m; r++) for (int c = 1; c < n; c++) row[c] += row[c - 1];
        return row[n - 1];
    }

    /** Combinatorics: choose which (m-1) of the (m+n-2) moves are "down". O(min(m, n)). */
    public static long combinatorics(int m, int n) {
        long result = 1;
        int moves = m + n - 2, k = Math.min(m - 1, n - 1);
        for (int i = 1; i <= k; i++) result = result * (moves - k + i) / i;   // stays an integer at every step
        return result;
    }

    /** With obstacles (1 = blocked): same rolling row, but a blocked cell has 0 paths. */
    public static long withObstacles(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid[0].length;
        long[] row = new long[n];
        row[0] = grid[0][0] == 1 ? 0 : 1;
        for (int[] cells : grid)
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                if (cells[c] == 1) row[c] = 0;
                else if (c > 0) row[c] += row[c - 1];
            }
        return row[n - 1];
    }
}

docs.title: Word break
docs.text: Expert 1D DP over prefixes Memoization

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Can s be split into a sequence of dictionary words (each reusable)? "leetcode", [leet, code] → true · "catsandog", [cats, dog, sand, and, cat] → false.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Recursion: try every dictionary word that is a prefix of s, then solve the rest.
  2. Why it explodes: "aaaa…ab" with [a, aa, aaa, aaaa] reaches the same suffix along exponentially many paths, and every one fails.
  3. State = the start index of the remaining suffix, so there are only n + 1 states. Memoize on it.
  4. Bottom-up: dp[i] = "the prefix s[0..i) can be segmented". dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] and s[j..i) is a word.
  5. Optimisation: only check j ≥ i − maxWordLength, and use a HashSet for O(1) word lookups.

docs.title: dp for "leetcode"
docs.text: i 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 dp T F F F T ("leet") F F F T ("code")

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.dp;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.HashSet;

/** Can s be segmented into dictionary words (reusable)? "leetcode", [leet, code] → true. */
public final class WordBreak {
    private WordBreak() {}

    /** Recursion: try every dictionary word as a prefix. Exponential on inputs like "aaaa…ab". */
    public static boolean recursive(String s, List<String> dict) {
        if (s.isEmpty()) return true;
        for (String w : dict) if (s.startsWith(w) && recursive(s.substring(w.length()), dict)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    /** Memoized on the start index. O(n · |dict| · L). */
    public static boolean memo(String s, List<String> dict) {
        return memo(s, 0, dict, new HashMap<>());
    }

    private static boolean memo(String s, int start, List<String> dict, Map<Integer, Boolean> cache) {
        if (start == s.length()) return true;
        Boolean hit = cache.get(start);
        if (hit != null) return hit;
        boolean ok = false;
        for (String w : dict) {
            if (s.startsWith(w, start) && memo(s, start + w.length(), dict, cache)) {
                ok = true;
                break;
            }
        }
        cache.put(start, ok);
        return ok;
    }

    /**
     * Bottom-up: dp[i] = prefix s[0..i) can be segmented. dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] and s[j..i) is a word.
     * Limit j to the longest word length. O(n · maxLen) substring checks.
     */
    public static boolean dp(String s, List<String> dict) {
        Set<String> words = new HashSet<>(dict);
        int maxLen = 0;
        for (String w : dict) maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, w.length());
        boolean[] can = new boolean[s.length() + 1];
        can[0] = true;
        for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++)
            for (int j = Math.max(0, i - maxLen); j < i && !can[i]; j++)
                can[i] = can[j] && words.contains(s.substring(j, i));
        return can[s.length()];
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Recursion: exponential · memo: O(n · |dict| · L) · DP: O(n · maxLen) substring checks (each substring is O(maxLen) to hash).

docs.title: Why it's "Expert"
docs.text: You have to see the hidden overlap, choose the right state (the index, not the substring), and handle the adversarial input. The tests include "a"×40 + "b", which the memoized versions answer instantly. Word break II (return every sentence) adds memoized lists of sentences, and its output can be exponential.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it. When it works, it's usually the simplest and fastest solution (often just a sort plus one pass). When it doesn't, it's silently wrong.

docs.title: How to know greedy is safe
docs.text:
1. Try to break it: look for a small counter-example. Greedy coin change fails on [1,3,4] for amount 6 (4+1+1 vs 3+3), and greedy-by-ratio fails on the 0/1 knapsack.
  2. Exchange argument: take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one at the first choice, swap in the greedy choice, and show it's no worse. If you can, greedy is optimal.
  3. If the exchange fails, the problem needs DP.

The most common greedy shapes

Sort by end time (intervals), sort both lists and match (cookies, boats), track the furthest reach (jump game), reset when a running total goes negative (gas station, Kadane), always combine the two smallest (Huffman, ropes).

docs.title: Activity selection / non-overlapping intervals
docs.text: Medium Sort by end Exchange argument

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals [start, end) (touching is allowed). Twin (LeetCode 435): the minimum number to remove so the rest don't overlap, which is n − max kept.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every subset, 2ⁿ of them.
  2. DP O(n²): sort by end, then dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over compatible j.
  3. Which greedy? Try the candidates against counter-examples:
    • shortest first fails: [0,5) [4,6) [5,10) keeps 1 instead of 2.
    • earliest start fails: [0,100) [1,2) [2,3) keeps 1 instead of 2.
    • earliest finish works.
  4. Why earliest finish is safe: the activity that ends first leaves the most time for everything else. Swap it into any optimal solution in place of that solution's first activity, and nothing else conflicts.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Comparator;

/**
 * Activity selection: max number of non-overlapping intervals [start, end) (touching is fine).
 * Twin (LeetCode 435): minimum intervals to REMOVE so the rest don't overlap = n - max kept.
 */
public final class ActivitySelection {
    private ActivitySelection() {}

    /** Brute force: try every subset (2^n) — reference for small n. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[][] iv) {
        int n = iv.length, best = 0;
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {
            if (Integer.bitCount(mask) <= best) continue;
            boolean ok = true;
            for (int i = 0; i < n && ok; i++)
                for (int j = i + 1; j < n && ok; j++)
                    if ((mask >> i & 1) == 1 && (mask >> j & 1) == 1 && iv[i][0] < iv[j][1] && iv[j][0] < iv[i][1]) ok = false;
            if (ok) best = Integer.bitCount(mask);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /** DP O(n^2): sort by end; dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] with end[j] ≤ start[i]. Correct but slower than greedy. */
    public static int dp(int[][] iv) {
        int[][] a = sortedByEnd(iv);
        int[] dp = new int[a.length];
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            dp[i] = 1;
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j][1] <= a[i][0]) dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Greedy: sort by END time, always take the activity that finishes first among those that fit.
     * Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the rest (exchange argument). O(n log n).
     */
    public static int greedy(int[][] iv) {
        int count = 0;
        long lastEnd = Long.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int[] x : sortedByEnd(iv)) {
            if (x[0] >= lastEnd) {
                count++;
                lastEnd = x[1];
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    public static int minRemovals(int[][] iv) {
        return iv.length - greedy(iv);
    }

    private static int[][] sortedByEnd(int[][] iv) {
        int[][] a = iv.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a, Comparator.comparingInt(x -> x[1]));
        return a;
    }
}

docs.title: Assign cookies
docs.text: Easy Sort + two pointers Exchange argument

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Child i is content with a cookie of size ≥ greed[i]. Each child gets at most one cookie. Maximise the number of content children. greed [1,2,3], cookies [1,1] → 1 · greed [1,2], cookies [1,2,3] → 2.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: try every assignment. Exponential.
  2. Intuition: don't waste a big cookie on an easy child, and don't skip an easy child that a small cookie can satisfy.
  3. Greedy: sort both lists. Walk the cookies from smallest to largest. If the current cookie satisfies the least greedy unsatisfied child, give it to them. Otherwise the cookie is too small for everyone left, so discard it.
  4. Exchange argument: if an optimal solution gives the least greedy child a bigger cookie, swapping it for the smallest cookie that works never makes things worse.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Child i is content with a cookie of size ≥ greed[i]; each child gets at most one cookie. Max content children. */
public final class AssignCookies {
    private AssignCookies() {}

    /** Brute force: try giving each child each unused cookie (or nothing). Exponential — reference only. */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] greed, int[] cookies) {
        return brute(greed, 0, cookies, new boolean[cookies.length]);
    }

    private static int brute(int[] g, int i, int[] s, boolean[] used) {
        if (i == g.length) return 0;
        int best = brute(g, i + 1, s, used);                 // child i gets nothing
        for (int j = 0; j < s.length; j++) {
            if (!used[j] && s[j] >= g[i]) {
                used[j] = true;
                best = Math.max(best, 1 + brute(g, i + 1, s, used));
                used[j] = false;
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Greedy: sort both; give the SMALLEST cookie that satisfies the LEAST greedy remaining child.
     * Exchange argument: any optimal assignment can be rearranged into this one without losing a child. O(n log n).
     */
    public static int greedy(int[] greed, int[] cookies) {
        int[] g = greed.clone(), s = cookies.clone();
        Arrays.sort(g);
        Arrays.sort(s);
        int child = 0;
        for (int cookie = 0; cookie < s.length && child < g.length; cookie++) {
            if (s[cookie] >= g[child]) child++;              // satisfied; otherwise this cookie is too small for everyone left
        }
        return child;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n log n + m log m) for the sorting, plus an O(n + m) scan. Brute force is exponential.

docs.title: Fractional knapsack
docs.text: Hard Value/weight ratio Greedy vs DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: As in the 0/1 knapsack, but you may take any fraction of an item. weights [10,20,30], values [60,100,120], capacity 50 → 240 (all of items 1 and 2, plus ⅔ of item 3).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Since items are divisible, every unit of weight is interchangeable, so you should fill the bag with the most valuable weight first. That means sorting by value / weight, descending.
  2. Take whole items while they fit, then take a fraction of the next one, and stop.
  3. Compare ratios without division: v₁/w₁ > v₂/w₂ ⇔ v₁·w₂ > v₂·w₁. Use long to avoid overflow and floating-point ties.
  4. Why the same greedy fails for 0/1: you can't take ⅔ of an item. With capacity 50 above, ratio-greedy takes items 1 and 2 (160) and has 20 left with nothing that fits, but the optimum is items 2 and 3 (220).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Items can be taken FRACTIONALLY. Max value within capacity. Greedy is optimal here (unlike 0/1 knapsack). */
public final class FractionalKnapsack {
    private FractionalKnapsack() {}

    /** Sort by value/weight descending, take whole items while they fit, then a fraction of the next. O(n log n). */
    public static double maxValue(int[] weight, int[] value, int capacity) {
        Integer[] idx = new Integer[weight.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < idx.length; i++) idx[i] = i;
        // compare ratios without division: v1/w1 > v2/w2  ⇔  v1·w2 > v2·w1
        Arrays.sort(idx, (x, y) -> Long.compare((long) value[y] * weight[x], (long) value[x] * weight[y]));
        double total = 0;
        int left = capacity;
        for (int i : idx) {
            if (left == 0) break;
            if (weight[i] <= left) {
                total += value[i];
                left -= weight[i];
            } else {
                total += (double) value[i] * left / weight[i];   // the fraction that still fits
                left = 0;
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n log n) for the sort, plus an O(n) fill.

docs.title: The interview point
docs.text: This pair, fractional (greedy works) versus 0/1 (needs DP), is the textbook demonstration of why you must justify a greedy choice. Expect to be asked "why doesn't this work for the 0/1 version?".

docs.title: Gas station
docs.text: Medium Running total Restart

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Stations sit on a circle. gas[i] is the fuel at station i, and cost[i] is the fuel to drive from i to i+1. Find the start index from which you can drive around once, or −1. The answer is unique if it exists. gas [1,2,3,4,5], cost [3,4,5,1,2] → 3.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: simulate from every start. O(n²).
  2. Feasibility: if total gas < total cost, no start can work.
  3. Key insight: suppose you start at s and run out of fuel arriving after station i. Then no start between s and i works either. Each of them would arrive at i with at most the fuel you had, because you reached each of them with ≥ 0 fuel in the tank. So skip them all and restart at i+1.
  4. With total ≥ total cost, the last restart point is the answer. This is the same "drop a negative prefix" idea as Kadane's algorithm.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: i gas − cost tank Action 0 −2 −2 restart at 1 1 −2 −2 restart at 2 2 −2 −2 restart at 3 3 +3 3 4 +3 6 total = 0 ≥ 0 → 3

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

/** Circular route: gas[i] fuel at station i, cost[i] to drive to i+1. Start index to complete the loop, or -1 (unique if exists). */
public final class GasStation {
    private GasStation() {}

    /** Brute force: simulate from every start. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] gas, int[] cost) {
        int n = gas.length;
        for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) {
            long tank = 0;
            int k;
            for (k = 0; k < n; k++) {
                int i = (s + k) % n;
                tank += gas[i] - cost[i];
                if (tank < 0) break;
            }
            if (k == n) return s;
        }
        return -1;
    }

    /**
     * Greedy O(n): (1) if total gas < total cost, impossible. (2) If the tank goes negative arriving after station i,
     * then NO start between the current start and i works either (they'd arrive with even less) → restart at i+1.
     */
    public static int greedy(int[] gas, int[] cost) {
        long total = 0, tank = 0;
        int start = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < gas.length; i++) {
            total += gas[i] - cost[i];
            tank += gas[i] - cost[i];
            if (tank < 0) {
                start = i + 1;
                tank = 0;
            }
        }
        return total < 0 ? -1 : start;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Brute force O(n²) · greedy O(n), O(1).

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: The tests check more than "both say possible". They rotate the arrays so greedy's start becomes index 0 and confirm that the brute force accepts it.

docs.title: Huffman coding
docs.text: Expert Greedy Min-heap Prefix-free codes

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given symbol frequencies, build prefix-free binary codes (no code is a prefix of another) that minimise the total encoded length Σ freq × codeLength. a:5 b:9 c:12 d:13 e:16 f:45 → 224 bits.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Frequent symbols should get short codes and rare symbols long ones.
  2. Codes are root-to-leaf paths in a binary tree (left = 0, right = 1). Leaves-only symbols guarantee the codes are prefix-free, so decoding is unambiguous.
  3. Greedy: the two rarest symbols should be the deepest siblings. Merge them into one node whose weight is their sum, and repeat with a min-heap until one tree remains.
  4. Each merge adds its combined weight to the total cost, because every symbol under it gets one more bit. So the total bits = the sum of all merge weights. That's the same calculation as the GfG "minimum cost of connecting ropes" problem.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.PriorityQueue;

/** Optimal prefix-free binary codes for symbol frequencies (data compression). */
public final class HuffmanCoding {
    private HuffmanCoding() {}

    /** Tree node: leaves carry a symbol. */
    private record Node(long freq, char symbol, Node left, Node right, int order) {
        boolean isLeaf() {
            return left == null;
        }
    }

    /**
     * Greedy: repeatedly merge the two LEAST frequent trees (min-heap); the merged weight is their sum.
     * Rare symbols end up deepest → longest codes. Ties broken by creation order for deterministic codes. O(n log n).
     */
    public static Map<Character, String> codes(Map<Character, Long> freq) {
        Map<Character, String> out = new HashMap<>();
        if (freq.isEmpty()) return out;
        PriorityQueue<Node> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) ->
                a.freq != b.freq ? Long.compare(a.freq, b.freq) : Integer.compare(a.order, b.order));
        int order = 0;
        for (Map.Entry<Character, Long> e : new java.util.TreeMap<>(freq).entrySet())
            pq.offer(new Node(e.getValue(), e.getKey(), null, null, order++));
        if (pq.size() == 1) {                                // single symbol still needs a 1-bit code
            out.put(pq.peek().symbol(), "0");
            return out;
        }
        while (pq.size() > 1) {
            Node a = pq.poll(), b = pq.poll();
            pq.offer(new Node(a.freq + b.freq, '\0', a, b, order++));
        }
        assign(pq.poll(), "", out);
        return out;
    }

    private static void assign(Node n, String prefix, Map<Character, String> out) {
        if (n.isLeaf()) {
            out.put(n.symbol(), prefix);
            return;
        }
        assign(n.left(), prefix + "0", out);                 // left edge = 0
        assign(n.right(), prefix + "1", out);                // right edge = 1
    }

    /** Total encoded length in bits = Σ freq × codeLength (the quantity Huffman minimises). */
    public static long encodedBits(Map<Character, Long> freq, Map<Character, String> codes) {
        long bits = 0;
        for (Map.Entry<Character, Long> e : freq.entrySet()) bits += e.getValue() * codes.get(e.getKey()).length();
        return bits;
    }

    /** Same total via merge costs only (classic GfG "minimum cost of ropes"): sum of all merged weights. */
    public static long minMergeCost(long[] freq) {
        PriorityQueue<Long> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
        for (long f : freq) pq.offer(f);
        long cost = 0;
        while (pq.size() > 1) {
            long merged = pq.poll() + pq.poll();
            cost += merged;
            pq.offer(merged);
        }
        return cost;
    }

    public static String encode(String text, Map<Character, String> codes) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (char c : text.toCharArray()) sb.append(codes.get(c));
        return sb.toString();
    }

    /** Prefix-free codes decode greedily: read bits until they match a code. */
    public static String decode(String bits, Map<Character, String> codes) {
        Map<String, Character> reverse = new HashMap<>();
        codes.forEach((k, v) -> reverse.put(v, k));
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(), cur = new StringBuilder();
        for (char b : bits.toCharArray()) {
            cur.append(b);
            Character c = reverse.get(cur.toString());
            if (c != null) {
                out.append(c);
                cur.setLength(0);
            }
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(n log n) with a heap of n symbols. Encoding and decoding take O(total bits).

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text:
For 200 random alphabets, the tests check that: - the codes are prefix-free; - the code length times frequency equals the merge cost; - encoding then decoding random text gives the original back.

A single-symbol alphabet still gets a 1-bit code, which is a classic edge case.

docs.title: Jump game I & II
docs.text: Medium Furthest reach Implicit BFS

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: a[i] = the maximum jump length from index i. 1. Can you reach the last index? [2,3,1,1,4] → yes · [3,2,1,0,4] → no. 2. The minimum number of jumps. [2,3,1,1,4] → 2 (0 → 1 → 4).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. DP O(n²): index i is reachable if some reachable j < i can jump to it. Min jumps is dp[i] = 1 + min dp[j].
  2. Greedy for I: keep furthest = the furthest index reachable so far. Scan i. If i > furthest, you're stuck. Otherwise extend furthest = max(furthest, i + a[i]).
  3. Greedy for II, as an implicit BFS: every index reachable with k jumps forms a contiguous window [start, currentEnd]. While scanning that window, track the furthest reach. When i passes currentEnd, you must jump again, and the next window ends at furthest.

docs.title: BFS windows for [2,3,1,1,4]
docs.text: Jumps Window Furthest from the window 0 [0, 0] 2 1 [1, 2] 1 + 3 = 4 ≥ last 2 reached 2 jumps

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** a[i] = max jump length from index i. (I) Can you reach the last index? (II) Minimum jumps to reach it. */
public final class JumpGame {
    private JumpGame() {}

    /** DP O(n^2): reachable[i] if some reachable j < i can jump to i. */
    public static boolean canReachDp(int[] a) {
        boolean[] ok = new boolean[a.length];
        ok[0] = true;
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++)
            for (int j = 0; j < i && !ok[i]; j++) ok[i] = ok[j] && j + a[j] >= i;
        return ok[a.length - 1];
    }

    /** Greedy O(n): track the furthest index reachable so far; if we ever stand beyond it, we're stuck. */
    public static boolean canReach(int[] a) {
        int furthest = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
            if (i > furthest) return false;
            furthest = Math.max(furthest, i + a[i]);
        }
        return true;
    }

    /** DP O(n^2) min jumps; Integer.MAX_VALUE marks unreachable. Returns -1 if the end is unreachable. */
    public static int minJumpsDp(int[] a) {
        int[] dp = new int[a.length];
        Arrays.fill(dp, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++)
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
                if (dp[j] != Integer.MAX_VALUE && j + a[j] >= i) dp[i] = Math.min(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
        return dp[a.length - 1] == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : dp[a.length - 1];
    }

    /**
     * Greedy O(n) — "implicit BFS": [start, currentEnd] is the set of indexes reachable with `jumps` jumps.
     * Scanning it, track the furthest reach; when we pass currentEnd we must jump once more. -1 if stuck.
     */
    public static int minJumps(int[] a) {
        int jumps = 0, currentEnd = 0, furthest = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
            if (i > furthest) return -1;
            furthest = Math.max(furthest, i + a[i]);
            if (i == currentEnd) {                           // exhausted this BFS level
                if (furthest <= i) return -1;
                jumps++;
                currentEnd = furthest;
            }
        }
        return jumps;
    }
}

docs.title: Minimum platforms
docs.text: Hard Sweep line Two pointers

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given the arrival and departure times of trains on one day, find the minimum number of platforms so no train waits. A train arriving at the same minute another departs needs its own platform (the GfG convention). arr [900,940,950,1100,1500,1800], dep [910,1200,1120,1130,1900,2000] → 3.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for each train, count the trains present at its arrival time. The maximum is the answer. O(n²).
  2. Insight: the answer is the maximum number of overlapping intervals at any moment. It changes only at arrivals (+1) and departures (−1).
  3. You don't need to know which train is which, only the event times. So sort the arrivals and departures separately and merge them like merge sort. An arrival ≤ the next departure means +1 (the ≤ makes simultaneous events overlap). Otherwise −1.
  4. The maximum of the running count is the answer.

docs.title: Sweep
docs.text: Event Time Platforms arr 900 1 dep 910 0 arr 940 1 arr 950 2 arr 1100 3 dep 1120 2 …

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.greedy;

import java.util.Arrays;

/** Trains arrive/depart (same day); minimum platforms so no train waits. A train arriving when another departs needs a new platform (GfG rule: dep inclusive). */
public final class MinimumPlatforms {
    private MinimumPlatforms() {}

    /** Brute force: for each train, count trains present at its arrival time. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] arr, int[] dep) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
            int present = 0;
            for (int j = 0; j < arr.length; j++) if (arr[j] <= arr[i] && arr[i] <= dep[j]) present++;
            best = Math.max(best, present);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Sweep: sort arrivals and departures independently (we only need COUNTS, not which train). Walk both with two
     * pointers: an arrival before (or at) the next departure adds a platform; otherwise a departure frees one. O(n log n).
     */
    public static int sweep(int[] arr, int[] dep) {
        int[] a = arr.clone(), d = dep.clone();
        Arrays.sort(a);
        Arrays.sort(d);
        int i = 0, j = 0, current = 0, best = 0;
        while (i < a.length) {
            if (a[i] <= d[j]) {                              // inclusive: arriving at a departure minute still overlaps
                current++;
                i++;
                best = Math.max(best, current);
            } else {
                current--;
                j++;
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

docs.text: Brute force O(n²) · sweep O(n log n), O(n) for the copies.

docs.title: Concept primer
docs.text:
• Java int is a 32-bit two's complement number: −x = ~x + 1, and the top bit is the sign.
  • >> is an arithmetic shift (copies the sign bit). >>> is a logical shift (fills with 0). Use >>> when looping over the bits of a possibly negative number, or the loop never ends.
  • Bit tricks turn O(n) loops into O(1) expressions, and let you store a set of up to 32/64 flags in one integer.

docs.title: The cheat sheet
docs.text: Goal Expression Is bit k set? (n >> k & 1) == 1 Set / clear / toggle bit k n \| 1<<k · n & ~(1<<k) · n ^ 1<<k Lowest set bit n & -n Clear the lowest set bit n & (n − 1) Power of two? n > 0 && (n & (n−1)) == 0 Odd? (also for negatives) (n & 1) == 1 x ^ x, x ^ 0 0, x (the basis of every "single number" trick) All subsets of n items for (mask = 0; mask < 1<<n; mask++)

docs.title: Check, set, clear & toggle a bit
docs.text: Easy Masks

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Given n and a bit position k (0 = least significant), check, set, clear or toggle that bit. Also isolate and clear the lowest set bit.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Build a mask with only bit k set: 1 << k.
  2. Check: AND keeps only that bit, then compare with 0.
  3. Set: OR forces it to 1. Clear: AND with the inverted mask forces it to 0. Toggle: XOR flips it.
  4. Lowest set bit: n & −n. In two's complement, −n = ~n + 1, which flips every bit above the lowest 1 and keeps that 1.
  5. Clear the lowest set bit: n & (n − 1). Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and the zeros below it into 1s, and AND removes them all.

docs.title: Worked example (n = 1010₂ = 10)
docs.text: Operation Expression Result check bit 1 10 & 0010 0010 ≠ 0 → set set bit 0 10 \| 0001 1011 clear bit 1 10 & 1101 1000 toggle bit 3 10 ^ 1000 0010 lowest set bit of 12 (1100) 12 & −12 0100 = 4

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

/** The four single-bit operations every bit problem is built from (bit positions are 0-based from the right). */
public final class BitBasics {
    private BitBasics() {}

    /** Is bit k set? Shift a 1 to position k and AND. */
    public static boolean isSet(int n, int k) {
        return (n & (1 << k)) != 0;
    }

    /** Turn bit k on: OR with the mask. */
    public static int set(int n, int k) {
        return n | (1 << k);
    }

    /** Turn bit k off: AND with the inverted mask. */
    public static int clear(int n, int k) {
        return n & ~(1 << k);
    }

    /** Flip bit k: XOR with the mask. */
    public static int toggle(int n, int k) {
        return n ^ (1 << k);
    }

    /** Lowest set bit as a value (12 = 1100 → 4). Two's complement: -n = ~n + 1 keeps only the lowest 1. */
    public static int lowestSetBit(int n) {
        return n & -n;
    }

    /** Clear the lowest set bit (12 → 8). The engine behind Kernighan's bit count and power-of-two test. */
    public static int clearLowestSetBit(int n) {
        return n & (n - 1);
    }

    /** Binary string padded to `width` bits (for teaching / debugging). */
    public static String toBinary(int n, int width) {
        String s = Integer.toBinaryString(n);
        if (s.length() >= width) return s.substring(s.length() - width);
        return "0".repeat(width - s.length()) + s;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(1) for every operation.

docs.text: Permission flags (READ | WRITE), EnumSet internals, chess bitboards, compact visited sets in bitmask DP.

docs.title: Subsets via bitmask, submasks & Gray code
docs.text: Hard Bitmask enumeration

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
1. Generate all 2ⁿ subsets of n items using bitmasks.
  2. Enumerate all submasks of a given mask.
  3. Generate the n-bit Gray code, a sequence where consecutive values differ in exactly one bit.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Subsets: the integers 0 … 2ⁿ − 1 are exactly the n-bit patterns, so each mask is a subset (bit j ⇔ item j). No recursion needed. Compare with the recursive version in Subsets.
  2. Submasks: sub = (sub − 1) & mask. Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and every bit below it into 1. ANDing with the mask keeps only the allowed bits. That gives the next smaller submask, ending at 0.
  3. Cost of all submasks of all masks: each item is "not in mask", "in mask but not in sub", or "in both", which gives 3ⁿ. This is the bound behind subset DP (for example, the travelling salesman problem in O(2ⁿ·n²)).
  4. Gray code: g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1). Going from i to i+1 flips a run of trailing bits, and XOR with the shifted value collapses that run into a single change.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

/** Enumerating subsets with bitmasks: all subsets, all submasks of a mask, and Gray code. */
public final class BitmaskSubsets {
    private BitmaskSubsets() {}

    /** Each mask in [0, 2^n) IS a subset: bit j set ⇔ include a[j]. O(n·2^n). */
    public static List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] a) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << a.length); mask++) {
            List<Integer> s = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) if ((mask >> j & 1) == 1) s.add(a[j]);
            out.add(s);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /**
     * All submasks of `mask` in decreasing order (including mask and 0): sub = (sub - 1) & mask.
     * Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and everything below; & mask keeps only allowed bits.
     * Iterating submasks of every mask costs O(3^n) total — the basis of subset-DP.
     */
    public static List<Integer> submasks(int mask) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int sub = mask; ; sub = (sub - 1) & mask) {
            out.add(sub);
            if (sub == 0) break;
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Gray code: successive values differ in exactly one bit; g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1). */
    public static List<Integer> grayCode(int n) {
        List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < (1 << n); i++) out.add(i ^ (i >> 1));
        return out;
    }

    /** Subsets whose sum equals target, counted by brute-force mask enumeration (n ≤ ~20). */
    public static int countSubsetsWithSum(int[] a, int target) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << a.length); mask++) {
            int sum = 0;
            for (int j = 0; j < a.length; j++) if ((mask >> j & 1) == 1) sum += a[j];
            if (sum == target) count++;
        }
        return count;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Subsets O(n·2ⁿ) · submasks of one mask O(2^popcount) · all submasks of all masks O(3ⁿ) · Gray code O(2ⁿ).

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: For every mask under 64, the submask count must equal 2^popcount. The tests also check that consecutive Gray codes differ by exactly one bit.

docs.title: Count set bits (Hamming weight)
docs.text: Easy Brian Kernighan DP

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Count the 1 bits of an int, treated as unsigned, so −1 → 32. Follow-up: return the bit counts of every number from 0 to n in O(n) (LeetCode 338).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Shift loop: add n & 1, then shift right. Use >>>: >> copies the sign bit, so a negative n never reaches 0 and the loop runs forever.
  2. Brian Kernighan: n &= n − 1 removes one set bit per iteration, so the loop runs only as many times as there are 1s.
  3. Library: Integer.bitCount compiles to a single POPCNT CPU instruction.
  4. All numbers 0..n: bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) + (i & 1). Dropping the last bit gives a smaller number you've already solved.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

/** Number of 1 bits (Hamming weight / popcount) of an int, treating it as UNSIGNED (so -1 → 32). */
public final class CountSetBits {
    private CountSetBits() {}

    /** Check all 32 bits. O(32). Unsigned shift >>> so negative numbers terminate. */
    public static int shiftLoop(int n) {
        int count = 0;
        while (n != 0) {
            count += n & 1;
            n >>>= 1;                                        // >> would keep shifting in 1s for negatives → infinite loop
        }
        return count;
    }

    /** Brian Kernighan: n & (n-1) removes one set bit per iteration → O(number of set bits). */
    public static int kernighan(int n) {
        int count = 0;
        while (n != 0) {
            n &= n - 1;
            count++;
        }
        return count;
    }

    /** Library (a single CPU instruction on modern hardware). */
    public static int library(int n) {
        return Integer.bitCount(n);
    }

    /** Counting bits for every number 0..n (LeetCode 338): bits(i) = bits(i >> 1) + (i & 1). O(n) DP. */
    public static int[] countAll(int n) {
        int[] bits = new int[n + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1);
        return bits;
    }

    /** Bits to flip to turn a into b = popcount(a XOR b) (Hamming distance). */
    public static int hammingDistance(int a, int b) {
        return Integer.bitCount(a ^ b);
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Shift loop O(32) · Kernighan O(number of set bits) · all-n DP O(n).

docs.title: Related
docs.text: Hamming distance (bitCount(a ^ b)) · total Hamming distance (count per bit position: ones × zeros).

docs.title: Maximum XOR of two numbers
docs.text: Expert Bitwise trie Greedy by bit

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Return the maximum a[i] XOR a[j] for non-negative ints. [3,10,5,25,2,8] → 28 (5 ^ 25 = 00101 ^ 11001 = 11100).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: every pair. O(n²).
  2. Greedy insight: a 1 in a higher bit beats anything the lower bits can add. So decide the answer from the top bit down, always trying to make the current bit 1.
  3. Bitwise trie: insert each number's 31 bits, from the top, into a binary trie. To find the best partner for x, walk down preferring the opposite bit at each level, since that makes the XOR bit 1. O(31) per number.
  4. Prefix-set alternative: build the answer bit by bit. Guess that the next bit is 1 (candidate). That's achievable if two prefixes p and q satisfy p ^ q == candidate, which is the same as (candidate ^ p) being in the prefix set. It's the two-sum trick, with XOR instead of +.

docs.title: Trie walk for x = 5 (00101), best partner 25 (11001)
docs.text: Bit x has Want Exists? XOR bit 4 0 1 ✅ (25) 1 3 0 1 ✅ 1 2 1 0 ✅ 1 1 0 1 ❌ → take 0 0 0 1 0 ❌ → take 1 0 → 11100 = 28

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

/** Maximum a[i] XOR a[j] over all pairs (i may equal j) of NON-NEGATIVE ints. [3,10,5,25,2,8] → 28 (5 ^ 25). */
public final class MaximumXor {
    private MaximumXor() {}

    /** Brute force: every pair. O(n^2). */
    public static int bruteForce(int[] a) {
        int best = 0;
        for (int x : a) for (int y : a) best = Math.max(best, x ^ y);
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Bitwise trie: insert every number's 31 bits from the top. For each number, walk the trie preferring the
     * OPPOSITE bit at every level (a 1 in a higher bit beats anything below). O(31·n).
     */
    public static int trie(int[] a) {
        int[][] child = new int[a.length * 31 + 1][2];       // node 0 = root; 0 = "no child"
        int nodes = 1, best = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            int node = 0;
            for (int b = 30; b >= 0; b--) {                  // insert
                int bit = (x >> b) & 1;
                if (child[node][bit] == 0) child[node][bit] = nodes++;
                node = child[node][bit];
            }
            node = 0;
            int cur = 0;
            for (int b = 30; b >= 0; b--) {                  // query: greedily take the opposite bit
                int want = ((x >> b) & 1) ^ 1;
                if (child[node][want] != 0) {
                    cur |= 1 << b;
                    node = child[node][want];
                } else node = child[node][want ^ 1];
            }
            best = Math.max(best, cur);
        }
        return best;
    }

    /**
     * Prefix greedy with a HashSet: decide the answer bit by bit from the top. Guess the next bit is 1 (candidate);
     * it's achievable iff two prefixes p, q exist with p ^ q == candidate ⇔ (candidate ^ p) is in the set. O(31·n).
     */
    public static int prefixSet(int[] a) {
        int best = 0, mask = 0;
        for (int b = 30; b >= 0; b--) {
            mask |= 1 << b;
            Set<Integer> prefixes = new HashSet<>();
            for (int x : a) prefixes.add(x & mask);
            int candidate = best | (1 << b);
            for (int p : prefixes) {
                if (prefixes.contains(candidate ^ p)) {
                    best = candidate;
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Brute force O(n²) · trie O(31·n) time and O(31·n) nodes · prefix set O(31·n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: Related

docs.title: Power of two (and power of four)
docs.text: Easy n & (n−1)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Is n a power of two? 1, 2, 4, 8, … → yes. 0, negatives, 6 → no. Follow-up: is n a power of four?

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Loop: divide by 2 while n is even, and check you end at 1. O(log n).
  2. Binary insight: a power of two has exactly one set bit (1000…0). n − 1 turns it into 0111…1, so n & (n−1) == 0. O(1). Guard against n > 0, because 0 & −1 == 0 and Integer.MIN_VALUE also has a single bit.
  3. Library: Integer.bitCount(n) == 1.
  4. Power of four: a power of two whose single bit is at an even position (1, 4, 16 → bits 0, 2, 4). Check with the mask 0x55555555 (…0101).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

/** Is n a power of two? (and of four). Negative numbers and 0 are not. */
public final class PowerOfTwo {
    private PowerOfTwo() {}

    /** Divide by 2 while even. O(log n). */
    public static boolean loop(int n) {
        if (n <= 0) return false;
        while (n % 2 == 0) n /= 2;
        return n == 1;
    }

    /** A power of two has exactly ONE set bit; n & (n-1) clears it → 0. O(1). */
    public static boolean bitTrick(int n) {
        return n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;
    }

    /** Library: exactly one set bit. */
    public static boolean bitCount(int n) {
        return n > 0 && Integer.bitCount(n) == 1;
    }

    /** Power of four: a power of two whose single bit is at an EVEN position (mask 0101…0101 = 0x55555555). */
    public static boolean powerOfFour(int n) {
        return bitTrick(n) && (n & 0x55555555) != 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Loop O(log n) · bit trick O(1).

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: Every n from −5 to 5000, plus Integer.MIN_VALUE. All methods must agree.

docs.title: Single number I, II, III
docs.text: Medium XOR Bit counting State machine

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
• I: every element appears twice except one. Find it. [4,1,2,1,2] → 4.
  • II: every element appears three times except one. [0,1,0,1,0,1,99] → 99.
  • III: every element appears twice except two. Find both. [1,2,1,3,2,5] → [3,5].

All in O(n) time and O(1) space. A HashMap count is the baseline, but it uses O(n) space.

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. I, XOR: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and XOR is commutative. XOR everything, the pairs cancel, and the single number remains.
  2. II, why XOR fails: three copies XOR to x, not 0. Count per bit instead: for each of the 32 positions, count how many numbers have a 1 there. Triples contribute multiples of 3, so count % 3 is the single number's bit.
  3. II, expert: track the bits seen once (ones) and twice (twos) with ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos and twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones. A third occurrence clears both.
  4. III: XOR everything to get p ^ q, which is non-zero. Pick any set bit, (p ^ q) & −(p ^ q). p and q differ there, so splitting all numbers by that bit separates p from q, and pairs stay together. XOR each group.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * I:   every element appears twice except one → find it.
 * II:  every element appears three times except one → find it.
 * III: every element appears twice except TWO → find both (returned sorted).
 */
public final class SingleNumber {
    private SingleNumber() {}

    /** Hash map count — works for all variants, O(n) space. */
    public static int countingI(int[] a) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> c = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : a) c.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : c.entrySet()) if (e.getValue() == 1) return e.getKey();
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("no single element");
    }

    /** I: XOR everything. x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, XOR is commutative → pairs cancel. O(n), O(1). */
    public static int xorI(int[] a) {
        int r = 0;
        for (int x : a) r ^= x;
        return r;
    }

    /** II: for each of the 32 bit positions, count ones; mod 3 leaves the single number's bit. O(32n), O(1). */
    public static int bitCountII(int[] a) {
        int result = 0;
        for (int bit = 0; bit < 32; bit++) {
            int ones = 0;
            for (int x : a) ones += (x >>> bit) & 1;
            if (ones % 3 != 0) result |= 1 << bit;
        }
        return result;
    }

    /**
     * II, expert: two-variable state machine. `ones` holds bits seen 1 (mod 3) times, `twos` bits seen 2 times;
     * a third occurrence clears both. O(n), O(1), no per-bit loop.
     */
    public static int stateMachineII(int[] a) {
        int ones = 0, twos = 0;
        for (int x : a) {
            ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos;
            twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones;
        }
        return ones;
    }

    /**
     * III: XOR of all = p ^ q (non-zero since p != q). Any set bit of it is a bit where p and q differ;
     * split the numbers by that bit → each group contains one of them plus cancelling pairs.
     */
    public static int[] xorIII(int[] a) {
        int both = 0;
        for (int x : a) both ^= x;
        int diffBit = both & -both;                          // lowest bit where p and q differ
        int p = 0;
        for (int x : a) if ((x & diffBit) != 0) p ^= x;
        int q = both ^ p;
        return p < q ? new int[]{p, q} : new int[]{q, p};
    }
}

docs.title: XOR tricks: swap, odd/even, signs, add without +
docs.text: Medium XOR identities

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A set of warm-up questions interviewers ask to check that you're comfortable with bits:

Question Answer Swap two variables without a temp a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; (but guard a and b being the same memory location!) Is n odd? (n & 1) == 1. Note n % 2 == 1 is wrong for negatives (−3 % 2 == −1) Do x and y have opposite signs? (x ^ y) < 0: the sign bits differ XOR of 1..n in O(1) n, 1, n+1, 0 repeating with period 4 Reverse the 32 bits of n shift the lowest bit of n into the result 32 times Add two ints without + XOR is addition without carry, and (a & b) << 1 is the carry. Repeat until the carry is 0

docs.title: Thinking process (add without +)
docs.text:
1. Single-bit addition: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=10. The sum bit is XOR and the carry bit is AND.
  2. For whole numbers: sum = a ^ b, carry = (a & b) << 1. Then add sum + carry the same way.
  3. The carry moves left each round, so it reaches 0 within 32 rounds, even for negative numbers in two's complement.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.bits;

/** Small XOR / bit tricks interviewers like to ask as warm-ups. */
public final class XorTricks {
    private XorTricks() {}

    /** Swap two array cells without a temp variable. Guard i == j: x ^= x would zero it! */
    public static void xorSwap(int[] a, int i, int j) {
        if (i == j) return;
        a[i] ^= a[j];                                        // a = a^b
        a[j] ^= a[i];                                        // b = b^(a^b) = a
        a[i] ^= a[j];                                        // a = (a^b)^a = b
    }

    /** Odd check via the lowest bit — works for negatives too (n % 2 == 1 does NOT: -3 % 2 == -1). */
    public static boolean isOdd(int n) {
        return (n & 1) == 1;
    }

    /** Do x and y have opposite signs? The sign bit of x ^ y is 1 exactly when they differ. */
    public static boolean oppositeSigns(int x, int y) {
        return (x ^ y) < 0;
    }

    /** XOR of 1..n in O(1): the prefix XOR repeats with period 4 → n, 1, n+1, 0. */
    public static int xorUpTo(int n) {
        return switch (n & 3) {
            case 0 -> n;
            case 1 -> 1;
            case 2 -> n + 1;
            default -> 0;
        };
    }

    /** Reverse the 32 bits of n (LeetCode 190): take the lowest bit of n, push it into the result. */
    public static int reverseBits(int n) {
        int r = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
            r = (r << 1) | (n & 1);
            n >>>= 1;
        }
        return r;
    }

    /** Add without + (LeetCode 371): XOR adds without carry, AND<<1 is the carry; repeat until no carry. */
    public static int addWithoutPlus(int a, int b) {
        while (b != 0) {
            int carry = (a & b) << 1;
            a ^= b;
            b = carry;
        }
        return a;
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(1) each, at most 32 iterations for reverse and add.

docs.title: Senior caveat
docs.text: The XOR swap is a puzzle answer, not production code. The JIT optimises a plain temp swap just as well, and the XOR version silently zeroes the value when both references point to the same cell. The code guards that case, and a test proves it.

docs.title: Autocomplete / search suggestions
docs.text: Hard Trie Binary search

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: After each character typed in search, return up to 3 products that start with the typed prefix, in lexicographic order (LeetCode 1268). products [mobile, mouse, moneypot, monitor, mousepad], search "mouse" → m: [mobile, moneypot, monitor] … mou: [mouse, mousepad] …

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Brute force: for every prefix, filter and sort all products.
  2. Sort once + binary search: in sorted order, the products sharing a prefix form a contiguous block starting at lowerBound(prefix). Take up to 3 from there. As the prefix grows, the block only moves right, so the next search can start from the previous position.
  3. Trie with cached suggestions: insert the products in sorted order, and store at each node the first 3 words that pass through it. Each keystroke is then one child step plus a list copy, which is how real autocomplete backends feel instant.
  4. Once the prefix leaves the trie, every following keystroke has no suggestions.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.advanced;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;

/**
 * Search suggestions (LeetCode 1268): after each typed character of `search`, return up to 3 products that start
 * with the typed prefix, in lexicographic order.
 */
public final class Autocomplete {
    private Autocomplete() {}

    /** Brute force: for every prefix, filter + sort all products. O(L · n · m log). */
    public static List<List<String>> bruteForce(String[] products, String search) {
        List<List<String>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 1; i <= search.length(); i++) {
            String p = search.substring(0, i);
            out.add(Arrays.stream(products).filter(s -> s.startsWith(p)).sorted().distinct().limit(3).toList());
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Sort once + binary search: products with a prefix form a contiguous block starting at lowerBound(prefix). */
    public static List<List<String>> binarySearch(String[] products, String search) {
        String[] sorted = Arrays.stream(products).sorted().distinct().toArray(String[]::new);
        List<List<String>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        int start = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= search.length(); i++) {
            String p = search.substring(0, i);
            int lo = start, hi = sorted.length;
            while (lo < hi) {                                // lower bound of p (only moves right as p grows)
                int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
                if (sorted[mid].compareTo(p) < 0) lo = mid + 1;
                else hi = mid;
            }
            start = lo;
            List<String> level = new ArrayList<>();
            for (int k = lo; k < Math.min(lo + 3, sorted.length) && sorted[k].startsWith(p); k++) level.add(sorted[k]);
            out.add(level);
        }
        return out;
    }

    /** Trie where every node stores its top-3 words (inserted in sorted order, so the first 3 are the smallest). */
    public static List<List<String>> trie(String[] products, String search) {
        Node root = new Node();
        for (String p : Arrays.stream(products).sorted().distinct().toArray(String[]::new)) {
            Node n = root;
            for (char c : p.toCharArray()) {
                n = n.next[c - 'a'] == null ? (n.next[c - 'a'] = new Node()) : n.next[c - 'a'];
                if (n.top.size() < 3) n.top.add(p);
            }
        }
        List<List<String>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : search.toCharArray()) {
            n = n == null ? null : n.next[c - 'a'];
            out.add(n == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(n.top));
        }
        return out;
    }

    private static final class Node {
        final Node[] next = new Node[26];
        final List<String> top = new ArrayList<>(3);
    }
}

docs.title: Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
docs.text: Expert Lowbit Prefix sums

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Support add(i, delta) and prefixSum(i), and therefore rangeSum(l, r), in O(log n), using one array and about 10 lines of code. Application: count inversions in O(n log M).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Idea: each slot tree[i] (1-based) stores the sum of a block of lowbit(i) = i & −i elements ending at i. For example, tree[12] covers a[9..12] (lowbit 4), and tree[8] covers a[1..8].
  2. prefixSum(i): add tree[i], then jump to i − lowbit(i) (the block just before), until 0. Each jump removes one set bit, so there are at most log n steps.
  3. add(i, delta): update every block that contains i. Those are found at i + lowbit(i), repeatedly. Also O(log n).
  4. O(n) build: each node adds its total into its parent i + lowbit(i), once.
  5. Inversions: walk from the right. For each x, prefixSum(x − 1) counts the values already seen that are smaller than x, which are exactly the inversions involving x. Then add(x, 1).

docs.title: Which blocks does prefixSum(13) read?
docs.text:
13 = 1101₂ → tree[13] covers a[13]
12 = 1100₂ → tree[12] covers a[9..12]
 8 = 1000₂ → tree[8]  covers a[1..8]
 0         → stop: 3 reads instead of 13

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.advanced;

/**
 * Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree): point add and prefix sum in O(log n) with a single array and ~10 lines.
 * Internally 1-based: tree[i] stores the sum of the (i & -i) elements ending at i.
 */
public final class FenwickTree {
    private final long[] tree;

    public FenwickTree(int n) {
        tree = new long[n + 1];
    }

    /** Build in O(n): each node pushes its total to the next node that covers it. */
    public static FenwickTree of(int[] a) {
        FenwickTree f = new FenwickTree(a.length);
        for (int i = 1; i <= a.length; i++) {
            f.tree[i] += a[i - 1];
            int parent = i + (i & -i);
            if (parent <= a.length) f.tree[parent] += f.tree[i];
        }
        return f;
    }

    /** a[index] += delta (0-based index). Climb to every node whose range covers index: i += lowbit(i). */
    public void add(int index, long delta) {
        for (int i = index + 1; i < tree.length; i += i & -i) tree[i] += delta;
    }

    /** Sum of a[0..index] inclusive. Descend by removing the lowest set bit: i -= lowbit(i). */
    public long prefixSum(int index) {
        long s = 0;
        for (int i = index + 1; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += tree[i];
        return s;
    }

    /** Sum of a[l..r] inclusive = prefix(r) − prefix(l−1). */
    public long rangeSum(int l, int r) {
        return prefixSum(r) - (l == 0 ? 0 : prefixSum(l - 1));
    }

    /**
     * Application: count inversions in O(n log M) for values in [0, maxValue]. Walk from the right; for each x, the
     * number of already-seen values < x are inversions with x.
     */
    public static long countInversions(int[] a, int maxValue) {
        FenwickTree f = new FenwickTree(maxValue + 1);
        long inv = 0;
        for (int i = a.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (a[i] > 0) inv += f.prefixSum(a[i] - 1);
            f.add(a[i], 1);
        }
        return inv;
    }
}

docs.title: LFU cache
docs.text: Expert HashMap LinkedHashSet buckets Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A fixed-capacity cache with O(1) get and put. When full, evict the key with the lowest use count. Among ties, evict the least recently used. Both get and put count as a use (LeetCode 460).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. LRU needs one ordering (recency). LFU needs two: frequency first, then recency.
  2. Frequency buckets: freq → LinkedHashSet<key>. A LinkedHashSet gives O(1) removal and remembers insertion order, so the first key in a bucket is that bucket's least recently used.
  3. Touching a key (on get or an update): move it from bucket f to bucket f+1. If bucket f becomes empty and f was minFreq, then minFreq becomes f+1. That's the only way the minimum can change during a touch.
  4. Evicting: take the first key of the minFreq bucket.
  5. Inserting a new key: frequency 1, so minFreq = 1. A brand-new key always has the lowest possible count.
  6. Together with values and counts maps, every step is O(1).

docs.title: Trace (capacity 2)
docs.text: Op Buckets (freq: keys, oldest first) minFreq Result put 1 1: [1] 1 put 2 1: [1, 2] 1 get 1 1: [2] · 2: [1] 1 1 put 3 evict 2 → 1: [3] · 2: [1] 1 get 3 2: [1, 3] 2 3 put 4 evict 1 (oldest at freq 2) → 1: [4] · 2: [3] 1

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.advanced;

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Map;

/**
 * Least-Frequently-Used cache, O(1) get/put (LeetCode 460). On eviction remove the key with the LOWEST use count;
 * among ties, the least RECENTLY used. get returns -1 if missing.
 */
public final class LfuCache {
    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> values = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
    /** frequency → keys with that frequency, in recency order (LinkedHashSet = O(1) remove + insertion order). */
    private final Map<Integer, LinkedHashSet<Integer>> buckets = new HashMap<>();
    private int minFreq;

    public LfuCache(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    public int get(int key) {
        Integer v = values.get(key);
        if (v == null) return -1;
        touch(key);
        return v;
    }

    public void put(int key, int value) {
        if (capacity <= 0) return;
        if (values.containsKey(key)) {
            values.put(key, value);
            touch(key);
            return;
        }
        if (values.size() == capacity) {                     // evict LFU, oldest among ties = first in its bucket
            LinkedHashSet<Integer> lowest = buckets.get(minFreq);
            int victim = lowest.iterator().next();
            lowest.remove(victim);
            values.remove(victim);
            counts.remove(victim);
        }
        values.put(key, value);
        counts.put(key, 1);
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(1, f -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
        minFreq = 1;                                         // a brand-new key always has the minimum frequency
    }

    /** Move key from bucket f to f+1; if bucket f was the minimum and is now empty, the minimum becomes f+1. */
    private void touch(int key) {
        int f = counts.get(key);
        counts.put(key, f + 1);
        LinkedHashSet<Integer> from = buckets.get(f);
        from.remove(key);
        if (from.isEmpty()) {
            buckets.remove(f);
            if (minFreq == f) minFreq = f + 1;
        }
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(f + 1, x -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
    }

    public int size() {
        return values.size();
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: O(1) for get and put. O(capacity) space.

docs.text: A naive reference LFU (a linear scan for the minimum (count, lastUsedTick)) is compared with the O(1) version on 50 random workloads × 400 operations, including capacity 0.

docs.text: Two orderings have to be kept consistent at the same time, and minFreq maintenance has subtle cases. Many candidates get get/put right but break the tie-breaking or minFreq after an update.

docs.title: Segment tree
docs.text: Expert Divide & conquer Range queries

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: An array changes over time. Support update(i, value) and the range queries sum(l, r) and min(l, r), all in O(log n).

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Plain array: update O(1), query O(n). Prefix sums: query O(1), update O(n). Interleaved operations make both too slow.
  2. Segment tree: a binary tree where each node stores the answer (sum, min, …) for a range. The root covers [0, n−1], and each node's two children cover its two halves. It's stored in an array: the children of node i are 2i and 2i+1, and 4n slots are always enough.

  3. Query(l, r) at a node covering [lo, hi]:

    • no overlap: return the neutral value (0 for a sum, +∞ for a min);
    • total overlap: return the stored value;
    • partial overlap: ask both children and combine.

    Any range splits into O(log n) fully covered nodes. 4. Update(i): walk from the root to the leaf, then recompute every ancestor on the way back up (pull). O(log n). 5. It works for any associative operation: sum, min, max, gcd, XOR, matrix product.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.advanced;

/**
 * Segment tree over an int array: point update and range SUM / range MIN queries, each O(log n).
 * Node i covers a range; its children 2i and 2i+1 cover the two halves. Size 4n is always enough.
 */
public final class SegmentTree {
    private final int n;
    private final long[] sum;
    private final int[] min;

    public SegmentTree(int[] a) {
        n = a.length;
        sum = new long[4 * Math.max(1, n)];
        min = new int[4 * Math.max(1, n)];
        if (n > 0) build(a, 1, 0, n - 1);
    }

    private void build(int[] a, int node, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) {
            sum[node] = min[node] = a[lo];
            return;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        build(a, 2 * node, lo, mid);
        build(a, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi);
        pull(node);
    }

    private void pull(int node) {                            // recompute a parent from its children
        sum[node] = sum[2 * node] + sum[2 * node + 1];
        min[node] = Math.min(min[2 * node], min[2 * node + 1]);
    }

    /** a[index] = value. Walk root → leaf, then fix every ancestor on the way back. O(log n). */
    public void update(int index, int value) {
        update(1, 0, n - 1, index, value);
    }

    private void update(int node, int lo, int hi, int idx, int value) {
        if (lo == hi) {
            sum[node] = min[node] = value;
            return;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        if (idx <= mid) update(2 * node, lo, mid, idx, value);
        else update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, idx, value);
        pull(node);
    }

    /** Sum of a[l..r] inclusive. A query range is covered by O(log n) whole nodes. */
    public long sum(int l, int r) {
        return sum(1, 0, n - 1, l, r);
    }

    private long sum(int node, int lo, int hi, int l, int r) {
        if (r < lo || hi < l) return 0;                      // no overlap
        if (l <= lo && hi <= r) return sum[node];            // total overlap: use the stored answer
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;                           // partial overlap: ask both children
        return sum(2 * node, lo, mid, l, r) + sum(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, l, r);
    }

    /** Minimum of a[l..r] inclusive. */
    public int min(int l, int r) {
        return min(1, 0, n - 1, l, r);
    }

    private int min(int node, int lo, int hi, int l, int r) {
        if (r < lo || hi < l) return Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        if (l <= lo && hi <= r) return min[node];
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        return Math.min(min(2 * node, lo, mid, l, r), min(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, l, r));
    }
}

docs.title: Longest common prefix via a trie
docs.text: Medium Trie

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: The longest common prefix of an array of words, solved with a trie. ["flower","flow","flight"] → "fl".

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Insert every word.
  2. Walk down from the root while the current node has exactly one child and no word ends there. Every character on that path is shared by all words.
  3. Stop at a branch (the words diverge) or a word end (a shorter word is itself the prefix: ["ab","abc"] → "ab").
  4. When is this better than scanning? For a single query, the vertical scan from the Strings topic is simpler. The trie wins when the word set stays fixed and you answer many prefix questions.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
The method longestCommonPrefix lives in the Trie class: 

package com.playbook.advanced;

/** Prefix tree over lowercase a–z: insert, search, startsWith, countWordsWithPrefix and delete — all O(L). */
public final class Trie {
    /** One node per character position; children indexed by c - 'a'. */
    static final class Node {
        final Node[] next = new Node[26];
        boolean isWord;                                      // a word ENDS here (not just passes through)
        int prefixCount;                                     // words in this subtree (for countWordsWithPrefix)
    }

    final Node root = new Node();

    public void insert(String word) {
        if (search(word)) return;                            // keep counts correct for duplicates
        Node n = root;
        n.prefixCount++;
        for (char c : word.toCharArray()) {
            int i = c - 'a';
            if (n.next[i] == null) n.next[i] = new Node();
            n = n.next[i];
            n.prefixCount++;
        }
        n.isWord = true;
    }

    /** Whole word present? Must end on a node flagged isWord ("app" is not a word just because "apple" is). */
    public boolean search(String word) {
        Node n = walk(word);
        return n != null && n.isWord;
    }

    public boolean startsWith(String prefix) {
        Node n = walk(prefix);
        return n != null && n.prefixCount > 0;
    }

    public int countWordsWithPrefix(String prefix) {
        Node n = walk(prefix);
        return n == null ? 0 : n.prefixCount;
    }

    /** Remove a word; prune nodes no word passes through any more. Returns false if it wasn't present. */
    public boolean delete(String word) {
        if (!search(word)) return false;
        Node n = root;
        n.prefixCount--;
        for (char c : word.toCharArray()) {
            int i = c - 'a';
            Node child = n.next[i];
            if (--child.prefixCount == 0) {                  // nothing else below: cut the branch here
                n.next[i] = null;
                return true;
            }
            n = child;
        }
        n.isWord = false;
        return true;
    }

    Node walk(String s) {
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            n = n.next[c - 'a'];
            if (n == null) return null;
        }
        return n;
    }

    /** Longest common prefix of all words: walk down while the node has exactly one child and isn't a word end. */
    public static String longestCommonPrefix(String[] words) {
        if (words.length == 0) return "";
        Trie t = new Trie();
        for (String w : words) {
            if (w.isEmpty()) return "";
            t.insert(w);
        }
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        Node n = t.root;
        while (!n.isWord) {
            int only = -1, children = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++) if (n.next[i] != null) {
                children++;
                only = i;
            }
            if (children != 1) break;
            sb.append((char) ('a' + only));
            n = n.next[only];
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}

docs.title: Implement a trie (prefix tree)
docs.text: Medium Trie Design

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Support insert(word), search(word), startsWith(prefix), countWordsWithPrefix(prefix) and delete(word) over lowercase words.

insert: apple, app, apt
            (root)
              a
              p
            /   \
          p*     t*        * = isWord
          l
          e*

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. A HashSet answers search in O(L), but startsWith would need to scan every word.
  2. A trie shares prefixes: each node is a character position, and its children are the possible next characters (Node[26]). Walking a prefix takes O(L), no matter how many words are stored.
  3. isWord flag: "app" is a word only if a word ends there, not merely because "apple" passes through it.
  4. prefixCount per node (the number of words in its subtree) makes countWordsWithPrefix O(L), and makes delete easy: decrement the counts along the path, and when a count hits 0, cut off that branch.

docs.title: Design trade-offs (the senior discussion)
docs.text:
• Node[26] is fast but uses a lot of memory. A HashMap<Character, Node> per node saves memory for sparse or Unicode alphabets.
  • A compressed trie (radix tree) merges single-child chains, which is how routers store IP prefixes.
  • delete with counters avoids a second recursive pruning pass.

docs.title: Word search II
docs.text: Hard Trie Backtracking

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Given a letter board and a list of words, return every word that can be traced through adjacent cells (up/down/left/right), using each cell at most once per word. 

o a a n
e t a e        words = [oath, pea, eat, rain]  →  [eat, oath]
i h k r
i f l v

docs.title: Thinking process
docs.text:
1. Per-word backtracking: for each word, start a DFS from every cell. This repeats the same exploration for words sharing a prefix ("oath", "oat", "oats"…), so it costs O(W · R·C · 4^L).
  2. Flip it: run one DFS from each cell and walk the trie at the same time. The path is still worth extending only if it's a prefix of some word, which the trie answers with one child lookup.
  3. When you reach a trie node holding a word, report it and set it to null so it's reported once.
  4. Prune exhausted branches: if a trie node has no children and no word left, delete it from its parent. Later searches stop even earlier. This is the optimisation that makes the hardest test cases pass.
  5. Backtracking: mark the cell '#' while it's on the path, and restore it afterwards.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
package com.playbook.advanced;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.TreeSet;

/**
 * Find every dictionary word that can be traced on a letter board through adjacent (4-dir) cells, each cell used at
 * most once per word (LeetCode 212). Result sorted.
 */
public final class WordSearchII {
    private WordSearchII() {}

    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

    /** Brute force: run a separate backtracking search for each word from each cell. O(W · R·C · 4^L). */
    public static List<String> perWord(char[][] board, String[] words) {
        TreeSet<String> found = new TreeSet<>();
        for (String w : words) {
            outer:
            for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
                for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
                    if (match(board, w, 0, r, c)) {
                        found.add(w);
                        break outer;
                    }
        }
        return new ArrayList<>(found);
    }

    private static boolean match(char[][] b, String w, int k, int r, int c) {
        if (k == w.length()) return true;
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length || b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;
        char saved = b[r][c];
        b[r][c] = '#';                                       // mark used on this path
        boolean ok = false;
        for (int[] d : DIRS) if (!ok) ok = match(b, w, k + 1, r + d[0], c + d[1]);
        b[r][c] = saved;                                     // backtrack
        return ok;
    }

    /**
     * Trie + one DFS per cell: walk the board and the trie TOGETHER; stop as soon as the path is not a prefix of any
     * word. All words share the work of common prefixes. Found words are un-flagged so each is reported once.
     */
    public static List<String> trie(char[][] board, String[] words) {
        TrieNode root = new TrieNode();
        for (String w : words) {
            TrieNode n = root;
            for (char ch : w.toCharArray()) n = n.next.computeIfAbsent(ch, x -> new TrieNode());
            n.word = w;
        }
        TreeSet<String> found = new TreeSet<>();
        for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++) dfs(board, r, c, root, found);
        return new ArrayList<>(found);
    }

    private static final class TrieNode {
        final java.util.Map<Character, TrieNode> next = new java.util.HashMap<>();
        String word;                                         // non-null where a word ends
    }

    private static void dfs(char[][] b, int r, int c, TrieNode parent, TreeSet<String> found) {
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length) return;
        char ch = b[r][c];
        TrieNode node = parent.next.get(ch);
        if (node == null) return;                            // '#' or no word continues this way → prune
        if (node.word != null) {
            found.add(node.word);
            node.word = null;                                // report once
        }
        b[r][c] = '#';
        for (int[] d : DIRS) dfs(b, r + d[0], c + d[1], node, found);
        b[r][c] = ch;
        if (node.next.isEmpty() && node.word == null) parent.next.remove(ch);   // prune exhausted branches
    }
}

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: Per word: O(W · R·C · 4^L). Trie: O(R·C · 4^L) in the worst case, but shared prefixes and pruning make it far faster in practice.

docs.title: Testing note
docs.text: 200 random boards (up to 4×4) with random word lists over a 3-letter alphabet, which forces many shared prefixes. Both methods must find the same words.
